content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 1: Short title, extent and commencement

Q: What is the short title of the Indian criminal procedure code enacted in 2023?
A: The Act may be called the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. [Source: Section 1, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Short title, extent and commencement

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 1: Short title, extent and commencement

Q: What does Section 1 of BNSS 2023 say?
A: Section 1 of BNSS 2023 outlines the short title, extent, and commencement of the Act, establishing its name and geographical applicability. [Source: Section 1, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Short title, extent and commencement

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 1: Short title, extent and commencement

Q: Does the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 apply to the tribal areas of Assam?
A: Under sub-section (2), the provisions do not automatically apply to the tribal areas, but the State Government may apply them by notification with necessary modifications. [Source: Section 1, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Short title, extent and commencement

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 1: Short title, extent and commencement

Q: What condition must be met for the entire Sanhita to apply to the State of Nagaland?
A: Under sub-section (2), the concerned State Government must issue a notification applying the provisions to the State of Nagaland. [Source: Section 1, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Short title, extent and commencement

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 1: Short title, extent and commencement

Q: Are there any specific chapters of the Sanhita that apply to the State of Nagaland without a special notification?
A: Yes, under sub-section (2), the provisions relating to Chapters IX, XI, and XII apply to the State of Nagaland and the tribal areas automatically. [Source: Section 1, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Short title, extent and commencement

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 1: Short title, extent and commencement

Q: What happens when the Central Government appoints a date in the Official Gazette?
A: Under sub-section (3), the Sanhita shall come into force on the date appointed by the Central Government through that notification. [Source: Section 1, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Short title, extent and commencement

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 2: Definitions

Q: What is the definition of "bail" under the criminal procedure code?
A: Bail means the release of a person accused of or suspected of commission of an offence from the custody of law upon certain conditions imposed by an officer or Court on execution by such person of a bond or a bail bond. [Source: Section 2, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Definitions

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 2: Definitions

Q: Can you explain Section 2 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 2 of BNSS 2023 provides the definitions for key legal terms used throughout the Sanhita, such as cognizable offence, complaint, inquiry, and police report. [Source: Section 2, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Definitions

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 2: Definitions

Q: If an officer investigates a case and the resulting police report discloses a non-cognizable offence, how is it legally categorized?
A: According to the Explanation under clause (h), a report made by a police officer which discloses the commission of a non-cognizable offence shall be deemed to be a complaint, and the police officer shall be deemed to be the complainant. [Source: Section 2, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Definitions

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 2: Definitions

Q: What elements define an "electronic communication"?
A: Under clause (i), electronic communication means the communication of any written, verbal, pictorial information or video content transmitted by means of an electronic device, including a telephone, mobile phone, computer, or camera. [Source: Section 2, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Definitions

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 2: Definitions

Q: Whose provisions prevail if the provisions of a special Act are inconsistent with this Sanhita?
A: Under the Explanation in clause (l), where any provisions of a special Act are inconsistent with this Sanhita, the provisions of the special Act shall prevail. [Source: Section 2, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Definitions

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 2: Definitions

Q: What is the consequence if a word is used in this Sanhita but lacks a definition here?
A: Under sub-section (2), words and expressions not defined herein but defined in the Information Technology Act, 2000 and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 shall have the meanings respectively assigned to them in those Acts. [Source: Section 2, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Definitions

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 3: Construction of references

Q: How should general references to a Magistrate be interpreted legally?
A: Any reference to a Magistrate without qualifying words shall be construed as a reference to a Judicial Magistrate of the first class or Judicial Magistrate of the second class exercising jurisdiction in that area. [Source: Section 3, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Construction of references

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 3: Construction of references

Q: What is Section 3 of BNSS 2023 about?
A: Section 3 of BNSS 2023 covers the construction of references, detailing how mentions of Magistrates in other laws should be interpreted and divided between Judicial and Executive Magistrates. [Source: Section 3, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Construction of references

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 3: Construction of references

Q: If a separate law gives a Magistrate the power to grant or cancel a license, which type of Magistrate should perform this function?
A: Under clause (b) of sub-section (2), functions which are administrative or executive in nature, such as granting or cancelling a licence, shall be exercisable by an Executive Magistrate. [Source: Section 3, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Construction of references

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 3: Construction of references

Q: What condition requires a function to be exercised specifically by a Judicial Magistrate?
A: Under clause (a) of sub-section (2), functions involving the appreciation of evidence or formulating a decision that exposes a person to punishment or detention must be exercisable by a Judicial Magistrate. [Source: Section 3, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Construction of references

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 3: Construction of references

Q: Is the assignment of administrative duties to an Executive Magistrate absolute?
A: No, under clause (b) of sub-section (2), the exercise of administrative functions by an Executive Magistrate is subject to the provisions of clause (a). [Source: Section 3, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Construction of references

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 3: Construction of references

Q: What happens if a function involves sending a person for trial before a Court?
A: Under clause (a) of sub-section (2), the consequence is that such a function shall be exercisable by a Judicial Magistrate. [Source: Section 3, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Construction of references

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 4: Trial of offences under Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and other laws

Q: Which code's procedures govern the investigation and trial of criminal offences in India?
A: All offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and other laws shall be investigated, inquired into, tried, and otherwise dealt with according to the provisions of this Sanhita. [Source: Section 4, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Trial of offences under Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and other laws

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 4: Trial of offences under Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and other laws

Q: What does Section 4 of BNSS 2023 state?
A: Section 4 of BNSS 2023 states the rules for the trial of offences, confirming that offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and other laws must be dealt with according to this Sanhita. [Source: Section 4, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Trial of offences under Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and other laws

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 4: Trial of offences under Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and other laws

Q: If a person commits an offence under a different law that has its own specific rules for how the investigation must take place, which procedure applies?
A: Under sub-section (2), the offence shall be dealt with under the Sanhita, but subject to any enactment for the time being in force regulating the manner or place of investigating or trying such offences. [Source: Section 4, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Trial of offences under Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and other laws

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 4: Trial of offences under Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and other laws

Q: What must occur for an offence under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 to be prosecuted?
A: Under sub-section (1), all such offences must be investigated, inquired into, tried, and otherwise dealt with according to the provisions contained in the Sanhita. [Source: Section 4, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Trial of offences under Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and other laws

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 4: Trial of offences under Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and other laws

Q: Are offences under laws other than the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita completely bound by this Sanhita without exception?
A: No, under sub-section (2), while they are dealt with under this Sanhita, this is explicitly subject to any enactment regulating the manner or place of dealing with such offences. [Source: Section 4, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Trial of offences under Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and other laws

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 4: Trial of offences under Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and other laws

Q: What is the practical application of this section for police investigating an offence under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita?
A: The consequence is that police must follow the procedures laid out in the BNSS 2023 when investigating, inquiring into, and trying those offences. [Source: Section 4, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Trial of offences under Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and other laws

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 5: Saving

Q: Does this criminal procedure code automatically override any local or special laws currently in effect?
A: Nothing contained in this Sanhita shall, in the absence of a specific provision to the contrary, affect any special or local law for the time being in force. [Source: Section 5, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Saving

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 5: Saving

Q: What is Section 5 of BNSS 2023 about?
A: Section 5 of BNSS 2023 is a saving clause that protects the operation of special or local laws and special jurisdictions from being overridden by this Sanhita unless explicitly stated. [Source: Section 5, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Saving

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 5: Saving

Q: If a separate special law prescribes a unique form of procedure for a specific crime, does the BNSS 2023 invalidate that unique procedure?
A: No, the Sanhita does not affect any special form of procedure prescribed by any other law for the time being in force, in the absence of a specific provision to the contrary. [Source: Section 5, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Saving

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 5: Saving

Q: Under what condition would this Sanhita actually override a special or local law?
A: It would only affect a special or local law if there is a "specific provision to the contrary" present within the Sanhita. [Source: Section 5, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Saving

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 5: Saving

Q: What exception exists regarding the preservation of special jurisdictions?
A: The preservation of special jurisdiction or power conferred by another law only applies "in the absence of a specific provision to the contrary" within the Sanhita. [Source: Section 5, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Saving

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 5: Saving

Q: What is the consequence of this saving clause for courts dealing with local laws?
A: Courts must continue to apply the special procedures and powers prescribed by those local laws, rather than defaulting strictly to the Sanhita, unless the Sanhita explicitly overrides them. [Source: Section 5, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Saving

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 6: Classes of Criminal Courts

Q: What are the different types of criminal courts that exist in a State?
A: Besides High Courts and other legally constituted Courts, there shall be Courts of Session, Judicial Magistrates of the first class, Judicial Magistrates of the second class, and Executive Magistrates. [Source: Section 6, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Classes of Criminal Courts

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 6: Classes of Criminal Courts

Q: Can you explain Section 6 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 6 of BNSS 2023 establishes the classes of Criminal Courts, listing the specific hierarchy and types of courts that operate in every State. [Source: Section 6, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Classes of Criminal Courts

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 6: Classes of Criminal Courts

Q: A new state is formed and needs to establish its criminal justice system. Which specific classes of courts must it create alongside the High Court?
A: The State must create Courts of Session, Judicial Magistrates of the first class, Judicial Magistrates of the second class, and Executive Magistrates. [Source: Section 6, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Classes of Criminal Courts

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 6: Classes of Criminal Courts

Q: What must exist in every State besides the High Courts and Courts constituted under other laws?
A: There must be the four specific classes of Criminal Courts enumerated: Courts of Session, Judicial Magistrates of the first class, Judicial Magistrates of the second class, and Executive Magistrates. [Source: Section 6, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Classes of Criminal Courts

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 6: Classes of Criminal Courts

Q: Does this section limit criminal courts exclusively to the four classes listed?
A: No, the section explicitly mentions these are "Besides the High Courts and the Courts constituted under any law, other than this Sanhita". [Source: Section 6, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Classes of Criminal Courts

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 6: Classes of Criminal Courts

Q: What is the structural outcome of this section on the state's judiciary?
A: It mandates a uniform baseline structure of criminal courts across every State, ensuring cases can be appropriately routed to Sessions Courts, Judicial Magistrates, or Executive Magistrates. [Source: Section 6, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Classes of Criminal Courts

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 7: Territorial divisions

Q: How are states geographically organized for the purposes of criminal jurisdiction?
A: Every State shall be a sessions division or shall consist of sessions divisions, and every sessions division shall be a district or consist of districts. [Source: Section 7, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Territorial divisions

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 7: Territorial divisions

Q: What does Section 7 of BNSS 2023 say?
A: Section 7 of BNSS 2023 governs territorial divisions, dictating how States are divided into sessions divisions, districts, and sub-divisions for criminal administration. [Source: Section 7, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Territorial divisions

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 7: Territorial divisions

Q: The State Government wants to redraw the boundaries of a sessions division to balance caseloads. What procedural step must they take first?
A: Under sub-section (2), the State Government may alter the limits or the number of such divisions and districts only "after consultation with the High Court." [Source: Section 7, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Territorial divisions

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 7: Territorial divisions

Q: What condition must be met for a district to be divided into smaller sub-divisions?
A: Under sub-section (3), the State Government may divide a district into sub-divisions "after consultation with the High Court." [Source: Section 7, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Territorial divisions

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 7: Territorial divisions

Q: Are the sessions divisions that existed before this Sanhita was enacted considered invalid?
A: No, under sub-section (4), the sessions divisions, districts, and sub-divisions existing in a State at the commencement of this Sanhita shall be deemed to have been formed under this section. [Source: Section 7, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Territorial divisions

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 7: Territorial divisions

Q: What is the practical result of establishing these territorial divisions?
A: The consequence is that it provides a defined geographic area for Courts of Session and Magistrates to exercise their jurisdiction and manage criminal cases locally. [Source: Section 7, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Territorial divisions

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 8: Court of Session

Q: Who is responsible for establishing a Court of Session in a division?
A: The State Government shall establish a Court of Session for every sessions division, and it shall be presided over by a Judge appointed by the High Court. [Source: Section 8, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Court of Session

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 8: Court of Session

Q: What is Section 8 of BNSS 2023 about?
A: Section 8 of BNSS 2023 details the establishment and functioning of the Court of Session, including the appointment of Judges, Additional Sessions Judges, and rules for their sittings. [Source: Section 8, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Court of Session

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 8: Court of Session

Q: A Sessions Judge's office becomes vacant, and an urgent bail application is filed. Who handles it if there are no Additional Sessions Judges available?
A: Under sub-section (5), the High Court may make arrangements for the urgent application to be disposed of by a Chief Judicial Magistrate in the sessions division. [Source: Section 8, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Court of Session

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 8: Court of Session

Q: What conditions allow a Court of Session to hold its sittings at a place other than its ordinarily specified location?
A: Under sub-section (6), it must be of the opinion that it will tend to the general convenience of the parties and witnesses, and it must have the consent of the prosecution and the accused. [Source: Section 8, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Court of Session

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 8: Court of Session

Q: Does the term "appointment" in this section cover the very first time a person is promoted into government service?
A: No, according to the Explanation, "appointment" does not include the first appointment, posting, or promotion of a person by the Government to any Service where such appointment is required to be made by the Government. [Source: Section 8, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Court of Session

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 8: Court of Session

Q: What happens when the High Court appoints a Sessions Judge of one division to be an Additional Sessions Judge of another division?
A: Under sub-section (4), the consequence is that the Judge may sit for the disposal of cases at such place or places in the other division as the High Court may direct. [Source: Section 8, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Court of Session

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 9: Courts of Judicial Magistrates

Q: How are the locations and quantities of Judicial Magistrate Courts determined in a district?
A: The State Government, after consultation with the High Court, shall establish as many Courts of Judicial Magistrates of the first and second class, and at such places, as it may specify by notification. [Source: Section 9, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Courts of Judicial Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 9: Courts of Judicial Magistrates

Q: What does Section 9 of BNSS 2023 say?
A: Section 9 of BNSS 2023 provides for the establishment of Courts of Judicial Magistrates, the appointment of their presiding officers, and the creation of Special Courts. [Source: Section 9, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Courts of Judicial Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 9: Courts of Judicial Magistrates

Q: The government sets up a Special Court of Judicial Magistrate to handle solely cybercrime cases in a local area. Can a regular Magistrate Court in that area also try a cybercrime case?
A: No, the proviso to sub-section (1) states that where a Special Court is established, no other Court of Magistrate in the local area shall have jurisdiction to try any case for which the Special Court has been established. [Source: Section 9, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Courts of Judicial Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 9: Courts of Judicial Magistrates

Q: What authority is required to appoint the presiding officers of the Courts of Judicial Magistrates?
A: Under sub-section (2), the presiding officers of such Courts shall be appointed by the High Court. [Source: Section 9, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Courts of Judicial Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 9: Courts of Judicial Magistrates

Q: Is it possible for a Civil Court Judge to exercise the powers of a Criminal Magistrate?
A: Yes, under sub-section (3), the High Court may confer the powers of a Judicial Magistrate of the first or second class on any member of the Judicial Service functioning as a Judge in a Civil Court. [Source: Section 9, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Courts of Judicial Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 9: Courts of Judicial Magistrates

Q: What is the consequence of establishing a Special Court of Judicial Magistrate for a particular class of cases?
A: The consequence, as per the proviso to sub-section (1), is that it strips all other Magistrate Courts in that local area of the jurisdiction to try that specific class of cases. [Source: Section 9, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Courts of Judicial Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 10: Chief Judicial Magistrate and Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, etc

Q: Who appoints the Chief Judicial Magistrate for a district?
A: In every district, the High Court shall appoint a Judicial Magistrate of the first class to be the Chief Judicial Magistrate. [Source: Section 10, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Chief Judicial Magistrate and Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 10: Chief Judicial Magistrate and Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, etc

Q: What is Section 10 of BNSS 2023 about?
A: Section 10 of BNSS 2023 covers the appointment of the Chief Judicial Magistrate, Additional Chief Judicial Magistrates, and Sub-divisional Judicial Magistrates, outlining their supervisory roles. [Source: Section 10, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Chief Judicial Magistrate and Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 10: Chief Judicial Magistrate and Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, etc

Q: The High Court wants to ensure a specific sub-division has a dedicated Magistrate with supervisory powers. What designation can they use?
A: Under sub-section (3), the High Court may designate any Judicial Magistrate of the first class in a sub-division as the Sub-divisional Judicial Magistrate. [Source: Section 10, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Chief Judicial Magistrate and Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 10: Chief Judicial Magistrate and Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, etc

Q: What condition applies to the powers of supervision exercised by a Sub-divisional Judicial Magistrate over other Magistrates?
A: Under sub-section (4), their powers of supervision and control are subject to the general control of the Chief Judicial Magistrate and must be specified by the High Court. [Source: Section 10, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Chief Judicial Magistrate and Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 10: Chief Judicial Magistrate and Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, etc

Q: Does a Sub-divisional Judicial Magistrate have supervisory control over an Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate in their sub-division?
A: No, under sub-section (4), the Sub-divisional Judicial Magistrate has supervision and control over Judicial Magistrates "other than Additional Chief Judicial Magistrates." [Source: Section 10, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Chief Judicial Magistrate and Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 10: Chief Judicial Magistrate and Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, etc

Q: What happens when a Judicial Magistrate of the first class is appointed as an Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate?
A: Under sub-section (2), the consequence is that such Magistrate shall have all or any of the powers of a Chief Judicial Magistrate under this Sanhita or any other law as the High Court may direct. [Source: Section 10, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Chief Judicial Magistrate and Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 11: Special Judicial Magistrates

Q: What is the process for appointing a Special Judicial Magistrate?
A: The High Court may, if requested by the Central or State Government, confer upon any person holding a government post the powers of a Judicial Magistrate to handle particular cases. [Source: Section 11, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Special Judicial Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 11: Special Judicial Magistrates

Q: What does Section 11 of BNSS 2023 say?
A: Section 11 of BNSS 2023 details the appointment of Special Judicial Magistrates by the High Court for specific cases, including their qualifications and term limits. [Source: Section 11, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Special Judicial Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 11: Special Judicial Magistrates

Q: The government requests the High Court to appoint a civil servant as a Special Judicial Magistrate, but the civil servant has no legal background. Can the High Court appoint them?
A: No, the proviso to sub-section (1) states no such power shall be conferred unless the person possesses such qualification or experience in relation to legal affairs as the High Court may specify by rules. [Source: Section 11, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Special Judicial Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 11: Special Judicial Magistrates

Q: What is the maximum term for which a Special Judicial Magistrate can be appointed at one time?
A: Under sub-section (2), they shall be appointed for such term, not exceeding one year at a time, as the High Court may direct. [Source: Section 11, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Special Judicial Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 11: Special Judicial Magistrates

Q: Can the High Court proactively appoint a Special Judicial Magistrate without any outside request?
A: No, under sub-section (1), the High Court may do so "if requested by the Central or State Government so to do." [Source: Section 11, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Special Judicial Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 11: Special Judicial Magistrates

Q: What is the practical application of appointing a Special Judicial Magistrate?
A: It allows the government and High Court to dedicate a specific magistrate with necessary legal qualifications to handle "particular cases or to particular classes of cases" in a specific local area. [Source: Section 11, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Special Judicial Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 12: Local Jurisdiction of Judicial Magistrates

Q: Who defines the specific local boundaries where a Judicial Magistrate can exercise their powers?
A: Subject to the control of the High Court, the Chief Judicial Magistrate may, from time to time, define the local limits of the areas within which Magistrates may exercise their powers. [Source: Section 12, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Local Jurisdiction of Judicial Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 12: Local Jurisdiction of Judicial Magistrates

Q: What is Section 12 of BNSS 2023 about?
A: Section 12 of BNSS 2023 covers the local jurisdiction of Judicial Magistrates, explaining how their operational boundaries are defined and how their jurisdiction interacts with district borders. [Source: Section 12, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Local Jurisdiction of Judicial Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 12: Local Jurisdiction of Judicial Magistrates

Q: A Magistrate is appointed to a district but no specific local limits are defined for them by the Chief Judicial Magistrate. Where can they exercise their powers?
A: Under sub-section (2), except as otherwise provided by such definition, the jurisdiction and powers of every such Magistrate shall extend throughout the district. [Source: Section 12, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Local Jurisdiction of Judicial Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 12: Local Jurisdiction of Judicial Magistrates

Q: Where is the Court of a Special Judicial Magistrate permitted to hold its sitting?
A: The proviso to sub-section (1) states that the Court of Special Judicial Magistrate may hold its sitting at any place within the local area for which it is established. [Source: Section 12, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Local Jurisdiction of Judicial Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 12: Local Jurisdiction of Judicial Magistrates

Q: Are the Chief Judicial Magistrate's decisions on defining local limits final and absolute?
A: No, under sub-section (1), the defining of local limits by the Chief Judicial Magistrate is "Subject to the control of the High Court." [Source: Section 12, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Local Jurisdiction of Judicial Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 12: Local Jurisdiction of Judicial Magistrates

Q: What happens if a Magistrate's local jurisdiction extends into an area beyond the district where they normally hold Court?
A: Under sub-section (3), any reference in the Sanhita to the Court of Session or Chief Judicial Magistrate shall be construed as a reference to the Court of Session or Chief Judicial Magistrate exercising jurisdiction in relation to that specific district. [Source: Section 12, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Local Jurisdiction of Judicial Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 13: Subordination of Judicial Magistrates

Q: Who is the immediate superior to a regular Judicial Magistrate in the judicial hierarchy?
A: Every Judicial Magistrate shall be subordinate to the Chief Judicial Magistrate, subject to the general control of the Sessions Judge. [Source: Section 13, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Subordination of Judicial Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 13: Subordination of Judicial Magistrates

Q: What does Section 13 of BNSS 2023 cover?
A: Section 13 of BNSS 2023 covers the subordination of Judicial Magistrates, establishing the chain of command under the Chief Judicial Magistrate and the Sessions Judge. [Source: Section 13, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Subordination of Judicial Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 13: Subordination of Judicial Magistrates

Q: A Chief Judicial Magistrate wants to assign specific types of cases to a newly appointed Judicial Magistrate. Does the Chief Judicial Magistrate have the authority to do this?
A: Yes, under sub-section (2), the Chief Judicial Magistrate may make rules or give special orders as to the distribution of business among the Judicial Magistrates subordinate to him. [Source: Section 13, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Subordination of Judicial Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 13: Subordination of Judicial Magistrates

Q: What is the hierarchical condition placed on the Chief Judicial Magistrate themselves?
A: Under sub-section (1), every Chief Judicial Magistrate shall be subordinate to the Sessions Judge. [Source: Section 13, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Subordination of Judicial Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 13: Subordination of Judicial Magistrates

Q: Is the subordination of Judicial Magistrates to the Chief Judicial Magistrate absolute and independent?
A: No, under sub-section (1), their subordination to the Chief Judicial Magistrate is "subject to the general control of the Sessions Judge." [Source: Section 13, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Subordination of Judicial Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 13: Subordination of Judicial Magistrates

Q: What is the practical outcome of the Chief Judicial Magistrate's power to distribute business?
A: It allows the Chief Judicial Magistrate to actively manage the caseloads and allocate specific cases or duties among the lower Judicial Magistrates to ensure efficient administration. [Source: Section 13, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Subordination of Judicial Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 14: Executive Magistrates

Q: How is the highest executive officer of a district appointed for criminal procedure purposes?
A: The State Government appoints Executive Magistrates in every district and shall appoint one of them to be the District Magistrate. [Source: Section 14, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Executive Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 14: Executive Magistrates

Q: What is Section 14 of BNSS 2023 about?
A: Section 14 of BNSS 2023 outlines the appointment and hierarchy of Executive Magistrates, including the District Magistrate, Additional District Magistrates, and Sub-divisional Magistrates. [Source: Section 14, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Executive Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 14: Executive Magistrates

Q: The District Magistrate suddenly resigns, leaving the office vacant. An officer temporarily takes over the executive administration of the district. Can this officer issue orders as the District Magistrate?
A: Yes, under sub-section (3), the officer succeeding temporarily shall exercise all the powers and perform all the duties conferred on the District Magistrate pending the orders of the State Government. [Source: Section 14, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Executive Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 14: Executive Magistrates

Q: What defines a Sub-divisional Magistrate under this section?
A: Under sub-section (4), a Sub-divisional Magistrate is an Executive Magistrate who has been placed in charge of a sub-division by the State Government. [Source: Section 14, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Executive Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 14: Executive Magistrates

Q: Can the State Government allow someone else to assign Executive Magistrates to head sub-divisions?
A: Yes, under sub-section (5), the State Government may delegate its powers to place an Executive Magistrate in charge of a sub-division to the District Magistrate. [Source: Section 14, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Executive Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 14: Executive Magistrates

Q: What happens when the State Government designates an Executive Magistrate as an Additional District Magistrate?
A: Under sub-section (2), the consequence is that such Magistrate shall have such of the powers of a District Magistrate under this Sanhita or other laws as directed by the State Government. [Source: Section 14, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Executive Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 15: Special Executive Magistrates

Q: Can a senior police officer be granted magisterial powers for specific tasks?
A: Yes, the State Government may appoint a police officer not below the rank of Superintendent of Police or equivalent to be a Special Executive Magistrate for particular functions. [Source: Section 15, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Special Executive Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 15: Special Executive Magistrates

Q: What does Section 15 of BNSS 2023 say?
A: Section 15 of BNSS 2023 authorizes the State Government to appoint Special Executive Magistrates, including senior police officers, for particular areas or functions. [Source: Section 15, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Special Executive Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 15: Special Executive Magistrates

Q: The State Government wants to appoint a local police Inspector as a Special Executive Magistrate to handle crowd control during a festival. Is this appointment valid?
A: No, the section specifies that any police officer appointed as a Special Executive Magistrate must be "not below the rank of Superintendent of Police or equivalent." [Source: Section 15, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Special Executive Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 15: Special Executive Magistrates

Q: What are the two specific circumstances for which a Special Executive Magistrate can be appointed?
A: They can be appointed for "particular areas" or for the "performance of particular functions." [Source: Section 15, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Special Executive Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 15: Special Executive Magistrates

Q: Is a Special Executive Magistrate appointed permanently?
A: No, the State Government may appoint them "for such term as it may think fit." [Source: Section 15, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Special Executive Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 15: Special Executive Magistrates

Q: What powers does a Special Executive Magistrate actually wield once appointed?
A: They exercise such of the powers as are conferrable under this Sanhita on Executive Magistrates, specifically as the State Government "may deem fit" to confer on them. [Source: Section 15, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Special Executive Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 16: Local Jurisdiction of Executive

Q: Who has the authority to define the local operational boundaries for Executive Magistrates?
A: Subject to the control of the State Government, the District Magistrate may, from time to time, define the local limits of the areas within which the Executive Magistrates may exercise their powers. [Source: Section 16, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Local Jurisdiction of Executive

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 16: Local Jurisdiction of Executive

Q: What is Section 16 of BNSS 2023 about?
A: Section 16 of BNSS 2023 explains the local jurisdiction of Executive Magistrates and the role of the District Magistrate in defining those limits. [Source: Section 16, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Local Jurisdiction of Executive

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 16: Local Jurisdiction of Executive

Q: An Executive Magistrate is assigned to a district but the District Magistrate has not yet explicitly defined their local limits. Where does the Executive Magistrate have jurisdiction?
A: Under sub-section (2), except as otherwise provided by such definition, the jurisdiction and powers of every such Magistrate shall extend throughout the district. [Source: Section 16, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Local Jurisdiction of Executive

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 16: Local Jurisdiction of Executive

Q: What condition applies to the District Magistrate's power to define these local limits?
A: Under sub-section (1), the District Magistrate's power to define local limits is "Subject to the control of the State Government." [Source: Section 16, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Local Jurisdiction of Executive

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 16: Local Jurisdiction of Executive

Q: Is an Executive Magistrate's jurisdiction automatically limited to a sub-division if no special order is given?
A: No, under sub-section (2), unless specifically defined otherwise, their jurisdiction extends "throughout the district." [Source: Section 16, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Local Jurisdiction of Executive

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 16: Local Jurisdiction of Executive

Q: What is the consequence of the District Magistrate defining a specific local area for an Executive Magistrate?
A: The consequence is that the Executive Magistrate may only exercise all or any of the powers with which they may be invested within those specific local limits, rather than the whole district. [Source: Section 16, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Local Jurisdiction of Executive

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 17: Subordination of Executive Magistrates

Q: Who is the direct superior of all Executive Magistrates in a district?
A: All Executive Magistrates shall be subordinate to the District Magistrate. [Source: Section 17, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Subordination of Executive Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 17: Subordination of Executive Magistrates

Q: What does Section 17 of BNSS 2023 state?
A: Section 17 of BNSS 2023 outlines the chain of command for Executive Magistrates, making them subordinate to the District Magistrate and Sub-divisional Magistrates. [Source: Section 17, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Subordination of Executive Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 17: Subordination of Executive Magistrates

Q: An Executive Magistrate is working within a specific sub-division. Are they only accountable to the District Magistrate?
A: No, under sub-section (1), every Executive Magistrate exercising powers in a sub-division shall also be subordinate to the Sub-divisional Magistrate, subject to the general control of the District Magistrate. [Source: Section 17, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Subordination of Executive Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 17: Subordination of Executive Magistrates

Q: What condition must a District Magistrate follow when distributing work among Executive Magistrates?
A: Under sub-section (2), the District Magistrate may make rules or give special orders "consistent with this Sanhita" regarding the distribution or allocation of business. [Source: Section 17, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Subordination of Executive Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 17: Subordination of Executive Magistrates

Q: Does a Sub-divisional Magistrate have absolute control over the Executive Magistrates in their sub-division?
A: No, under sub-section (1), the subordination of Executive Magistrates to the Sub-divisional Magistrate is "subject, to the general control of the District Magistrate." [Source: Section 17, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Subordination of Executive Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 17: Subordination of Executive Magistrates

Q: What happens practically when the District Magistrate issues rules regarding business allocation?
A: The consequence is that the workload and specific cases are legally distributed and allocated among the subordinate Executive Magistrates according to those rules. [Source: Section 17, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Subordination of Executive Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 18: Public Prosecutors

Q: Who is responsible for appointing a Public Prosecutor for a High Court?
A: For every High Court, the Central Government or the State Government shall, after consultation with the High Court, appoint a Public Prosecutor. [Source: Section 18, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public Prosecutors

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 18: Public Prosecutors

Q: What is Section 18 of BNSS 2023 about?
A: Section 18 of BNSS 2023 provides the rules and qualifications for the appointment of Public Prosecutors, Additional Public Prosecutors, and Special Public Prosecutors at both the High Court and district levels. [Source: Section 18, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public Prosecutors

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 18: Public Prosecutors

Q: A district needs a new Public Prosecutor. Can the State Government appoint anyone who meets the experience requirement without consulting local officials?
A: No, under sub-section (5), the State Government cannot appoint a person for the district unless their name appears in the panel of names prepared by the District Magistrate in consultation with the Sessions Judge. [Source: Section 18, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public Prosecutors

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 18: Public Prosecutors

Q: What is the minimum experience required to be appointed as a Public Prosecutor or Additional Public Prosecutor?
A: Under sub-section (7), a person shall be eligible only if he has been in practice as an advocate for not less than seven years. [Source: Section 18, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public Prosecutors

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 18: Public Prosecutors

Q: If a State has a regular Cadre of Prosecuting Officers, must the State Government only appoint from that Cadre?
A: Yes, but with an exception: under the proviso to sub-section (6), if no suitable person is available in the Cadre, the Government may appoint someone from the panel prepared by the District Magistrate. [Source: Section 18, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public Prosecutors

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 18: Public Prosecutors

Q: What is the practical application of appointing a Special Public Prosecutor?
A: Under sub-section (8), the Central or State Government may appoint an advocate with at least ten years of practice to conduct a specific "case or class of cases," allowing specialized legal expertise for complex prosecutions. [Source: Section 18, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public Prosecutors

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 19: Assistant Public Prosecutors

Q: Who conducts prosecutions in the Courts of Magistrates on behalf of the state?
A: The State Government shall appoint in every district one or more Assistant Public Prosecutors for conducting prosecutions in the Courts of Magistrates. [Source: Section 19, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assistant Public Prosecutors

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 19: Assistant Public Prosecutors

Q: What does Section 19 of BNSS 2023 say?
A: Section 19 of BNSS 2023 covers the appointment of Assistant Public Prosecutors for Magistrate Courts and outlines when a police officer is prohibited from serving in this role. [Source: Section 19, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assistant Public Prosecutors

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 19: Assistant Public Prosecutors

Q: During a trial in a Magistrate's Court, no Assistant Public Prosecutor is available. Can the District Magistrate appoint a police officer who investigated the crime to act as the prosecutor?
A: No, under proviso (a) to sub-section (3), no police officer shall be eligible if he "has taken any part in the investigation into the offence with respect to which the accused is being prosecuted." [Source: Section 19, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assistant Public Prosecutors

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 19: Assistant Public Prosecutors

Q: What conditions allow the District Magistrate to appoint any other person to be the Assistant Public Prosecutor in charge of a case?
A: Under sub-section (3), this can occur where no Assistant Public Prosecutor is available, and it must be done after giving notice of fourteen days to the State Government. [Source: Section 19, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assistant Public Prosecutors

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 19: Assistant Public Prosecutors

Q: Can any police officer whatsoever be appointed as an Assistant Public Prosecutor in an emergency?
A: No, under proviso (b) to sub-section (3), a police officer is not eligible if he is "below the rank of Inspector." [Source: Section 19, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assistant Public Prosecutors

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 19: Assistant Public Prosecutors

Q: What happens when the Central Government appoints an Assistant Public Prosecutor?
A: Under sub-section (2), the consequence is that the appointee is tasked with conducting "any case or class of cases" specifically in the Courts of Magistrates on behalf of the Central Government. [Source: Section 19, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assistant Public Prosecutors

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 20: Directorate of Prosecution

Q: What structural body monitors serious criminal cases on behalf of the State?
A: The State Government may establish a Directorate of Prosecution in the State consisting of a Director of Prosecution and Deputy Directors, as well as District Directorates. [Source: Section 20, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Directorate of Prosecution

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 20: Directorate of Prosecution

Q: What is Section 20 of BNSS 2023 about?
A: Section 20 of BNSS 2023 establishes the Directorate of Prosecution, defining its hierarchy, eligibility requirements for its officers, and their duties in monitoring specific categories of offenses. [Source: Section 20, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Directorate of Prosecution

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 20: Directorate of Prosecution

Q: An advocate with 8 years of practice wants to become a Deputy Director of Prosecution. Are they eligible based on experience?
A: No, under clause (a) of sub-section (2), a person is eligible to be a Director or Deputy Director only if he has been in practice as an advocate for "not less than fifteen years or is or has been a Sessions Judge." [Source: Section 20, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Directorate of Prosecution

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 20: Directorate of Prosecution

Q: What are the conditions for eligibility as an Assistant Director of Prosecution?
A: Under clause (b) of sub-section (2), a person must have been in practice as an advocate for not less than seven years or has been a Magistrate of the first class. [Source: Section 20, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Directorate of Prosecution

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 20: Directorate of Prosecution

Q: Does this section apply to the Advocate General of the State?
A: No, under sub-section (12), the provisions of this section shall not apply to the Advocate General for the State while performing the functions of a Public Prosecutor. [Source: Section 20, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Directorate of Prosecution

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 20: Directorate of Prosecution

Q: What is the consequence of establishing the Director of Prosecution role?
A: Under sub-section (7), the Director monitors cases involving offenses punishable by ten years or more, life imprisonment, or death, expedites proceedings, and gives opinions on filing appeals. [Source: Section 20, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Directorate of Prosecution

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 21: Courts by which offences are triable

Q: Which courts have the authority to try an offence under the new criminal code?
A: Subject to other provisions, any offence under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 may be tried by the High Court, the Court of Session, or any other Court shown in the First Schedule to be triable. [Source: Section 21, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Courts by which offences are triable

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 21: Courts by which offences are triable

Q: What does Section 21 of BNSS 2023 state?
A: Section 21 of BNSS 2023 outlines which specific courts possess the jurisdiction to try offenses under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and other laws. [Source: Section 21, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Courts by which offences are triable

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 21: Courts by which offences are triable

Q: A man is charged with an offence under section 64 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. What specific arrangement must the court make for the trial?
A: According to the proviso in clause (a), any offence under section 64 shall be tried "as far as practicable by a Court presided over by a woman." [Source: Section 21, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Courts by which offences are triable

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 21: Courts by which offences are triable

Q: How does a court determine its jurisdiction to try an offence under a law other than the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita?
A: Under clause (b), if a Court is mentioned in that specific law, it shall be tried by such Court; if no Court is mentioned, it may be tried by the High Court or any Court shown in the First Schedule. [Source: Section 21, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Courts by which offences are triable

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 21: Courts by which offences are triable

Q: Is the rule that certain sexual or domestic offenses must be tried by a woman judge absolute?
A: No, the proviso to clause (a) states that offenses under sections 64 to 71 shall be tried by a Court presided over by a woman "as far as practicable." [Source: Section 21, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Courts by which offences are triable

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 21: Courts by which offences are triable

Q: What happens if a special law does not specify which court should try its offences?
A: The consequence, under clause (b), is that the offence falls back to being triable by the High Court or the Court specified for it in the First Schedule of the Sanhita. [Source: Section 21, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Courts by which offences are triable

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 22: Sentences which High Courts and Sessions Judges may pass

Q: What are the limits on the types of sentences a High Court can issue?
A: A High Court may pass any sentence authorised by law. [Source: Section 22, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sentences which High Courts and Sessions Judges may pass

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 22: Sentences which High Courts and Sessions Judges may pass

Q: What is Section 22 of BNSS 2023 about?
A: Section 22 of BNSS 2023 defines the sentencing powers of High Courts, Sessions Judges, and Additional Sessions Judges, including the requirement for confirming death sentences. [Source: Section 22, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sentences which High Courts and Sessions Judges may pass

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 22: Sentences which High Courts and Sessions Judges may pass

Q: A Sessions Judge presides over a murder trial and decides the appropriate punishment is the death penalty. Does this sentence take immediate effect?
A: No, under sub-section (2), any sentence of death passed by a Sessions Judge or Additional Sessions Judge "shall be subject to confirmation by the High Court." [Source: Section 22, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sentences which High Courts and Sessions Judges may pass

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 22: Sentences which High Courts and Sessions Judges may pass

Q: What conditions restrict the sentencing power of a Sessions Judge?
A: Under sub-section (2), while they may pass any sentence authorised by law, a death sentence requires the specific condition of confirmation by the High Court. [Source: Section 22, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sentences which High Courts and Sessions Judges may pass

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 22: Sentences which High Courts and Sessions Judges may pass

Q: Are there any types of legal sentences that a High Court cannot pass?
A: No, under sub-section (1), the High Court may pass "any sentence authorised by law" without listed exceptions. [Source: Section 22, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sentences which High Courts and Sessions Judges may pass

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 22: Sentences which High Courts and Sessions Judges may pass

Q: What is the practical procedural consequence when an Additional Sessions Judge passes a death sentence?
A: The consequence is that the execution of the sentence is halted, and the case must be submitted to the High Court for confirmation before the death penalty can be carried out. [Source: Section 22, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sentences which High Courts and Sessions Judges may pass

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 23: Sentences which Magistrates may pass

Q: What is the maximum prison term a Chief Judicial Magistrate can sentence a convicted person to?
A: The Court of a Chief Judicial Magistrate may pass any sentence authorised by law except a sentence of death, imprisonment for life, or imprisonment for a term exceeding seven years. [Source: Section 23, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sentences which Magistrates may pass

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 23: Sentences which Magistrates may pass

Q: What does Section 23 of BNSS 2023 cover?
A: Section 23 of BNSS 2023 sets out the specific sentencing powers and limitations for Chief Judicial Magistrates, Magistrates of the first class, and Magistrates of the second class, and defines "community service." [Source: Section 23, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sentences which Magistrates may pass

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 23: Sentences which Magistrates may pass

Q: A Magistrate of the first class finds an accused guilty. The prosecutor asks for a sentence of five years. Can the Magistrate grant this?
A: No, under sub-section (2), the Court of a Magistrate of the first class may pass a sentence of imprisonment for a term "not exceeding three years." [Source: Section 23, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sentences which Magistrates may pass

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 23: Sentences which Magistrates may pass

Q: What constitutes "community service" as a form of punishment?
A: According to the Explanation, community service shall mean the work which the Court may order a convict to perform as a form of punishment that benefits the community, for which he shall not be entitled to any remuneration. [Source: Section 23, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sentences which Magistrates may pass

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 23: Sentences which Magistrates may pass

Q: Can a Magistrate of the second class impose a fine of fifteen thousand rupees?
A: No, under sub-section (3), the Court of Magistrate of the second class may pass a sentence of fine "not exceeding ten thousand rupees." [Source: Section 23, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sentences which Magistrates may pass

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 23: Sentences which Magistrates may pass

Q: What is the consequence if a Magistrate decides that a convict should perform unpaid work to benefit the community?
A: Under sub-sections (2) and (3), Magistrates of the first and second class have the specific legal authority to pass a sentence of "community service" upon the convict. [Source: Section 23, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sentences which Magistrates may pass

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 24: Sentence of imprisonment in default of fine

Q: How does a court penalize someone who fails to pay a legally imposed fine?
A: The Court of a Magistrate may award such term of imprisonment in default of payment of fine as is authorised by law. [Source: Section 24, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sentence of imprisonment in default of fine

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 24: Sentence of imprisonment in default of fine

Q: What does Section 24 of BNSS 2023 state?
A: Section 24 of BNSS 2023 explains the rules and limits for sentencing a person to a term of imprisonment when they default on paying a court-ordered fine. [Source: Section 24, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sentence of imprisonment in default of fine

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 24: Sentence of imprisonment in default of fine

Q: A Magistrate of the first class sentences a convict to two years in prison and a fine. The convict refuses to pay the fine. The Magistrate wants to add an extra one-year prison term for the default. Is this allowed?
A: No, under proviso (b) to sub-section (1), the imprisonment in default cannot exceed one-fourth of the maximum term the Magistrate is competent to inflict (which is 3 years), so the default term cannot exceed 9 months. [Source: Section 24, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sentence of imprisonment in default of fine

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 24: Sentence of imprisonment in default of fine

Q: What two conditions limit the term of imprisonment a Magistrate can impose for default of fine?
A: Under the proviso to sub-section (1), the term must not be in excess of the Magistrate's powers under section 23, and it shall not exceed one-fourth of the term of imprisonment the Magistrate is competent to inflict if awarded as part of a substantive sentence. [Source: Section 24, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sentence of imprisonment in default of fine

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 24: Sentence of imprisonment in default of fine

Q: Is imprisonment for defaulting on a fine considered part of the substantive sentence?
A: No, under sub-section (2), the imprisonment awarded under this section may be "in addition to a substantive sentence of imprisonment" for the maximum term awardable by the Magistrate. [Source: Section 24, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sentence of imprisonment in default of fine

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 24: Sentence of imprisonment in default of fine

Q: What is the consequence if an offender receives the absolute maximum prison sentence from a Magistrate and then defaults on their fine?
A: Under sub-section (2), the Magistrate may still award an additional term of imprisonment for the default, meaning the total time served can legally exceed the Magistrate's normal maximum substantive sentence limit. [Source: Section 24, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sentence of imprisonment in default of fine

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 25: Sentence in cases of conviction of several offences at one trial

Q: How does a judge handle sentencing when a person is convicted of multiple distinct crimes in a single trial?
A: When a person is convicted at one trial of two or more offences, the Court may sentence him for such offences to several punishments and order such punishments to run concurrently or consecutively, considering the gravity of the offences. [Source: Section 25, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sentence in cases of conviction of several offences at one trial

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 25: Sentence in cases of conviction of several offences at one trial

Q: What is Section 25 of BNSS 2023 about?
A: Section 25 of BNSS 2023 dictates how sentences are applied and calculated when a defendant is convicted of several offences at one trial, outlining limits on consecutive sentences. [Source: Section 25, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sentence in cases of conviction of several offences at one trial

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 25: Sentence in cases of conviction of several offences at one trial

Q: A Magistrate competent to inflict a maximum of 3 years imprisonment convicts a defendant of three offences. The Magistrate orders consecutive sentences of 2 years each, totaling 6 years. Must the Magistrate send the case to a higher Court because 6 years exceeds their 3-year limit?
A: No, under sub-section (2), it shall not be necessary for the Court to send the offender for trial before a higher Court by reason only of the aggregate punishment being in excess of the punishment it is competent to inflict on conviction of a single offence. [Source: Section 25, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sentence in cases of conviction of several offences at one trial

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 25: Sentence in cases of conviction of several offences at one trial

Q: What two conditions limit the aggregate consecutive punishment a Court can impose?
A: Under the proviso to sub-section (2), in no case shall such person be sentenced to imprisonment for longer than twenty years, and the aggregate punishment shall not exceed twice the amount of punishment the Court is competent to inflict for a single offence. [Source: Section 25, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sentence in cases of conviction of several offences at one trial

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 25: Sentence in cases of conviction of several offences at one trial

Q: Are consecutive sentences calculated individually if the convicted person wants to file an appeal?
A: No, under sub-section (3), for the purpose of appeal by a convicted person, the aggregate of the consecutive sentences passed against him shall be deemed to be a "single sentence." [Source: Section 25, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sentence in cases of conviction of several offences at one trial

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 25: Sentence in cases of conviction of several offences at one trial

Q: What is the practical result when a Court orders punishments to run consecutively?
A: The consequence is that the defendant serves the sentences back-to-back, adding the time together, subject to the maximum limit of twenty years or twice the Court's single-offence limit. [Source: Section 25, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sentence in cases of conviction of several offences at one trial

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 26: Mode of conferring powers

Q: How do authorities grant powers to officials under this criminal code?
A: The High Court or the State Government may, by order, empower persons specially by name or in virtue of their offices or classes of officials generally by their official titles. [Source: Section 26, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Mode of conferring powers

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 26: Mode of conferring powers

Q: What does Section 26 of BNSS 2023 say?
A: Section 26 of BNSS 2023 details the method for conferring powers under the Sanhita, specifying that powers can be granted by name or official title and defining when such orders take effect. [Source: Section 26, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Mode of conferring powers

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 26: Mode of conferring powers

Q: A government order granting new powers to a Magistrate is signed on Monday but not communicated to the Magistrate until Thursday. When does the Magistrate actually have those new powers?
A: Under sub-section (2), every such order shall take effect "from the date on which it is communicated to the person so empowered," which means Thursday. [Source: Section 26, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Mode of conferring powers

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 26: Mode of conferring powers

Q: What condition determines when an order conferring power becomes active?
A: Under sub-section (2), the order must be "communicated to the person so empowered" for it to take effect. [Source: Section 26, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Mode of conferring powers

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 26: Mode of conferring powers

Q: Are powers only granted to individuals specifically by their personal names?
A: No, under sub-section (1), they can also be empowered "in virtue of their offices or classes of officials generally be their official titles." [Source: Section 26, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Mode of conferring powers

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 26: Mode of conferring powers

Q: What happens when the High Court signs an order empowering a class of officials?
A: The consequence is that the officials in that class receive the conferred powers, but only starting from the date the order is actually communicated to them. [Source: Section 26, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Mode of conferring powers

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 27: Powers of officers appointed

Q: What happens to a government official's special powers if they are promoted to a similar job within the same state?
A: Whenever any person holding an office in the service of Government who has been invested with powers is appointed to an equal or higher office of the same nature within a like local area under the same State Government, he shall exercise the same powers in the local area in which he is so appointed. [Source: Section 27, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Powers of officers appointed

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 27: Powers of officers appointed

Q: What is Section 27 of BNSS 2023 about?
A: Section 27 of BNSS 2023 ensures continuity of authority by allowing government officers to retain their conferred powers under the Sanhita when they are transferred or promoted to an equal or higher office of the same nature. [Source: Section 27, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Powers of officers appointed

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 27: Powers of officers appointed

Q: A Magistrate with specific conferred powers in District A is transferred to an equal position in District B. Does the Magistrate need a new order to exercise those specific powers in District B?
A: No, under Section 27, he shall exercise the same powers in the local area in which he is so appointed, unless the High Court or the State Government directs otherwise. [Source: Section 27, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Powers of officers appointed

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 27: Powers of officers appointed

Q: What conditions must exist for an officer to automatically retain their powers upon a new appointment?
A: The officer must be appointed to an equal or higher office of the same nature, within a like local area under the same State Government. [Source: Section 27, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Powers of officers appointed

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 27: Powers of officers appointed

Q: Is the automatic retention of powers upon transfer guaranteed without exception?
A: No, the retention of powers applies "unless the High Court or the State Government, as the case may be, otherwise directs, or has otherwise directed." [Source: Section 27, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Powers of officers appointed

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 27: Powers of officers appointed

Q: What is the consequence if the State Government promotes a police officer with special powers to a higher rank of the same nature?
A: The consequence is that the officer automatically carries those same special powers into their new role, avoiding administrative delays in re-authorizing them. [Source: Section 27, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Powers of officers appointed

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 28: Withdrawal of powers

Q: How can special legal authority granted to an official be revoked?
A: The High Court or the State Government may withdraw all or any of the powers conferred by it under this Sanhita on any person or by any officer subordinate to it. [Source: Section 28, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Withdrawal of powers

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 28: Withdrawal of powers

Q: What does Section 28 of BNSS 2023 state?
A: Section 28 of BNSS 2023 provides the rules for the withdrawal of powers, allowing the High Court, State Government, Chief Judicial Magistrate, or District Magistrate to revoke authority they previously granted. [Source: Section 28, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Withdrawal of powers

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 28: Withdrawal of powers

Q: The Chief Judicial Magistrate conferred specific powers on a subordinate Magistrate. Does the State Government have to be the one to withdraw those specific powers?
A: No, under sub-section (2), any powers conferred by the Chief Judicial Magistrate may be withdrawn "by the respective Magistrate by whom such powers were conferred." [Source: Section 28, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Withdrawal of powers

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 28: Withdrawal of powers

Q: What is required for the District Magistrate to withdraw powers from someone?
A: Under sub-section (2), the condition is that those specific powers must have been conferred by that respective Magistrate. [Source: Section 28, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Withdrawal of powers

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 28: Withdrawal of powers

Q: Can the High Court withdraw powers that were conferred by an officer subordinate to the High Court?
A: Yes, under sub-section (1), the High Court may withdraw powers conferred "by any officer subordinate to it." [Source: Section 28, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Withdrawal of powers

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 28: Withdrawal of powers

Q: What is the practical result when the State Government decides an official should no longer have a specific power?
A: The consequence is that the State Government can issue an order to "withdraw all or any of the powers," instantly stripping the official of that legal authority. [Source: Section 28, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Withdrawal of powers

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 29: Powers of Judges and Magistrates exercisable by their successors-in office

Q: When a judge retires or transfers, what happens to their ongoing judicial duties and powers?
A: Subject to the other provisions of this Sanhita, the powers and duties of a Judge or Magistrate may be exercised or performed by his successor-in-office. [Source: Section 29, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Powers of Judges and Magistrates exercisable by their successors-in office

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 29: Powers of Judges and Magistrates exercisable by their successors-in office

Q: What is Section 29 of BNSS 2023 about?
A: Section 29 of BNSS 2023 ensures continuity in the courts by allowing the powers and duties of a Judge or Magistrate to be passed on to and exercised by their official successor. [Source: Section 29, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Powers of Judges and Magistrates exercisable by their successors-in office

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 29: Powers of Judges and Magistrates exercisable by their successors-in office

Q: Two new Judges are assigned to a district and there is confusion over which one is the exact successor to a Judge who just retired. How is this resolved?
