Q: A constable is given a written order to arrest a man. Upon finding the man, he just cuffs him and puts him in the car without explaining anything. Is this lawful?
A: No, the constable "shall, before making the arrest, notify to the person to be arrested the substance of the order." [Source: Section 55, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure when police officer deputes subordinate to arrest without warrant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 55: Procedure when police officer deputes subordinate to arrest without warrant

Q: What two things must be specified in the written order given to the subordinate officer?
A: The written order must specify "the person to be arrested" and "the offence or other cause for which the arrest is to be made." [Source: Section 55, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure when police officer deputes subordinate to arrest without warrant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 55: Procedure when police officer deputes subordinate to arrest without warrant

Q: Does this strict written order requirement prevent a subordinate officer from making an independent arrest if they witness a crime?
A: No, sub-section (2) explicitly states that nothing in this section "shall affect the power of a police officer to arrest a person under section 35." [Source: Section 55, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure when police officer deputes subordinate to arrest without warrant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 55: Procedure when police officer deputes subordinate to arrest without warrant

Q: What is the consequence if the arrested person demands to see the written order during the arrest?
A: The consequence is that the subordinate officer "if so required by such person, shall show him the order" before completing the arrest. [Source: Section 55, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure when police officer deputes subordinate to arrest without warrant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 56: Health and safety of arrested person

Q: Are police officers responsible for the well-being of the people they arrest?
A: Yes, it shall be the duty of the person having the custody of an accused to take reasonable care of the health and safety of the accused. [Source: Section 56, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Health and safety of arrested person

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 56: Health and safety of arrested person

Q: What is the mandate of Section 56 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 56 of BNSS 2023 creates a statutory duty for whoever has custody of an accused person to ensure they are provided with reasonable care regarding their health and safety. [Source: Section 56, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Health and safety of arrested person

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 56: Health and safety of arrested person

Q: A suspect in lockup informs the guard that they need their daily insulin injection to survive. The guard ignores them. Is this a violation?
A: Yes, ignoring a serious medical need violates the duty "to take reasonable care of the health and safety of the accused." [Source: Section 56, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Health and safety of arrested person

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 56: Health and safety of arrested person

Q: To whom does the duty of care in this section apply?
A: The duty applies to "the person having the custody of an accused." [Source: Section 56, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Health and safety of arrested person

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 56: Health and safety of arrested person

Q: Does this section only apply to police officers?
A: No, it applies broadly to "the person having the custody of an accused," which could include prison officials or other authorized individuals holding the person. [Source: Section 56, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Health and safety of arrested person

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 56: Health and safety of arrested person

Q: What is the legal consequence of taking someone into custody?
A: The legal consequence is that the custodian immediately assumes a statutory duty to actively "take reasonable care of the health and safety" of that individual. [Source: Section 56, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Health and safety of arrested person

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 57: Person arrested to be taken before Magistrate or officer in charge of police station

Q: What must a police officer do immediately after arresting someone without a warrant?
A: A police officer making an arrest without warrant shall, without unnecessary delay, take or send the person arrested before a Magistrate having jurisdiction in the case, or before the officer in charge of a police station. [Source: Section 57, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Person arrested to be taken before Magistrate or officer in charge of police station

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 57: Person arrested to be taken before Magistrate or officer in charge of police station

Q: What does Section 57 of BNSS 2023 state?
A: Section 57 of BNSS 2023 mandates that individuals arrested without a warrant must be brought before a Magistrate or the officer in charge of a police station without unnecessary delay. [Source: Section 57, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Person arrested to be taken before Magistrate or officer in charge of police station

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 57: Person arrested to be taken before Magistrate or officer in charge of police station

Q: An officer arrests a suspect and decides to keep them in an unmarked warehouse for two days for interrogation before taking them to the station. Is this permitted?
A: No, the officer must take or send the person before a Magistrate or officer in charge "without unnecessary delay." [Source: Section 57, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Person arrested to be taken before Magistrate or officer in charge of police station

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 57: Person arrested to be taken before Magistrate or officer in charge of police station

Q: What condition applies to the general rule of taking the person before a Magistrate or officer in charge?
A: This requirement is "subject to the provisions herein contained as to bail." [Source: Section 57, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Person arrested to be taken before Magistrate or officer in charge of police station

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 57: Person arrested to be taken before Magistrate or officer in charge of police station

Q: Does the arresting officer absolutely have to bring the person to a Magistrate?
A: No, they have the option to take or send the person "before a Magistrate having jurisdiction in the case, or before the officer in charge of a police station." [Source: Section 57, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Person arrested to be taken before Magistrate or officer in charge of police station

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 57: Person arrested to be taken before Magistrate or officer in charge of police station

Q: What is the consequence of making a warrantless arrest?
A: The consequence is that the arresting officer is legally bound to swiftly transport the suspect to a higher authority (Magistrate or station head) to legitimize and process the detention. [Source: Section 57, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Person arrested to be taken before Magistrate or officer in charge of police station

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 58: Person arrested not to be detained more than twenty-four hours

Q: Are police station chiefs required to report warrantless arrests to higher authorities?
A: Yes, officers in charge of police stations shall report to the District Magistrate, or to the Sub-divisional Magistrate if directed, the cases of all persons arrested without warrant within their limits. [Source: Section 58, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Person arrested not to be detained more than twenty-four hours

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 58: Person arrested not to be detained more than twenty-four hours

Q: What does Section 58 of BNSS 2023 dictate?
A: Section 58 of BNSS 2023 dictates that officers in charge of police stations must report all warrantless arrests occurring within their station's limits to the District or Sub-divisional Magistrate. [Source: Section 58, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Person arrested not to be detained more than twenty-four hours

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 58: Person arrested not to be detained more than twenty-four hours

Q: A station chief arrests a person without a warrant but immediately releases them on bail. Does the chief still need to report this arrest to the District Magistrate?
A: Yes, the report must include the cases of all persons arrested without warrant, "whether such persons have been admitted to bail or otherwise." [Source: Section 58, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Person arrested not to be detained more than twenty-four hours

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 58: Person arrested not to be detained more than twenty-four hours

Q: To whom must the officer in charge ordinarily send the report of apprehensions?
A: They must report to the "District Magistrate, or, if he so directs, to the Sub-divisional Magistrate." [Source: Section 58, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Person arrested not to be detained more than twenty-four hours

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 58: Person arrested not to be detained more than twenty-four hours

Q: Do police have to report arrests made with a warrant under this specific provision?
A: No, the section specifies reporting the cases of "all persons arrested without warrant." [Source: Section 58, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Person arrested not to be detained more than twenty-four hours

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 58: Person arrested not to be detained more than twenty-four hours

Q: What is the consequence of this reporting requirement for the District Magistrate?
A: The consequence is that the District Magistrate is kept continuously informed of all warrantless deprivations of liberty occurring within their territorial jurisdiction. [Source: Section 58, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Person arrested not to be detained more than twenty-four hours

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 59: Police to report apprehensions

Q: What obligation do police stations have regarding reporting arrests to the District Magistrate?
A: Officers in charge of police stations are obligated to report to the District Magistrate (or Sub-divisional Magistrate) the cases of all persons arrested without warrant within their station limits. [Source: Section 59, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Police to report apprehensions

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 59: Police to report apprehensions

Q: What is the purpose of Section 59 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 59 of BNSS 2023 establishes a mandatory reporting mechanism where station heads must notify the magistracy of all warrantless apprehensions in their jurisdiction. [Source: Section 59, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Police to report apprehensions

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 59: Police to report apprehensions

Q: The District Magistrate directs the local station chief to send all arrest reports to the Sub-divisional Magistrate instead. Is the station chief legally allowed to do this?
A: Yes, the section explicitly states they shall report to the District Magistrate, "or, if he so directs, to the Sub-divisional Magistrate." [Source: Section 59, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Police to report apprehensions

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 59: Police to report apprehensions

Q: What detail about the arrested person's status must be included in the report to the Magistrate?
A: The report must cover all such arrested persons, "whether such persons have been admitted to bail or otherwise." [Source: Section 59, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Police to report apprehensions

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 59: Police to report apprehensions

Q: Are arrests made outside the limits of the officer's respective station required to be reported by them?
A: No, they must report the cases of persons arrested "within the limits of their respective stations." [Source: Section 59, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Police to report apprehensions

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 59: Police to report apprehensions

Q: What is the consequence of an officer releasing a suspect on bail after a warrantless arrest?
A: The consequence is that the officer is still required to report the apprehension to the Magistrate, ensuring oversight even when detention is brief. [Source: Section 59, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Police to report apprehensions

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 60: Discharge of person apprehended

Q: Once someone is arrested by the police, how can they be legally released?
A: No person who has been arrested by a police officer shall be discharged except on his bond, or bail bond, or under the special order of a Magistrate. [Source: Section 60, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Discharge of person apprehended

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 60: Discharge of person apprehended

Q: What is stated in Section 60 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 60 of BNSS 2023 states that an arrested person cannot be simply let go; they must be formally discharged via a bond, a bail bond, or a special order from a Magistrate. [Source: Section 60, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Discharge of person apprehended

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 60: Discharge of person apprehended

Q: An officer arrests a man but later realizes it's a case of mistaken identity. Can the officer just open the cell and tell him to go home without any paperwork?
A: No, the arrested person cannot be discharged "except on his bond, or bail bond, or under the special order of a Magistrate." [Source: Section 60, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Discharge of person apprehended

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 60: Discharge of person apprehended

Q: What are the three exclusive conditions under which an arrested person can be discharged?
A: They can only be discharged "on his bond", "or bail bond", or "under the special order of a Magistrate." [Source: Section 60, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Discharge of person apprehended

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 60: Discharge of person apprehended

Q: Can a police inspector issue a general verbal order to release an arrested suspect?
A: No, if it is an order, it must be "the special order of a Magistrate" to constitute a valid discharge without a bond. [Source: Section 60, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Discharge of person apprehended

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 60: Discharge of person apprehended

Q: What is the consequence of this section for the integrity of police custody?
A: The consequence is that it prevents arbitrary or undocumented releases by police officers, ensuring there is always a formal legal record (bond, bail, or Magistrate's order) justifying a discharge. [Source: Section 60, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Discharge of person apprehended

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 61: Power, on escape, to pursue and retake

Q: What can the person who had custody do if an arrested person escapes?
A: If a person in lawful custody escapes or is rescued, the person from whose custody he escaped may immediately pursue and arrest him in any place in India. [Source: Section 61, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power, on escape, to pursue and retake

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 61: Power, on escape, to pursue and retake

Q: What does Section 61 of BNSS 2023 authorize?
A: Section 61 of BNSS 2023 authorizes a custodian to immediately pursue and retake an escaped or rescued prisoner anywhere within India, applying the entry and search provisions of section 44 to the pursuit. [Source: Section 61, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power, on escape, to pursue and retake

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 61: Power, on escape, to pursue and retake

Q: A suspect escapes from custody in Mumbai and flees to Delhi. Can the Mumbai officer pursue and arrest them in Delhi without getting a new warrant?
A: Yes, under sub-section (1), the person from whose custody he escaped may immediately pursue and arrest him "in any place in India." [Source: Section 61, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power, on escape, to pursue and retake

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 61: Power, on escape, to pursue and retake

Q: What powers apply to an officer trying to recapture an escapee who has hidden inside a house?
A: Under sub-section (2), "The provisions of section 44 shall apply to arrests under sub-section (1)," which governs the procedures for entering and searching places to make an arrest. [Source: Section 61, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power, on escape, to pursue and retake

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 61: Power, on escape, to pursue and retake

Q: Does the pursuing officer need a formal arrest warrant to retake an escaped prisoner?
A: No, sub-section (2) explicitly states section 44 provisions apply "although the person making any such arrest is not acting under a warrant and is not a police officer having authority to arrest." [Source: Section 61, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power, on escape, to pursue and retake

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 61: Power, on escape, to pursue and retake

Q: What is the consequence of an individual escaping lawful custody?
A: The consequence is that the custodian immediately gains sweeping jurisdictional authority to pursue and arrest the escapee anywhere in India without needing a warrant. [Source: Section 61, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power, on escape, to pursue and retake

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 62: Arrest to be made strictly according to Sanhita

Q: Can police invent their own procedures for arresting people if it saves time?
A: No, no arrest shall be made except in accordance with the provisions of this Sanhita or any other law for the time being in force providing for arrest. [Source: Section 62, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Arrest to be made strictly according to Sanhita

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 62: Arrest to be made strictly according to Sanhita

Q: What does Section 62 of BNSS 2023 mandate?
A: Section 62 of BNSS 2023 mandates strict compliance with established legal codes, ensuring that no arrest is lawful unless it strictly adheres to the provisions of the Sanhita or other applicable laws. [Source: Section 62, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Arrest to be made strictly according to Sanhita

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 62: Arrest to be made strictly according to Sanhita

Q: A local police department creates a new "rapid arrest" policy that skips the required paperwork to save time. Is this legal?
A: No, the section states "No arrest shall be made except in accordance with the provisions of this Sanhita," making the circumvention of established procedures unlawful. [Source: Section 62, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Arrest to be made strictly according to Sanhita

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 62: Arrest to be made strictly according to Sanhita

Q: What condition must be met for any arrest to be considered legally valid?
A: The arrest must be made "in accordance with the provisions of this Sanhita or any other law for the time being in force providing for arrest." [Source: Section 62, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Arrest to be made strictly according to Sanhita

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 62: Arrest to be made strictly according to Sanhita

Q: Is the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita the absolute only law that can govern an arrest in India?
A: No, arrests can also be made in accordance with "any other law for the time being in force providing for arrest." [Source: Section 62, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Arrest to be made strictly according to Sanhita

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 62: Arrest to be made strictly according to Sanhita

Q: What is the overarching legal consequence of this section for law enforcement?
A: The consequence is that it strips law enforcement of arbitrary or extrajudicial arrest powers, rendering any arrest made outside of statutory frameworks illegal. [Source: Section 62, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Arrest to be made strictly according to Sanhita

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 63: Form of summons

Q: What does an official court summons look like?
A: Every summons issued by a Court under this Sanhita shall be in writing, in duplicate, signed by the presiding officer or other directed officer, and shall bear the seal of the Court. [Source: Section 63, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Form of summons

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 63: Form of summons

Q: What is Section 63 of BNSS 2023 about?
A: Section 63 of BNSS 2023 dictates the formal physical requirements for a valid court summons and outlines the acceptable electronic methods for issuing one. [Source: Section 63, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Form of summons

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 63: Form of summons

Q: A judge sends a WhatsApp message telling a witness to come to court tomorrow. There is no physical document or digital seal. Is this a valid summons?
A: No, under sub-section (1), every summons must be "in writing, in duplicate, signed by the presiding officer" and bear the seal of the Court, or if electronic, must be "in an encrypted or any other form of electronic communication" that bears the image of the Court's seal. [Source: Section 63, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Form of summons

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 63: Form of summons

Q: What condition applies if the court chooses to issue a summons in an electronic communication?
A: Under sub-section (2), the electronic summons must bear the "image of the seal of the Court" or digital signature. [Source: Section 63, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Form of summons

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 63: Form of summons

Q: Must a physical summons always be signed specifically by the presiding officer of the Court?
A: No, under sub-section (1), it can be signed by the presiding officer "or by such other officer as the High Court may, from time to time, by rule direct." [Source: Section 63, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Form of summons

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 63: Form of summons

Q: What is the consequence if a physical summons lacks the official court seal?
A: The consequence is that the document is legally invalid, as sub-section (1) strictly mandates that the summons "shall bear the seal of the Court." [Source: Section 63, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Form of summons

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 64: Summons how served

Q: How is a court summons delivered to the person who needs to receive it?
A: The summons shall, if practicable, be served personally by delivering or tendering one of the duplicates, and the recipient must sign a receipt; electronic service is also legally recognized. [Source: Section 64, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Summons how served

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 64: Summons how served

Q: What does Section 64 of BNSS 2023 detail?
A: Section 64 of BNSS 2023 details the primary methods for serving a summons, preferring personal delivery to the individual and outlining the requirements for electronic service and receipt of delivery. [Source: Section 64, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Summons how served

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 64: Summons how served

Q: An officer delivers a physical summons to a witness. The witness takes it but refuses to sign the back of the other copy. Did the officer complete their duty under this section?
A: The officer must attempt to get the signature; under sub-section (2), every person on whom a summons is so served "shall, if so required by the serving officer, sign a receipt therefor on the back of the other duplicate." [Source: Section 64, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Summons how served

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 64: Summons how served

Q: What is the condition for an electronic summons to be considered legally served?
A: Under sub-section (3), it is considered served when it is "delivered or transmitted to the device of the summoned person and the record of such delivery is available." [Source: Section 64, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Summons how served

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 64: Summons how served

Q: Must a summons always be served by a police officer?
A: No, under sub-section (1), it may be served by a police officer, or subject to rules, by "an officer of the Court issuing it or other public servant." [Source: Section 64, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Summons how served

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 64: Summons how served

Q: What is the documentary consequence of personally serving a physical summons?
A: The consequence is that the serving officer obtains a signed receipt on the back of the duplicate copy, providing legal proof that the individual received the document. [Source: Section 64, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Summons how served

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 65: Service of summons on corporate bodies, firms, and societies

Q: How do you serve a court summons to an entire company rather than just a person?
A: Service of a summons on a corporation may be effected by serving it on the Director, Manager, Secretary or other officer, or by a letter sent by registered post addressed to the chief officer of the corporation in India. [Source: Section 65, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Service of summons on corporate bodies, firms, and societies

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 65: Service of summons on corporate bodies, firms, and societies

Q: What is Section 65 of BNSS 2023 about?
A: Section 65 of BNSS 2023 outlines the specific legal procedures for serving a summons on corporate bodies, societies, and other incorporated associations. [Source: Section 65, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Service of summons on corporate bodies, firms, and societies

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 65: Service of summons on corporate bodies, firms, and societies

Q: A court needs to serve a summons on a registered society. The court sends the summons via registered post to the society's chief officer in India. When is the summons considered officially served?
A: Under the section, the service shall be deemed to have been effected "when the letter would arrive in ordinary course of post." [Source: Section 65, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Service of summons on corporate bodies, firms, and societies

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 65: Service of summons on corporate bodies, firms, and societies

Q: What condition validates the service of a summons sent by letter to a corporation?
A: The letter must be sent by "registered post" and addressed to the "chief officer of the corporation in India." [Source: Section 65, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Service of summons on corporate bodies, firms, and societies

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 65: Service of summons on corporate bodies, firms, and societies

Q: Does the term "corporation" in this section only apply to private businesses?
A: No, the Explanation states that "corporation" means an incorporated company or other body corporate and includes a "society registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860." [Source: Section 65, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Service of summons on corporate bodies, firms, and societies

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 65: Service of summons on corporate bodies, firms, and societies

Q: What is the consequence if an officer hands a summons intended for a corporation to the company's local branch Manager?
A: The consequence is that the service on the corporation is legally effected, as the section allows serving it on the "Manager... of the corporation." [Source: Section 65, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Service of summons on corporate bodies, firms, and societies

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 66: Service when persons summoned cannot be found

Q: What happens if the police try to deliver a summons but the person is never home?
A: If the person summoned cannot be found after due diligence, the summons may be served by leaving one of the duplicates with some adult member of his family residing with him, who shall then sign the receipt. [Source: Section 66, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Service when persons summoned cannot be found

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 66: Service when persons summoned cannot be found

Q: What does Section 66 of BNSS 2023 establish?
A: Section 66 of BNSS 2023 establishes the fallback procedure for serving a summons by leaving it with an adult family member when the actual target cannot be located. [Source: Section 66, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Service when persons summoned cannot be found

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 66: Service when persons summoned cannot be found

Q: An officer goes to serve a summons, but the man is out of town. The officer leaves the summons with the man's 14-year-old daughter who lives there. Is this valid service?
A: No, the section requires leaving the duplicate with "some adult member of his family residing with him." [Source: Section 66, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Service when persons summoned cannot be found

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 66: Service when persons summoned cannot be found

Q: What specific condition regarding the family member must be met for this type of service to be valid?
A: The family member must be an "adult," must be "residing with him," and the Explanation explicitly states a servant is "not a member of the family within the meaning of this section." [Source: Section 66, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Service when persons summoned cannot be found

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 66: Service when persons summoned cannot be found

Q: Can the serving officer immediately use this fallback method on their first attempt without trying to find the actual person?
A: No, the section explicitly requires that the person summoned cannot be found "by the exercise of due diligence." [Source: Section 66, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Service when persons summoned cannot be found

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 66: Service when persons summoned cannot be found

Q: What is the documentary consequence of leaving the summons with the adult family member?
A: The consequence is that the person with whom the summons is left "shall, if so required by the serving officer, sign a receipt therefor on the back of the other duplicate." [Source: Section 66, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Service when persons summoned cannot be found

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 67: Procedure when service cannot be effected as before provided

Q: How is a summons served if the person is hiding and their family won't accept it?
A: If service cannot be effected by personal delivery or leaving it with family, the serving officer shall affix one of the duplicates to some conspicuous part of the house where the person ordinarily resides. [Source: Section 67, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure when service cannot be effected as before provided

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 67: Procedure when service cannot be effected as before provided

Q: What is Section 67 of BNSS 2023 about?
A: Section 67 of BNSS 2023 provides the final fallback method for serving a summons, known as "substituted service," which involves affixing the document to the person's residence when other methods fail. [Source: Section 67, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure when service cannot be effected as before provided

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 67: Procedure when service cannot be effected as before provided

Q: An officer tries to serve a summons at a suspect's house. Nobody answers the door, so the officer immediately tapes the summons to the front door and leaves. Is this valid?
A: Only if service cannot by the exercise of due diligence be effected under section 64, section 65 or section 66. The officer cannot skip to this step without first attempting the earlier methods. [Source: Section 67, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure when service cannot be effected as before provided

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 67: Procedure when service cannot be effected as before provided

Q: What condition triggers the use of the procedure described in Section 67?
A: The condition is that "service cannot by the exercise of due diligence be effected as provided in section 64, section 65 or section 66." [Source: Section 67, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure when service cannot be effected as before provided

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 67: Procedure when service cannot be effected as before provided

Q: Once the officer affixes the summons to the door, is the service automatically deemed completely finished without further court action?
A: No, the Court must review the action; the Court "may either declare that the summons has been duly served or order fresh service in such manner as it considers proper." [Source: Section 67, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure when service cannot be effected as before provided

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 67: Procedure when service cannot be effected as before provided

Q: What is the physical consequence of employing this method of service?
A: The consequence is that the serving officer physically affixes one of the duplicates of the summons "to some conspicuous part of the house or homestead in which the person summoned ordinarily resides." [Source: Section 67, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure when service cannot be effected as before provided

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 68: Service on Government servant

Q: How do you serve a summons to someone who works for the government?
A: Where the person summoned is in the active service of the Government, the Court shall ordinarily send the summons in duplicate to the head of the office in which such person is employed. [Source: Section 68, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Service on Government servant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 68: Service on Government servant

Q: What does Section 68 of BNSS 2023 dictate?
A: Section 68 of BNSS 2023 dictates the specific procedure for serving a summons on an active Government servant by routing it through the head of their office. [Source: Section 68, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Service on Government servant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 68: Service on Government servant

Q: A court sends a summons for a government clerk to the Head of the Department. The Head of the Department gives it to the clerk and signs the duplicate, but forgets to put the office seal on it. Is the signature alone sufficient proof?
A: No, under sub-section (2), such signature "shall be evidence of due service" only when it is signed "with the seal of the office." [Source: Section 68, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Service on Government servant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 68: Service on Government servant

Q: What condition applies to the head of the office when they receive the summons?
A: Under sub-section (1), the head of the office shall "cause the summons to be served in the manner provided by section 64, and shall return it to the Court under his signature with the endorsement required by that section." [Source: Section 68, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Service on Government servant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 68: Service on Government servant

Q: Does the Court send the summons directly to the government employee's desk?
A: No, sub-section (1) requires the Court to ordinarily send the summons in duplicate "to the head of the office in which such person is employed." [Source: Section 68, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Service on Government servant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 68: Service on Government servant

Q: What is the legal consequence of the head of the office signing the returned summons with the office seal?
A: The consequence, under sub-section (2), is that the signature with the seal "shall be evidence of due service." [Source: Section 68, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Service on Government servant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 69: Service of summons outside local limits

Q: How does a court serve a summons on someone who lives in a completely different district?
A: When a Court desires that a summons issued by it shall be served outside its local jurisdiction, it shall ordinarily send such summons in duplicate to a Magistrate within whose local jurisdiction the person summoned resides or is. [Source: Section 69, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Service of summons outside local limits

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 69: Service of summons outside local limits

Q: What is Section 69 of BNSS 2023 about?
A: Section 69 of BNSS 2023 explains the procedure for serving a summons across jurisdictional boundaries by routing it through the local Magistrate where the target currently resides. [Source: Section 69, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Service of summons outside local limits

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 69: Service of summons outside local limits

Q: A court in Delhi wants to summon a witness living in Chennai. The Delhi court mails the summons directly to the witness's house in Chennai via normal post. Is this the ordinary procedure?
A: No, the ordinary procedure is that the Court shall send the summons in duplicate "to a Magistrate within whose local jurisdiction the person summoned resides or is, to be there served." [Source: Section 69, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Service of summons outside local limits

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 69: Service of summons outside local limits

Q: What condition triggers the use of the procedure in this section?
A: This procedure is triggered when a Court desires that a summons "shall be served at any place outside its local jurisdiction." [Source: Section 69, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Service of summons outside local limits

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 69: Service of summons outside local limits

Q: Must the outside Magistrate serve the summons themselves personally?
A: The section implies the Magistrate handles the process locally ("to be there served"), meaning they use their local officers to execute the service according to the rules. [Source: Section 69, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Service of summons outside local limits

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 69: Service of summons outside local limits

Q: What is the consequence for the originating court when it needs an out-of-jurisdiction summons served?
A: The consequence is that the originating court relies on the cooperation of the destination Magistrate, forwarding the documents to them for execution within their respective local limits. [Source: Section 69, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Service of summons outside local limits

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 70: Proof of service in such cases and when serving officer not present

Q: How does a court prove a summons was served if the officer who delivered it is far away and cannot testify in person?
A: When a summons is served outside the court's jurisdiction, an affidavit sworn before a Magistrate stating the summons was served, along with the endorsed duplicate, shall be admissible in evidence to prove service without the officer's physical presence. [Source: Section 70, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Proof of service in such cases and when serving officer not present

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 70: Proof of service in such cases and when serving officer not present

Q: What does Section 70 of BNSS 2023 state?
A: Section 70 of BNSS 2023 states the methods for proving a summons was served when the serving officer cannot be present in court, primarily utilizing sworn affidavits and endorsed duplicates. [Source: Section 70, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Proof of service in such cases and when serving officer not present

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 70: Proof of service in such cases and when serving officer not present

Q: A summons is served locally, but the serving officer falls ill on the day of the hearing and cannot be present in court. Can an affidavit be used to prove service?
A: Yes, under sub-section (1), if "the officer who has served a summons is not present at the hearing of the case," an affidavit made before a Magistrate may be used as proof. [Source: Section 70, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Proof of service in such cases and when serving officer not present

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 70: Proof of service in such cases and when serving officer not present

Q: What two documents must be presented to the court to prove service under this section?
A: An "affidavit, made before a Magistrate, that such summons has been served" and the "duplicate of the summons purporting to be endorsed (in the manner provided by section 64 or section 66)." [Source: Section 70, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Proof of service in such cases and when serving officer not present

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 70: Proof of service in such cases and when serving officer not present

Q: Does the serving officer always have to swear the affidavit in person before a Magistrate?
A: No, under sub-section (2), the affidavit may be attached to the duplicate of the summons and returned to the Court, preventing the need for the officer to travel to the originating court. [Source: Section 70, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Proof of service in such cases and when serving officer not present

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 70: Proof of service in such cases and when serving officer not present

Q: What is the evidentiary consequence of presenting the proper affidavit and endorsed duplicate to the court?
A: The consequence, under sub-section (1), is that these documents "shall be admissible in evidence and the statements made therein shall be deemed to be correct unless and until the contrary is proved." [Source: Section 70, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Proof of service in such cases and when serving officer not present

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 71: Service of summons on witness

Q: Can a court just mail a summons to a witness instead of sending a police officer?
A: Yes, the Court issuing a summons to a witness may, in addition to and simultaneously with the issue of such summons, direct that a copy be served by registered post addressed to the witness at their place of residence or business. [Source: Section 71, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Service of summons on witness

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 71: Service of summons on witness

Q: What is Section 71 of BNSS 2023 about?
A: Section 71 of BNSS 2023 allows courts to serve summons on witnesses via registered post as an additional method, and defines what constitutes proof of delivery or refusal. [Source: Section 71, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Service of summons on witness

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 71: Service of summons on witness

Q: A court sends a summons to an accused person via registered post under this section. Is this valid?
A: No, sub-section (1) explicitly states this procedure is for a Court "issuing a summons to a witness," not an accused person. [Source: Section 71, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Service of summons on witness

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 71: Service of summons on witness

Q: What condition regarding the address is required for sending a summons by registered post?
A: The summons must be "addressed to the witness at the place where he ordinarily resides or carries on business or personally works for gain." [Source: Section 71, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Service of summons on witness

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 71: Service of summons on witness

Q: Does sending a summons by post replace the traditional method of sending an officer?
A: Not necessarily; sub-section (1) says the Court may direct postal service "in addition to and simultaneously with the issue of such summons" through traditional means. [Source: Section 71, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Service of summons on witness

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 71: Service of summons on witness

Q: What is the consequence if the postal employee returns the letter with an endorsement that the witness refused to sign for it?
A: The consequence is that, under sub-section (2), the Court issuing the summons "may declare that the summons has been duly served." [Source: Section 71, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Service of summons on witness

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 72: Form of warrant of arrest and duration

Q: What are the legal requirements for a valid arrest warrant issued by a court?
A: Every warrant of arrest issued by a Court must be in writing, signed by the presiding officer, bear the seal of the Court, and remains in force until cancelled by the issuing Court or until it is executed. [Source: Section 72, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Form of warrant of arrest and duration

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 72: Form of warrant of arrest and duration

Q: What does Section 72 of BNSS 2023 dictate?
A: Section 72 of BNSS 2023 dictates the formal physical requirements for a warrant of arrest and establishes that a warrant remains perpetually valid until either executed or officially cancelled. [Source: Section 72, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Form of warrant of arrest and duration

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 72: Form of warrant of arrest and duration

Q: A judge signs a warrant of arrest but forgets to stamp it with the court's official seal. The police arrest the suspect a month later. Was the warrant technically valid?
A: No, under sub-section (1), every warrant of arrest "shall bear the seal of the Court." Without it, the formal requirements are not met. [Source: Section 72, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Form of warrant of arrest and duration

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 72: Form of warrant of arrest and duration

Q: Under what conditions does an arrest warrant finally stop being active?
A: Under sub-section (2), every such warrant shall remain in force "until it is cancelled by the Court which issued it, or until it is executed." [Source: Section 72, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Form of warrant of arrest and duration

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 72: Form of warrant of arrest and duration

Q: Do arrest warrants automatically expire after a certain number of days?
A: No, sub-section (2) clearly states the warrant remains in force until cancelled or executed, meaning it does not have an automatic time-based expiration. [Source: Section 72, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Form of warrant of arrest and duration

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 72: Form of warrant of arrest and duration

Q: What is the consequence if a person with an active arrest warrant hides for ten years?
A: The consequence is that the warrant remains fully in force for those ten years, allowing the police to arrest the person at any time, unless the issuing Court proactively cancels it. [Source: Section 72, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Form of warrant of arrest and duration

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 73: Power to direct security to be taken

Q: Can a court issue an arrest warrant but allow the police to release the person if they promise to show up in court?
A: Yes, a Court may endorse the warrant directing that if the person executes a bond with sufficient sureties for his attendance before the Court at a specified time, the officer shall take such security and release him from custody. [Source: Section 73, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to direct security to be taken

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 73: Power to direct security to be taken

Q: What is Section 73 of BNSS 2023 about?
A: Section 73 of BNSS 2023 grants courts the power to issue "bailable warrants," allowing the arresting officer to take security (a bond with sureties) and immediately release the arrested person. [Source: Section 73, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to direct security to be taken

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 73: Power to direct security to be taken

Q: A police officer arrests someone on a bailable warrant. The suspect provides the required bond and sureties. Can the officer refuse to release them because they seem dangerous?
A: No, under sub-section (1), if the person executes the bond, the officer to whom the warrant is directed "shall take such security and shall release such person from custody." [Source: Section 73, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to direct security to be taken

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 73: Power to direct security to be taken

Q: What three specific details must the court's endorsement on the warrant state?
A: Under sub-section (2), the endorsement shall state "(a) the number of sureties; (b) the amount in which they and the person for whose arrest the warrant is issued, are to be respectively bound; (c) the time at which he is to attend before the Court." [Source: Section 73, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to direct security to be taken

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 73: Power to direct security to be taken

Q: Is it the police officer's job to decide the amount of the bond for a bailable warrant?
A: No, under sub-section (2), the "amount in which they... are to be respectively bound" is specified by the Court in the endorsement on the warrant. [Source: Section 73, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to direct security to be taken

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 73: Power to direct security to be taken

Q: What is the procedural consequence once the police officer takes the security and releases the person?
A: The consequence, under sub-section (3), is that the officer "shall forward the bond to the Court" so the Court has official record of the guarantee of attendance. [Source: Section 73, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to direct security to be taken

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 74: Warrants to whom directed

Q: Who actually goes out and executes an arrest warrant?
A: A warrant of arrest is ordinarily directed to one or more police officers, but if immediate execution is necessary and no police officer is available, the Court may direct it to any other person or persons. [Source: Section 74, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Warrants to whom directed

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 74: Warrants to whom directed

Q: What does Section 74 of BNSS 2023 state?
A: Section 74 of BNSS 2023 states that warrants are primarily directed to police officers for execution, but permits courts to direct warrants to other individuals in emergencies, and allows multiple officers to execute a shared warrant. [Source: Section 74, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Warrants to whom directed

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 74: Warrants to whom directed

Q: A court issues a warrant and directs it simultaneously to three different police officers. Only one of those officers is present when they spot the suspect. Can that single officer execute the warrant?
A: Yes, under sub-section (2), when a warrant is directed to more officers or persons than one, "it may be executed by all, or by any one or more of them." [Source: Section 74, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Warrants to whom directed

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 74: Warrants to whom directed

Q: What condition must be met for a court to direct a warrant to someone other than a police officer?
A: Under sub-section (1), the condition is that "its immediate execution is necessary and no police officer is immediately available." [Source: Section 74, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Warrants to whom directed

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 74: Warrants to whom directed

Q: Are warrants absolutely always directed only to police officers?
A: No, the section states a warrant is "ordinarily" directed to police officers, allowing exceptions under specific circumstances. [Source: Section 74, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Warrants to whom directed

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 74: Warrants to whom directed

Q: What is the consequence if the court directs a warrant to a specific non-police individual during an emergency?
A: The consequence is that "such person or persons shall execute the same," granting them temporary legal authority to make the arrest. [Source: Section 74, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Warrants to whom directed

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 75: Warrant may be directed to any person

Q: Can a judge order a normal citizen to arrest a dangerous criminal hiding in their neighborhood?
A: Yes, a Chief Judicial Magistrate or a Magistrate of the first class may direct a warrant to any person within his local jurisdiction for the arrest of any escaped convict, proclaimed offender, or a person accused of a non-bailable offence who is evading arrest. [Source: Section 75, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Warrant may be directed to any person

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 75: Warrant may be directed to any person

Q: What is Section 75 of BNSS 2023 about?
A: Section 75 of BNSS 2023 empowers higher Magistrates to direct arrest warrants to any private person within their jurisdiction specifically for capturing serious offenders like escapees or proclaimed offenders. [Source: Section 75, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Warrant may be directed to any person

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 75: Warrant may be directed to any person

Q: A Magistrate of the second class directs a warrant to a local farmer to arrest a proclaimed offender hiding on his farm. Is this a valid order?
A: No, under sub-section (1), only "The Chief Judicial Magistrate or a Magistrate of the first class" has the authority to direct a warrant to any person in this manner. [Source: Section 75, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Warrant may be directed to any person

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 75: Warrant may be directed to any person

Q: What specific types of suspects can be targeted by a warrant directed to a private person under this section?
A: The warrant can be for the arrest of "any escaped convict, proclaimed offender or of any person who is accused of a non-bailable offence and is evading arrest." [Source: Section 75, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Warrant may be directed to any person

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 75: Warrant may be directed to any person

Q: Can the private person refuse to acknowledge the warrant if it is directed to them?
A: No, under sub-section (2), such person "shall acknowledge in writing the receipt of the warrant, and shall execute it" if the suspect is on their property. [Source: Section 75, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Warrant may be directed to any person

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 75: Warrant may be directed to any person

Q: What is the immediate procedural consequence after the private person successfully arrests the suspect?
A: Under sub-section (3), the arrested person "shall be made over with the warrant to the nearest police officer, who shall cause him to be taken before a Magistrate having jurisdiction." [Source: Section 75, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Warrant may be directed to any person

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 76: Warrant directed to police officer

Q: Can a police officer ask another police officer to execute an arrest warrant for them?
A: Yes, a warrant directed to any police officer may also be executed by any other police officer whose name is endorsed upon the warrant by the officer to whom it is directed or endorsed. [Source: Section 76, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Warrant directed to police officer

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 76: Warrant directed to police officer

Q: What does Section 76 of BNSS 2023 dictate?
A: Section 76 of BNSS 2023 dictates the process of delegation for arrest warrants, allowing a police officer to endorse a warrant over to another police officer for execution. [Source: Section 76, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Warrant directed to police officer

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 76: Warrant directed to police officer

Q: An arrest warrant is directed to Inspector Smith. Inspector Smith gives the physical warrant to Constable Jones and verbally tells him to go arrest the suspect. Can Constable Jones legally execute the warrant?
A: No, to be legally valid, Constable Jones's name must be "endorsed upon the warrant by the officer to whom it is directed" (Inspector Smith). Verbal delegation is not sufficient. [Source: Section 76, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Warrant directed to police officer

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 76: Warrant directed to police officer

Q: What condition is required for a secondary police officer to execute a warrant not originally directed to them?
A: The condition is that their name must be "endorsed upon the warrant by the officer to whom it is directed or endorsed." [Source: Section 76, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Warrant directed to police officer

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 76: Warrant directed to police officer

Q: Can a police officer endorse a warrant over to a private citizen?
A: No, the section specifies it may be executed by "any other police officer" whose name is endorsed upon it. [Source: Section 76, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Warrant directed to police officer

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 76: Warrant directed to police officer

Q: What is the practical consequence of this section for police operations?
A: The consequence is flexibility; it allows a busy investigating officer to legally transfer the physical task of making an arrest to a subordinate or available colleague via a simple written endorsement. [Source: Section 76, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Warrant directed to police officer

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 77: Notification of substance of warrant

Q: Does a police officer have to show the arrest warrant to the person they are arresting?
A: The police officer or other person executing a warrant of arrest shall notify the substance thereof to the person to be arrested, and, if so required, shall show him the warrant. [Source: Section 77, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Notification of substance of warrant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 77: Notification of substance of warrant

Q: What is Section 77 of BNSS 2023 about?
A: Section 77 of BNSS 2023 outlines the requirement for the arresting officer to inform the suspect of the contents of the arrest warrant and to physically show the document if the suspect asks to see it. [Source: Section 77, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Notification of substance of warrant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 77: Notification of substance of warrant

Q: An officer arrests a suspect under a warrant. The suspect immediately demands to read the warrant. The officer refuses, saying he'll read it at the station. Is the officer acting legally?
A: No, the section clearly states that the officer "if so required, shall show him the warrant." Refusing to show it upon demand violates this provision. [Source: Section 77, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Notification of substance of warrant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 77: Notification of substance of warrant

Q: What condition triggers the officer's obligation to physically produce the warrant during the arrest?
A: The obligation is triggered "if so required" by the person being arrested. [Source: Section 77, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Notification of substance of warrant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 77: Notification of substance of warrant

Q: Is it enough for the officer to just silently handcuff the person and show them the warrant later?
A: No, the officer "shall notify the substance thereof to the person to be arrested" at the time of execution, meaning they must verbally explain the reason for the arrest. [Source: Section 77, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Notification of substance of warrant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 77: Notification of substance of warrant

Q: What is the informational consequence of this section for an arrested individual?
A: The consequence is that the individual is legally guaranteed to know exactly why they are being deprived of their liberty at the moment of arrest, preventing secret or unexplained detentions. [Source: Section 77, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Notification of substance of warrant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 78: Person arrested to be brought before Court without delay

Q: How long can police keep someone they've arrested with a warrant before showing them to a judge?
A: The arresting officer must bring the person before the Court without unnecessary delay, and such delay shall not exceed twenty-four hours exclusive of travel time. [Source: Section 78, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Person arrested to be brought before Court without delay

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 78: Person arrested to be brought before Court without delay

Q: What does Section 78 of BNSS 2023 establish?
A: Section 78 of BNSS 2023 establishes a strict 24-hour limit (excluding travel time) for an officer to bring an individual arrested under a warrant before the relevant Court. [Source: Section 78, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Person arrested to be brought before Court without delay

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 78: Person arrested to be brought before Court without delay

Q: An officer arrests a suspect on Friday evening. The officer keeps them in the station cell until Monday morning because the courts are closed. Is this lawful?
A: No, the proviso states that "such delay shall not, in any case, exceed twenty-four hours" exclusive of travel time. Weekends do not pause this clock. [Source: Section 78, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Person arrested to be brought before Court without delay

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 78: Person arrested to be brought before Court without delay

Q: What is the absolute maximum time allowed for delay under this section?
A: The delay shall not exceed "twenty-four hours exclusive of the time necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the Magistrate's Court." [Source: Section 78, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Person arrested to be brought before Court without delay

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 78: Person arrested to be brought before Court without delay

Q: Does this 24-hour rule apply if the person has already been released on security by the arresting officer?
A: No, the requirement to bring the person before the court is "subject to the provisions of section 73 as to security." [Source: Section 78, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Person arrested to be brought before Court without delay

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 78: Person arrested to be brought before Court without delay

Q: What is the consequence of holding a person for more than 24 hours (excluding travel) after arresting them under a warrant?
A: The consequence is that the detention becomes unlawful, as it directly violates the explicit statutory maximum limit set by this section. [Source: Section 78, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Person arrested to be brought before Court without delay

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 79: Where warrant may be executed

Q: Can an arrest warrant issued by a local city court be used in another state?
A: Yes, a warrant of arrest may be executed at any place in India. [Source: Section 79, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Where warrant may be executed

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 79: Where warrant may be executed

Q: What is Section 79 of BNSS 2023 about?
A: Section 79 of BNSS 2023 establishes the universal territorial jurisdiction for the execution of arrest warrants within the nation. [Source: Section 79, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Where warrant may be executed

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 79: Where warrant may be executed

Q: A court in Chennai issues an arrest warrant. The suspect flees to a remote village in Punjab. Can police execute the Chennai warrant in Punjab?
A: Yes, the section explicitly states that "A warrant of arrest may be executed at any place in India." [Source: Section 79, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Where warrant may be executed

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 79: Where warrant may be executed

Q: What geographical limit does this section place on the execution of an arrest warrant?
A: The only geographical limit is that it must be executed "at any place in India." [Source: Section 79, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Where warrant may be executed

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 79: Where warrant may be executed

Q: Does an arrest warrant lose its power once it crosses a state border?
A: No, it remains fully valid, as it may be executed "at any place in India." [Source: Section 79, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Where warrant may be executed

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 79: Where warrant may be executed

Q: What is the jurisdictional consequence of this single-sentence section?
A: The consequence is that it eliminates safe havens within the country, allowing the legal reach of any issuing court to span the entirety of India. [Source: Section 79, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Where warrant may be executed

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 80: Warrant forwarded for execution outside jurisdiction

Q: How does a court get police in another district to arrest someone for them?
A: The Court may forward the warrant by post to any Executive Magistrate, District Superintendent, or Commissioner of Police in the destination jurisdiction, who will endorse it and cause it to be executed. [Source: Section 80, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Warrant forwarded for execution outside jurisdiction

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 80: Warrant forwarded for execution outside jurisdiction

Q: What does Section 80 of BNSS 2023 dictate?
A: Section 80 of BNSS 2023 dictates the procedure for a court to remotely send an arrest warrant to authorities in another jurisdiction for execution, rather than sending its own local officers. [Source: Section 80, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Warrant forwarded for execution outside jurisdiction

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 80: Warrant forwarded for execution outside jurisdiction

Q: A court mails an arrest warrant to a Superintendent in another district but sends no other documents. The suspect applies for bail. Did the court follow the full procedure?
A: No, under sub-section (2), the Court "shall forward, along with the warrant, the substance of the information against the person... together with such documents, if any, as may be sufficient to enable the Court... to decide whether bail should or should not be granted." [Source: Section 80, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Warrant forwarded for execution outside jurisdiction

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 80: Warrant forwarded for execution outside jurisdiction

Q: What must the receiving Magistrate or Superintendent do with the forwarded warrant before it is executed?
A: Under sub-section (1), they "shall endorse his name thereon, and if practicable, cause it to be executed." [Source: Section 80, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Warrant forwarded for execution outside jurisdiction

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 80: Warrant forwarded for execution outside jurisdiction

Q: Does a court have to use this postal forwarding method for out-of-jurisdiction arrests?
A: No, sub-section (1) says the Court "may, instead of directing the warrant to a police officer within its jurisdiction, forward it." It is an alternative option. [Source: Section 80, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Warrant forwarded for execution outside jurisdiction

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 80: Warrant forwarded for execution outside jurisdiction

Q: What is the consequence of the originating court failing to send the supporting information documents alongside the warrant?
A: The consequence is that the distant court handling the arrested person will lack the necessary context to make an informed decision on whether to grant bail under section 83. [Source: Section 80, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Warrant forwarded for execution outside jurisdiction

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 81: Warrant directed to police officer for execution outside jurisdiction

Q: What should a police officer do if they travel to another district to execute an arrest warrant?
A: The officer should ordinarily take the warrant to a local Executive Magistrate or a local police station chief for endorsement before executing it. [Source: Section 81, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Warrant directed to police officer for execution outside jurisdiction

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 81: Warrant directed to police officer for execution outside jurisdiction

Q: What is Section 81 of BNSS 2023 about?
A: Section 81 of BNSS 2023 outlines the protocol for a police officer executing a warrant outside their home jurisdiction, requiring them to obtain a local endorsement, but allowing exceptions for emergencies. [Source: Section 81, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Warrant directed to police officer for execution outside jurisdiction

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 81: Warrant directed to police officer for execution outside jurisdiction

Q: An officer tracks a fleeing suspect into the next district. If the officer stops to find a local magistrate for an endorsement, the suspect will board a train and vanish. Can the officer arrest them immediately?
A: Yes, under sub-section (3), if there is reason to believe the delay occasioned by obtaining the endorsement will prevent execution, the officer "may execute the same without such endorsement." [Source: Section 81, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Warrant directed to police officer for execution outside jurisdiction

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 81: Warrant directed to police officer for execution outside jurisdiction

Q: Who are the two types of local officials from whom the traveling officer can obtain the endorsement?
A: Either an "Executive Magistrate" or a "police officer not below the rank of an officer in charge of a police station." [Source: Section 81, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Warrant directed to police officer for execution outside jurisdiction

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 81: Warrant directed to police officer for execution outside jurisdiction

Q: If the visiting officer gets the endorsement, can the local police refuse to help them make the arrest?
A: No, sub-section (2) mandates that "the local police shall, if so required, assist such officer in executing such warrant." [Source: Section 81, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Warrant directed to police officer for execution outside jurisdiction

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 81: Warrant directed to police officer for execution outside jurisdiction

Q: What is the legal consequence of the local Magistrate or station chief endorsing their name on the visiting officer's warrant?
A: The consequence, under sub-section (2), is that the endorsement provides "sufficient authority to the police officer... to execute the same" within that new territory. [Source: Section 81, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Warrant directed to police officer for execution outside jurisdiction

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 82: Procedure on arrest of person against whom warrant issued

Q: If police arrest someone in another district, where do they take the person first?
A: The arrested person must be taken before the local Magistrate or Superintendent/Commissioner of Police in the district of arrest, unless the originating Court is within 30 kilometers or closer than the local authorities. [Source: Section 82, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure on arrest of person against whom warrant issued

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 82: Procedure on arrest of person against whom warrant issued

Q: What does Section 82 of BNSS 2023 state?
A: Section 82 of BNSS 2023 dictates that a person arrested out-of-district must generally be presented to local authorities first, and requires immediate police-to-police notification regarding the arrest and holding location. [Source: Section 82, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure on arrest of person against whom warrant issued

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 82: Procedure on arrest of person against whom warrant issued

Q: Police arrest a suspect 20 kilometers away from the issuing court, which happens to be across the district line. Do they have to find the local Magistrate in the new district first?
A: No, because the Court which issued the warrant "is within thirty kilometres of the place of arrest." They can take the person directly to the issuing Court. [Source: Section 82, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure on arrest of person against whom warrant issued

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 82: Procedure on arrest of person against whom warrant issued

Q: Who must the arresting officer forthwith notify about the arrest and holding location under sub-section (2)?
A: The officer must give information to "the designated police officer in the district" and to "such officer of another district where the arrested person normally resides." [Source: Section 82, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure on arrest of person against whom warrant issued

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 82: Procedure on arrest of person against whom warrant issued

Q: Is the arresting officer always required to take the person before a local Magistrate if the issuing court is far away?
A: No, there is an exception if "security is taken under section 73," meaning if the person posts bail immediately, they do not need to be hauled before the local Magistrate. [Source: Section 82, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure on arrest of person against whom warrant issued

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 82: Procedure on arrest of person against whom warrant issued

Q: What is the protective consequence of the mandatory 30-kilometer rule?
