metadata.section_title: Magistrate may direct search in his presence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 109: Power to impound document, etc., produced

Q: If a witness brings a crucial document to court, can the judge confiscate it to keep it safe?
A: Yes, any Court has the power to impound any document or thing produced before it under this Sanhita if it thinks fit to do so. [Source: Section 109, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to impound document, etc., produced

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 109: Power to impound document, etc., produced

Q: What power does Section 109 of BNSS 2023 give to the courts?
A: Section 109 of BNSS 2023 gives courts the discretionary power to impound any document or object that is produced before them during proceedings. [Source: Section 109, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to impound document, etc., produced

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 109: Power to impound document, etc., produced

Q: A defendant voluntarily presents their passport in court to prove their identity, but the judge believes they are a flight risk and decides to seize the passport. Is the judge allowed to do this under this section?
A: Yes, the section explicitly states that "Any Court may, if it thinks fit, impound any document or thing produced before it." [Source: Section 109, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to impound document, etc., produced

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 109: Power to impound document, etc., produced

Q: What are the conditions required for a court to impound an item?
A: The only conditions are that the "document or thing" must be "produced before it under this Sanhita," and the Court must "think fit" to impound it. [Source: Section 109, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to impound document, etc., produced

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 109: Power to impound document, etc., produced

Q: Is the court mandated to impound every piece of evidence presented?
A: No, it is a discretionary power; the Court may impound items only "if it thinks fit." [Source: Section 109, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to impound document, etc., produced

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 109: Power to impound document, etc., produced

Q: What is the consequence of a court utilizing its power under this section?
A: The consequence is that the physical custody of the document or thing transfers from the person producing it to the Court, preventing its alteration, destruction, or removal. [Source: Section 109, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to impound document, etc., produced

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 110: Reciprocal arrangements regarding processes

Q: How does an Indian court serve a summons on someone living in another country?
A: If the Central Government has arrangements with that contracting State, the Indian Court can send the summons in duplicate, directed to the foreign Court or Judge, through the transmission authority specified by the Central Government. [Source: Section 110, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Reciprocal arrangements regarding processes

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 110: Reciprocal arrangements regarding processes

Q: What does Section 110 of BNSS 2023 regulate?
A: Section 110 of BNSS 2023 regulates the reciprocal service and execution of summonses, arrest warrants, and search warrants between domestic Indian courts and courts in both external Indian territories and foreign contracting States. [Source: Section 110, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Reciprocal arrangements regarding processes

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 110: Reciprocal arrangements regarding processes

Q: An Indian court receives a search warrant issued by a court in a foreign contracting State. The Indian police execute it and seize stolen jewelry. Do they keep the jewelry in India?
A: No, under the proviso to sub-section (2), the "things found in the search shall be forwarded to the Court issuing the summons or search-warrant" through the authority specified by the Central Government. [Source: Section 110, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Reciprocal arrangements regarding processes

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 110: Reciprocal arrangements regarding processes

Q: What four types of legal processes are explicitly covered under sub-section (1) for reciprocal execution?
A: The four processes are "a summons to an accused person," "a warrant for the arrest of an accused person," "a summons to any person requiring him to attend and produce a document or other thing," and "a search-warrant." [Source: Section 110, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Reciprocal arrangements regarding processes

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 110: Reciprocal arrangements regarding processes

Q: If an Indian court sends a summons to another State in India outside its local jurisdiction, how should it be sent?
A: Under sub-section (1)(i), it may "send such summons or warrant in duplicate by post or otherwise, to the presiding officer of that Court to be served or executed." [Source: Section 110, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Reciprocal arrangements regarding processes

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 110: Reciprocal arrangements regarding processes

Q: What is the jurisdictional consequence when an Indian court receives a valid warrant from a contracting State?
A: Under sub-section (2), the consequence is that the Indian court "shall cause the same to be served or executed as if it were a summons or warrant received by it from another Court in the said territories." [Source: Section 110, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Reciprocal arrangements regarding processes

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 111: Definitions

Q: In international legal assistance, what does "proceeds of crime" mean?
A: It means any property derived or obtained, directly or indirectly, by any person as a result of criminal activity, including currency transfers, or the value of such property. [Source: Section 111, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Definitions

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 111: Definitions

Q: What does Section 111 of BNSS 2023 provide?
A: Section 111 of BNSS 2023 provides the definitions for key terms used in Chapter VIII, such as "contracting State," "identifying," "proceeds of crime," "property," and "tracing." [Source: Section 111, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Definitions

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 111: Definitions

Q: Investigators need to figure out who officially owns a piece of land suspected of being bought with illegal funds. Which defined term covers this activity?
A: This activity falls under "tracing," which clause (e) defines as "determining the nature, source, disposition, movement, title or ownership of property." [Source: Section 111, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Definitions

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 111: Definitions

Q: Under clause (d), what types of assets are included in the definition of "property"?
A: Property includes assets of every description, whether "corporeal or incorporeal, movable or immovable, tangible or intangible," and includes deeds, instruments evidencing title, and property obtained through proceeds of crime. [Source: Section 111, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Definitions

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 111: Definitions

Q: What constitutes a "contracting State" under this section?
A: Clause (a) states it means "any country or place outside India in respect of which arrangements have been made by the Central Government with the Government of such country through a treaty or otherwise." [Source: Section 111, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Definitions

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 111: Definitions

Q: What is the consequence of "identifying" property under this chapter?
A: Clause (b) establishes that "identifying" has the evidentiary consequence of "establishment of a proof that the property was derived from, or used in, the commission of an offence." [Source: Section 111, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Definitions

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 112: Letter of request to competent authority for investigation in a country or place outside India

Q: How can Indian police legally gather evidence located in another country?
A: During an investigation, the investigating officer can apply to a Criminal Court, which may issue a letter of request to a competent foreign Court or authority to examine witnesses, record statements, or require the production of documents. [Source: Section 112, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Letter of request to competent authority for investigation in a country or place outside India

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 112: Letter of request to competent authority for investigation in a country or place outside India

Q: What mechanism does Section 112 of BNSS 2023 outline?
A: Section 112 of BNSS 2023 outlines the mechanism for Indian courts to issue a "letter of request" to foreign authorities to collect evidence, record statements, and seize documents abroad during a domestic investigation. [Source: Section 112, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Letter of request to competent authority for investigation in a country or place outside India

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 112: Letter of request to competent authority for investigation in a country or place outside India

Q: A foreign authority complies with an Indian letter of request, records a witness's statement abroad, and sends it back. Can the defense argue this statement wasn't collected legally under Indian law?
A: No, under sub-section (3), every statement, document, or thing received under this process "shall be deemed to be the evidence collected during the course of investigation under this Sanhita." [Source: Section 112, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Letter of request to competent authority for investigation in a country or place outside India

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 112: Letter of request to competent authority for investigation in a country or place outside India

Q: What specific actions can the foreign authority be requested to perform under sub-section (1)?
A: They can be requested to "examine orally any person supposed to be acquainted with the facts," "record his statement," "require such person or any other person to produce any document or thing," and "forward all the evidence" back to the issuing Court. [Source: Section 112, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Letter of request to competent authority for investigation in a country or place outside India

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 112: Letter of request to competent authority for investigation in a country or place outside India

Q: Can a junior police constable directly apply to the court for a letter of request to a foreign country?
A: No, the application must be made by "the investigating officer or any officer superior in rank to the investigating officer." [Source: Section 112, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Letter of request to competent authority for investigation in a country or place outside India

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 112: Letter of request to competent authority for investigation in a country or place outside India

Q: How is the letter of request physically routed to the foreign country?
A: The consequence of sub-section (2) is that the letter "shall be transmitted in such manner as the Central Government may specify in this behalf," preventing courts from sending them directly through unapproved channels. [Source: Section 112, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Letter of request to competent authority for investigation in a country or place outside India

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 113: Letter of request from a country or place outside India to a Court or an authority for investigation in India

Q: What happens when a foreign country asks India to interrogate a witness for a foreign crime?
A: Upon receiving a letter of request, the Central Government may forward it to a designated Magistrate to summon and examine the witness, or send it to a police officer to investigate the offence as if it occurred in India. [Source: Section 113, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Letter of request from a country or place outside India to a Court or an authority for investigation in India

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 113: Letter of request from a country or place outside India to a Court or an authority for investigation in India

Q: What procedure does Section 113 of BNSS 2023 detail?
A: Section 113 of BNSS 2023 details how the Central Government and Indian authorities handle incoming letters of request from foreign countries seeking assistance in examining witnesses or producing evidence within India. [Source: Section 113, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Letter of request from a country or place outside India to a Court or an authority for investigation in India

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 113: Letter of request from a country or place outside India to a Court or an authority for investigation in India

Q: A French court sends a letter of request to India asking police to investigate a suspect residing in Mumbai. Does the Mumbai police officer treat this as a civil inquiry?
A: No, under sub-section (1)(ii), the police officer "shall thereupon investigate into the offence in the same manner, as if the offence had been committed within India." [Source: Section 113, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Letter of request from a country or place outside India to a Court or an authority for investigation in India

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 113: Letter of request from a country or place outside India to a Court or an authority for investigation in India

Q: What are the two distinct procedural routes the Central Government can choose under sub-section (1) when honoring a foreign request?
A: The government may either (i) forward it to a Chief Judicial Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate to record statements and produce documents, or (ii) send it to a police officer to investigate the offence. [Source: Section 113, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Letter of request from a country or place outside India to a Court or an authority for investigation in India

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 113: Letter of request from a country or place outside India to a Court or an authority for investigation in India

Q: Is the Central Government legally obligated to execute every letter of request it receives from a foreign country?
A: No, sub-section (1) grants discretion by stating the Central Government may take action "if it thinks fit." [Source: Section 113, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Letter of request from a country or place outside India to a Court or an authority for investigation in India

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 113: Letter of request from a country or place outside India to a Court or an authority for investigation in India

Q: What must be done with the evidence collected by the Indian Magistrate or police officer?
A: Under sub-section (2), all collected evidence or authenticated copies "shall be forwarded... to the Central Government for transmission to the Court or the authority issuing the letter of request." [Source: Section 113, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Letter of request from a country or place outside India to a Court or an authority for investigation in India

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 114: Assistance in securing transfer of persons

Q: How does an Indian court secure the attendance of a person located in a contracting State?
A: An Indian court, upon satisfaction that the person's attendance is required for an investigation or inquiry, can issue a summons or warrant to a foreign Court or Judge through the authority specified by the Central Government. [Source: Section 114, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assistance in securing transfer of persons

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 114: Assistance in securing transfer of persons

Q: What does Section 114 of BNSS 2023 manage?
A: Section 114 of BNSS 2023 manages the reciprocal transfer of persons between India and contracting States for the execution of warrants, summonses, and investigations. [Source: Section 114, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assistance in securing transfer of persons

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 114: Assistance in securing transfer of persons

Q: A foreign prisoner is temporarily transferred to India to testify in a criminal trial under a specific set of conditions. Once the trial ends, can the Indian court ignore those conditions and keep the prisoner indefinitely?
A: No, under sub-section (5), the Court in India "shall ensure that the conditions subject to which the prisoner is transferred to India are complied with." [Source: Section 114, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assistance in securing transfer of persons

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 114: Assistance in securing transfer of persons

Q: What conditions must be met under sub-section (2) before a Court issues a summons for someone in a contracting State?
A: An application must be made by the investigating officer or a superior officer, and the Court must be "satisfied that such attendance is so required." [Source: Section 114, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assistance in securing transfer of persons

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 114: Assistance in securing transfer of persons

Q: When an Indian prisoner is transferred to a contracting State to testify there, who has the power to impose conditions on the transfer?
A: Under sub-section (4), either "the Court in India or the Central Government may impose such conditions as that Court or Government deems fit." [Source: Section 114, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assistance in securing transfer of persons

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 114: Assistance in securing transfer of persons

Q: What is the procedural consequence when an Indian court receives a valid foreign warrant for an arrest in India?
A: Under sub-section (3), the consequence is that the warrant "shall be executed as if it is the warrant received by it from another Court in India for execution within its local limits." [Source: Section 114, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assistance in securing transfer of persons

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 115: Assistance in relation to orders of attachment or forfeiture of property

Q: How does India handle requests from foreign countries to seize crime-related assets located in India?
A: When the Central Government receives a letter of request from a contracting State, it may forward the letter to an Indian Court for the attachment or forfeiture of the property in accordance with Indian law. [Source: Section 115, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assistance in relation to orders of attachment or forfeiture of property

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 115: Assistance in relation to orders of attachment or forfeiture of property

Q: What is the focus of Section 115 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 115 of BNSS 2023 focuses on international assistance for executing orders of attachment or forfeiture of property believed to be obtained from the commission of an offence. [Source: Section 115, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assistance in relation to orders of attachment or forfeiture of property

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 115: Assistance in relation to orders of attachment or forfeiture of property

Q: An Indian court discovers that a suspect convicted in India has hidden millions in a bank account in a contracting State. Can the Indian court directly order the foreign bank to freeze the account?
A: No, under sub-section (2), the Indian Court "may issue a letter of request to a Court or an authority in the contracting State for execution of such order." [Source: Section 115, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assistance in relation to orders of attachment or forfeiture of property

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 115: Assistance in relation to orders of attachment or forfeiture of property

Q: What must a Court in India establish under sub-section (1) before making an order of attachment or forfeiture?
A: The Court must have "reasonable grounds to believe that any property obtained by any person is derived or obtained, directly or indirectly, by such person from the commission of an offence." [Source: Section 115, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assistance in relation to orders of attachment or forfeiture of property

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 115: Assistance in relation to orders of attachment or forfeiture of property

Q: Is the Central Government required to forward every foreign letter of request for property attachment to an Indian court?
A: No, sub-section (3) states that the Central Government "may forward such letter of request to the Court, as it thinks fit," maintaining discretionary power. [Source: Section 115, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assistance in relation to orders of attachment or forfeiture of property

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 115: Assistance in relation to orders of attachment or forfeiture of property

Q: What is the consequence if the Central Government forwards a foreign request for attachment to an Indian Court?
A: The consequence is that the Indian Court must execute the request "in accordance with the provisions of sections 116 to 122... or, as the case may be, any other law for the time being in force." [Source: Section 115, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assistance in relation to orders of attachment or forfeiture of property

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 116: Identifying unlawfully acquired property

Q: How do courts investigate unlawfully acquired property tied to international crimes?
A: The Court directs a police officer, not below the rank of Sub-Inspector, to take all necessary steps, including inquiries, investigations, or surveys, to trace and identify the property. [Source: Section 116, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Identifying unlawfully acquired property

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 116: Identifying unlawfully acquired property

Q: What does Section 116 of BNSS 2023 establish?
A: Section 116 of BNSS 2023 establishes the procedure and authority for directing police officers to trace, identify, and investigate unlawfully acquired property. [Source: Section 116, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Identifying unlawfully acquired property

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 116: Identifying unlawfully acquired property

Q: A constable is ordered by a court to conduct a survey of bank accounts to identify criminal assets. Is this a valid order under this section?
A: No, sub-section (1) strictly requires the Court to direct a "police officer not below the rank of Sub-Inspector of Police." A constable does not meet this rank requirement. [Source: Section 116, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Identifying unlawfully acquired property

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 116: Identifying unlawfully acquired property

Q: Under sub-section (2), what types of actions are explicitly included in the steps for identifying property?
A: The steps may include "any inquiry, investigation or survey in respect of any person, place, property, assets, documents, books of account in any bank or public financial institutions or any other relevant matters." [Source: Section 116, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Identifying unlawfully acquired property

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 116: Identifying unlawfully acquired property

Q: Who controls how the inquiry, investigation, or survey is carried out by the police officer?
A: Under sub-section (3), the inquiry must be carried out "in accordance with such directions issued by the said Court in this behalf." [Source: Section 116, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Identifying unlawfully acquired property

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 116: Identifying unlawfully acquired property

Q: What is the practical consequence of the Court issuing a directive under sub-section (1)?
A: The consequence is that designated police officers are empowered to deeply investigate personal assets and financial institutions specifically to trace criminal property for potential forfeiture. [Source: Section 116, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Identifying unlawfully acquired property

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 117: Seizure or attachment of property

Q: Can an officer freeze a property if they think the owner is about to sell it during an investigation?
A: Yes, if the officer believes the property is likely to be concealed, transferred, or disposed of, they can make an order seizing it, or if seizure is impractical, make an order of attachment. [Source: Section 117, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Seizure or attachment of property

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 117: Seizure or attachment of property

Q: What is the purpose of Section 117 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 117 of BNSS 2023 empowers investigating officers to urgently seize or attach property to prevent its disposal, subject to swift judicial confirmation. [Source: Section 117, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Seizure or attachment of property

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 117: Seizure or attachment of property

Q: An officer investigating money laundering attaches a suspect's house but forgets to notify the court. Forty days pass. Is the house still legally attached under the officer's order?
A: No, under sub-section (2), the officer's order "shall have no effect unless the said order is confirmed by an order of the said Court, within a period of thirty days of its being made." [Source: Section 117, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Seizure or attachment of property

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 117: Seizure or attachment of property

Q: What must an investigating officer have reason to believe before making an order to seize or attach property under this section?
A: The officer must have reason to believe that the property "is likely to be concealed, transferred or dealt with in any manner which will result in disposal of such property." [Source: Section 117, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Seizure or attachment of property

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 117: Seizure or attachment of property

Q: If an officer orders an attachment on a piece of land, can the owner still sell it if they get permission?
A: Yes, the order of attachment directs that the property shall not be transferred "except with the prior permission of the officer making such order." [Source: Section 117, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Seizure or attachment of property

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 117: Seizure or attachment of property

Q: What is the immediate consequence for the property owner when an order of attachment is made?
A: The consequence is that "a copy of such order shall be served on the person concerned," placing them on formal legal notice not to transfer or deal with the asset. [Source: Section 117, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Seizure or attachment of property

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 118: Management of properties seized or forfeited under this Chapter

Q: Who takes care of properties that have been seized or forfeited to the government?
A: The Court may appoint the District Magistrate or a nominated officer to act as the Administrator to receive, manage, and dispose of such properties. [Source: Section 118, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Management of properties seized or forfeited under this Chapter

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 118: Management of properties seized or forfeited under this Chapter

Q: What does Section 118 of BNSS 2023 address?
A: Section 118 of BNSS 2023 addresses the management of seized or forfeited properties by authorizing the appointment of an Administrator to oversee and dispose of them. [Source: Section 118, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Management of properties seized or forfeited under this Chapter

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 118: Management of properties seized or forfeited under this Chapter

Q: A luxury hotel is seized under this Chapter. The Court appoints a local business owner as the Administrator to run the hotel. Is this lawful?
A: No, under sub-section (1), the Court may only appoint "the District Magistrate of the area where the property is situated, or any other officer that may be nominated by the District Magistrate." [Source: Section 118, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Management of properties seized or forfeited under this Chapter

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 118: Management of properties seized or forfeited under this Chapter

Q: What are the primary duties of the Administrator regarding forfeited property under sub-section (3)?
A: The Administrator must "take such measures, as the Central Government may direct, to dispose of the property which is forfeited to the Central Government." [Source: Section 118, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Management of properties seized or forfeited under this Chapter

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 118: Management of properties seized or forfeited under this Chapter

Q: Does the Administrator have total independent control over how to manage seized property?
A: No, under sub-section (2), the Administrator must receive and manage the property "in such manner and subject to such conditions as may be specified by the Central Government." [Source: Section 118, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Management of properties seized or forfeited under this Chapter

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 118: Management of properties seized or forfeited under this Chapter

Q: What is the consequence of appointing an Administrator under this section?
A: The consequence is that the daily management and eventual disposal of seized complex assets are handled systematically by government officers rather than leaving the property to decay during legal proceedings. [Source: Section 118, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Management of properties seized or forfeited under this Chapter

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 119: Notice of forfeiture of property

Q: What must a court do before declaring a person's property as proceeds of crime to be forfeited?
A: The Court must serve a notice on the affected person, giving them thirty days to indicate the source of their income and show cause why the property should not be forfeited. [Source: Section 119, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Notice of forfeiture of property

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 119: Notice of forfeiture of property

Q: What is the function of Section 119 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 119 of BNSS 2023 provides the procedural safeguard of a show-cause notice, requiring the court to demand proof of legitimate income before forfeiting suspected criminal property. [Source: Section 119, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Notice of forfeiture of property

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 119: Notice of forfeiture of property

Q: The Court believes a suspect's brother is holding the suspect's illegally acquired property in his name. The Court serves a forfeiture notice only on the suspect. Is this sufficient?
A: No, under sub-section (2), if the notice specifies property held on behalf of the affected person by another, "a copy of the notice shall also be served upon such other person." [Source: Section 119, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Notice of forfeiture of property

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 119: Notice of forfeiture of property

Q: What specific information must the affected person indicate in their response to the show-cause notice?
A: They must indicate "the source of income, earnings or assets, out of which or by means of which he has acquired such property, the evidence on which he relies and other relevant information and particulars." [Source: Section 119, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Notice of forfeiture of property

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 119: Notice of forfeiture of property

Q: How long does the affected person have to respond to the notice of forfeiture?
A: The notice calls upon the person to respond "within a period of thirty days specified in the notice." [Source: Section 119, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Notice of forfeiture of property

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 119: Notice of forfeiture of property

Q: What is the consequence if the person cannot adequately explain their source of income?
A: The consequence is that they fail to show cause, leading the Court closer to declaring the properties "to be proceeds of crime and forfeited to the Central Government." [Source: Section 119, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Notice of forfeiture of property

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 120: Forfeiture of property in certain cases

Q: How does the court finalize the confiscation of property determined to be proceeds of crime?
A: After considering explanations, giving a reasonable opportunity to be heard, and examining evidence, the Court records a finding; if the property is criminal proceeds, it stands forfeited to the Central Government free from all encumbrances. [Source: Section 120, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Forfeiture of property in certain cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 120: Forfeiture of property in certain cases

Q: What does Section 120 of BNSS 2023 dictate?
A: Section 120 of BNSS 2023 dictates the final procedure and legal effect of declaring property as proceeds of crime, resulting in its absolute forfeiture to the Central Government. [Source: Section 120, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Forfeiture of property in certain cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 120: Forfeiture of property in certain cases

Q: The Court issues a 30-day notice to a suspect to prove how they bought a yacht. The suspect ignores the notice and never shows up. Can the Court forfeit the yacht without hearing from them?
A: Yes, under the proviso to sub-section (1), if the affected person does not appear or represent their case within thirty days, "the Court may proceed to record a finding under this sub-section ex parte on the basis of evidence available before it." [Source: Section 120, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Forfeiture of property in certain cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 120: Forfeiture of property in certain cases

Q: If the Court is sure a person has criminal proceeds but cannot trace the exact specific assets, what can the Court do under sub-section (2)?
A: It is lawful for the Court to "specify the properties which, to the best of its judgment, are proceeds of crime and record a finding accordingly." [Source: Section 120, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Forfeiture of property in certain cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 120: Forfeiture of property in certain cases

Q: If forfeited property consists of company shares, can the company use its Articles of Association to block the government from taking ownership?
A: No, under sub-section (4), the company shall register the Central Government as the transferee "notwithstanding anything contained in the Companies Act, 2013... or the Articles of Association of the company." [Source: Section 120, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Forfeiture of property in certain cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 120: Forfeiture of property in certain cases

Q: What happens to existing mortgages or liens on property that the court declares as proceeds of crime?
A: Under sub-section (3), the consequence is that "such property shall stand forfeited to the Central Government free from all encumbrances," effectively wiping out those liens. [Source: Section 120, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Forfeiture of property in certain cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 121: Fine in lieu of forfeiture

Q: Can a person pay a penalty to keep their property if only part of it was bought with illegal money?
A: Yes, if the source of only a part of the property is unproved, the Court must offer the person an option to pay a fine equal to the market value of that part in lieu of forfeiting the whole property. [Source: Section 121, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fine in lieu of forfeiture

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 121: Fine in lieu of forfeiture

Q: What mechanism does Section 121 of BNSS 2023 provide?
A: Section 121 of BNSS 2023 provides the mechanism for an affected person to save their partially tainted property from forfeiture by paying a fine equivalent to the unproven portion's market value. [Source: Section 121, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fine in lieu of forfeiture

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 121: Fine in lieu of forfeiture

Q: A suspect proves that 80% of their house was bought with legitimate salary, but cannot prove the source for the remaining 20%. Can the judge outright confiscate the entire house without offering an alternative?
A: No, under sub-section (1), because the source of only a part of the property has not been proved, the Court "shall make an order giving an option to the person affected to pay... a fine equal to the market value of such part." [Source: Section 121, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fine in lieu of forfeiture

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 121: Fine in lieu of forfeiture

Q: What must the Court do before it actually imposes the calculated fine on the affected person?
A: Under sub-section (2), "the person affected shall be given a reasonable opportunity of being heard." [Source: Section 121, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fine in lieu of forfeiture

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 121: Fine in lieu of forfeiture

Q: What is the exact amount of the fine that must be paid to avoid forfeiture?
A: The fine must be "equal to the market value of such part" of the property whose legitimate source could not be proved. [Source: Section 121, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fine in lieu of forfeiture

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 121: Fine in lieu of forfeiture

Q: What happens once the affected person successfully pays the ordered fine within the allowed time?
A: Under sub-section (3), the consequence is that the Court "may, by order, revoke the declaration of forfeiture under section 120 and thereupon such property shall stand released." [Source: Section 121, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fine in lieu of forfeiture

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 122: Certain transfers to be null and void

Q: What happens if a suspect tries to sell or gift their property after receiving a forfeiture notice?
A: Any transfer of property made after an order of attachment or the issuance of a forfeiture notice is ignored during proceedings, and if forfeited, the transfer is deemed null and void. [Source: Section 122, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Certain transfers to be null and void

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 122: Certain transfers to be null and void

Q: What does Section 122 of BNSS 2023 ensure?
A: Section 122 of BNSS 2023 ensures that suspects cannot evade asset forfeiture by rapidly selling or transferring their property after being officially notified or attached by authorities. [Source: Section 122, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Certain transfers to be null and void

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 122: Certain transfers to be null and void

Q: After receiving a show-cause notice for forfeiture, a suspect quickly "sells" his car to his cousin to hide it. Does the court have to respect the cousin's new ownership during the hearings?
A: No, the section dictates that "such transfers shall, for the purposes of the proceedings under this Chapter, be ignored." [Source: Section 122, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Certain transfers to be null and void

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 122: Certain transfers to be null and void

Q: What two specific triggering events make any subsequent transfer of the property null and void upon forfeiture?
A: The triggers are "the making of an order under sub-section (1) of section 117" (attachment/seizure) or "the issue of a notice under section 119" (show-cause for forfeiture). [Source: Section 122, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Certain transfers to be null and void

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 122: Certain transfers to be null and void

Q: Does this section only void written or formal sales of the property?
A: No, it applies if the property is "transferred by any mode whatsoever," covering all forms of conveyance. [Source: Section 122, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Certain transfers to be null and void

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 122: Certain transfers to be null and void

Q: What is the ultimate legal status of the rushed transfer if the Central Government successfully forfeits the property under Section 120?
A: The ultimate consequence is that "the transfer of such property shall be deemed to be null and void." [Source: Section 122, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Certain transfers to be null and void

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 123: Procedure in respect of letter of request

Q: How are official international letters of request formatted and sent?
A: Every letter of request, summons, or warrant sent to or received from a contracting State must be transmitted in the specific form and manner notified by the Central Government. [Source: Section 123, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in respect of letter of request

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 123: Procedure in respect of letter of request

Q: What is the scope of Section 123 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 123 of BNSS 2023 grants the Central Government the authority to specify the standardized procedures, forms, and transmission channels for all international letters of request, summonses, and warrants under Chapter VIII. [Source: Section 123, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in respect of letter of request

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 123: Procedure in respect of letter of request

Q: A local court decides to email a summons directly to a police station in a contracting State because it seems faster. Is this allowed under the rules of Chapter VIII?
A: No, the section requires that the transmission to a contracting State shall be done "in such form and in such manner as the Central Government may, by notification, specify in this behalf." [Source: Section 123, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in respect of letter of request

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 123: Procedure in respect of letter of request

Q: What three types of legal documents are explicitly governed by the transmission rules in this section?
A: The three documents are "Every letter of request, summons or warrant." [Source: Section 123, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in respect of letter of request

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 123: Procedure in respect of letter of request

Q: Does this section only cover documents sent outward from India to other countries?
A: No, it applies both to documents "received by the Central Government from" and those "to be transmitted to a contracting State." [Source: Section 123, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in respect of letter of request

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 123: Procedure in respect of letter of request

Q: What is the administrative consequence of this section for the Central Government?
A: The consequence is that the Central Government acts as the central coordinating authority, responsible for notifying the proper form and manner of international judicial communications. [Source: Section 123, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in respect of letter of request

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 124: Application of this Chapter

Q: Can Chapter IX on security for keeping the peace be applied to a foreign country?
A: Yes, the Central Government may direct its application in relation to a contracting State with which reciprocal arrangements have been made, subject to specified conditions. [Source: Section 124, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Application of this Chapter

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 124: Application of this Chapter

Q: What is the function of Section 124 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 124 of BNSS 2023 provides the Central Government with the authority to apply the provisions of Chapter IX to contracting States through an official notification. [Source: Section 124, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Application of this Chapter

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 124: Application of this Chapter

Q: The government decides to apply this chapter to a neighboring contracting state, but wants to exempt certain types of bonds. Is this allowed?
A: Yes, the application "shall be subject to such conditions, exceptions or qualifications as are specified in the said notification." [Source: Section 124, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Application of this Chapter

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 124: Application of this Chapter

Q: What condition must exist between India and the foreign State for this chapter to apply?
A: It must be a "contracting State with which reciprocal arrangements have been made." [Source: Section 124, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Application of this Chapter

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 124: Application of this Chapter

Q: Who has the exclusive authority to direct the application of this Chapter to a contracting State?
A: The "Central Government" has the authority to do so by notification in the Official Gazette. [Source: Section 124, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Application of this Chapter

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 124: Application of this Chapter

Q: What is the consequence of the Central Government issuing a notification under this section?
A: The consequence is that the legal mechanisms for demanding security for peace and good behaviour are extended internationally to the specified contracting State, modified by any stated exceptions. [Source: Section 124, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Application of this Chapter

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 125: Security for keeping peace on conviction

Q: Can a court force a convicted criminal to sign a bond to behave themselves after sentencing?
A: Yes, if a Court of Session or Magistrate of the first class convicts someone of specific offences and thinks it necessary, they can order the person to execute a bond for keeping the peace for up to three years. [Source: Section 125, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Security for keeping peace on conviction

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 125: Security for keeping peace on conviction

Q: What does Section 125 of BNSS 2023 authorize?
A: Section 125 of BNSS 2023 authorizes specific courts to demand a bond for keeping the peace from individuals convicted of offences like assault, criminal intimidation, or breach of peace, at the time of sentencing. [Source: Section 125, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Security for keeping peace on conviction

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 125: Security for keeping peace on conviction

Q: A person is convicted of assault and ordered to sign a three-year peace bond. Later, a higher court overturns the assault conviction. Does the person still have to follow the peace bond?
A: No, under sub-section (3), if the conviction is set aside on appeal or otherwise, "the bond or bail bond so executed shall become void." [Source: Section 125, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Security for keeping peace on conviction

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 125: Security for keeping peace on conviction

Q: What specific offences listed in sub-section (2) can trigger a peace bond requirement upon conviction?
A: The offences include specific ones under Chapter XI of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, offences involving assault or criminal force or mischief, criminal intimidation, or any other offence intended to cause a breach of the peace. [Source: Section 125, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Security for keeping peace on conviction

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 125: Security for keeping peace on conviction

Q: What is the maximum duration for which a court can order someone to keep the peace under this section?
A: The bond can be for a period "not exceeding three years, as it thinks fit." [Source: Section 125, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Security for keeping peace on conviction

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 125: Security for keeping peace on conviction

Q: What is the procedural consequence if an Appellate Court reviews the case?
A: Under sub-section (4), the consequence is that an order for security "may also be made by an Appellate Court or by a Court when exercising its powers of revision." [Source: Section 125, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Security for keeping peace on conviction

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 126: Security for keeping peace in other cases

Q: What happens if a Magistrate receives information that a person might disturb the public peace, even if they haven't committed a crime yet?
A: The Executive Magistrate can require the person to show cause why they should not be ordered to execute a bond for keeping the peace for a period not exceeding one year. [Source: Section 126, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Security for keeping peace in other cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 126: Security for keeping peace in other cases

Q: What is the purpose of Section 126 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 126 of BNSS 2023 serves as a preventive measure, allowing Executive Magistrates to demand a peace bond from individuals deemed likely to breach the peace or disturb public tranquillity. [Source: Section 126, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Security for keeping peace in other cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 126: Security for keeping peace in other cases

Q: An Executive Magistrate hears a person living in their district is planning to cause a riot in the neighboring district. Can the Magistrate initiate proceedings against this person?
A: Yes, under sub-section (2), proceedings may be taken when "there is within such jurisdiction a person who is likely to commit a breach of the peace or disturb the public tranquillity or to do any wrongful act as aforesaid beyond such jurisdiction." [Source: Section 126, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Security for keeping peace in other cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 126: Security for keeping peace in other cases

Q: What must the Executive Magistrate be of the opinion of before requiring a person to show cause under sub-section (1)?
A: The Magistrate must be of the opinion that "there is sufficient ground for proceeding." [Source: Section 126, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Security for keeping peace in other cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 126: Security for keeping peace in other cases

Q: What is the maximum duration for a peace bond demanded by an Executive Magistrate under this preventive section?
A: The bond is for a period "not exceeding one year, as the Magistrate thinks fit." [Source: Section 126, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Security for keeping peace in other cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 126: Security for keeping peace in other cases

Q: What is the immediate procedural consequence for a person suspected under this section?
A: The consequence is that they are formally summoned to "show cause why he should not be ordered to execute a bond or bail bond," forcing them to justify their conduct before the Magistrate. [Source: Section 126, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Security for keeping peace in other cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 127: Security for good behaviour from persons disseminating certain matters

Q: Can a Magistrate demand a good behaviour bond from someone spreading seditious or defamatory materials?
A: Yes, an Executive Magistrate can require a person to show cause why they shouldn't execute a bond for good behaviour for up to one year if they intentionally disseminate matters punishable under specific laws, like defamation of a Judge or distributing obscene matter. [Source: Section 127, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Security for good behaviour from persons disseminating certain matters

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 127: Security for good behaviour from persons disseminating certain matters

Q: What does Section 127 of BNSS 2023 cover?
A: Section 127 of BNSS 2023 covers the preventive power of Executive Magistrates to demand good behaviour bonds from individuals disseminating inflammatory, defamatory, or obscene materials. [Source: Section 127, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Security for good behaviour from persons disseminating certain matters

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 127: Security for good behaviour from persons disseminating certain matters

Q: A registered newspaper publishes an article highly critical of a local judge. Can the local Executive Magistrate independently start proceedings against the editor under this section?
A: No, under sub-section (2), no proceedings shall be taken against the editor of a registered publication "except by the order or under the authority of the State Government or some officer empowered by the State Government in this behalf." [Source: Section 127, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Security for good behaviour from persons disseminating certain matters

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 127: Security for good behaviour from persons disseminating certain matters

Q: Under sub-section (1), what two broad categories of actions can trigger a demand for a good behaviour bond?
A: The two actions are intentionally disseminating specific punishable or defamatory matters, or making, producing, publishing, or circulating "any obscene matter such as is referred to in section 294 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023." [Source: Section 127, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Security for good behaviour from persons disseminating certain matters

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 127: Security for good behaviour from persons disseminating certain matters

Q: Does the Magistrate need proof of actual harm before demanding a bond from someone distributing obscene matter?
A: No, the Magistrate only needs information that the person is disseminating the material and the "opinion that there is sufficient ground for proceeding." [Source: Section 127, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Security for good behaviour from persons disseminating certain matters

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 127: Security for good behaviour from persons disseminating certain matters

Q: What is the consequence of this section for individuals circulating material that defames a Judge?
A: The consequence is that they can be preemptively forced by an Executive Magistrate to secure their future good behaviour through a bond, rather than just facing a standalone defamation trial. [Source: Section 127, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Security for good behaviour from persons disseminating certain matters

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 128: Security for good behaviour from suspected persons

Q: What action can be taken against someone who is sneaking around and hiding their presence to commit a crime?
A: An Executive Magistrate can require such a person to show cause why they should not execute a bond for good behaviour for a period not exceeding one year. [Source: Section 128, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Security for good behaviour from suspected persons

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 128: Security for good behaviour from suspected persons

Q: What is the scope of Section 128 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 128 of BNSS 2023 empowers an Executive Magistrate to demand a good behaviour bond from suspected persons who are taking precautions to conceal their presence in order to commit a cognizable offence. [Source: Section 128, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Security for good behaviour from suspected persons

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 128: Security for good behaviour from suspected persons

Q: A person is found hiding in an alley. The Magistrate believes they are just a homeless person seeking shelter, with no intent to commit a crime. Can the Magistrate still demand a bond under this section?
A: No, the section requires that there is reason to believe the person is concealing their presence "with a view to committing a cognizable offence." [Source: Section 128, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Security for good behaviour from suspected persons

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 128: Security for good behaviour from suspected persons

Q: What two conditions must be met for a Magistrate to proceed against a suspected person under this section?
A: The Magistrate must receive information that the person is "taking precautions to conceal his presence" and that there is reason to believe they are doing so "with a view to committing a cognizable offence." [Source: Section 128, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Security for good behaviour from suspected persons

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 128: Security for good behaviour from suspected persons

Q: Who has the authority to require a suspected person to show cause under this section?
A: An "Executive Magistrate" has the authority to initiate these proceedings within their local jurisdiction. [Source: Section 128, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Security for good behaviour from suspected persons

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 128: Security for good behaviour from suspected persons

Q: What is the procedural consequence if the Magistrate believes the information about the lurking suspect is credible?
A: The consequence is that the Magistrate initiates a formal inquiry, forcing the suspect to publicly justify their presence or execute a bond ensuring their good behaviour. [Source: Section 128, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Security for good behaviour from suspected persons

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 129: Security for good behaviour from habitual offenders

Q: How does the law deal with repeat offenders like habitual thieves or forgers to prevent future crimes?
A: An Executive Magistrate can demand that a habitual offender show cause why they should not execute a bail bond for good behaviour for a period of up to three years. [Source: Section 129, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Security for good behaviour from habitual offenders

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 129: Security for good behaviour from habitual offenders

Q: What does Section 129 of BNSS 2023 target?
A: Section 129 of BNSS 2023 targets habitual offenders—including thieves, receivers of stolen property, and those who chronically commit specific offences—allowing Magistrates to bind them to good behaviour for up to three years. [Source: Section 129, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Security for good behaviour from habitual offenders

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 129: Security for good behaviour from habitual offenders

Q: A person has never been convicted of a crime but is known in the community to be "so desperate and dangerous as to render his being at large without security hazardous to the community." Can they be bound over under this section?
A: Yes, clause (g) explicitly includes any person who "is so desperate and dangerous as to render his being at large without security hazardous to the community." [Source: Section 129, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Security for good behaviour from habitual offenders

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 129: Security for good behaviour from habitual offenders

Q: According to clause (f), habitual commission of offences under which specific Acts can lead to security proceedings?
A: The Acts include the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, the Foreigners Act, the Employees' Provident Fund Act, the Essential Commodities Act, the Protection of Civil Rights Act, the Customs Act, and the Food Safety and Standards Act. [Source: Section 129, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Security for good behaviour from habitual offenders

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 129: Security for good behaviour from habitual offenders

Q: Is the duration of the bond for a habitual offender the same as for a suspected person under Section 128?
A: No, while Section 128 limits the bond to one year, Section 129 allows a bond for a period "not exceeding three years." [Source: Section 129, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Security for good behaviour from habitual offenders

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 129: Security for good behaviour from habitual offenders

Q: What is the consequence of being legally classified as a habitual protector of thieves under clause (c)?
A: The consequence is that the person can be brought before a Magistrate and forced to provide security for their good behaviour, curbing their ability to continuously aid criminal networks. [Source: Section 129, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Security for good behaviour from habitual offenders

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 130: Order to be made

Q: What must a Magistrate do formally before requiring a person to show cause why they should not provide security?
A: The Magistrate must make an order in writing that sets forth the substance of the information received, the amount of the bond, the term it will be in force, and the number of sureties required. [Source: Section 130, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order to be made

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 130: Order to be made

Q: What is the purpose of Section 130 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 130 of BNSS 2023 outlines the mandatory components of the written order a Magistrate must issue when initiating proceedings to demand a peace or good behaviour bond under the preceding sections. [Source: Section 130, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order to be made

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 130: Order to be made

Q: A Magistrate verbally tells a habitual offender to show up in court next week to sign a 10,000 rupee peace bond. Is this verbal instruction sufficient?
A: No, the Magistrate "shall make an order in writing" setting forth the specific details; a verbal demand is not sufficient. [Source: Section 130, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order to be made

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 130: Order to be made

Q: What four specific pieces of information must be included in the written order according to this section?
A: The order must include "the substance of the information received, the amount of the bond to be executed, the term for which it is to be in force and the number of sureties." [Source: Section 130, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order to be made

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 130: Order to be made

Q: Does the section apply to all bond orders made by any court?
A: No, it specifically applies to a "Magistrate acting under section 126, section 127, section 128 or section 129." [Source: Section 130, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order to be made

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 130: Order to be made

Q: What is the legal consequence of the Magistrate issuing this written order?
A: The consequence is that the formal parameters of the inquiry are locked in, ensuring the accused knows exactly what allegations they must answer and the potential financial and temporal scope of the demanded bond. [Source: Section 130, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order to be made

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 131: Procedure in respect of person present in Court

Q: If the person against whom a bond order is made is already sitting in the courtroom, how is the order communicated?
A: The order shall be read over to the person, or if they desire, the substance of the order shall be explained to them. [Source: Section 131, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in respect of person present in Court

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 131: Procedure in respect of person present in Court

Q: What does Section 131 of BNSS 2023 prescribe?
A: Section 131 of BNSS 2023 prescribes the immediate procedural step of reading or explaining the show-cause order to the targeted individual if they are physically present in the Court when it is made. [Source: Section 131, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in respect of person present in Court

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 131: Procedure in respect of person present in Court

Q: A Magistrate makes a bond order against a person in the gallery, but the person does not speak the language of the court. What must be done?
A: Because the person "so desires" to understand, "the substance thereof shall be explained to him" rather than just read out in a language they don't grasp. [Source: Section 131, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in respect of person present in Court

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 131: Procedure in respect of person present in Court

Q: Under what condition is the substance of the order explained rather than just strictly read over?
A: The substance shall be explained to him "if he so desires." [Source: Section 131, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in respect of person present in Court

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 131: Procedure in respect of person present in Court

Q: Does the Magistrate need to issue a summons to the person if this procedure is followed?
A: No, this specific procedure applies only "If the person in respect of whom such order is made is present in Court," making a summons unnecessary. [Source: Section 131, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in respect of person present in Court

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 131: Procedure in respect of person present in Court

Q: What is the procedural consequence of reading the order to the person present in Court?
A: The consequence is that the person is immediately put on formal notice of the proceedings against them, bypassing the need for physical service of a summons. [Source: Section 131, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in respect of person present in Court

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 132: Summons or warrant in case of person not so present

Q: How does a Magistrate get a person to court for a bond hearing if they aren't already there?
A: The Magistrate issues a summons requiring them to appear, or if they are already in custody, a warrant directing the custodial officer to bring them before the Court. [Source: Section 132, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Summons or warrant in case of person not so present

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 132: Summons or warrant in case of person not so present

Q: What is the function of Section 132 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 132 of BNSS 2023 provides the mechanisms—summons, warrant to a custodian, or direct arrest warrant—to secure the attendance of a person against whom a show-cause order for a bond has been made. [Source: Section 132, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Summons or warrant in case of person not so present

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 132: Summons or warrant in case of person not so present

Q: A Magistrate issues a show-cause order for a peace bond, but gets a police report that the person is violently destroying property right now. Can the Magistrate skip the summons and send an arrest warrant?
A: Yes, under the proviso, if there is reason to fear a breach of the peace that cannot be prevented otherwise, "the Magistrate may at any time issue a warrant for his arrest." [Source: Section 132, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Summons or warrant in case of person not so present

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 132: Summons or warrant in case of person not so present

Q: If the targeted person is currently locked up in jail on another charge, how does the Magistrate compel their attendance?
A: The Magistrate issues "a warrant directing the officer in whose custody he is to bring him before the Court." [Source: Section 132, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Summons or warrant in case of person not so present

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 132: Summons or warrant in case of person not so present

Q: What must the Magistrate do before issuing an immediate arrest warrant under the proviso?
A: The Magistrate must rely upon a police report or other information and "the substance of which report or information shall be recorded by the Magistrate." [Source: Section 132, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Summons or warrant in case of person not so present

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 132: Summons or warrant in case of person not so present

Q: What is the consequence of applying the proviso to this section?
A: The consequence is that the Magistrate can escalate from a mere summons to a forcible arrest to pre-emptively neutralize an imminent threat to public peace. [Source: Section 132, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Summons or warrant in case of person not so present

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 133: Copy of order to accompany summons or warrant

Q: When a person receives a summons to appear for a bond hearing, do they get to see the actual allegations against them beforehand?
A: Yes, every summons or warrant must be accompanied by a copy of the Magistrate's order, which is delivered to the person being served or arrested. [Source: Section 133, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Copy of order to accompany summons or warrant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 133: Copy of order to accompany summons or warrant

Q: What does Section 133 of BNSS 2023 mandate?
A: Section 133 of BNSS 2023 mandates that a copy of the foundational show-cause order must always accompany the summons or warrant and be physically delivered to the targeted individual. [Source: Section 133, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Copy of order to accompany summons or warrant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 133: Copy of order to accompany summons or warrant

Q: An officer arrests a man under a warrant issued for a bond hearing. The officer forgets to bring the copy of the Magistrate's order and just throws the man in the van. Is this procedurally sound?
A: No, the section requires that a copy of the order "shall be delivered by the officer serving or executing such summons or warrant to the person served with, or arrested under, the same." [Source: Section 133, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Copy of order to accompany summons or warrant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 133: Copy of order to accompany summons or warrant

Q: What specific documents are linked together by this section?
A: It links "Every summons or warrant issued under section 132" with "a copy of the order made under section 130." [Source: Section 133, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Copy of order to accompany summons or warrant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 133: Copy of order to accompany summons or warrant

Q: Who is responsible for ensuring the person actually receives the copy of the order?
A: The delivery is the responsibility of "the officer serving or executing such summons or warrant." [Source: Section 133, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Copy of order to accompany summons or warrant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 133: Copy of order to accompany summons or warrant

Q: What is the practical consequence of this delivery requirement for the accused?
A: The consequence is that the accused is fully informed of the substance of the information against them and the bond requirements before they even step foot in the courtroom, allowing them to prepare their defense. [Source: Section 133, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Copy of order to accompany summons or warrant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 134: Power to dispense with personal attendance

Q: Can a person send a lawyer to a peace bond hearing instead of showing up in person?
A: Yes, the Magistrate may, if there is sufficient cause, dispense with the personal attendance of the person called upon to show cause and permit them to appear by an advocate. [Source: Section 134, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to dispense with personal attendance

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 134: Power to dispense with personal attendance

Q: What does Section 134 of BNSS 2023 allow?
A: Section 134 of BNSS 2023 allows a Magistrate to dispense with the personal attendance of an individual required to show cause for a peace or good behaviour bond, permitting them to appear via an advocate instead. [Source: Section 134, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to dispense with personal attendance

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 134: Power to dispense with personal attendance

Q: A person is summoned for a good behaviour bond hearing but is severely ill in the hospital. Can they send their advocate instead?
A: Yes, because the Magistrate "may, if he sees sufficient cause, dispense with the personal attendance" and permit appearance by an advocate. Severe illness would be sufficient cause. [Source: Section 134, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to dispense with personal attendance

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 134: Power to dispense with personal attendance

Q: What condition must the Magistrate find before excusing someone's personal attendance?
A: The Magistrate must find that "he sees sufficient cause" to dispense with their attendance. [Source: Section 134, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to dispense with personal attendance

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 134: Power to dispense with personal attendance

Q: Is the right to skip a bond hearing and send a lawyer automatic for everyone?
A: No, it is not automatic; the Magistrate "may" grant it only if they see "sufficient cause." [Source: Section 134, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to dispense with personal attendance

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 134: Power to dispense with personal attendance

Q: What is the practical consequence of a Magistrate invoking this section?
A: The consequence is that the legal inquiry into whether the person must execute a bond can proceed without dragging them physically into court, easing the burden on individuals with valid reasons to be absent. [Source: Section 134, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to dispense with personal attendance

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 135: Inquiry as to truth of information

Q: What kind of trial process does a Magistrate follow to figure out if a peace bond is actually needed?
A: The Magistrate proceeds to inquire into the truth of the information using a process that is as near as practicable to the manner prescribed for conducting a trial and recording evidence in summons-cases. [Source: Section 135, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Inquiry as to truth of information

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 135: Inquiry as to truth of information

Q: What does Section 135 of BNSS 2023 govern?
