A: Section 135 of BNSS 2023 governs the formal inquiry process to ascertain the truth of the information against a person, including rules on interim bonds, evidence of repute, joint inquiries, and strict time limits. [Source: Section 135, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Inquiry as to truth of information

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 135: Inquiry as to truth of information

Q: A Magistrate starts an inquiry against a suspected riot leader. Before the inquiry finishes, the Magistrate fears the person will start a riot tonight. Can the Magistrate demand a bond immediately?
A: Yes, under sub-section (3), if immediate measures are necessary to prevent a breach of peace, the Magistrate may, "for reasons to be recorded in writing, direct the person... to execute a bond or bail bond... until the conclusion of the inquiry." [Source: Section 135, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Inquiry as to truth of information

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 135: Inquiry as to truth of information

Q: How long does a Magistrate have to complete an inquiry under this section?
A: Under sub-section (6), the inquiry "shall be completed within a period of six months from the date of its commencement," unless extended for special recorded reasons. [Source: Section 135, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Inquiry as to truth of information

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 135: Inquiry as to truth of information

Q: Can a Magistrate demand an interim bond for maintaining good behaviour from someone simply suspected of disturbing the peace under Section 126?
A: No, the proviso to sub-section (3) states that no person "against whom proceedings are not being taken under section 127, section 128, or section 129 shall be directed to execute a bond or bail bond for maintaining good behaviour." [Source: Section 135, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Inquiry as to truth of information

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 135: Inquiry as to truth of information

Q: What happens if the six-month inquiry period expires and the Magistrate has not recorded any special reasons for extending it?
A: Under sub-section (6), the consequence is that "the proceedings under this Chapter shall, on the expiry of the said period, stand terminated." [Source: Section 135, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Inquiry as to truth of information

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 136: Order to give security

Q: What happens if the court inquiry proves that a person actually does pose a threat to public peace?
A: If the inquiry proves that a bond is necessary, the Magistrate shall make an order requiring the person to execute a bond or bail bond for keeping the peace or maintaining good behaviour. [Source: Section 136, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order to give security

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 136: Order to give security

Q: What is the function of Section 136 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 136 of BNSS 2023 dictates the final step where a Magistrate formally orders a person to give security, provided that the terms do not exceed what was initially stated in the show-cause order. [Source: Section 136, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order to give security

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 136: Order to give security

Q: A Magistrate initially issues a show-cause order for a bond of 50,000 rupees. During the inquiry, the Magistrate realizes the person is very wealthy and decides to order a final bond of 200,000 rupees instead. Is this lawful?
A: No, under proviso (a), "no person shall be ordered to give security of a nature different from, or of an amount larger than, or for a period longer than, that specified in the order made under section 130." [Source: Section 136, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order to give security

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 136: Order to give security

Q: What standard must the Magistrate use when fixing the exact amount of the bond to be executed?
A: Under proviso (b), the amount "shall be fixed with due regard to the circumstances of the case and shall not be excessive." [Source: Section 136, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order to give security

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 136: Order to give security

Q: If the person required to execute a bond is a child, do they sign the bond themselves?
A: No, under proviso (c), "when the person in respect of whom the inquiry is made is a child, the bond shall be executed only by his sureties." [Source: Section 136, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order to give security

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 136: Order to give security

Q: What is the legal consequence of the inquiry proving the necessity of the security?
A: The consequence is that the Magistrate transitions from merely investigating the person to imposing a legally binding obligation on them to maintain the peace or face imprisonment in default. [Source: Section 136, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order to give security

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 137: Discharge of person informed against

Q: What happens if the Magistrate investigates the allegations but finds no proof that a peace bond is needed?
A: If it is not proved that a bond is necessary, the Magistrate must make an entry on the record and discharge the person, or release them if they were held in custody just for the inquiry. [Source: Section 137, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Discharge of person informed against

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 137: Discharge of person informed against

Q: What does Section 137 of BNSS 2023 mandate?
A: Section 137 of BNSS 2023 mandates the immediate release and formal discharge of an individual when an inquiry fails to prove that requiring them to give security is necessary. [Source: Section 137, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Discharge of person informed against

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 137: Discharge of person informed against

Q: An inquiry concludes that a suspect is not a threat. The suspect is currently in jail serving a sentence for an unrelated theft. Must the Magistrate order their release from jail completely?
A: No, the section says the Magistrate shall release him "if such person is in custody only for the purposes of the inquiry." They will remain in custody for their other sentence. [Source: Section 137, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Discharge of person informed against

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 137: Discharge of person informed against

Q: What specific action must the Magistrate take on the official record before discharging the person?
A: The Magistrate "shall make an entry on the record to that effect," confirming that the necessity of a bond was not proved. [Source: Section 137, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Discharge of person informed against

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 137: Discharge of person informed against

Q: Is there any scenario under this section where a person is kept under a bond even if the inquiry fails to prove it is necessary?
A: No, if it is not proved, the Magistrate "shall discharge him" or release him, with no exceptions for maintaining a bond. [Source: Section 137, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Discharge of person informed against

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 137: Discharge of person informed against

Q: What is the consequence for a person who successfully defends themselves during the inquiry?
A: The consequence is full exoneration from the bond requirement, resulting in either a formal discharge or physical release from preventative custody. [Source: Section 137, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Discharge of person informed against

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 138: Commencement of period for which security is required

Q: When exactly does the clock start ticking on the time period for a peace bond?
A: Usually, it starts on the date the order is made, unless the Magistrate fixes a later date, but if the person is currently serving a prison sentence, it starts when that sentence expires. [Source: Section 138, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Commencement of period for which security is required

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 138: Commencement of period for which security is required

Q: What does Section 138 of BNSS 2023 dictate?
A: Section 138 of BNSS 2023 dictates the commencement date for security periods, ensuring that bonds run consecutively after prison sentences rather than concurrently. [Source: Section 138, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Commencement of period for which security is required

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 138: Commencement of period for which security is required

Q: A convicted prisoner has exactly one year left on their prison sentence. A Magistrate orders them to execute a two-year bond for good behaviour. When does the two-year bond period end?
A: Because the bond period commences "on the expiration of such sentence" under sub-section (1), the two-year period starts after they are released, meaning it ends three years from the date of the Magistrate's order. [Source: Section 138, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Commencement of period for which security is required

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 138: Commencement of period for which security is required

Q: Who has the authority to delay the start date of a bond in cases where the person is not in prison?
A: Under sub-section (2), "the Magistrate, for sufficient reason, fixes a later date" for the period to commence. [Source: Section 138, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Commencement of period for which security is required

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 138: Commencement of period for which security is required

Q: Does a peace bond period always start immediately on the day the Magistrate issues the order?
A: No, it is delayed if the person is "sentenced to, or undergoing a sentence of, imprisonment," or if the Magistrate explicitly "fixes a later date." [Source: Section 138, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Commencement of period for which security is required

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 138: Commencement of period for which security is required

Q: What is the consequence of applying sub-section (1) to a currently imprisoned individual?
A: The consequence is that the state maximizes the post-release monitoring period, preventing the bond's duration from being wasted while the person is already safely locked up. [Source: Section 138, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Commencement of period for which security is required

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 139: Contents of bond

Q: What specific actions actually violate a bond for good behaviour?
A: The commission, attempt to commit, or abetment of any offence punishable with imprisonment, wherever it is committed, constitutes a breach of a bond for good behaviour. [Source: Section 139, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Contents of bond

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 139: Contents of bond

Q: What does Section 139 of BNSS 2023 define?
A: Section 139 of BNSS 2023 defines the contents of the bonds and explicitly outlines what constitutes a breach of a bond for good behaviour. [Source: Section 139, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Contents of bond

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 139: Contents of bond

Q: A man signs a good behaviour bond in Delhi. He then travels to Goa and attempts to commit an offence punishable by imprisonment there. Has he breached his Delhi bond?
A: Yes, because the commission or attempt of an offence punishable with imprisonment "wherever it may be committed, is a breach of the bond." [Source: Section 139, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Contents of bond

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 139: Contents of bond

Q: What are the three forms of involvement in an offence that will trigger a breach of a good behaviour bond?
A: The three forms are the "commission or attempt to commit, or the abetment of" an offence. [Source: Section 139, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Contents of bond

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 139: Contents of bond

Q: Does committing a minor offence that only carries a fine constitute a breach of a good behaviour bond under this section?
A: No, the section specifies that it is a breach if the offence is "punishable with imprisonment." [Source: Section 139, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Contents of bond

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 139: Contents of bond

Q: What is the consequence of executing a bond under this section for the targeted individual?
A: The consequence is that they are legally bound to keep the peace or behave well, and any subsequent imprisonable offence they commit anywhere immediately violates this formal promise, triggering further penalties. [Source: Section 139, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Contents of bond

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 140: Power to reject sureties

Q: Can a Magistrate reject a person who offers to be a guarantor for someone's peace bond?
A: Yes, a Magistrate can refuse to accept or reject any previously accepted surety if they determine, after an inquiry, that the surety is an unfit person for the purposes of the bail bond. [Source: Section 140, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to reject sureties

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 140: Power to reject sureties

Q: What is the purpose of Section 140 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 140 of BNSS 2023 establishes the power of Magistrates to scrutinize and reject unfit sureties, detailing the inquiry, notice, and reporting procedures required before making such a rejection. [Source: Section 140, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to reject sureties

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 140: Power to reject sureties

Q: A Magistrate arbitrarily refuses to accept a surety without giving any reason or holding an inquiry, just because they don't like the person. Is this valid?
A: No, under the proviso to sub-section (1), before refusing, the Magistrate "shall either himself hold an inquiry on oath into the fitness of the surety, or cause such inquiry to be held." [Source: Section 140, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to reject sureties

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 140: Power to reject sureties

Q: What must a Magistrate do before holding an inquiry into the fitness of a surety?
A: Under sub-section (2), the Magistrate must "give reasonable notice to the surety and to the person by whom the surety was offered." [Source: Section 140, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to reject sureties

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 140: Power to reject sureties

Q: If a Magistrate decides to reject a surety who was already previously accepted, what extra step must they take?
A: Under the proviso to sub-section (3), they "shall issue his summons or warrant, as he thinks fit, and cause the person for whom the surety is bound to appear or to be brought before him." [Source: Section 140, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to reject sureties

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 140: Power to reject sureties

Q: What is the consequence of a Magistrate officially recording that a surety is an unfit person under sub-section (3)?
A: The consequence is that the Magistrate "shall make an order refusing to accept or rejecting... such surety," forcing the bound person to find a new, acceptable guarantor or face default. [Source: Section 140, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to reject sureties

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 141: Imprisonment in default of security

Q: What happens to a person who is ordered to provide security for good behaviour but fails to do so?
A: If the person does not give the security by the start date, they shall be committed to prison, or if already in prison, detained there, until the period expires or they provide the security. [Source: Section 141, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Imprisonment in default of security

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 141: Imprisonment in default of security

Q: What does Section 141 of BNSS 2023 dictate?
A: Section 141 of BNSS 2023 dictates the penalties for defaulting on a security order, including automatic imprisonment, the referral process for periods exceeding one year, and the nature of the imprisonment. [Source: Section 141, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Imprisonment in default of security

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 141: Imprisonment in default of security

Q: A Magistrate orders a man to give security for three years. The man fails to provide the bond. Can the Magistrate immediately sentence him to three years in prison?
A: No, under sub-section (2), for periods exceeding one year, the Magistrate must issue a warrant detaining him pending the orders of the Sessions Judge, and the proceedings "shall be laid... before such Court." [Source: Section 141, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Imprisonment in default of security

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 141: Imprisonment in default of security

Q: Under sub-section (7), what is the specific nature of the imprisonment if a person fails to give security for keeping the peace?
A: The section explicitly states that "Imprisonment for failure to give security for keeping the peace shall be simple." [Source: Section 141, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Imprisonment in default of security

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 141: Imprisonment in default of security

Q: If proceedings are laid before a Sessions Court under sub-section (2), is there an absolute maximum time the person can be imprisoned for failing to give security?
A: Yes, the proviso to sub-section (3) states that "the period (if any) for which any person is imprisoned for failure to give security shall not exceed three years." [Source: Section 141, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Imprisonment in default of security

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 141: Imprisonment in default of security

Q: What is the consequence under sub-section (1)(b) if a person actually signs a bond but later breaches it?
A: The consequence is that the Magistrate may "order that the person be arrested and detained in prison until the expiry of the period of the bond," separate from any other punishment they face for the breach. [Source: Section 141, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Imprisonment in default of security

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 142: Power to release persons imprisoned for failing to give security

Q: Can a prisoner be released early if they were jailed just because they couldn't afford to pay a peace bond?
A: Yes, the District Magistrate or Chief Judicial Magistrate can order their discharge if they believe the person can be released without hazard to the community or any other person. [Source: Section 142, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to release persons imprisoned for failing to give security

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 142: Power to release persons imprisoned for failing to give security

Q: What powers are outlined in Section 142 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 142 of BNSS 2023 outlines the powers of higher Magistrates and Courts to release individuals imprisoned for failing to give security, reduce bond amounts, and enforce or cancel conditional discharges. [Source: Section 142, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to release persons imprisoned for failing to give security

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 142: Power to release persons imprisoned for failing to give security

Q: A person imprisoned for not giving a peace bond is granted a conditional early release. They immediately break the conditions. Can they be arrested without a new court warrant?
A: Yes, under sub-section (6), when a conditional order is cancelled for non-fulfillment, "such person may be arrested by any police officer without warrant." [Source: Section 142, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to release persons imprisoned for failing to give security

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 142: Power to release persons imprisoned for failing to give security

Q: According to sub-section (2), what three specific reductions can a High Court or Court of Session make regarding a security order?
A: They may make an order "reducing the amount of the security or the number of sureties or the time for which security has been required." [Source: Section 142, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to release persons imprisoned for failing to give security

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 142: Power to release persons imprisoned for failing to give security

Q: Are conditions imposed on a discharged person meant to last forever?
A: No, the proviso to sub-section (3) states that "any condition imposed shall cease to be operative when the period for which such person was ordered to give security has expired." [Source: Section 142, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to release persons imprisoned for failing to give security

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 142: Power to release persons imprisoned for failing to give security

Q: What happens to a person who is arrested and remanded after violating their conditional early discharge under sub-section (7)?
A: The consequence is that they must "undergo such unexpired portion" of their original term in prison, unless they finally provide the required security for that remaining time. [Source: Section 142, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to release persons imprisoned for failing to give security

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 143: Security for unexpired period of bond

Q: What happens when a person's original surety bond is cancelled by the court and they are brought in?
A: The Magistrate or Court cancels the old bond and orders the person to give fresh security of the exact same description to cover the remaining, unexpired portion of the original term. [Source: Section 143, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Security for unexpired period of bond

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 143: Security for unexpired period of bond

Q: What does Section 143 of BNSS 2023 handle?
A: Section 143 of BNSS 2023 handles the procedure for securing a fresh bond for the unexpired period when a previous surety is rejected or asks to be discharged from their obligation. [Source: Section 143, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Security for unexpired period of bond

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 143: Security for unexpired period of bond

Q: A person's surety for a one-year peace bond backs out after six months. The person is summoned to court. Does the Magistrate issue a brand new order for a full year?
A: No, the Magistrate shall order the person "to give, for the unexpired portion of the term of such bond, fresh security of the same description as the original security," which would only be for the remaining six months. [Source: Section 143, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Security for unexpired period of bond

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 143: Security for unexpired period of bond

Q: Under sub-section (2), the fresh order is legally deemed to be an order made under which specific sections for procedural purposes?
A: It shall "be deemed to be an order made under section 125 or section 136, as the case may be." [Source: Section 143, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Security for unexpired period of bond

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 143: Security for unexpired period of bond

Q: Can the court demand a harsher type of security when replacing the cancelled bond?
A: No, the fresh security must be "of the same description as the original security." [Source: Section 143, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Security for unexpired period of bond

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 143: Security for unexpired period of bond

Q: What is the consequence of applying sub-section (2) to the fresh security order?
A: The consequence is that all the subsequent rules from sections 139 to 142 regarding imprisonment for default, bond contents, and appeal rights apply identically to this newly replacement bond. [Source: Section 143, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Security for unexpired period of bond

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 144: Order for maintenance of wives, children and parents

Q: Who is legally required to provide a monthly maintenance allowance to their dependent family members?
A: Any person having sufficient means who neglects or refuses to maintain their wife, legitimate or illegitimate minor child, disabled adult child, or their father or mother who are unable to maintain themselves. [Source: Section 144, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order for maintenance of wives, children and parents

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 144: Order for maintenance of wives, children and parents

Q: What does Section 144 of BNSS 2023 cover?
A: Section 144 of BNSS 2023 covers the power of a Magistrate of the first class to order a person with sufficient means to pay a monthly allowance for the maintenance of their dependent wife, children, or parents. [Source: Section 144, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order for maintenance of wives, children and parents

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 144: Order for maintenance of wives, children and parents

Q: A man refuses to pay maintenance to his wife, claiming she shouldn't get any because she left him. The wife proves he had secretly married another woman, prompting her to leave. Does the wife still get maintenance?
A: Yes, because the Explanation states: "If a husband has contracted marriage with another woman... it shall be considered to be just ground for his wife's refusal to live with him," so the Magistrate may still make the order under sub-section (3). [Source: Section 144, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order for maintenance of wives, children and parents

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 144: Order for maintenance of wives, children and parents

Q: According to the second proviso of sub-section (1), within what timeframe should an application for interim maintenance be disposed of?
A: The application "shall, as far as possible, be disposed of within sixty days from the date of the service of notice of the application to such person." [Source: Section 144, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order for maintenance of wives, children and parents

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 144: Order for maintenance of wives, children and parents

Q: Under sub-section (4), what specific actions by a wife completely disqualify her from receiving an allowance from her husband?
A: She is not entitled to receive an allowance if "she is living in adultery, or if, without any sufficient reason, she refuses to live with her husband, or if they are living separately by mutual consent." [Source: Section 144, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order for maintenance of wives, children and parents

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 144: Order for maintenance of wives, children and parents

Q: What is the consequence under sub-section (3) if a person fails to comply with the maintenance order without sufficient cause?
A: The consequence is that the Magistrate may issue a warrant for levying the amount due, and sentence the person to imprisonment for up to one month or until payment if sooner made, for every breach of the order. [Source: Section 144, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order for maintenance of wives, children and parents

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 145: Procedure

Q: Where can a wife file a case to claim maintenance from her husband?
A: She can file the proceedings against him in any district where he is, where he or his wife resides, where he last resided with his wife, or where his parents reside. [Source: Section 145, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 145: Procedure

Q: What does Section 145 of BNSS 2023 regulate?
A: Section 145 of BNSS 2023 regulates the procedure for maintenance proceedings, establishing the territorial jurisdiction for filing cases and the requirement that evidence be taken in the presence of the respondent. [Source: Section 145, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 145: Procedure

Q: A man intentionally ignores all court summons for his maintenance hearing to delay the process. What can the Magistrate do?
A: Under the proviso to sub-section (2), if the Magistrate is satisfied the person is "wilfully avoiding service, or willfully neglecting to attend the Court, the Magistrate may proceed to hear and determine the case ex parte." [Source: Section 145, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 145: Procedure

Q: How must the evidence in maintenance proceedings be recorded according to sub-section (2)?
A: It "shall be recorded in the manner prescribed for summons-cases." [Source: Section 145, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 145: Procedure

Q: Does an ex parte order made against an absent husband remain permanent forever?
A: No, the order "may be set aside for good cause shown on an application made within three months from the date thereof." [Source: Section 145, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 145: Procedure

Q: What is the consequence of a person willfully avoiding court under this section?
A: The consequence is that they lose their right to present evidence, as the court is empowered to determine the maintenance order based solely on the applicant's evidence, resulting in an ex parte decision. [Source: Section 145, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 146: Alteration in allowance

Q: Can a court change the amount of monthly maintenance if someone loses their job or gets a huge salary increase?
A: Yes, on proof of a change in the circumstances of any person receiving or paying the monthly allowance, the Magistrate may make such alteration in the allowance as they think fit. [Source: Section 146, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Alteration in allowance

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 146: Alteration in allowance

Q: What is the function of Section 146 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 146 of BNSS 2023 provides the function for altering or cancelling a previously ordered maintenance allowance based on changes in circumstances, civil court decisions, or the remarriage of a divorced woman. [Source: Section 146, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Alteration in allowance

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 146: Alteration in allowance

Q: A divorced woman has been receiving maintenance from her ex-husband. She then gets remarried to someone else. Does the ex-husband still have to pay?
A: No, under sub-section (3)(a), if she has remarried after the divorce, the Magistrate shall "cancel such order as from the date of her remarriage." [Source: Section 146, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Alteration in allowance

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 146: Alteration in allowance

Q: According to sub-section (4), what must a Civil Court do if it makes a decree for the recovery of maintenance or dowry?
A: The Civil Court "shall take into account the sum which has been paid to, or recovered by, such person as monthly allowance" under section 144. [Source: Section 146, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Alteration in allowance

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 146: Alteration in allowance

Q: If a woman received her full customary divorce settlement (like Mahr) before the maintenance order was even made, does the maintenance order stand?
A: No, under sub-section (3)(b)(i), the Magistrate shall cancel the order "from the date on which such order was made." [Source: Section 146, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Alteration in allowance

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 146: Alteration in allowance

Q: What is the consequence of a competent Civil Court making a decision that contradicts an existing Magisterial maintenance order?
A: Under sub-section (2), the consequence is that the Magistrate "shall cancel the order or, as the case may be, vary the same accordingly," ensuring the civil court's superior jurisdiction takes precedence. [Source: Section 146, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Alteration in allowance

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 147: Enforcement of order of maintenance

Q: Does a person who wins a maintenance case have to pay a court fee to get a copy of the final order?
A: No, a copy of the order of maintenance or interim maintenance shall be given without payment to the person in whose favour it is made or their guardian. [Source: Section 147, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Enforcement of order of maintenance

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 147: Enforcement of order of maintenance

Q: What does Section 147 of BNSS 2023 dictate?
A: Section 147 of BNSS 2023 dictates the free provision of the maintenance order copy to the beneficiary and establishes that the order can be enforced by any Magistrate where the liable person is located. [Source: Section 147, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Enforcement of order of maintenance

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 147: Enforcement of order of maintenance

Q: A wife wins a maintenance order in Mumbai, but her husband immediately moves to Chennai to avoid paying. Must she start a new case in Chennai?
A: No, the order "may be enforced by any Magistrate in any place where the person against whom it is made may be," as long as the Magistrate is satisfied as to the identity of the parties and the non-payment. [Source: Section 147, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Enforcement of order of maintenance

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 147: Enforcement of order of maintenance

Q: What two facts must a new Magistrate be satisfied of before enforcing an order made by a different Magistrate?
A: The Magistrate must be satisfied "as to the identity of the parties and the non-payment of the allowance, or as the case may be, expenses, due." [Source: Section 147, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Enforcement of order of maintenance

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 147: Enforcement of order of maintenance

Q: Are there any circumstances where the court charges the dependent person for the copy of the maintenance order?
A: No, the section strictly mandates that it "shall be given without payment." [Source: Section 147, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Enforcement of order of maintenance

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 147: Enforcement of order of maintenance

Q: What is the practical consequence of this section for a dependent spouse?
A: The consequence is that the dependent spouse receives immediate, free documentation of their rights and gains the ability to seamlessly enforce their claim across jurisdictions, preventing the defaulter from escaping by simply relocating. [Source: Section 147, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Enforcement of order of maintenance

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 148: Dispersal of assembly by use of civil force

Q: Who has the authority to order an angry mob or unlawful assembly to disperse?
A: Any Executive Magistrate, officer in charge of a police station, or any police officer not below the rank of a sub-inspector can command them to disperse. [Source: Section 148, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dispersal of assembly by use of civil force

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 148: Dispersal of assembly by use of civil force

Q: What does Section 148 of BNSS 2023 authorize?
A: Section 148 of BNSS 2023 authorizes Executive Magistrates and specific police officers to use civil force to disperse unlawful assemblies or assemblies of five or more persons likely to disturb the public peace. [Source: Section 148, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dispersal of assembly by use of civil force

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 148: Dispersal of assembly by use of civil force

Q: A police inspector commands a violent mob to disperse. The mob refuses and starts throwing rocks. Can the inspector ask local civilian shopkeepers to help arrest the rioters?
A: Yes, under sub-section (2), the officer may proceed to disperse the assembly by force and "may require the assistance of any person, not being an officer or member of the armed forces... for the purpose of dispersing such assembly." [Source: Section 148, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dispersal of assembly by use of civil force

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 148: Dispersal of assembly by use of civil force

Q: How many people must be in an assembly likely to cause a disturbance of public peace for this section to apply?
A: It applies to "any assembly of five or more persons likely to cause a disturbance of the public peace." [Source: Section 148, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dispersal of assembly by use of civil force

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 148: Dispersal of assembly by use of civil force

Q: Can a police officer ask an off-duty army soldier who happens to be passing by to assist in dispersing the mob under this specific section?
A: No, the section allows requiring the assistance of any person "not being an officer or member of the armed forces and acting as such." [Source: Section 148, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dispersal of assembly by use of civil force

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 148: Dispersal of assembly by use of civil force

Q: What is the legal consequence for members of the assembly once the lawful command to disperse is given?
A: The consequence is that "it shall thereupon be the duty of the members of such assembly to disperse accordingly," and failing to do so exposes them to forcible dispersal and arrest. [Source: Section 148, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dispersal of assembly by use of civil force

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 149: Use of armed forces to disperse assembly

Q: When can the military or armed forces be called in to break up a riot?
A: If the assembly cannot be dispersed by civil force and it is necessary for public security, the District Magistrate or an authorized Executive Magistrate may cause it to be dispersed by the armed forces. [Source: Section 149, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Use of armed forces to disperse assembly

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 149: Use of armed forces to disperse assembly

Q: What does Section 149 of BNSS 2023 enable?
A: Section 149 of BNSS 2023 enables a District Magistrate or authorized Executive Magistrate to requisition the armed forces to disperse an unlawful assembly that poses a threat to public security and cannot otherwise be controlled. [Source: Section 149, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Use of armed forces to disperse assembly

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 149: Use of armed forces to disperse assembly

Q: An Executive Magistrate orders an army captain to disperse a mob. The Magistrate orders the captain to "shoot to kill" immediately to send a message. Must the captain obey this specific tactical instruction?
A: No, under sub-section (3), the officer shall obey the requisition "in such manner as he thinks fit," and is legally bound to "use as little force, and do as little injury to person and property, as may be consistent with dispersing the assembly." [Source: Section 149, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Use of armed forces to disperse assembly

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 149: Use of armed forces to disperse assembly

Q: Who has the primary authority to require the armed forces to disperse an assembly under this section?
A: The "District Magistrate or any other Executive Magistrate authorised by him, who is present" holds this authority. [Source: Section 149, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Use of armed forces to disperse assembly

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 149: Use of armed forces to disperse assembly

Q: Can the armed forces be called in just because a protest is loud and annoying?
A: No, they can only be called if the assembly "cannot otherwise be dispersed, and it is necessary for the public security that it should be dispersed." [Source: Section 149, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Use of armed forces to disperse assembly

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 149: Use of armed forces to disperse assembly

Q: What is the consequence for an armed forces officer receiving a requisition under sub-section (2)?
A: The consequence is that the officer is legally compelled to act ("shall obey such requisition"), shifting the responsibility for the physical dispersal to the military, while bound by the principle of minimum necessary force. [Source: Section 149, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Use of armed forces to disperse assembly

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 150: Power of certain armed force officers to disperse assembly

Q: Can a military officer break up a violent riot on their own without waiting for a Magistrate's permission?
A: Yes, if public security is manifestly endangered and no Executive Magistrate can be communicated with, any commissioned or gazetted officer of the armed forces may disperse the assembly with troops under their command. [Source: Section 150, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power of certain armed force officers to disperse assembly

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 150: Power of certain armed force officers to disperse assembly

Q: What power does Section 150 of BNSS 2023 grant?
A: Section 150 of BNSS 2023 grants exceptional, independent power to commissioned or gazetted officers of the armed forces to disperse dangerous assemblies when an Executive Magistrate is utterly unreachable. [Source: Section 150, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power of certain armed force officers to disperse assembly

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 150: Power of certain armed force officers to disperse assembly

Q: A major in the army disperses a dangerous mob without a Magistrate's order because communications are down. An hour later, the radio starts working and they contact the District Magistrate. What must the major do now?
A: The section dictates that "if... it becomes practicable for him to communicate with an Executive Magistrate, he shall do so, and shall thenceforward obey the instructions of the Magistrate." [Source: Section 150, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power of certain armed force officers to disperse assembly

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 150: Power of certain armed force officers to disperse assembly

Q: What two specific conditions must exist for an armed forces officer to act independently under this section?
A: "When the public security is manifestly endangered by any such assembly" and "no Executive Magistrate can be communicated with." [Source: Section 150, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power of certain armed force officers to disperse assembly

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 150: Power of certain armed force officers to disperse assembly

Q: Can a low-ranking army private independently decide to disperse an assembly under this section?
A: No, this exceptional power is granted only to "any commissioned or gazetted officer of the armed forces." [Source: Section 150, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power of certain armed force officers to disperse assembly

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 150: Power of certain armed force officers to disperse assembly

Q: What is the consequence of applying this section during an extreme crisis?
A: The consequence is that military commanders can take immediate, decisive action to save civilian lives and property without being paralyzed by a lack of civilian communication, temporarily superseding the normal chain of civil authority. [Source: Section 150, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power of certain armed force officers to disperse assembly

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 151: Protection against prosecution for acts done under sections 148, 149 and 150

Q: Can a police officer or army soldier be sued or prosecuted for injuring someone while lawfully breaking up a riot?
A: No, no prosecution can be instituted for acts done in good faith under these dispersal sections without the specific sanction of either the Central or State Government. [Source: Section 151, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Protection against prosecution for acts done under sections 148, 149 and 150

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 151: Protection against prosecution for acts done under sections 148, 149 and 150

Q: What does Section 151 of BNSS 2023 provide?
A: Section 151 of BNSS 2023 provides legal immunity and protection against un-sanctioned prosecution for Executive Magistrates, police officers, and armed forces personnel who act in good faith to disperse unlawful assemblies. [Source: Section 151, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Protection against prosecution for acts done under sections 148, 149 and 150

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 151: Protection against prosecution for acts done under sections 148, 149 and 150

Q: A citizen wants to file a criminal case against an army lieutenant for excessive force during a riot dispersal under section 150. Who must approve this prosecution?
A: Under sub-section (1)(a), the prosecution requires "the sanction of the Central Government where such person is an officer or member of the armed forces." [Source: Section 151, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Protection against prosecution for acts done under sections 148, 149 and 150

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 151: Protection against prosecution for acts done under sections 148, 149 and 150

Q: Under sub-section (2), what core standard of behavior protects an Executive Magistrate or police officer from being deemed to have committed an offence?
A: They must be "acting under any of the said sections in good faith." [Source: Section 151, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Protection against prosecution for acts done under sections 148, 149 and 150

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 151: Protection against prosecution for acts done under sections 148, 149 and 150

Q: Is an ordinary civilian who helps disperse a riot legally protected, or only government officials?
A: Civilians are protected too; sub-section (2)(b) protects "no person doing any act in good faith in compliance with a requisition under section 148 or section 149." [Source: Section 151, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Protection against prosecution for acts done under sections 148, 149 and 150

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 151: Protection against prosecution for acts done under sections 148, 149 and 150

Q: What is the institutional consequence of the protections in sub-section (1)?
A: The consequence is that state actors are shielded from frivolous or retaliatory lawsuits by rioters, ensuring they can perform their duty to restore order without fear of personal legal ruin, unless the government explicitly sanctions their trial. [Source: Section 151, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Protection against prosecution for acts done under sections 148, 149 and 150

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 152: Conditional order for removal of nuisance

Q: What can a Magistrate do if someone illegally blocks a public road, builds a dangerous structure, or keeps a dangerous animal?
A: The Magistrate can make a conditional order requiring the person to remove the obstruction, secure the building, or destroy/confine the animal within a fixed time, or appear to show cause why they shouldn't have to. [Source: Section 152, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Conditional order for removal of nuisance

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 152: Conditional order for removal of nuisance

Q: What does Section 152 of BNSS 2023 address?
A: Section 152 of BNSS 2023 addresses the issuance of conditional orders by Executive Magistrates for the immediate removal of public nuisances, hazardous structures, dangerous animals, and health risks. [Source: Section 152, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Conditional order for removal of nuisance

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 152: Conditional order for removal of nuisance

Q: A factory is keeping highly explosive materials right next to a residential neighborhood. Can a Magistrate intervene before an explosion happens?
A: Yes, under clause (c), if the Magistrate considers that "the disposal of any substance, as is likely to occasion conflagration or explosion, should be prevented or stopped," they can make a conditional order. [Source: Section 152, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Conditional order for removal of nuisance

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 152: Conditional order for removal of nuisance

Q: If a person objects to the conditional order to remove a nuisance, what alternative does the order provide them?
A: The order requires them to "appear before himself or some other Executive Magistrate subordinate to him at a time and place to be fixed by the order, and show cause... why the order should not be made absolute." [Source: Section 152, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Conditional order for removal of nuisance

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 152: Conditional order for removal of nuisance

Q: Can a person who receives a conditional order from a Magistrate go to a Civil Court and get an injunction to stop the Magistrate's order?
A: No, sub-section (2) explicitly states, "No order duly made by a Magistrate under this section shall be called in question in any Civil Court." [Source: Section 152, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Conditional order for removal of nuisance

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 152: Conditional order for removal of nuisance

Q: What is the legal consequence of a Magistrate issuing a conditional order under this section?
A: The consequence is that the burden immediately shifts to the creator of the nuisance; they must either physically abate the hazard at their own expense or formally defend their actions in a magisterial inquiry, bypassing slow civil litigation. [Source: Section 152, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Conditional order for removal of nuisance

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 153: Service or notification of order

Q: How does the government ensure that a person actually receives the order to remove a public nuisance?
A: If practicable, the order is served directly on the person like a summons; if that's not possible, it is proclaimed publicly and a copy is stuck up at a fit place to convey the information. [Source: Section 153, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Service or notification of order

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 153: Service or notification of order

Q: What is the function of Section 153 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 153 of BNSS 2023 outlines the procedural methods for serving or notifying an individual about a conditional order for the removal of a nuisance. [Source: Section 153, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Service or notification of order

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 153: Service or notification of order

Q: A Magistrate issues an order to tear down a dangerous, abandoned building, but the owner has fled the state and cannot be found for direct service. How is the order legally delivered?
A: Under sub-section (2), "it shall be notified by proclamation published in such manner as the State Government may, by rules, direct, and a copy thereof shall be stuck up at such place or places as may be fittest for conveying the information." [Source: Section 153, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Service or notification of order

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 153: Service or notification of order

Q: What is the primary method of delivery for an order under this section, if it is practicable?
A: It shall be "served on the person against whom it is made, in the manner herein provided for service of summons." [Source: Section 153, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Service or notification of order

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 153: Service or notification of order

Q: Is physical hand-delivery strictly required in absolutely every single case?
A: No, it is only required "if practicable"; otherwise, the alternative method of proclamation and posting is used. [Source: Section 153, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Service or notification of order

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 153: Service or notification of order

Q: What is the consequence of posting the order at the "fittest" place under sub-section (2)?
A: The consequence is that the legal requirement for notice is deemed fulfilled, preventing the absentee owner from later claiming ignorance to stall the demolition or removal of the nuisance. [Source: Section 153, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Service or notification of order

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 154: Person to whom order is addressed to obey or show cause

Q: What must a person do when they receive an order from a Magistrate to remove a nuisance?
A: The person must either perform the directed act within the specified time and manner, or appear in accordance with the order to show cause against it, which may be permitted through audio-video conferencing. [Source: Section 154, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Person to whom order is addressed to obey or show cause

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 154: Person to whom order is addressed to obey or show cause

Q: What does Section 154 of BNSS 2023 require?
A: Section 154 of BNSS 2023 requires that a person addressed by a conditional nuisance order must either obey the order by performing the act or appear to formally show cause against it. [Source: Section 154, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Person to whom order is addressed to obey or show cause

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 154: Person to whom order is addressed to obey or show cause

Q: A person living abroad receives an order to repair their falling building in India. They want to show cause but cannot travel. Can they attend the hearing remotely?
A: Yes, because clause (b) specifies that "such appearance or hearing may be permitted through audio-video conferencing." [Source: Section 154, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Person to whom order is addressed to obey or show cause

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 154: Person to whom order is addressed to obey or show cause

Q: What two specific parameters are dictated by clause (a) regarding the performance of the act?
A: The act must be performed "within the time and in the manner specified in the order." [Source: Section 154, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Person to whom order is addressed to obey or show cause

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 154: Person to whom order is addressed to obey or show cause

Q: Is a person absolutely forced to perform the physical act directed by the order immediately?
A: No, they have the alternative option under clause (b) to "appear in accordance with such order and show cause against the same." [Source: Section 154, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Person to whom order is addressed to obey or show cause

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 154: Person to whom order is addressed to obey or show cause

Q: What is the immediate legal consequence of this section for the recipient of the order?
A: The consequence is that the recipient is placed under a strict legal obligation to take action—either by complying physically or contesting legally—leaving them no option to simply ignore the Magistrate's directive. [Source: Section 154, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Person to whom order is addressed to obey or show cause

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 155: Penalty for failure to comply with section 154

Q: What happens if a person just ignores a Magistrate's order to remove a public nuisance?
A: If the person does not perform the act or appear to show cause, they become liable to a penalty under section 223 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, and the Magistrate's order is made absolute. [Source: Section 155, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Penalty for failure to comply with section 154

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 155: Penalty for failure to comply with section 154

Q: What does Section 155 of BNSS 2023 state?
A: Section 155 of BNSS 2023 states the penalties for failing to comply with a conditional order, imposing criminal liability under the BNS and automatically converting the conditional order into an absolute one. [Source: Section 155, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Penalty for failure to comply with section 154

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 155: Penalty for failure to comply with section 154

Q: A factory owner receives an order to stop polluting but throws it away and doesn't show up to court. Later, they want to contest the order. Can they still argue against it?
A: No, because by failing to perform the act or show cause, "the order shall be made absolute," meaning it is finalized and they have forfeited their right to contest it. [Source: Section 155, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Penalty for failure to comply with section 154

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 155: Penalty for failure to comply with section 154

Q: Under what specific section of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, is the penalty specified for this failure?
A: The penalty is specified "in section 223 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023." [Source: Section 155, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Penalty for failure to comply with section 154

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 155: Penalty for failure to comply with section 154

Q: Is there any leniency provided in this section for someone who accidentally forgot about the order?
A: No, the section dictates that if they fail to perform or appear, "he shall be liable to the penalty" and the order "shall be made absolute," without providing statutory exceptions for forgetfulness. [Source: Section 155, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Penalty for failure to comply with section 154

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 155: Penalty for failure to comply with section 154

Q: What is the procedural consequence of the order being "made absolute"?
A: The consequence is that the conditional nature of the order evaporates, locking in the legal mandate for the nuisance's removal and exposing the person to immediate enforcement actions and costs. [Source: Section 155, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Penalty for failure to comply with section 154

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 156: Procedure where existence of public right is denied

Q: How does a Magistrate handle a situation where a person claims that the obstructed road is actually their private property, not a public way?
A: The Magistrate must question the person about this denial. If there is reliable evidence supporting the denial, the Magistrate must stay the proceedings until a Civil Court decides the matter. [Source: Section 156, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where existence of public right is denied

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 156: Procedure where existence of public right is denied

Q: What is the purpose of Section 156 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 156 of BNSS 2023 establishes the procedure for handling denials of public rights in nuisance cases, pausing Magisterial action if credible evidence shows a genuine dispute over whether a place is actually public. [Source: Section 156, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where existence of public right is denied

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 156: Procedure where existence of public right is denied

Q: A person is ordered to clear a path. When questioned, they say it's private land but provide zero documents, witnesses, or evidence. Should the Magistrate stop the proceedings?
A: No, under sub-section (2), if the Magistrate "finds that there is no such evidence, he shall proceed as laid down in section 157" instead of staying the proceedings. [Source: Section 156, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where existence of public right is denied

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 156: Procedure where existence of public right is denied

Q: What must a Magistrate actively do before proceeding under section 157 when the person appears?
A: The Magistrate must "question him as to whether he denies the existence of any public right in respect of the way, river, channel or place." [Source: Section 156, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where existence of public right is denied

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 156: Procedure where existence of public right is denied

Q: If a person initially admits the path is public but later changes their mind during the inquiry, can they then deny it?
A: No, under sub-section (3), a person who fails to deny it when questioned, or fails to adduce reliable evidence upon denial, "shall not in the subsequent proceedings be permitted to make any such denial." [Source: Section 156, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where existence of public right is denied

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 156: Procedure where existence of public right is denied

Q: What is the consequence of a Magistrate finding reliable evidence that a public right does not exist?
A: The consequence is a mandatory stay of the Magisterial proceedings, transferring the jurisdictional authority to resolve the underlying property right dispute to a "competent Court." [Source: Section 156, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where existence of public right is denied

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 157: Procedure where person against whom order is made under section 152 appears to show

Q: What happens when a person shows up to court and argues against an order to remove a public nuisance?
A: The Magistrate takes evidence as in a summons-case. If the order is found reasonable and proper, it is made absolute; if not, no further proceedings are taken. [Source: Section 157, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where person against whom order is made under section 152 appears to show

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 157: Procedure where person against whom order is made under section 152 appears to show

Q: What does Section 157 of BNSS 2023 outline?
A: Section 157 of BNSS 2023 outlines the evidentiary procedure when a person contests a conditional nuisance order, culminating in either the cancellation or finalization of the order within strict timeframes. [Source: Section 157, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where person against whom order is made under section 152 appears to show

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 157: Procedure where person against whom order is made under section 152 appears to show

Q: A Magistrate starts an inquiry into a contested nuisance order. The proceedings drag on for 150 days. Is this allowed under the law?
A: No, the proviso strictly states that proceedings "shall be completed, as soon as possible, within a period of ninety days, which may be extended... to one hundred and twenty days." 150 days exceeds the maximum limit. [Source: Section 157, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where person against whom order is made under section 152 appears to show

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 157: Procedure where person against whom order is made under section 152 appears to show

Q: What standard must the Magistrate meet before making the contested order absolute under sub-section (2)?
A: The Magistrate must be "satisfied that the order, either as originally made or subject to such modification as he considers necessary, is reasonable and proper." [Source: Section 157, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where person against whom order is made under section 152 appears to show

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 157: Procedure where person against whom order is made under section 152 appears to show

Q: Is the Magistrate forced to make the order absolute exactly exactly as it was originally written?
A: No, the Magistrate may make it absolute "either as originally made or subject to such modification as he considers necessary." [Source: Section 157, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where person against whom order is made under section 152 appears to show

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 157: Procedure where person against whom order is made under section 152 appears to show

Q: What is the consequence if the Magistrate is "not so satisfied" that the order is reasonable and proper?
A: Under sub-section (3), the consequence is that "no further proceedings shall be taken in the case," effectively dropping the matter against the person. [Source: Section 157, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where person against whom order is made under section 152 appears to show

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 158: Power of Magistrate to direct local investigation and examination of an expert

Q: Can a Magistrate hire an expert or send someone to physically inspect the site of a public nuisance?
A: Yes, for the purposes of an inquiry, the Magistrate may direct a local investigation by a fit person or summon and examine an expert. [Source: Section 158, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power of Magistrate to direct local investigation and examination of an expert

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 158: Power of Magistrate to direct local investigation and examination of an expert

Q: What power does Section 158 of BNSS 2023 grant?
A: Section 158 of BNSS 2023 grants Magistrates the power to direct local site investigations or summon expert witnesses to gather specialized evidence during a public nuisance inquiry. [Source: Section 158, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power of Magistrate to direct local investigation and examination of an expert

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 158: Power of Magistrate to direct local investigation and examination of an expert

Q: A Magistrate is deciding if a chemical factory is polluting a river but has no background in chemistry. How can they determine the truth?
A: The Magistrate can invoke clause (b) to "summon and examine an expert" to provide technical analysis of the pollution. [Source: Section 158, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power of Magistrate to direct local investigation and examination of an expert

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 158: Power of Magistrate to direct local investigation and examination of an expert

Q: Under what specific sections of BNSS 2023 are the inquiries for which these powers can be used?
A: The powers may be used "for the purposes of an inquiry under section 156 or section 157." [Source: Section 158, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power of Magistrate to direct local investigation and examination of an expert

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 158: Power of Magistrate to direct local investigation and examination of an expert

Q: Is the Magistrate restricted to only sending police officers for a local investigation?
A: No, the Magistrate may direct the investigation to be made "by such person as he thinks fit." [Source: Section 158, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power of Magistrate to direct local investigation and examination of an expert

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 158: Power of Magistrate to direct local investigation and examination of an expert

Q: What is the practical consequence of this section for Magisterial inquiries?
A: The consequence is that Magistrates are not limited to just hearing oral testimonies in court; they can actively acquire objective, specialized, and on-site evidence to make informed rulings on complex public hazards. [Source: Section 158, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power of Magistrate to direct local investigation and examination of an expert

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 159: Power of Magistrate to furnish written instructions, etc

Q: Who pays for the costs of bringing in an expert or conducting a local investigation during a nuisance hearing?
A: The Magistrate has the power to declare by whom the whole or any part of the necessary expenses of the local investigation or the costs of summoning the expert shall be paid. [Source: Section 159, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power of Magistrate to furnish written instructions, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 159: Power of Magistrate to furnish written instructions, etc

Q: What is defined in Section 159 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 159 of BNSS 2023 defines the Magistrate's authority to furnish written instructions to local investigators, treat their reports as evidence, and allocate the financial costs of investigations and experts. [Source: Section 159, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power of Magistrate to furnish written instructions, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 159: Power of Magistrate to furnish written instructions, etc

Q: A person conducts a local investigation of a hazardous building on a Magistrate's order and submits a written report. Can this report be used directly to decide the case without calling the investigator to testify?
A: Yes, under sub-section (2), "The report of such person may be read as evidence in the case." [Source: Section 159, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power of Magistrate to furnish written instructions, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 159: Power of Magistrate to furnish written instructions, etc

Q: What can a Magistrate provide to a person directed to make a local investigation under section 158?
A: Under sub-section (1)(a), the Magistrate may "furnish such person with such written instructions as may seem necessary for his guidance." [Source: Section 159, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power of Magistrate to furnish written instructions, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 159: Power of Magistrate to furnish written instructions, etc

Q: Is the government automatically responsible for paying the expenses of a local investigation ordered by a Magistrate?
A: No, the Magistrate has the discretion to "declare by whom the whole or any part of the necessary expenses of the local investigation shall be paid." [Source: Section 159, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power of Magistrate to furnish written instructions, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 159: Power of Magistrate to furnish written instructions, etc

Q: What is the consequence of the Magistrate's power to allocate costs under this section?
A: The consequence is that the financial burden of complex investigations does not automatically fall on the State; the Magistrate can order the offending party, or even the complaining party, to bear the costs. [Source: Section 159, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power of Magistrate to furnish written instructions, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 160: Procedure on order being made absolute and consequences of disobedience

Q: What happens if an order to remove a public nuisance is finalized, but the person still refuses to do the work?
A: The Magistrate may cause the act to be performed themselves and recover the costs by selling any property removed or by distraining and selling the person's movable property. [Source: Section 160, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure on order being made absolute and consequences of disobedience

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 160: Procedure on order being made absolute and consequences of disobedience

Q: What does Section 160 of BNSS 2023 establish?
A: Section 160 of BNSS 2023 establishes the procedure for enforcing an absolute order, detailing the notice given, the penalty for disobedience, and the methods for state execution and cost recovery. [Source: Section 160, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure on order being made absolute and consequences of disobedience

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 160: Procedure on order being made absolute and consequences of disobedience

Q: A Magistrate orders a local government body to tear down a dangerous wall because the owner refused. The owner then sues the Magistrate for destroying their property. Will the lawsuit succeed?
A: No, under sub-section (3), "No suit shall lie in respect of anything done in good faith under this section." [Source: Section 160, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure on order being made absolute and consequences of disobedience

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 160: Procedure on order being made absolute and consequences of disobedience

Q: What specific information must be included in the notice given to a person after an order is made absolute?
A: The notice must require them to perform the act within a fixed time and inform them that disobedience makes them "liable to the penalty provided by section 223 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023." [Source: Section 160, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure on order being made absolute and consequences of disobedience

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 160: Procedure on order being made absolute and consequences of disobedience

Q: Can a Magistrate only recover costs by selling property found within their own local jurisdiction?
A: No, they may recover costs by the sale of movable property "within or without such Magistrate's local jurisdiction," though selling property outside requires the endorsement of the local Magistrate there. [Source: Section 160, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure on order being made absolute and consequences of disobedience

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 160: Procedure on order being made absolute and consequences of disobedience

Q: What is the ultimate consequence of continued disobedience under sub-section (2)?
A: The consequence is that the State forcefully intervenes to physically eliminate the nuisance itself, and then aggressively recoups the financial cost directly from the disobedient person's assets. [Source: Section 160, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure on order being made absolute and consequences of disobedience

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 161: Injunction pending inquiry

Q: What can a Magistrate do if a public nuisance poses an immediate, serious danger before the court hearings are even finished?
A: The Magistrate can issue an immediate injunction to prevent the danger pending the determination of the matter, and if disobeyed, use necessary means to prevent the injury themselves. [Source: Section 161, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Injunction pending inquiry

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 161: Injunction pending inquiry

Q: What power is granted by Section 161 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 161 of BNSS 2023 grants Magistrates the power to issue emergency injunctions during pending inquiries to prevent imminent, serious danger to the public, and to enforce them immediately. [Source: Section 161, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Injunction pending inquiry

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 161: Injunction pending inquiry

Q: A chemical leak is actively poisoning a town's water supply. The factory owner demands a full inquiry before shutting off the pipes. Can the Magistrate bypass the inquiry temporarily?
