A: Yes, if the Magistrate considers immediate measures are needed to prevent imminent danger, they may "issue such an injunction... as is required to obviate or prevent such danger or injury pending the determination of the matter." [Source: Section 161, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Injunction pending inquiry

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 161: Injunction pending inquiry

Q: If a person disobeys an emergency injunction under this section, what action is the Magistrate authorized to take?
A: Under sub-section (2), "the Magistrate may himself use, or cause to be used, such means as he thinks fit to obviate such danger or to prevent such injury." [Source: Section 161, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Injunction pending inquiry

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 161: Injunction pending inquiry

Q: Are Magistrates liable for damages if they destroy someone's property while enforcing an emergency injunction under sub-section (2)?
A: No, sub-section (3) provides absolute immunity: "No suit shall lie in respect of anything done in good faith by a Magistrate under this section." [Source: Section 161, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Injunction pending inquiry

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 161: Injunction pending inquiry

Q: What is the practical consequence of this section in disaster scenarios?
A: The consequence is that bureaucratic procedural delays cannot be used to prolong a lethal or disastrous public hazard; the Magistrate has supreme, unchallengeable authority to stop the immediate threat first, and ask questions later. [Source: Section 161, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Injunction pending inquiry

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 162: Magistrate may prohibit repetition or Continuance of public nuisance

Q: Can a Magistrate permanently ban someone from continuously causing a public nuisance?
A: Yes, specific Magistrates empowered by the State Government can order any person not to repeat or continue a public nuisance as defined in law. [Source: Section 162, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Magistrate may prohibit repetition or Continuance of public nuisance

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 162: Magistrate may prohibit repetition or Continuance of public nuisance

Q: What does Section 162 of BNSS 2023 allow?
A: Section 162 of BNSS 2023 allows empowered Magistrates to issue orders prohibiting the repetition or continuance of a public nuisance, ensuring long-term prevention rather than just one-time removal. [Source: Section 162, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Magistrate may prohibit repetition or Continuance of public nuisance

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 162: Magistrate may prohibit repetition or Continuance of public nuisance

Q: A nightclub is shut down for being a noise nuisance. A week later, the owner tries to reopen it and play loud music again. Can a Magistrate issue an order specifically forbidding them from doing this again?
A: Yes, an empowered Magistrate "may order any person not to repeat or continue a public nuisance." [Source: Section 162, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Magistrate may prohibit repetition or Continuance of public nuisance

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 162: Magistrate may prohibit repetition or Continuance of public nuisance

Q: What specific legal texts define the "public nuisance" that can be prohibited under this section?
A: It is a public nuisance "as defined in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, or any special or local law." [Source: Section 162, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Magistrate may prohibit repetition or Continuance of public nuisance

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 162: Magistrate may prohibit repetition or Continuance of public nuisance

Q: Can any random Executive Magistrate issue a prohibition order under this section?
A: No, it must be a District Magistrate, Sub-divisional Magistrate, or an Executive Magistrate or Deputy Commissioner of Police specifically "empowered by the State Government or the District Magistrate in this behalf." [Source: Section 162, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Magistrate may prohibit repetition or Continuance of public nuisance

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 162: Magistrate may prohibit repetition or Continuance of public nuisance

Q: What is the legal consequence for an individual who receives an order under this section?
A: The consequence is that they are placed under a targeted, personalized legal injunction, transforming any future repetition of the nuisance from a general statutory violation into a direct defiance of a specific Magisterial order. [Source: Section 162, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Magistrate may prohibit repetition or Continuance of public nuisance

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 163: Power to issue order in urgent cases of nuisance or apprehended danger

Q: What sweeping power does a Magistrate have during extreme emergencies like riots, mass health threats, or major disturbances?
A: A Magistrate can issue an urgent, sometimes ex-parte, written order directing any person or the public to abstain from certain acts or manage their property in a certain way to immediately prevent danger, riots, or injury. [Source: Section 163, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to issue order in urgent cases of nuisance or apprehended danger

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 163: Power to issue order in urgent cases of nuisance or apprehended danger

Q: What does Section 163 of BNSS 2023 provide?
A: Section 163 of BNSS 2023 (historically akin to Section 144 CrPC) provides vast emergency powers to Magistrates to issue urgent, temporary restrictive orders to individuals or the general public to prevent imminent danger, riots, or health crises. [Source: Section 163, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to issue order in urgent cases of nuisance or apprehended danger

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 163: Power to issue order in urgent cases of nuisance or apprehended danger

Q: A violent riot breaks out in a specific neighborhood. The District Magistrate wants to impose an immediate curfew on anyone entering that area. Can they do this without serving notice to every single citizen?
A: Yes, under sub-section (2) the order may "be passed ex parte," and under sub-section (3) it may be directed "to the public generally when frequenting or visiting a particular place or area." [Source: Section 163, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to issue order in urgent cases of nuisance or apprehended danger

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 163: Power to issue order in urgent cases of nuisance or apprehended danger

Q: By default, what is the maximum duration an order under this section can remain in force?
A: Under sub-section (4), "No order under this section shall remain in force for more than two months from the making thereof." [Source: Section 163, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to issue order in urgent cases of nuisance or apprehended danger

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 163: Power to issue order in urgent cases of nuisance or apprehended danger

Q: Can an emergency order under this section ever last longer than two months?
A: Yes, the proviso to sub-section (4) states the State Government may direct it to remain in force for a "further period not exceeding six months" to prevent danger to human life, health, safety, or riots. [Source: Section 163, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to issue order in urgent cases of nuisance or apprehended danger

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 163: Power to issue order in urgent cases of nuisance or apprehended danger

Q: What is the consequence if a person aggrieved by such an order applies to the Magistrate to have it altered or rescinded?
A: Under sub-section (7), the consequence is that the Magistrate "shall afford to the applicant an early opportunity of appearing... and showing cause against the order," and must record written reasons if they reject the application. [Source: Section 163, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to issue order in urgent cases of nuisance or apprehended danger

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 164: Procedure where dispute concerning land or water is likely to cause breach of

Q: What happens if two people are violently fighting over who owns a piece of land or a crop?
A: An Executive Magistrate can require the parties to attend court and submit written statements of their claims regarding actual possession. The Magistrate will then decide who was in actual possession and declare them entitled to it until a formal eviction. [Source: Section 164, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where dispute concerning land or water is likely to cause breach of

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 164: Procedure where dispute concerning land or water is likely to cause breach of

Q: What does Section 164 of BNSS 2023 establish?
A: Section 164 of BNSS 2023 establishes the procedure for Executive Magistrates to intervene in disputes concerning land or water that are likely to cause a breach of the peace, by determining immediate possession without deciding legal title. [Source: Section 164, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where dispute concerning land or water is likely to cause breach of

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 164: Procedure where dispute concerning land or water is likely to cause breach of

Q: A farmer is violently thrown off their land by thugs. Three weeks later, a Magistrate hears about the dispute. When the Magistrate investigates, the thugs claim they are currently in possession. Does the Magistrate have to rule in favor of the thugs?
A: No, under the proviso to sub-section (4), if a party "has been forcibly and wrongfully dispossessed within two months next before the date on which the report... was received," the Magistrate may treat the dispossessed farmer as if they were in possession. [Source: Section 164, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where dispute concerning land or water is likely to cause breach of

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 164: Procedure where dispute concerning land or water is likely to cause breach of

Q: According to sub-section (2), what specific things are included in the expression "land or water"?
A: It includes "buildings, markets, fisheries, crops or other produce of land, and the rents or profits of any such property." [Source: Section 164, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where dispute concerning land or water is likely to cause breach of

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 164: Procedure where dispute concerning land or water is likely to cause breach of

Q: If the parties are summoned to court, are they allowed to argue that there is actually no risk of violence or breach of peace at all?
A: Yes, sub-section (5) states nothing shall preclude any party "from showing that no such dispute as aforesaid exists or has existed," and if proven, the Magistrate "shall cancel his said order." [Source: Section 164, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where dispute concerning land or water is likely to cause breach of

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 164: Procedure where dispute concerning land or water is likely to cause breach of

Q: What is the legal consequence of the Magistrate issuing an order under sub-section (6)?
A: The consequence is that the declared party's physical possession is legally protected from any disturbance, forcing the losing party to seek formal eviction through a lengthy civil lawsuit rather than resorting to immediate violence. [Source: Section 164, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where dispute concerning land or water is likely to cause breach of

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 165: Power to attach subject of dispute and to appoint receiver

Q: What happens if a land dispute is so chaotic that the Magistrate can't figure out who was actually in possession, but a riot is about to happen?
A: The Magistrate may attach the subject of dispute and appoint a receiver to look after the property until a competent Court determines the rightful owner. [Source: Section 165, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to attach subject of dispute and to appoint receiver

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 165: Power to attach subject of dispute and to appoint receiver

Q: What power does Section 165 of BNSS 2023 grant?
A: Section 165 of BNSS 2023 grants the Magistrate the power to attach disputed land or water and appoint a receiver in cases of emergency, or when actual possession cannot be determined. [Source: Section 165, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to attach subject of dispute and to appoint receiver

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 165: Power to attach subject of dispute and to appoint receiver

Q: A Magistrate attaches a disputed market and appoints a receiver. A month later, a Civil Court ruling on the same property also appoints its own receiver. What must the Magistrate's receiver do?
A: Under the proviso to sub-section (2), the Magistrate shall order their receiver "to hand over the possession of the subject of dispute to the receiver appointed by the Civil Court and shall thereafter discharge the receiver appointed by him." [Source: Section 165, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to attach subject of dispute and to appoint receiver

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 165: Power to attach subject of dispute and to appoint receiver

Q: What are the three specific situations under sub-section (1) where a Magistrate may attach the subject of dispute?
A: If the Magistrate considers it "a case of emergency," or decides "none of the parties was then in such possession," or is "unable to satisfy himself as to which of them was then in such possession." [Source: Section 165, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to attach subject of dispute and to appoint receiver

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 165: Power to attach subject of dispute and to appoint receiver

Q: Is an attachment order under this section permanent until a Civil Court rules?
A: No, under the proviso to sub-section (1), the Magistrate "may withdraw the attachment at any time if he is satisfied that there is no longer any likelihood of breach of the peace." [Source: Section 165, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to attach subject of dispute and to appoint receiver

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 165: Power to attach subject of dispute and to appoint receiver

Q: What is the immediate consequence of the Magistrate attaching the property?
A: The consequence is that all disputing parties are stripped of physical control over the asset, neutralizing the immediate trigger for violence while shifting management to a neutral, state-appointed receiver. [Source: Section 165, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to attach subject of dispute and to appoint receiver

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 166: Dispute concerning right of use of land or water

Q: What can a Magistrate do if people are fighting over the right to use a specific road or draw water from a well?
A: The Magistrate can require the parties to submit written statements, hear evidence, and if the right of use exists, make an order prohibiting interference with that right or removing obstructions. [Source: Section 166, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dispute concerning right of use of land or water

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 166: Dispute concerning right of use of land or water

Q: What does Section 166 of BNSS 2023 address?
A: Section 166 of BNSS 2023 addresses disputes concerning the alleged right of user of land or water (such as easements), allowing Magistrates to protect established usage rights to prevent a breach of the peace. [Source: Section 166, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dispute concerning right of use of land or water

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 166: Dispute concerning right of use of land or water

Q: A farmer claims a right to use a seasonal path across a neighbor's land every monsoon. They haven't used it for two years because it didn't rain. Can the Magistrate protect this right right now?
A: No, under the proviso to sub-section (3), for rights exercisable only at particular seasons, the order cannot be made "unless the right has been exercised during the last of such seasons... before such receipt" of information. [Source: Section 166, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dispute concerning right of use of land or water

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 166: Dispute concerning right of use of land or water

Q: For a right that is exercisable at all times of the year, within what timeframe must it have been exercised to be protected under this section?
A: It must have been "exercised within three months next before the receipt under sub-section (1) of the report of a police officer or other information." [Source: Section 166, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dispute concerning right of use of land or water

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 166: Dispute concerning right of use of land or water

Q: If a Magistrate starts a proceeding about who "owns" a piece of land under section 164, but realizes it's just a dispute about a right of "way" across it, must they throw the case out and start over?
A: No, under sub-section (4), the Magistrate "may, after recording his reasons, continue with the proceedings as if they had been commenced under sub-section (1)" of section 166. [Source: Section 166, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dispute concerning right of use of land or water

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 166: Dispute concerning right of use of land or water

Q: What is the consequence if the Magistrate makes an order under sub-section (3)?
A: The consequence is that the party claiming the right of use is legally shielded from interference and any physical barricades can be forcefully removed, restoring the status quo usage. [Source: Section 166, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dispute concerning right of use of land or water

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 167: Local inquiry

Q: Can a higher-up Magistrate send a subordinate to go inspect a disputed piece of land?
A: Yes, whenever a local inquiry is necessary for disputes over land or water, a District Magistrate or Sub-divisional Magistrate may depute any subordinate Magistrate to make the inquiry. [Source: Section 167, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Local inquiry

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 167: Local inquiry

Q: What is the function of Section 167 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 167 of BNSS 2023 authorizes District and Sub-divisional Magistrates to depute subordinate Magistrates for local inquiries in land disputes and to allocate the costs of those inquiries and proceedings. [Source: Section 167, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Local inquiry

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 167: Local inquiry

Q: A subordinate Magistrate conducts a local inquiry and submits a report to the District Magistrate. The opposing party objects, saying the subordinate must take the witness stand to testify about the report. Is this required?
A: No, under sub-section (2), "The report of the person so deputed may be read as evidence in the case" without requiring them to testify. [Source: Section 167, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Local inquiry

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 167: Local inquiry

Q: What specific types of expenses can the Magistrate include when directing who pays the costs under sub-section (3)?
A: The costs may include "any expenses incurred in respect of witnesses and of advocates' fees, which the Court may consider reasonable." [Source: Section 167, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Local inquiry

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 167: Local inquiry

Q: Does the District Magistrate have to pay for the subordinate's inquiry out of the government budget?
A: No, under sub-section (1), they "may declare by whom the whole or any part of the necessary expenses of the inquiry shall be paid." [Source: Section 167, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Local inquiry

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 167: Local inquiry

Q: What is the financial consequence for a party found to be aggressively and baselessly disputing land under these sections?
A: The consequence is that the Magistrate passing the decision can penalize them by directing them to pay the other party's costs, including reasonable advocate fees and witness expenses. [Source: Section 167, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Local inquiry

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 168: Police to prevent cognizable offences

Q: Do police officers have to wait for a crime to happen before they stop it?
A: No, every police officer may interpose to prevent, and shall to the best of their ability prevent, the commission of any cognizable offence. [Source: Section 168, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Police to prevent cognizable offences

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 168: Police to prevent cognizable offences

Q: What does Section 168 of BNSS 2023 mandate?
A: Section 168 of BNSS 2023 mandates the proactive duty of every police officer to intervene and use their best efforts to prevent cognizable offences before they are committed. [Source: Section 168, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Police to prevent cognizable offences

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 168: Police to prevent cognizable offences

Q: A police officer sees a group of people gathering with weapons, clearly intending to commit a robbery. Does the officer need a Magistrate's order to step in and break up the group?
A: No, the officer "may interpose for the purpose of preventing... the commission of any cognizable offence" entirely on their own authority. [Source: Section 168, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Police to prevent cognizable offences

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 168: Police to prevent cognizable offences

Q: What specific standard of effort is required from the police officer under this section?
A: The officer "shall, to the best of his ability, prevent" the commission of the offence. [Source: Section 168, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Police to prevent cognizable offences

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 168: Police to prevent cognizable offences

Q: Does this proactive duty apply to minor, non-cognizable offences like simple defamation?
A: No, the section explicitly restricts this duty to preventing the commission of "any cognizable offence." [Source: Section 168, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Police to prevent cognizable offences

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 168: Police to prevent cognizable offences

Q: What is the institutional consequence of this section for police conduct?
A: The consequence is that police are legally transformed from merely being a reactionary investigative force into a proactive, preventative body with a statutory mandate to intervene before harm occurs. [Source: Section 168, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Police to prevent cognizable offences

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 169: Information of design to commit cognizable offences

Q: What must a police officer do if they hear a rumor that a major crime is being planned?
A: The officer must communicate that information to their subordinate officer and to any other officer whose duty it is to prevent or take cognizance of the offence. [Source: Section 169, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Information of design to commit cognizable offences

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 169: Information of design to commit cognizable offences

Q: What is the requirement of Section 169 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 169 of BNSS 2023 requires police officers to immediately share intelligence regarding the design to commit cognizable offences up the chain of command and laterally to relevant officers. [Source: Section 169, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Information of design to commit cognizable offences

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 169: Information of design to commit cognizable offences

Q: A traffic cop hears from an informant that a bank will be robbed tomorrow. The traffic cop thinks it's not their jurisdiction and decides to investigate it alone. Is this a violation?
A: Yes, the section mandates that the officer "shall communicate such information to the police officer to whom he is subordinate, and to any other officer whose duty it is to prevent" it. [Source: Section 169, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Information of design to commit cognizable offences

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 169: Information of design to commit cognizable offences

Q: What specific type of information triggers this mandatory communication?
A: "Information of a design to commit any cognizable offence." [Source: Section 169, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Information of design to commit cognizable offences

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 169: Information of design to commit cognizable offences

Q: Can the officer choose to only tell their boss, and ignore the specific anti-robbery squad who actually handles such crimes?
A: No, they must communicate it to their subordinate officer "and to any other officer whose duty it is to prevent or take cognizance" of that offence. [Source: Section 169, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Information of design to commit cognizable offences

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 169: Information of design to commit cognizable offences

Q: What is the operational consequence of this section for a police department?
A: The consequence is that critical intelligence cannot be legally siloed or hoarded by individual officers; it forces a coordinated, multi-officer response to prevent serious crimes. [Source: Section 169, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Information of design to commit cognizable offences

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 170: Arrest to prevent commission of cognizable offences

Q: Can the police arrest someone just because they are planning to commit a crime, even before they actually attempt it?
A: Yes, a police officer knowing of a design to commit a cognizable offence can arrest the person without a warrant if it appears the offence cannot be prevented any other way. [Source: Section 170, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Arrest to prevent commission of cognizable offences

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 170: Arrest to prevent commission of cognizable offences

Q: What does Section 170 of BNSS 2023 authorize?
A: Section 170 of BNSS 2023 authorizes police officers to make preventative, warrantless arrests of individuals designing to commit cognizable offences, subject to a strict 24-hour detention limit. [Source: Section 170, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Arrest to prevent commission of cognizable offences

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 170: Arrest to prevent commission of cognizable offences

Q: A police officer overhears someone planning a kidnapping. The officer immediately arrests the person but keeps them locked up in the station for three days without seeing a judge. Is this lawful?
A: No, under sub-section (2), "No person arrested under sub-section (1) shall be detained in custody for a period exceeding twenty-four hours... unless his further detention is required or authorised." [Source: Section 170, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Arrest to prevent commission of cognizable offences

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 170: Arrest to prevent commission of cognizable offences

Q: What specific subjective belief must the police officer hold to justify making a preventative arrest under sub-section (1)?
A: The officer must believe that "it appears to such officer that the commission of the offence cannot be otherwise prevented." [Source: Section 170, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Arrest to prevent commission of cognizable offences

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 170: Arrest to prevent commission of cognizable offences

Q: Does the police officer need to get a warrant from a Magistrate to make an arrest under this section?
A: No, they may arrest the person "without orders from a Magistrate and without a warrant." [Source: Section 170, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Arrest to prevent commission of cognizable offences

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 170: Arrest to prevent commission of cognizable offences

Q: What is the consequence of the 24-hour limit imposed by sub-section (2)?
A: The consequence is that the police cannot use preventative arrests as a tool for indefinite, extrajudicial detention; they must either release the suspect or formally justify continued detention under another law within a day. [Source: Section 170, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Arrest to prevent commission of cognizable offences

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 171: Prevention of injury to public property

Q: Can a police officer stop someone from vandalizing a public monument?
A: Yes, a police officer may on their own authority intervene to prevent any attempted injury to public property or navigation marks. [Source: Section 171, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prevention of injury to public property

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 171: Prevention of injury to public property

Q: What is the purpose of Section 171 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 171 of BNSS 2023 empowers police officers to proactively interpose on their own authority to prevent vandalism, injury, or removal of public property and navigational landmarks. [Source: Section 171, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prevention of injury to public property

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 171: Prevention of injury to public property

Q: An officer sees someone trying to steal a buoy marking a safe channel for boats. Can the officer stop them immediately, or must they wait for a complaint from the port authority?
A: The officer "may of his own authority interpose to prevent... the removal or injury of any public landmark, buoy or other mark used for navigation," without waiting for a complaint. [Source: Section 171, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prevention of injury to public property

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 171: Prevention of injury to public property

Q: What two categories of public property are specifically protected under this section?
A: "any public property, movable or immovable" and "any public landmark, buoy or other mark used for navigation." [Source: Section 171, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prevention of injury to public property

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 171: Prevention of injury to public property

Q: Is this power limited only to property owned by the local municipality?
A: No, it broadly applies to "any public property," regardless of which specific government body owns it. [Source: Section 171, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prevention of injury to public property

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 171: Prevention of injury to public property

Q: What is the consequence of granting this power "of his own authority"?
A: The consequence is that it removes any bureaucratic hesitation; officers have the absolute, immediate legal mandate to physically protect state assets from destruction the moment they see an attempt occurring. [Source: Section 171, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prevention of injury to public property

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 172: Persons bound to conform to lawful directions of police

Q: If a police officer tells you to step back from a crime scene, do you legally have to obey?
A: Yes, all persons are bound to conform to the lawful directions of a police officer given in fulfillment of their duties, and can be detained if they refuse. [Source: Section 172, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Persons bound to conform to lawful directions of police

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 172: Persons bound to conform to lawful directions of police

Q: What does Section 172 of BNSS 2023 stipulate?
A: Section 172 of BNSS 2023 stipulates the legal obligation of the public to obey lawful police directions and grants police the power to detain or remove those who resist or disregard such directions. [Source: Section 172, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Persons bound to conform to lawful directions of police

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 172: Persons bound to conform to lawful directions of police

Q: A police officer cordons off a street to prevent a riot. A civilian ignores the officer and tries to walk through. Can the officer arrest them and hold them in a cell for two days?
A: No, under sub-section (2), the officer may detain them but in petty cases must "release him as soon as possible within a period of twenty-four hours" or take them to a Magistrate. [Source: Section 172, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Persons bound to conform to lawful directions of police

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 172: Persons bound to conform to lawful directions of police

Q: What specific behaviors by a person justify a police officer detaining or removing them under sub-section (2)?
A: "resisting, refusing, ignoring or disregarding to conform to any direction given by him." [Source: Section 172, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Persons bound to conform to lawful directions of police

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 172: Persons bound to conform to lawful directions of police

Q: Must a person obey a police officer if the officer tells them to do something completely unrelated to their duties, like buying the officer a coffee?
A: No, the section explicitly binds persons to conform only to "lawful directions of a police officer given in fulfilment of any of his duty under this Chapter." [Source: Section 172, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Persons bound to conform to lawful directions of police

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 172: Persons bound to conform to lawful directions of police

Q: What is the consequence of this section for civilian-police interactions during emergencies?
A: The consequence is that civilians cannot legally debate or ignore crowd-control or preventative instructions; non-compliance instantly empowers the police to physically remove or temporarily lock up the civilian to secure the area. [Source: Section 172, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Persons bound to conform to lawful directions of police

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 173: Information in cognizable cases

Q: How does the police officially record the first information of a serious crime (an FIR)?
A: Information about a cognizable offence can be given orally (and reduced to writing) or by electronic communication. It must be signed by the informant and entered into a specific police record book. [Source: Section 173, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Information in cognizable cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 173: Information in cognizable cases

Q: What is the core function of Section 173 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 173 of BNSS 2023 (historically Section 154 CrPC) governs the recording of the First Information Report (FIR) for cognizable offences, including provisions for electronic filing, zero FIRs, and special procedures for crimes against women. [Source: Section 173, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Information in cognizable cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 173: Information in cognizable cases

Q: A woman goes to the police station to report a sexual assault (an offence under section 64 BNS). The male officer on duty tells her she must recount the details to him. Is this procedurally correct?
A: No, the first proviso mandates that information regarding such offences "shall be recorded, by a woman police officer or any woman officer." [Source: Section 173, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Information in cognizable cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 173: Information in cognizable cases

Q: If a victim of an offence under section 64 BNS is physically disabled, where must the police record her information?
A: Under the second proviso, it must be recorded "at the residence of the person seeking to report such offence or at a convenient place of such person's choice, in the presence of an interpreter or a special educator." [Source: Section 173, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Information in cognizable cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 173: Information in cognizable cases

Q: If an informant files an FIR via an email or "electronic communication," is the process complete immediately upon sending?
A: No, under sub-section (1)(ii), it shall be taken on record "on being signed within three days by the person giving it." [Source: Section 173, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Information in cognizable cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 173: Information in cognizable cases

Q: What is the consequence if an officer in charge of a police station absolutely refuses to record a person's FIR?
A: Under sub-section (4), the consequence is that the aggrieved person may send the information by post to the Superintendent of Police, who can investigate it directly or direct a subordinate to do so, or the person can apply to a Magistrate. [Source: Section 173, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Information in cognizable cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 174: Information as to non-cognizable cases and investigation of such cases

Q: What happens when someone reports a minor crime (non-cognizable offence) to the police?
A: The police officer must enter the substance of the information into a prescribed book, refer the informant to the Magistrate, and forward a daily diary report to the Magistrate fortnightly. [Source: Section 174, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Information as to non-cognizable cases and investigation of such cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 174: Information as to non-cognizable cases and investigation of such cases

Q: What does Section 174 of BNSS 2023 dictate?
A: Section 174 of BNSS 2023 dictates the procedure for police handling non-cognizable offences, strictly prohibiting them from investigating such cases without a direct order from a Magistrate. [Source: Section 174, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Information as to non-cognizable cases and investigation of such cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 174: Information as to non-cognizable cases and investigation of such cases

Q: A person complains to the police about simple defamation (a non-cognizable offence). The officer feels sorry for them and immediately starts an investigation. Is this lawful?
A: No, under sub-section (2), "No police officer shall investigate a non-cognizable case without the order of a Magistrate having power to try such case or commit the case for trial." [Source: Section 174, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Information as to non-cognizable cases and investigation of such cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 174: Information as to non-cognizable cases and investigation of such cases

Q: Once a police officer does receive a Magistrate's order to investigate a non-cognizable case, what specific power do they still lack under sub-section (3)?
A: They may exercise all powers of an officer investigating a cognizable case, "(except the power to arrest without warrant)." [Source: Section 174, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Information as to non-cognizable cases and investigation of such cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 174: Information as to non-cognizable cases and investigation of such cases

Q: If a person reports two crimes at once—one non-cognizable and one cognizable—does the police have to split the case and get a Magistrate's order for the non-cognizable part?
A: No, under sub-section (4), "the case shall be deemed to be a cognizable case, notwithstanding that the other offences are non-cognizable." [Source: Section 174, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Information as to non-cognizable cases and investigation of such cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 174: Information as to non-cognizable cases and investigation of such cases

Q: What is the consequence of a case being deemed "cognizable" under sub-section (4)?
A: The consequence is that the police automatically gain the authority to investigate the entire matter, including the non-cognizable parts, without needing prior Magisterial permission. [Source: Section 174, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Information as to non-cognizable cases and investigation of such cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 175: Police officer’s power to investigate cognizable case

Q: Can a police officer start investigating a serious crime (cognizable offence) without waiting for a judge's permission?
A: Yes, an officer in charge of a police station can investigate any cognizable case within their local jurisdiction without the order of a Magistrate. [Source: Section 175, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Police officer’s power to investigate cognizable case

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 175: Police officer’s power to investigate cognizable case

Q: What is the core provision of Section 175 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 175 of BNSS 2023 empowers the police to independently initiate investigations into cognizable offences without Magisterial orders, while also allowing Magistrates to order such investigations under certain conditions. [Source: Section 175, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Police officer’s power to investigate cognizable case

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 175: Police officer’s power to investigate cognizable case

Q: A defense lawyer tries to throw out a murder investigation in court by claiming the specific police officer who investigated it lacked the exact territorial empowerment under section 175 to do so. Will this argument succeed?
A: No, under sub-section (2), "No proceeding of a police officer in any such case shall at any stage be called in question on the ground that the case was one which such officer was not empowered under this section to investigate." [Source: Section 175, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Police officer’s power to investigate cognizable case

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 175: Police officer’s power to investigate cognizable case

Q: Under sub-section (4), what two things must a Magistrate consider before ordering an investigation into a complaint against a public servant discharging their official duties?
A: The Magistrate must receive "a report containing facts and circumstances of the incident from the officer superior to him" and consider "the assertions made by the public servant as to the situation that led to the incident." [Source: Section 175, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Police officer’s power to investigate cognizable case

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 175: Police officer’s power to investigate cognizable case

Q: Can the Superintendent of Police take an investigation away from the regular station officer?
A: Yes, under the proviso to sub-section (1), considering the nature and gravity of the offence, the Superintendent "may require the Deputy Superintendent of Police to investigate the case." [Source: Section 175, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Police officer’s power to investigate cognizable case

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 175: Police officer’s power to investigate cognizable case

Q: What is the consequence of the protections offered to public servants in sub-section (4)?
A: The consequence is that public servants are shielded from immediate, frivolous criminal investigations by Magistrates over actions taken in their official capacity, ensuring their side of the story and a superior officer's report are considered first. [Source: Section 175, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Police officer’s power to investigate cognizable case

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 176: Procedure for investigation

Q: What must the police do immediately after they suspect a serious crime has been committed?
A: The officer in charge must send a report to the Magistrate and proceed (or depute a subordinate) to the spot to investigate the facts, discover the offender, and take necessary measures for arrest. [Source: Section 176, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure for investigation

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 176: Procedure for investigation

Q: What procedure does Section 176 of BNSS 2023 outline?
A: Section 176 of BNSS 2023 outlines the mandatory procedure for initiating a police investigation upon receiving information of a cognizable offence, including exceptions for minor offences and special rules for rape cases and forensic evidence gathering. [Source: Section 176, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure for investigation

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 176: Procedure for investigation

Q: A police officer receives a credible report of a murder (punishable by life/death). Do they have to call a forensic expert to the crime scene?
A: Yes, under sub-section (3), for offences punishable for seven years or more, the officer "shall... cause the forensic expert to visit the crime scene to collect forensic evidence... and also cause videography of the process." [Source: Section 176, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure for investigation

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 176: Procedure for investigation

Q: According to the second proviso to sub-section (1), where must the statement of a rape victim be recorded?
A: It "shall be conducted at the residence of the victim or in the place of her choice." [Source: Section 176, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure for investigation

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 176: Procedure for investigation

Q: If a person reports that their neighbor named 'John' stole a $5 garden gnome (a minor cognizable offence), does the police officer legally have to go to the house to investigate?
A: No, under proviso (a) to sub-section (1), when information is against a person by name and "the case is not of a serious nature," the officer "need not proceed in person or depute a subordinate officer to make an investigation on the spot." [Source: Section 176, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure for investigation

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 176: Procedure for investigation

Q: What is the consequence if a police officer decides under proviso (b) that there isn't sufficient ground to investigate a reported case?
A: The consequence is that under sub-section (2), the officer must state the reasons in their report to the Magistrate and must also "forthwith notify to the informant" that they will not investigate. [Source: Section 176, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure for investigation

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 177: Report how submitted

Q: How does the police report about a newly discovered crime actually reach the Magistrate?
A: If directed by the State Government, the report is submitted through a designated superior officer of police, who may add instructions before transmitting it to the Magistrate without delay. [Source: Section 177, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Report how submitted

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 177: Report how submitted

Q: What does Section 177 of BNSS 2023 regulate?
A: Section 177 of BNSS 2023 regulates the routing of the initial investigation report (often called the FIR or occurrence report) through superior police officers to the Magistrate. [Source: Section 177, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Report how submitted

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 177: Report how submitted

Q: A police station chief writes an initial crime report and sends it to their Superintendent as required by state rules. The Superintendent thinks the investigation approach is flawed. Can they intervene at this stage?
A: Yes, under sub-section (2), the superior officer "may give such instructions to the officer in charge of the police station as he thinks fit, and shall, after recording such instructions on such report, transmit the same." [Source: Section 177, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Report how submitted

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 177: Report how submitted

Q: What specific action must the superior officer take regarding the report after recording any instructions on it?
A: They must "transmit the same without delay to the Magistrate." [Source: Section 177, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Report how submitted

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 177: Report how submitted

Q: Do all reports across the entire country automatically have to go through a superior officer before reaching the Magistrate?
A: No, this routing is only required "if the State Government so directs" and through an officer it appoints "by general or special order." [Source: Section 177, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Report how submitted

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 177: Report how submitted

Q: What is the practical consequence of sub-section (2) for the investigation?
A: The consequence is that it provides a statutory mechanism for senior police leadership to review, correct, and guide the investigative strategy of subordinates right at the inception of a criminal case before the Magistrate even sees it. [Source: Section 177, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Report how submitted

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 178: Power to hold investigation or preliminary inquiry

Q: What can a Magistrate do once they receive the initial police report about a crime?
A: The Magistrate may direct a police investigation or decide to personally hold a preliminary inquiry, or depute a subordinate Magistrate to do so, or otherwise dispose of the case. [Source: Section 178, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to hold investigation or preliminary inquiry

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 178: Power to hold investigation or preliminary inquiry

Q: What power is given to the Magistrate in Section 178 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 178 of BNSS 2023 gives the Magistrate the power to control the direction of a new case upon receiving the police report (under Section 176), allowing them to order further police investigation or initiate a Magisterial inquiry. [Source: Section 178, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to hold investigation or preliminary inquiry

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 178: Power to hold investigation or preliminary inquiry

Q: The police send a report to the Magistrate stating they don't think there is enough evidence to investigate a reported kidnapping. The Magistrate disagrees. Can the Magistrate force the police to investigate?
A: Yes, under section 178, the Magistrate, on receiving the report under section 176, "may direct an investigation." [Source: Section 178, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to hold investigation or preliminary inquiry

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 178: Power to hold investigation or preliminary inquiry

Q: Under this section, what are the two distinct types of proceedings a Magistrate can initiate upon receiving the report?
A: The Magistrate may direct an "investigation" (which is done by the police) or hold a "preliminary inquiry" (which is done by a Magistrate). [Source: Section 178, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to hold investigation or preliminary inquiry

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 178: Power to hold investigation or preliminary inquiry

Q: Is the Magistrate forced to either order a police investigation or conduct a preliminary inquiry themselves?
A: No, the section gives them the broad discretion to "otherwise to dispose of, the case in the manner provided in this Sanhita." [Source: Section 178, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to hold investigation or preliminary inquiry

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 178: Power to hold investigation or preliminary inquiry

Q: What is the consequence of the powers granted in this section?
A: The consequence is that the police do not have the final say on whether a reported crime is pursued or dropped; the Magistrate serves as a vital judicial check, capable of overriding police inaction. [Source: Section 178, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to hold investigation or preliminary inquiry

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 179: Police officer's power to require attendance of witnesses

Q: Can a police officer force a witness to come to the police station for questioning?
A: Yes, a police officer can issue a written order requiring any acquainted person within their station's limits or adjoining stations to attend an investigation. [Source: Section 179, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Police officer's power to require attendance of witnesses

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 179: Police officer's power to require attendance of witnesses

Q: What does Section 179 of BNSS 2023 govern?
A: Section 179 of BNSS 2023 governs the police's power to compel the attendance of witnesses for investigation, while laying down strict protections against summoning vulnerable demographics to the police station. [Source: Section 179, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Police officer's power to require attendance of witnesses

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 179: Police officer's power to require attendance of witnesses

Q: A police officer issues a written order for a 65-year-old man to come to the police station for questioning about a robbery he witnessed. The man refuses to leave his home. Is the man breaking the law?
A: No, under the first proviso, no male person "above the age of sixty years... shall be required to attend at any place other than the place in which such person resides." The police order was unlawful. [Source: Section 179, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Police officer's power to require attendance of witnesses

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 179: Police officer's power to require attendance of witnesses

Q: What specific groups of people are protected from being required to attend an investigation at any place other than their residence?
A: A male person under fifteen or above sixty, a woman, a mentally or physically disabled person, or a person with acute illness. [Source: Section 179, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Police officer's power to require attendance of witnesses

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 179: Police officer's power to require attendance of witnesses

Q: If a woman witness actually wants to go to the police station to give her statement because she feels safer there than at home, is she allowed to?
A: Yes, the second proviso states: "if such person is willing to attend at the police station, such person may be permitted so to do." [Source: Section 179, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Police officer's power to require attendance of witnesses

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 179: Police officer's power to require attendance of witnesses

Q: What is the consequence of the State Government's power under sub-section (2)?
A: The consequence is that the State can establish rules to pay the "reasonable expenses" of witnesses who are compelled to travel to attend an investigation, preventing financial hardship for assisting law enforcement. [Source: Section 179, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Police officer's power to require attendance of witnesses

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 180: Examination of witnesses by police

Q: When the police are questioning a witness, does the witness have to answer every single question?
A: The witness is bound to answer all questions truly, except those questions whose answers would tend to expose them to a criminal charge, penalty, or forfeiture. [Source: Section 180, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Examination of witnesses by police

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 180: Examination of witnesses by police

Q: What is established by Section 180 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 180 of BNSS 2023 establishes the framework for the oral examination of witnesses by police, the obligation of witnesses to tell the truth (with self-incrimination protections), and the rules for recording these statements. [Source: Section 180, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Examination of witnesses by police

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 180: Examination of witnesses by police

Q: A police officer is typing out a witness's statement. The officer decides to merge the statements of three different witnesses into one document to save time. Is this allowed?
A: No, under sub-section (3), if the police officer reduces the statement to writing, "he shall make a separate and true record of the statement of each such person whose statement he records." [Source: Section 180, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Examination of witnesses by police

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 180: Examination of witnesses by police

Q: According to the second proviso of sub-section (3), who exactly is mandated to record the statement of a woman alleging a sexual offence (like under section 64 BNS)?
A: It "shall be recorded, by a woman police officer or any woman officer." [Source: Section 180, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Examination of witnesses by police

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 180: Examination of witnesses by police

Q: Are witnesses legally allowed to lie to the police during an investigation under this section if the truth wouldn't incriminate them?
A: No, sub-section (2) explicitly states that the person "shall be bound to answer truly all questions relating to such case." [Source: Section 180, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Examination of witnesses by police

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 180: Examination of witnesses by police

Q: What is the constitutional consequence of the exception provided in sub-section (2)?
A: The consequence is that it statutorily embeds the fundamental right against self-incrimination (Article 20(3) of the Constitution) directly into the police interrogation process, protecting witnesses from being forced to confess to crimes. [Source: Section 180, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Examination of witnesses by police

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 181: Statements to police and use thereof

Q: Do you have to sign the statement that the police write down after questioning you?
A: No, statements made to the police during an investigation and reduced to writing shall not be signed by the person making them. [Source: Section 181, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Statements to police and use thereof

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 181: Statements to police and use thereof

Q: What does Section 181 of BNSS 2023 govern?
A: Section 181 of BNSS 2023 governs the use of police statements (often called "161 statements" under the old CrPC) in court, strictly limiting their use primarily to contradicting the witness during cross-examination. [Source: Section 181, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Statements to police and use thereof

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 181: Statements to police and use thereof

Q: A witness tells the police the robber wore a blue shirt. At trial, the same witness testifies the robber wore a red shirt. Can the defense lawyer use the police statement to show the jury the witness changed their story?
A: Yes, under the proviso to sub-section (1), any part of the written statement "may be used by the accused... to contradict such witness in the manner provided by section 148 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023." [Source: Section 181, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Statements to police and use thereof

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 181: Statements to police and use thereof

Q: Can the prosecution (the state) use a police statement to contradict its own witness if the witness suddenly turns hostile in court?
A: Yes, but only "with the permission of the Court," as stated in the proviso to sub-section (1). [Source: Section 181, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Statements to police and use thereof

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 181: Statements to police and use thereof

Q: If a witness omitted a crucial fact when talking to the police but mentions it in court, can that omission be used as a "contradiction"?
A: Yes, the Explanation clarifies that an omission to state a fact "may amount to contradiction if the same appears to be significant and otherwise relevant having regard to the context." [Source: Section 181, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Statements to police and use thereof

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 181: Statements to police and use thereof

Q: What is the main legal consequence of prohibiting witnesses from signing their police statements?
A: The consequence is that witnesses are protected from being legally bound or overly pressured by police-drafted documents, ensuring that substantive evidence is given fresh in court under oath, rather than just rubber-stamping what the police wrote down. [Source: Section 181, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Statements to police and use thereof

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 182: No inducement to be offered

Q: Can the police offer you a bribe or threaten you to force you to make a statement?
A: No, no police officer or person in authority is allowed to offer any inducement, threat, or promise to influence a statement during an investigation. [Source: Section 182, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: No inducement to be offered

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 182: No inducement to be offered

Q: What is prohibited by Section 182 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 182 of BNSS 2023 strictly prohibits police officers from using inducements, threats, or promises to extract statements, while also ensuring police do not prevent individuals from making voluntary statements. [Source: Section 182, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: No inducement to be offered

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 182: No inducement to be offered

Q: An accused person decides they feel guilty and wants to confess everything to the investigating officer right there in the police station. Does the officer have to stop them and tell them to keep quiet?
A: No, under sub-section (2), "no police officer or other person shall prevent, by any caution or otherwise, any person from making... any statement which he may be disposed to make of his own free will." [Source: Section 182, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: No inducement to be offered

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 182: No inducement to be offered

Q: What specific section of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 defines the type of "inducement, threat or promise" forbidden here?
A: It is mentioned in "section 22 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023." [Source: Section 182, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: No inducement to be offered

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 182: No inducement to be offered

Q: Are there any circumstances under this section where an officer is allowed to legally threaten a suspect to get the truth?
A: No, sub-section (1) provides no exceptions; no police officer "shall offer or make... any such inducement, threat or promise." [Source: Section 182, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: No inducement to be offered

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 182: No inducement to be offered

Q: What is the intended consequence of this section on police interrogation methods?
A: The consequence is that it illegalizes coercive interrogation tactics, ensuring that any statements or confessions gathered during the investigation are the product of the witness or accused's free will, thereby safeguarding the integrity of the evidence. [Source: Section 182, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: No inducement to be offered

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 183: Recording of confessions and statements

Q: How is a formal confession or a victim's statement legally recorded by a judge before a trial starts?
A: A Magistrate records it after warning the person that they don't have to confess and that it can be used against them. The Magistrate must believe it is voluntary and signs a memorandum confirming this. [Source: Section 183, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Recording of confessions and statements

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 183: Recording of confessions and statements

Q: What does Section 183 of BNSS 2023 regulate?
A: Section 183 of BNSS 2023 (historically Section 164 CrPC) regulates the formal recording of confessions and statements by Magistrates during an investigation, with rigorous safeguards to ensure voluntariness and special rules for victims of sexual offences. [Source: Section 183, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Recording of confessions and statements

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 183: Recording of confessions and statements

Q: The police bring a suspect to a Magistrate to record a confession. The Magistrate warns the suspect. The suspect immediately says, "Actually, I changed my mind, I don't want to confess." What must the Magistrate do with the suspect now?
A: Under sub-section (3), "the Magistrate shall not authorise the detention of such person in police custody" if they state they are not willing to make the confession. [Source: Section 183, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Recording of confessions and statements

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 183: Recording of confessions and statements

Q: Before recording a confession, what two specific things must the Magistrate explain to the person making it?
A: The Magistrate must explain "that he is not bound to make a confession and that, if he does so, it may be used as evidence against him." [Source: Section 183, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Recording of confessions and statements

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 183: Recording of confessions and statements

Q: Can a police officer who has temporarily been granted the powers of a Magistrate record a legally binding confession under this section?
A: No, the second proviso to sub-section (1) explicitly states: "no confession shall be recorded by a police officer on whom any power of a Magistrate has been conferred." [Source: Section 183, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Recording of confessions and statements

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 183: Recording of confessions and statements

Q: For a victim of a sexual offence who is permanently physically disabled, what is the major consequence of having her statement recorded by a Magistrate under sub-section (6)(a)?
A: Under clause (b), the consequence is that this recorded statement "shall be considered a statement in lieu of examination-in-chief... such that the maker of the statement can be cross-examined on such statement, without the need for recording the same at the time of trial," sparing her the trauma of repeating the testimony. [Source: Section 183, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Recording of confessions and statements

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 184: Medical examination of victim of rape

Q: What must the police do if a woman is a victim of rape and needs a medical examination?
A: They must send her to a registered medical practitioner employed in a government or local authority hospital within 24 hours of receiving the information, and the doctor must examine her and prepare a detailed report. [Source: Section 184, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Medical examination of victim of rape

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 184: Medical examination of victim of rape

Q: What does Section 184 of BNSS 2023 dictate?
A: Section 184 of BNSS 2023 dictates the mandatory procedure and timeframe for the medical examination of rape victims, detailing the specific contents required in the medical report and the absolute necessity of consent. [Source: Section 184, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Medical examination of victim of rape

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 184: Medical examination of victim of rape

Q: A woman reports an attempted rape. The police take her to a private clinic because the government hospital is too far. The private doctor performs the examination with her consent. Is this allowed under the law?
A: Yes, sub-section (1) allows the examination to be conducted by "any other registered medical practitioner" in the "absence of such a practitioner" employed in a government or local authority hospital. [Source: Section 184, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Medical examination of victim of rape

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 184: Medical examination of victim of rape

Q: What specific detail about the timing of the examination must be noted in the medical report under sub-section (5)?
A: "The exact time of commencement and completion of the examination shall also be noted in the report." [Source: Section 184, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Medical examination of victim of rape

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 184: Medical examination of victim of rape

Q: Can a police officer order a doctor to medically examine a rape victim even if the victim refuses, in order to secure vital evidence?
A: No, sub-section (7) explicitly states: "Nothing in this section shall be construed as rendering lawful any examination without the consent of the woman or of any person competent to give such consent on her behalf." [Source: Section 184, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Medical examination of victim of rape

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 184: Medical examination of victim of rape

Q: What is the consequence of the 7-day rule in sub-section (6)?
A: The consequence is that the medical practitioner cannot indefinitely delay handing over crucial forensic evidence; they are legally bound to forward the report to the investigating officer within seven days, ensuring the investigation proceeds swiftly. [Source: Section 184, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Medical examination of victim of rape

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 185: Search by police officer

Q: Can a police officer search a house without a search warrant from a judge during an investigation?
A: Yes, if the officer has reasonable grounds to believe something necessary for the investigation is in a place within their station's limits and cannot be obtained otherwise without undue delay, they can record their reasons in writing and conduct the search. [Source: Section 185, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Search by police officer

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 185: Search by police officer

Q: What power is granted by Section 185 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 185 of BNSS 2023 grants police officers the power to conduct warrantless searches during investigations under exigent circumstances, requiring written justification, mandatory audio-video recording, and immediate reporting to a Magistrate. [Source: Section 185, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Search by police officer

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 185: Search by police officer

Q: An officer conducts a warrantless search of a suspect's warehouse. During the search, their phone dies so they don't record a video of it. Is this a violation of the procedure?
A: Yes, the proviso to sub-section (2) strictly mandates that "the search conducted under this section shall be recorded through audio-video electronic means preferably by mobile phone." [Source: Section 185, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Search by police officer

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 185: Search by police officer

Q: What two specific things must the police officer record in writing in the case-diary before conducting the warrantless search?
A: They must record "the grounds of his belief" and specify "so far as possible, the thing for which search is to be made." [Source: Section 185, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Search by police officer

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 185: Search by police officer

Q: Must the officer in charge of the police station personally conduct every single warrantless search?
A: No, under sub-section (3), if they are unable to conduct it in person, they may "require any officer subordinate to him to make the search" after recording the reasons and giving a written order. [Source: Section 185, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Search by police officer

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 185: Search by police officer

Q: What is the consequence of the requirement in sub-section (5) to send copies of the record to the nearest Magistrate within 48 hours?
A: The consequence is that the police are subjected to immediate judicial oversight; it prevents officers from secretly searching premises without a warrant and hiding the fact, ensuring accountability to both the judiciary and the property owner. [Source: Section 185, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Search by police officer

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 186: When officer in charge of police station may require another to issue search-warrant

Q: What happens if a police officer investigating a crime in Mumbai needs to search a house located in Pune?
A: The Mumbai officer can require the officer in charge of the Pune police station to conduct the search. In emergencies where delay would destroy evidence, the Mumbai officer can even search the Pune house themselves directly. [Source: Section 186, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: When officer in charge of police station may require another to issue search-warrant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 186: When officer in charge of police station may require another to issue search-warrant

Q: What does Section 186 of BNSS 2023 regulate?
A: Section 186 of BNSS 2023 regulates how a police officer can cause a search to be made outside the limits of their own police station, either by requesting the local officer or by executing an emergency search themselves. [Source: Section 186, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: When officer in charge of police station may require another to issue search-warrant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 186: When officer in charge of police station may require another to issue search-warrant

Q: A Delhi inspector needs to search a house in Noida right now because the suspect is currently burning evidence. Can the Delhi inspector just kick the door down and search it without asking the Noida police first?
A: Yes, under sub-section (3), if delay might result in evidence being concealed or destroyed, it is lawful for the officer "to search, or cause to be searched, any place in the limits of another police station... as if such place were within the limits of his own." [Source: Section 186, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: When officer in charge of police station may require another to issue search-warrant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 186: When officer in charge of police station may require another to issue search-warrant

Q: What must an officer conducting an emergency out-of-jurisdiction search under sub-section (3) send to the local police station officer afterwards?
A: Under sub-section (4), they must "forthwith send notice of the search... and shall also send with such notice a copy of the list (if any) prepared under section 103." [Source: Section 186, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: When officer in charge of police station may require another to issue search-warrant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 186: When officer in charge of police station may require another to issue search-warrant
