Q: Can a low-ranking police constable demand that another police station conduct a search for them?
A: No, under sub-section (1), only "An officer in charge of a police station or a police officer not being below the rank of sub-inspector making an investigation" can require this. [Source: Section 186, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: When officer in charge of police station may require another to issue search-warrant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 186: When officer in charge of police station may require another to issue search-warrant

Q: What is the operational consequence of sub-section (3)?
A: The consequence is that rigid territorial boundaries between police stations do not become a shield for criminals; investigating officers have the legal agility to cross jurisdictions instantly to secure evaporating evidence. [Source: Section 186, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: When officer in charge of police station may require another to issue search-warrant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 187: Procedure when investigation cannot be completed in twenty-four hours

Q: How long can the police keep someone in jail during an investigation before they must be released on bail?
A: A Magistrate can authorize detention in police or judicial custody, but the maximum total period before a right to default bail arises is 90 days for crimes punishable by 10+ years/life/death, and 60 days for all other offences. [Source: Section 187, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure when investigation cannot be completed in twenty-four hours

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 187: Procedure when investigation cannot be completed in twenty-four hours

Q: What is the primary function of Section 187 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 187 of BNSS 2023 (historically Section 167 CrPC) governs the procedure for extending an accused's detention beyond the initial 24 hours, setting strict maximum limits (60 or 90 days) after which "default bail" becomes a statutory right. [Source: Section 187, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure when investigation cannot be completed in twenty-four hours

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 187: Procedure when investigation cannot be completed in twenty-four hours

Q: The police arrest a suspect for a fraud punishable by 7 years. The investigation takes 70 days. The suspect applies for bail. Can the Magistrate refuse bail because the suspect might tamper with evidence?
A: No, under sub-section (3)(ii), for offences not punishable by 10+ years, the limit is 60 days. On expiry of 60 days, "the accused person shall be released on bail if he is prepared to and does furnish bail." The Magistrate has no discretion to refuse. [Source: Section 187, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure when investigation cannot be completed in twenty-four hours

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 187: Procedure when investigation cannot be completed in twenty-four hours

Q: Under sub-section (4), what is required before a Magistrate can authorise the detention of the accused in police custody?
A: The accused must be "produced before him in person for the first time and subsequently every time till the accused remains in the custody of the police." [Source: Section 187, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure when investigation cannot be completed in twenty-four hours

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 187: Procedure when investigation cannot be completed in twenty-four hours

Q: Can an Executive Magistrate (who is not a Judicial Magistrate) ever authorize the detention of an accused person?
A: Yes, under sub-section (6), if a Judicial Magistrate is not available, the police can transmit the accused to an Executive Magistrate, who can authorize detention for a term "not exceeding seven days in the aggregate." [Source: Section 187, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure when investigation cannot be completed in twenty-four hours

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 187: Procedure when investigation cannot be completed in twenty-four hours

Q: What is the consequence of Explanation I regarding the expiry of the 60/90 day period?
A: The consequence is that the release is not automatic or self-executing; if the accused does not actually furnish the required bail bond, they will continue to languish in custody despite the time limit expiring. [Source: Section 187, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure when investigation cannot be completed in twenty-four hours

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 188: Report of investigation by subordinate police officer

Q: What does a junior police officer do when they finish investigating a case?
A: When a subordinate police officer completes an investigation, they must report the results to the officer in charge of the police station. [Source: Section 188, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Report of investigation by subordinate police officer

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 188: Report of investigation by subordinate police officer

Q: What does Section 188 of BNSS 2023 state?
A: Section 188 of BNSS 2023 states the internal reporting requirement, mandating that subordinate investigating officers must submit the results of their investigations to the Station House Officer (SHO). [Source: Section 188, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Report of investigation by subordinate police officer

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 188: Report of investigation by subordinate police officer

Q: A Sub-Inspector finishes an investigation and directly files the final charge-sheet with the Magistrate without telling their Station House Officer. Is this procedurally correct?
A: No, under section 188, the subordinate officer "shall report the result of such investigation to the officer in charge of the police station," who is legally responsible for forwarding reports to the Magistrate. [Source: Section 188, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Report of investigation by subordinate police officer

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 188: Report of investigation by subordinate police officer

Q: Who exactly is bound by the requirement to report the results under this section?
A: "any subordinate police officer [who] has made any investigation under this Chapter." [Source: Section 188, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Report of investigation by subordinate police officer

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 188: Report of investigation by subordinate police officer

Q: Does this section allow the subordinate officer to skip the station officer and report directly to the Superintendent of Police?
A: No, the statute explicitly specifies they shall report "to the officer in charge of the police station." [Source: Section 188, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Report of investigation by subordinate police officer

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 188: Report of investigation by subordinate police officer

Q: What is the administrative consequence of this section within a police station?
A: The consequence is that the officer in charge of the police station maintains centralized oversight and ultimate legal accountability for all investigations conducted by personnel within their station. [Source: Section 188, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Report of investigation by subordinate police officer

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 189: Release of accused when evidence deficient

Q: What happens if the police arrest someone but then realize they don't have enough evidence against them?
A: If there isn't sufficient evidence or reasonable suspicion, the police officer must release the person from custody after having them sign a bond to appear before a Magistrate if required later. [Source: Section 189, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Release of accused when evidence deficient

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 189: Release of accused when evidence deficient

Q: What is the purpose of Section 189 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 189 of BNSS 2023 provides the mechanism for the police to release an accused person when an investigation reveals deficient evidence, preventing unnecessary forwarding of innocent or weakly-evidenced suspects to court. [Source: Section 189, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Release of accused when evidence deficient

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 189: Release of accused when evidence deficient

Q: The police arrest a man for theft but quickly realize it was a misunderstanding and there is zero evidence. Can the police just let him walk out the door unconditionally?
A: No, the officer shall "release him on his executing a bond or bail bond, as such officer may direct, to appear, if and when so required, before a Magistrate." [Source: Section 189, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Release of accused when evidence deficient

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 189: Release of accused when evidence deficient

Q: Under this section, who makes the subjective determination that there is "not sufficient evidence or reasonable ground of suspicion"?
A: "the officer in charge of the police station." [Source: Section 189, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Release of accused when evidence deficient

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 189: Release of accused when evidence deficient

Q: Does releasing the accused under this section completely close the case forever and guarantee they will never face trial?
A: No, the release is conditional; they are released on a bond "to appear, if and when so required, before a Magistrate... to try the accused or commit him for trial." [Source: Section 189, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Release of accused when evidence deficient

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 189: Release of accused when evidence deficient

Q: What is the consequence for the accused when this section is applied?
A: The consequence is that the accused regains their physical liberty immediately without enduring the delay and stigma of a court proceeding, though they remain legally tethered to the justice system via the bond. [Source: Section 189, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Release of accused when evidence deficient

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 190: Cases to be sent to Magistrate, when evidence is sufficient

Q: What do the police do when they finish an investigation and decide they have enough evidence to prosecute the suspect?
A: The police must forward the accused under custody to a Magistrate (or take security for their appearance if they are on bail), and make the witnesses sign bonds promising to show up in court to testify. [Source: Section 190, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cases to be sent to Magistrate, when evidence is sufficient

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 190: Cases to be sent to Magistrate, when evidence is sufficient

Q: What does Section 190 of BNSS 2023 require?
A: Section 190 of BNSS 2023 requires the police to forward the accused, the weapon/articles, and the bound-over witnesses to the Magistrate when an investigation yields sufficient evidence for trial. [Source: Section 190, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cases to be sent to Magistrate, when evidence is sufficient

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 190: Cases to be sent to Magistrate, when evidence is sufficient

Q: The police find enough evidence against a suspect who was never arrested during the investigation. They submit the report to the Magistrate. The Magistrate refuses to accept the report because the suspect isn't in custody. Is the Magistrate right?
A: No, under the proviso to sub-section (1), the Magistrate "shall not refuse to accept the same on the ground that the accused is not taken in custody." [Source: Section 190, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cases to be sent to Magistrate, when evidence is sufficient

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 190: Cases to be sent to Magistrate, when evidence is sufficient

Q: What specific items must the police officer send to the Magistrate along with forwarding the accused under sub-section (2)?
A: The officer "shall send to such Magistrate any weapon or other article which it may be necessary to produce before him." [Source: Section 190, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cases to be sent to Magistrate, when evidence is sufficient

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 190: Cases to be sent to Magistrate, when evidence is sufficient

Q: Do the police have to forward the accused in custody if the offence is a minor, bailable one?
A: No, under sub-section (1), "if the offence is bailable and the accused is able to give security, [the officer] shall take security from him for his appearance before such Magistrate." [Source: Section 190, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cases to be sent to Magistrate, when evidence is sufficient

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 190: Cases to be sent to Magistrate, when evidence is sufficient

Q: What is the consequence of the police requiring witnesses to execute a bond under sub-section (2)?
A: The consequence is that the prosecution's key witnesses are legally compelled to attend the upcoming trial, preventing the case from collapsing due to witnesses failing to show up at court. [Source: Section 190, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cases to be sent to Magistrate, when evidence is sufficient

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 191: Complainant and witnesses not to be required to accompany police officer and not to be

Q: Can a police officer force a witness to travel to court with them in the police car?
A: No, a complainant or witness on their way to court cannot be required to accompany a police officer or be subjected to unnecessary restraint, unless they refuse to attend court entirely. [Source: Section 191, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Complainant and witnesses not to be required to accompany police officer and not to be

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 191: Complainant and witnesses not to be required to accompany police officer and not to be

Q: What protection does Section 191 of BNSS 2023 offer?
A: Section 191 of BNSS 2023 offers protection to complainants and witnesses against police harassment and unnecessary restraint while traveling to court, preserving their dignity and independence. [Source: Section 191, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Complainant and witnesses not to be required to accompany police officer and not to be

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 191: Complainant and witnesses not to be required to accompany police officer and not to be

Q: A key witness refuses to sign the bond promising to appear in court under section 190. Can the police arrest the witness?
A: Yes, under the proviso, if a witness refuses to attend or execute a bond, the officer "may forward him in custody to the Magistrate, who may detain him in custody until he executes such bond, or until the hearing... is completed." [Source: Section 191, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Complainant and witnesses not to be required to accompany police officer and not to be

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 191: Complainant and witnesses not to be required to accompany police officer and not to be

Q: According to the main clause, what is the maximum level of security a police officer can normally require from a witness for their appearance?
A: They cannot be "required to give any security for his appearance other than his own bond." [Source: Section 191, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Complainant and witnesses not to be required to accompany police officer and not to be

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 191: Complainant and witnesses not to be required to accompany police officer and not to be

Q: Is there any situation where a witness can be subjected to restraint by the police while going to court?
A: Yes, as an exception in the proviso, if the witness "refuses to attend or to execute a bond," they may be forwarded in custody. [Source: Section 191, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Complainant and witnesses not to be required to accompany police officer and not to be

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 191: Complainant and witnesses not to be required to accompany police officer and not to be

Q: What is the intended consequence of this section for the justice system?
A: The consequence is that it encourages public cooperation by ensuring witnesses are treated as free citizens aiding the court, rather than being treated like suspects or prisoners by the investigating police. [Source: Section 191, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Complainant and witnesses not to be required to accompany police officer and not to be

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 192: Diary of proceedings in investigation

Q: Are police officers required to keep a daily log of their investigation activities?
A: Yes, every investigating officer must maintain a daily, paginated case diary detailing when information was received, times of investigation, places visited, and circumstances ascertained. [Source: Section 192, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Diary of proceedings in investigation

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 192: Diary of proceedings in investigation

Q: What does Section 192 of BNSS 2023 mandate?
A: Section 192 of BNSS 2023 mandates the creation and maintenance of a police case diary to chronologically track investigation proceedings, and strictly limits the accused's access to it during trial. [Source: Section 192, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Diary of proceedings in investigation

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 192: Diary of proceedings in investigation

Q: During a trial, the defense lawyer demands to see the police officer's case diary to check if the officer visited the crime scene on Tuesday. Does the court have to give the diary to the lawyer?
A: No, under sub-section (5), "Neither the accused nor his agents shall be entitled to call for such diaries, nor shall he or they be entitled to see them merely because they are referred to by the Court." [Source: Section 192, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Diary of proceedings in investigation

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 192: Diary of proceedings in investigation

Q: According to sub-section (2), what specific documents must be inserted into the case diary?
A: "The statements of witnesses recorded during the course of investigation under section 180 shall be inserted in the case diary." [Source: Section 192, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Diary of proceedings in investigation

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 192: Diary of proceedings in investigation

Q: Is there any situation where the accused is allowed to see the police diary during trial?
A: Yes, under sub-section (5), if the diaries "are used by the police officer who made them to refresh his memory, or if the Court uses them for the purpose of contradicting such police officer," then the accused gains access. [Source: Section 192, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Diary of proceedings in investigation

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 192: Diary of proceedings in investigation

Q: What is the consequence of the Court's power under sub-section (4) to use the diaries "to aid it in such inquiry or trial"?
A: The consequence is that the judge has a private, chronological roadmap of the entire police investigation to verify testimonies and clarify timelines, even though the diary itself cannot be used as formal evidence against the accused. [Source: Section 192, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Diary of proceedings in investigation

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 193: Report of police officer on completion of investigation

Q: What document does the police file with the court at the very end of an investigation?
A: They file a final report (often called a charge-sheet or challan) with the Magistrate, detailing the parties, the nature of the information, whether an offence was committed, and if the accused was arrested. [Source: Section 193, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Report of police officer on completion of investigation

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 193: Report of police officer on completion of investigation

Q: What is the function of Section 193 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 193 of BNSS 2023 (historically Section 173 CrPC) dictates the contents, timelines, and filing procedure of the final police report upon completion of an investigation, and establishes the right of the police to conduct further investigation even after filing it. [Source: Section 193, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Report of police officer on completion of investigation

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 193: Report of police officer on completion of investigation

Q: The police file their final report with the court. A week later, a new witness comes forward with a video of the crime. Can the police investigate this new evidence, or is the case closed because the report was filed?
A: They can investigate. Under sub-section (9), "Nothing in this section shall be deemed to preclude further investigation... and, where upon such investigation, the officer... obtains further evidence... he shall forward to the Magistrate a further report." [Source: Section 193, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Report of police officer on completion of investigation

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 193: Report of police officer on completion of investigation

Q: Under sub-section (2), what is the strict time limit for completing an investigation into child sexual abuse offences (POCSO Act) or severe rape offences?
A: It "shall be completed within two months from the date on which the information was recorded." [Source: Section 193, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Report of police officer on completion of investigation

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 193: Report of police officer on completion of investigation

Q: If a police officer thinks a witness's statement contains sensitive, irrelevant information that could harm the public interest, do they still have to give a copy to the accused?
A: Under sub-section (7), the officer can indicate that part of the statement, append a note requesting the Magistrate to exclude it from the copies granted to the accused, and state their reasons. [Source: Section 193, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Report of police officer on completion of investigation

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 193: Report of police officer on completion of investigation

Q: What is the consequence of sub-section (3)(ii) requiring the police to inform the informant/victim of the investigation's progress within 90 days?
A: The consequence is that victims are statutorily guaranteed transparency and updates regarding their case, preventing the police from leaving complainants in the dark about the fate of their FIRs. [Source: Section 193, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Report of police officer on completion of investigation

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 194: Police to enquire and report on suicide, etc

Q: What must the police do if they find out someone committed suicide or was killed in an accident?
A: The police must immediately inform the nearest Executive Magistrate empowered to hold inquests, proceed to the spot, investigate the apparent cause of death in front of local inhabitants, and draw up a detailed report. [Source: Section 194, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Police to enquire and report on suicide, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 194: Police to enquire and report on suicide, etc

Q: What duty does Section 194 of BNSS 2023 impose on the police?
A: Section 194 of BNSS 2023 imposes the duty on police to conduct an immediate inquest report (Panchnama) upon receiving information of unnatural deaths (suicide, murder, accident) and forward it to a Magistrate. [Source: Section 194, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Police to enquire and report on suicide, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 194: Police to enquire and report on suicide, etc

Q: A woman who has been married for 5 years commits suicide. The police investigate, find a suicide note, and conclude no one else was involved. Do they still have to send her body for a medical post-mortem examination?
A: Yes, under sub-section (3)(i), when "the case involves suicide by a woman within seven years of her marriage," the police officer "shall... forward the body, with a view to its being examined, to the nearest Civil Surgeon." [Source: Section 194, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Police to enquire and report on suicide, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 194: Police to enquire and report on suicide, etc

Q: According to sub-section (1), who must be present when the police officer makes the investigation and draws up the report of the apparent cause of death?
A: The investigation must be made "in the presence of two or more respectable inhabitants of the neighbourhood." [Source: Section 194, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Police to enquire and report on suicide, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 194: Police to enquire and report on suicide, etc

Q: Is there any situation where a police officer does not have to proceed to the place where the dead body is?
A: Yes, they do not have to proceed to the spot if "otherwise directed by any rule made by the State Government, or by any general or special order of the District or Sub-divisional Magistrate." [Source: Section 194, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Police to enquire and report on suicide, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 194: Police to enquire and report on suicide, etc

Q: What is the consequence of the 24-hour rule in sub-section (2)?
A: The consequence is that the initial police findings regarding an unnatural death are rapidly communicated to the District or Sub-divisional Magistrate, ensuring swift executive oversight and preventing evidence tampering or delayed reporting. [Source: Section 194, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Police to enquire and report on suicide, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 195: Power to summon persons

Q: Can the police force people in the neighborhood to come and answer questions when they are investigating a suspicious death?
A: Yes, the police can issue a written order summoning the respectable inhabitants and anyone else acquainted with the facts, and those summoned are bound to attend and answer truthfully. [Source: Section 195, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to summon persons

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 195: Power to summon persons

Q: What power is given to police officers by Section 195 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 195 of BNSS 2023 gives police officers conducting an inquest (under Section 194) the power to summon witnesses and compels those witnesses to answer questions truthfully, subject to protections against self-incrimination. [Source: Section 195, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to summon persons

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 195: Power to summon persons

Q: A police officer is investigating a fatal car crash. He issues a written summons to a 70-year-old man who witnessed it from his porch, ordering him to come down to the crash site to answer questions. Does the man have to go?
A: No, under the first proviso, no male person "above the age of sixty years... shall be required to attend at any place other than the place where such person resides." The officer must question him at his home. [Source: Section 195, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to summon persons

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 195: Power to summon persons

Q: When a witness is summoned under this section, what specific types of questions are they NOT bound to answer truly?
A: They are not bound to answer "questions the answers to which would have a tendency to expose him to a criminal charge or to a penalty or forfeiture." [Source: Section 195, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to summon persons

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 195: Power to summon persons

Q: If a woman witness wants to go to the police station to answer questions instead of having the police come to her house, is she allowed to do that?
A: Yes, under the second proviso, "if such person is willing to attend and answer at the police station, such person may be permitted so to do." [Source: Section 195, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to summon persons

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 195: Power to summon persons

Q: What is the consequence if the police investigation into the death reveals it was just an accident and no cognizable crime was committed?
A: Under sub-section (2), the consequence is that the summoned witnesses "shall not be required by the police officer to attend a Magistrate's Court," sparing them from unnecessary court appearances. [Source: Section 195, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to summon persons

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 196: Inquiry by Magistrate into cause of death

Q: Can a judge investigate a suspicious death themselves, instead of just relying on the police?
A: Yes, certain Magistrates are empowered to hold their own inquiry into the cause of an unnatural death, either instead of or in addition to the police investigation. [Source: Section 196, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Inquiry by Magistrate into cause of death

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 196: Inquiry by Magistrate into cause of death

Q: What does Section 196 of BNSS 2023 authorize?
A: Section 196 of BNSS 2023 authorizes and sometimes mandates Magisterial inquiries into unnatural deaths, particularly empowering them to order exhumations and mandating their involvement in cases of custodial death or custodial rape. [Source: Section 196, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Inquiry by Magistrate into cause of death

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 196: Inquiry by Magistrate into cause of death

Q: A person dies while in police custody at the station. The local police chief says his officers will investigate it thoroughly. Is a police investigation legally sufficient in this scenario?
A: No, under sub-section (2)(a), where any person dies or disappears in police custody, "in addition to the inquiry or investigation held by the police, an inquiry shall be held by the Magistrate within whose local jurisdiction the offence has been committed." [Source: Section 196, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Inquiry by Magistrate into cause of death

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 196: Inquiry by Magistrate into cause of death

Q: If a Magistrate decides to hold an inquiry into a death under this section, who must they try to inform and allow to be present?
A: Under sub-section (5), the Magistrate "shall, wherever practicable, inform the relatives of the deceased whose names and addresses are known, and shall allow them to remain present at the inquiry." [Source: Section 196, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Inquiry by Magistrate into cause of death

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 196: Inquiry by Magistrate into cause of death

Q: Is there any situation where a Magistrate can order a dead body that has already been buried to be dug up?
A: Yes, under sub-section (4), whenever the Magistrate "considers it expedient to make an examination of the dead body... in order to discover the cause of his death, the Magistrate may cause the body to be disinterred and examined." [Source: Section 196, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Inquiry by Magistrate into cause of death

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 196: Inquiry by Magistrate into cause of death

Q: What is the main consequence of making Magisterial inquiries mandatory for custodial deaths or rapes under sub-section (2)?
A: The consequence is that it provides an independent, judicial layer of scrutiny over incidents occurring while individuals are entirely under the state's control, preventing police cover-ups of custodial violence. [Source: Section 196, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Inquiry by Magistrate into cause of death

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 197: Ordinary place of inquiry and trial

Q: In which court should a criminal trial normally take place?
A: Normally, a crime should be inquired into and tried by a Court that has local jurisdiction over the specific area where the crime was committed. [Source: Section 197, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Ordinary place of inquiry and trial

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 197: Ordinary place of inquiry and trial

Q: What general rule is established by Section 197 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 197 of BNSS 2023 establishes the fundamental territorial rule of criminal jurisdiction: an offence is ordinarily to be inquired into and tried by the Court within whose local jurisdiction the offence occurred. [Source: Section 197, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Ordinary place of inquiry and trial

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 197: Ordinary place of inquiry and trial

Q: A man commits a robbery entirely within the city limits of Jaipur. He is later caught hiding in Delhi. Which city's court should ordinarily hold his trial?
A: The court in Jaipur. Under section 197, "Every offence shall ordinarily be inquired into and tried by a Court within whose local jurisdiction it was committed." [Source: Section 197, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Ordinary place of inquiry and trial

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 197: Ordinary place of inquiry and trial

Q: What is the key determining factor for deciding the "ordinary place" of inquiry and trial under this section?
A: The "local jurisdiction" where the offence "was committed." [Source: Section 197, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Ordinary place of inquiry and trial

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 197: Ordinary place of inquiry and trial

Q: Does the word "ordinarily" in this section mean that a trial can NEVER happen anywhere else?
A: No, the use of "ordinarily" indicates this is the general rule, but it is subject to exceptions provided in the subsequent sections of the Sanhita where jurisdiction might be shared or shifted. [Source: Section 197, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Ordinary place of inquiry and trial

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 197: Ordinary place of inquiry and trial

Q: What is the practical consequence of this territorial rule for the prosecution?
A: The consequence is that the prosecution must generally file the case in the geographical area where the crime happened, ensuring the trial is convenient for local witnesses and respects the specific jurisdiction's authority. [Source: Section 197, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Ordinary place of inquiry and trial

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 198: Place of inquiry or trial

Q: If a crime happens across the border of two different cities, which city's court handles the trial?
A: If an offence is committed partly in one area and partly in another, or if it's uncertain exactly where it happened, the court in *any* of those local areas can handle the inquiry or trial. [Source: Section 198, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Place of inquiry or trial

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 198: Place of inquiry or trial

Q: What jurisdictional issue does Section 198 of BNSS 2023 resolve?
A: Section 198 of BNSS 2023 resolves jurisdictional ambiguity by providing alternative venues for trial when an offence spans multiple local areas, is continuous, consists of several acts, or has an uncertain location. [Source: Section 198, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Place of inquiry or trial

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 198: Place of inquiry or trial

Q: A gang kidnaps a victim in District A, transports them through District B, and holds them hostage in District C. Which district court has jurisdiction to try the kidnapping case?
A: Under clause (c), because kidnapping is a "continuing one, and continues to be committed in more local areas than one," it may be tried by a Court having jurisdiction over District A, District B, or District C. [Source: Section 198, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Place of inquiry or trial

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 198: Place of inquiry or trial

Q: According to clause (a), what specific condition allows for multiple courts to potentially have jurisdiction over an offence?
A: "When it is uncertain in which of several local areas an offence was committed." [Source: Section 198, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Place of inquiry or trial

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 198: Place of inquiry or trial

Q: If an offence consists of planning a fraud in City X, executing it in City Y, and hiding the money in City Z, does the trial have to be held only where the final act occurred?
A: No, under clause (d), where an offence "consists of several acts done in different local areas, it may be inquired into or tried by a Court having jurisdiction over any of such local areas." [Source: Section 198, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Place of inquiry or trial

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 198: Place of inquiry or trial

Q: What is the consequence of allowing overlapping jurisdiction in these complex scenarios?
A: The consequence is that it prevents criminals from escaping justice on technicalities by claiming the prosecution filed the case in the "wrong" court when their criminal activities crossed municipal or district boundaries. [Source: Section 198, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Place of inquiry or trial

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 199: Offence triable where act is done or consequence ensues

Q: If someone does a criminal act in one place, but the bad result happens in another place, where is the trial held?
A: The trial can be held either in the court where the act was done OR in the court where the consequence occurred. [Source: Section 199, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Offence triable where act is done or consequence ensues

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 199: Offence triable where act is done or consequence ensues

Q: What jurisdictional rule does Section 199 of BNSS 2023 establish?
A: Section 199 of BNSS 2023 establishes that when an offence involves both a criminal act and a resulting consequence, jurisdiction lies concurrently with the Courts in both the location of the act and the location of the consequence. [Source: Section 199, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Offence triable where act is done or consequence ensues

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 199: Offence triable where act is done or consequence ensues

Q: A person mails a poisoned package from Chennai. The package is opened by the victim in Bengaluru, resulting in their death. Where can the murder trial take place?
A: The trial can take place in either Chennai (where the act of mailing the poison was done) or Bengaluru (where the consequence of death ensued), as per section 199. [Source: Section 199, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Offence triable where act is done or consequence ensues

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 199: Offence triable where act is done or consequence ensues

Q: Under this section, what two distinct components of an offence confer jurisdiction on a local court?
A: The "act which has been done" and the "consequence which has ensued." [Source: Section 199, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Offence triable where act is done or consequence ensues

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 199: Offence triable where act is done or consequence ensues

Q: Does the court where the consequence happened only get jurisdiction if the act itself was also committed within its borders?
A: No, the section uses the word "or", meaning jurisdiction vests in the Court within whose limits the consequence ensued, entirely regardless of where the originating act was performed. [Source: Section 199, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Offence triable where act is done or consequence ensues

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 199: Offence triable where act is done or consequence ensues

Q: What is the legal consequence of this "act and consequence" jurisdictional rule?
A: The consequence is that prosecutors have the flexibility to choose the most convenient or appropriate venue for trial based on where evidence and witnesses for either the wrongful act or the resulting harm are most accessible. [Source: Section 199, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Offence triable where act is done or consequence ensues

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 200: Place of trial where act is an offence by reason of relation to other offence

Q: If an act is only a crime because it is connected to another crime committed elsewhere, where can the trial happen?
A: The trial for the connected offence can take place either where that connected act was done or where the primary offence was committed. [Source: Section 200, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Place of trial where act is an offence by reason of relation to other offence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 200: Place of trial where act is an offence by reason of relation to other offence

Q: What does Section 200 of BNSS 2023 cover?
A: Section 200 of BNSS 2023 covers jurisdiction for related offences (like abetment or receiving stolen property), stating they can be tried either where the related act occurred or where the primary offence took place. [Source: Section 200, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Place of trial where act is an offence by reason of relation to other offence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 200: Place of trial where act is an offence by reason of relation to other offence

Q: A man in City A hires an assassin (abetment). The assassin commits the murder in City B. Can the man in City A be put on trial for abetment in City B's court?
A: Yes, under section 200, because abetment is an offence by reason of its relation to the murder, the abetment "may be inquired into or tried by a Court within whose local jurisdiction either act was done." Therefore, City B has jurisdiction. [Source: Section 200, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Place of trial where act is an offence by reason of relation to other offence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 200: Place of trial where act is an offence by reason of relation to other offence

Q: What specific type of relationship between two acts does this section address for determining jurisdiction?
A: It addresses a situation "When an act is an offence by reason of its relation to any other act which is also an offence". [Source: Section 200, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Place of trial where act is an offence by reason of relation to other offence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 200: Place of trial where act is an offence by reason of relation to other offence

Q: Does the primary actor actually have to be legally capable of committing the offence for this section to apply to the related act?
A: No, the section explicitly covers situations related to another act "which would be an offence if the doer were capable of committing an offence" (e.g., abetting a child or a person of unsound mind). [Source: Section 200, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Place of trial where act is an offence by reason of relation to other offence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 200: Place of trial where act is an offence by reason of relation to other offence

Q: What is the practical consequence of this rule for complex criminal conspiracies?
A: The consequence is that conspirators, abettors, and facilitators can be brought to trial in the same court as the principal offender where the main crime happened, enabling joint trials and a comprehensive presentation of evidence. [Source: Section 200, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Place of trial where act is an offence by reason of relation to other offence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 201: Place of trial in case of certain offences

Q: Where can a thief or someone caught with stolen property be put on trial?
A: They can be tried in the court where the theft happened, or in any court where the stolen property was possessed, received, or retained by someone who knew it was stolen. [Source: Section 201, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Place of trial in case of certain offences

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 201: Place of trial in case of certain offences

Q: What specific jurisdictional rules are detailed in Section 201 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 201 of BNSS 2023 details specific, expanded territorial jurisdictions for certain mobile or property-related offences, including dacoity, kidnapping, theft, extortion, robbery, and criminal misappropriation. [Source: Section 201, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Place of trial in case of certain offences

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 201: Place of trial in case of certain offences

Q: A criminal kidnaps a child in Delhi, transports them through Haryana, and hides them in a safehouse in Punjab. Can the trial for kidnapping ONLY happen in Delhi?
A: No, under sub-section (2), the offence of kidnapping "may be inquired into or tried by a Court within whose local jurisdiction the person was kidnapped or abducted or was conveyed or concealed or detained." Therefore, courts in Delhi, Haryana, or Punjab have jurisdiction. [Source: Section 201, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Place of trial in case of certain offences

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 201: Place of trial in case of certain offences

Q: According to sub-section (1), what two geographical locations provide jurisdiction for trying the offence of belonging to a gang of dacoits?
A: The court within whose local jurisdiction "the offence was committed" or where "the accused person is found." [Source: Section 201, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Place of trial in case of certain offences

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 201: Place of trial in case of certain offences

Q: If an employee commits criminal breach of trust by embezzling company funds in Mumbai but is supposed to account for those funds at the head office in Chennai, can they be tried in Chennai?
A: Yes, under sub-section (4), the offence may be tried where it was committed or where the property "was required to be returned or accounted for, by the accused person." [Source: Section 201, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Place of trial in case of certain offences

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 201: Place of trial in case of certain offences

Q: What is the consequence of these expanded jurisdictional rules for property offences?
A: The consequence is that law enforcement has the flexibility to prosecute thieves and fences in the jurisdiction where they are caught with the loot, rather than being forced to transfer the case back to the original site of the theft. [Source: Section 201, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Place of trial in case of certain offences

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 202: Offences committed by means of electronic communications, letters, etc

Q: If someone scams you over email or WhatsApp, which court handles the cheating case?
A: The cheating case can be tried in the court where the electronic message was sent from, where it was received, where the property was delivered by the victim, or where the scammer received the property. [Source: Section 202, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Offences committed by means of electronic communications, letters, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 202: Offences committed by means of electronic communications, letters, etc

Q: What modern issue does Section 202 of BNSS 2023 address regarding jurisdiction?
A: Section 202 of BNSS 2023 addresses jurisdiction for offences committed via electronic communications or letters (like cyber fraud and cheating), and also specifies jurisdiction for bigamy offences under the BNS. [Source: Section 202, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Offences committed by means of electronic communications, letters, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 202: Offences committed by means of electronic communications, letters, etc

Q: A scammer in Kolkata sends a fraudulent email to a victim in Hyderabad. The victim transfers money to the scammer's bank account in Mumbai. Can the victim file the case in Hyderabad?
A: Yes, under sub-section (1), cheating by electronic communications may be tried by a Court within whose local jurisdiction "such electronic communications... were received," which is Hyderabad. [Source: Section 202, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Offences committed by means of electronic communications, letters, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 202: Offences committed by means of electronic communications, letters, etc

Q: For offences punishable under section 82 of BNS (bigamy), what specific location related to the *first wife* grants jurisdiction to a court under sub-section (2)?
A: The court within whose local jurisdiction "the wife by the first marriage has taken up permanent residence after the commission of the offence." [Source: Section 202, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Offences committed by means of electronic communications, letters, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 202: Offences committed by means of electronic communications, letters, etc

Q: For a standard cheating case (not involving electronic messages/letters), does this section apply?
A: This specific section focuses on cheating where "the deception is practised by means of electronic communications or letters or telecommunication messages" and where property delivery is induced. General cheating without these elements would fall under general jurisdiction rules. [Source: Section 202, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Offences committed by means of electronic communications, letters, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 202: Offences committed by means of electronic communications, letters, etc

Q: What is the primary consequence of sub-section (1) for cybercrime victims?
A: The consequence is that cybercrime victims do not have to travel to the distant city where the cybercriminal is physically located to initiate a prosecution; they can seek justice in their own local courts where they received the deceptive message or lost their property. [Source: Section 202, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Offences committed by means of electronic communications, letters, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 203: Offence committed on journey or voyage

Q: If a crime happens on a moving train or a flying airplane, where does the trial take place?
A: The trial can take place in any court whose local jurisdiction the train, plane, or person passed through during that journey or voyage. [Source: Section 203, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Offence committed on journey or voyage

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 203: Offence committed on journey or voyage

Q: What specific scenario is addressed by Section 203 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 203 of BNSS 2023 addresses the jurisdictional challenge of offences committed during a journey or voyage, granting jurisdiction to any court along the route traversed by the person or thing involved. [Source: Section 203, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Offence committed on journey or voyage

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 203: Offence committed on journey or voyage

Q: A passenger's laptop is stolen on a train traveling from New Delhi to Bhopal. The theft is discovered when the train reaches Agra. Can the passenger file the case and have the trial in Gwalior (a city the train passed through between Agra and Bhopal)?
A: Yes, under section 203, the offence may be tried by a Court through whose local jurisdiction "that person or thing passed in the course of that journey," which includes Gwalior. [Source: Section 203, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Offence committed on journey or voyage

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 203: Offence committed on journey or voyage

Q: What specific entities must be "in the course of performing a journey or voyage" for this section to apply?
A: "the person by or against whom, or the thing in respect of which, the offence is committed". [Source: Section 203, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Offence committed on journey or voyage

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 203: Offence committed on journey or voyage

Q: If an offence happens at a train station *before* the journey begins, does this section apply to give jurisdiction to courts along the intended route?
A: No, the section specifically states "When an offence is committed *whilst* the person... or the thing... is *in the course of performing* a journey or voyage." [Source: Section 203, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Offence committed on journey or voyage

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 203: Offence committed on journey or voyage

Q: What is the practical consequence of this rule for law enforcement and travelers?
A: The consequence is that it eliminates the often impossible burden of proving exactly which territorial boundary a speeding vehicle was crossing at the exact moment a crime occurred inside it, allowing prosecution anywhere along the route. [Source: Section 203, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Offence committed on journey or voyage

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 204: Place of trial for offences triable together

Q: If a person is accused of multiple connected crimes, or if several people are accused together, which court handles the trial?
A: Any court that is competent to try *any* of the connected offences can handle the entire joint trial for all the offences and all the accused persons. [Source: Section 204, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Place of trial for offences triable together

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 204: Place of trial for offences triable together

Q: What jurisdictional principle is established by Section 204 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 204 of BNSS 2023 establishes that when offences or persons can be legally tried together (under joinder rules), any court competent to try one of those offences has jurisdiction to try the whole combined case. [Source: Section 204, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Place of trial for offences triable together

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 204: Place of trial for offences triable together

Q: A gang commits a robbery in District X and then immediately murders a witness in District Y. Because these acts form the same transaction, they can be tried together. Can District X's court conduct the trial for both the robbery AND the murder?
A: Yes, under section 204, if offences may be tried together, "the offences may be inquired into or tried by any Court competent to inquire into or try any of the offences." District X is competent to try the robbery, so it can try both. [Source: Section 204, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Place of trial for offences triable together

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 204: Place of trial for offences triable together

Q: What specific later sections of the Sanhita determine whether offences committed by one person can be "tried at one trial" under clause (a)?
A: "by virtue of the provisions of section 242, section 243 or section 244". [Source: Section 204, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Place of trial for offences triable together

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 204: Place of trial for offences triable together

Q: Does this section allow a very low-level court (like a Second Class Magistrate) to try a murder case just because it's joined with a minor theft case that the Magistrate is competent to try?
A: While section 204 grants territorial jurisdiction, it is implicitly subject to the court also having the substantive *power* to try the more severe offence (usually laid out in the First Schedule). A Magistrate cannot try a Sessions-triable offence, so the joint case must go to the higher competent court. [Source: Section 204, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Place of trial for offences triable together

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 204: Place of trial for offences triable together

Q: What is the practical consequence of this rule for the judicial system?
A: The consequence is judicial efficiency; it prevents the fragmentation of connected cases across multiple different territorial courts, saving time, reducing costs, and avoiding conflicting judgments on the same set of facts. [Source: Section 204, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Place of trial for offences triable together

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 205: Power to order cases to be tried in different sessions divisions

Q: Can a state government move a trial from one district to another within its state?
A: Yes, the State Government may direct that any case or class of cases committed for trial in a district may be tried in any sessions division, provided it doesn't conflict with High Court or Supreme Court orders. [Source: Section 205, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to order cases to be tried in different sessions divisions

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 205: Power to order cases to be tried in different sessions divisions

Q: What does Section 205 of BNSS 2023 allow the State Government to do?
A: Section 205 of BNSS 2023 allows the State Government to alter the normal territorial jurisdiction for trials by directing that cases committed in any district be tried in any sessions division. [Source: Section 205, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to order cases to be tried in different sessions divisions

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 205: Power to order cases to be tried in different sessions divisions

Q: The State Government issues an order to transfer a sensitive murder trial from District A to the Sessions division of District B. However, the High Court had previously issued an order keeping the trial in District A. Which order prevails?
A: The High Court's order prevails. The proviso to section 205 states that the State Government's direction must not be "repugnant to any direction previously issued by the High Court or the Supreme Court." [Source: Section 205, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to order cases to be tried in different sessions divisions

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 205: Power to order cases to be tried in different sessions divisions

Q: What specific type of "cases" does this section authorize the State Government to transfer?
A: "any case or class of cases committed for trial in any district". [Source: Section 205, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to order cases to be tried in different sessions divisions

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 205: Power to order cases to be tried in different sessions divisions

Q: Can the State Government use this section to transfer a case to a court outside the state?
A: No, the language allows transfer to "any sessions division," which implicitly means any sessions division within the jurisdiction of that specific State Government. [Source: Section 205, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to order cases to be tried in different sessions divisions

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 205: Power to order cases to be tried in different sessions divisions

Q: What is the intended consequence of this executive power?
A: The consequence is that the State Government can administratively manage the trial venue for reasons like security, public order, or judicial load, without needing complex judicial transfer proceedings, as long as higher courts haven't intervened. [Source: Section 205, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to order cases to be tried in different sessions divisions

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 206: High Court to decide, in case of doubt, district where inquiry or trial shall take place

Q: What happens if two different courts both think they have the right to try the exact same crime?
A: If both courts are under the same High Court, that High Court decides. If they are under different High Courts, the High Court where proceedings started first decides, and the other proceedings stop. [Source: Section 206, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: High Court to decide, in case of doubt, district where inquiry or trial shall take place

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 206: High Court to decide, in case of doubt, district where inquiry or trial shall take place

Q: What jurisdictional conflict does Section 206 of BNSS 2023 resolve?
A: Section 206 of BNSS 2023 resolves the conflict that arises when multiple courts take cognizance of the same offence, laying down the rule for which High Court acts as the final arbiter. [Source: Section 206, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: High Court to decide, in case of doubt, district where inquiry or trial shall take place

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 206: High Court to decide, in case of doubt, district where inquiry or trial shall take place

Q: A fraud case is registered in both a Mumbai court and a Pune court (both subordinate to the Bombay High Court). Both courts claim jurisdiction. Who resolves this?
A: Under clause (a), since both courts are subordinate to the same High Court, the question shall be decided "by that High Court" (the Bombay High Court). [Source: Section 206, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: High Court to decide, in case of doubt, district where inquiry or trial shall take place

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 206: High Court to decide, in case of doubt, district where inquiry or trial shall take place

Q: Under clause (b), if two courts under different High Courts take cognizance, which High Court has the power to decide the jurisdiction question?
A: "the High Court within the local limits of whose appellate criminal jurisdiction the proceedings were first commenced". [Source: Section 206, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: High Court to decide, in case of doubt, district where inquiry or trial shall take place

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 206: High Court to decide, in case of doubt, district where inquiry or trial shall take place

Q: Does the second court get to continue its trial while the High Court decides the issue under clause (b)?
A: No, the section explicitly states that once the High Court where proceedings first commenced takes up the question, "thereupon all other proceedings in respect of that offence shall be discontinued." [Source: Section 206, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: High Court to decide, in case of doubt, district where inquiry or trial shall take place

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 206: High Court to decide, in case of doubt, district where inquiry or trial shall take place

Q: What is the systemic consequence of the rule in clause (b)?
A: The consequence is the prevention of parallel trials, conflicting judgments, and double jeopardy across state lines, establishing a clear "first-in-time" rule for appellate jurisdiction over the dispute. [Source: Section 206, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: High Court to decide, in case of doubt, district where inquiry or trial shall take place

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 207: Power to issue summons or warrant for offence committed beyond local jurisdiction

Q: If a Magistrate knows a person in their town committed a crime somewhere else, can the Magistrate arrest them even if they don't have jurisdiction to try the case?
A: Yes, a First Class Magistrate can issue a summons or warrant, compel the person's appearance, and then send them to the correct Magistrate who actually has jurisdiction, or grant bail if applicable. [Source: Section 207, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to issue summons or warrant for offence committed beyond local jurisdiction

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 207: Power to issue summons or warrant for offence committed beyond local jurisdiction

Q: What does Section 207 of BNSS 2023 allow a Magistrate to do?
A: Section 207 of BNSS 2023 allows a Magistrate of the first class to initiate proceedings and compel the appearance of a person found within their local limits who committed an offence outside their jurisdiction. [Source: Section 207, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to issue summons or warrant for offence committed beyond local jurisdiction

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 207: Power to issue summons or warrant for offence committed beyond local jurisdiction

Q: A First Class Magistrate in Delhi learns that a man currently living in their jurisdiction committed a non-bailable theft in Chennai. The Magistrate summons him. Can the Delhi Magistrate try the theft case?
A: No, the Magistrate can inquire into it as if committed locally only to compel appearance, but must then "send such person to the Magistrate having jurisdiction to inquire into or try such offence." [Source: Section 207, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to issue summons or warrant for offence committed beyond local jurisdiction

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 207: Power to issue summons or warrant for offence committed beyond local jurisdiction

Q: If the offence committed outside the jurisdiction is not punishable with death or life imprisonment, what alternative does the Magistrate have instead of sending the person in custody to the correct court?
A: The Magistrate may "take a bond or bail bond for his appearance before the Magistrate having such jurisdiction." [Source: Section 207, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to issue summons or warrant for offence committed beyond local jurisdiction

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 207: Power to issue summons or warrant for offence committed beyond local jurisdiction

Q: What happens if there are multiple Magistrates who might have jurisdiction over the outside offence, and the current Magistrate isn't sure which one to send the accused to?
A: Under sub-section (2), "the case shall be reported for the orders of the High Court." [Source: Section 207, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to issue summons or warrant for offence committed beyond local jurisdiction

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 207: Power to issue summons or warrant for offence committed beyond local jurisdiction

Q: What is the practical consequence of this section for fugitives?
A: The consequence is that criminals cannot escape justice simply by crossing territorial boundaries and hiding in a different city; local Magistrates have the power to apprehend them and ship them back to the correct jurisdiction. [Source: Section 207, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to issue summons or warrant for offence committed beyond local jurisdiction

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 208: Offence committed outside India

Q: Can an Indian citizen be tried in India for a crime they committed in another country?
A: Yes, an Indian citizen committing an offence anywhere outside India can be tried at any place in India where they are found or where the offence is registered, subject to central government approval. [Source: Section 208, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Offence committed outside India

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 208: Offence committed outside India

Q: What does Section 208 of BNSS 2023 deal with?
A: Section 208 of BNSS 2023 deals with the extra-territorial jurisdiction of Indian courts, allowing the trial of Indian citizens for offences committed abroad, and foreigners for offences on Indian ships/aircraft. [Source: Section 208, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Offence committed outside India

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 208: Offence committed outside India

Q: A French citizen commits a murder while onboard a ship registered in India sailing in international waters. He is later found in Mumbai. Can he be tried in Mumbai?
A: Yes, under clause (b), an offence committed by a non-citizen "on any ship or aircraft registered in India" can be dealt with as if committed in India where he is found. [Source: Section 208, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Offence committed outside India

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 208: Offence committed outside India

Q: According to the proviso, what is the mandatory prerequisite before an Indian court can actually inquire into or try an offence committed outside India under this section?
A: It requires "the previous sanction of the Central Government." [Source: Section 208, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Offence committed outside India

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 208: Offence committed outside India

Q: If an Indian citizen commits an act in London that is a crime in India but legal in the UK, can they still be tried in India?
A: The section states "When an offence is committed...", implying it must be an offence under Indian law. Because of the extra-territorial application of the BNS, they can be tried in India as if the act was committed in India. [Source: Section 208, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Offence committed outside India

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 208: Offence committed outside India

Q: What is the consequence of the phrase "where he may be found or where the offence is registered in India"?
A: The consequence is that it provides flexible territorial jurisdiction; the trial doesn't have to wait until the fugitive is physically caught, as it can proceed where the FIR is registered, or alternatively, where they eventually land or are arrested. [Source: Section 208, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Offence committed outside India

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 209: Receipt of evidence relating to offences committed outside India

Q: In a trial in India for a crime committed abroad, can the court use evidence or witness statements collected by officials in that foreign country?
A: Yes, if the Central Government directs it, copies of depositions or exhibits produced before a foreign judicial officer or an Indian diplomat abroad can be received as evidence by the Indian court. [Source: Section 209, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Receipt of evidence relating to offences committed outside India

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 209: Receipt of evidence relating to offences committed outside India

Q: What does Section 209 of BNSS 2023 authorize?
A: Section 209 of BNSS 2023 authorizes the receipt of foreign evidence (depositions and exhibits) in Indian trials for offences committed outside India, subject to the Central Government's direction. [Source: Section 209, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Receipt of evidence relating to offences committed outside India

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 209: Receipt of evidence relating to offences committed outside India

Q: An Indian citizen is being tried in Delhi for a fraud committed in Dubai. A witness gave a sworn statement to an Indian consular representative in Dubai. The defense objects to this statement being used in court. Is it admissible?
A: Yes, if the Central Government directs it, depositions made "before a diplomatic or consular representative of India in or for that territory shall be received as evidence by the Court." [Source: Section 209, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Receipt of evidence relating to offences committed outside India

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 209: Receipt of evidence relating to offences committed outside India

Q: Under this section, what are the two types of officials abroad before whom the evidence must have been produced to be potentially admissible in India?
A: "before a judicial officer, in or for that territory or before a diplomatic or consular representative of India in or for that territory". [Source: Section 209, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Receipt of evidence relating to offences committed outside India

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 209: Receipt of evidence relating to offences committed outside India

Q: Can the Indian court automatically accept any foreign deposition it wants?
A: No, it requires that "the Central Government may, if it thinks fit, direct" that the copies be received as evidence. [Source: Section 209, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Receipt of evidence relating to offences committed outside India

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 209: Receipt of evidence relating to offences committed outside India

Q: What is the consequence of allowing this foreign evidence?
A: The consequence is that it overcomes the massive logistical and jurisdictional hurdles of compelling foreign witnesses to travel to India for a trial, making extra-territorial prosecutions under Section 208 practically feasible. [Source: Section 209, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Receipt of evidence relating to offences committed outside India

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 210: Cognizance of offences by Magistrate

Q: How does a Magistrate formally start dealing with a criminal case (take cognizance)?
A: A Magistrate takes cognizance in three ways: by receiving a complaint, upon a police report, or upon information received from any person or their own knowledge that a crime occurred. [Source: Section 210, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cognizance of offences by Magistrate

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 210: Cognizance of offences by Magistrate

Q: What is the core function of Section 210 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 210 of BNSS 2023 (historically Section 190 CrPC) outlines the three specific methods by which Magistrates are empowered to take "cognizance" of an offence, effectively initiating the judicial process. [Source: Section 210, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cognizance of offences by Magistrate

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 210: Cognizance of offences by Magistrate

Q: A Magistrate is walking down the street and personally witnesses a man assaulting another. Nobody files a police report or a formal complaint. Can the Magistrate initiate a case against the attacker?
A: Yes, under sub-section (1)(c), a Magistrate may take cognizance "upon his own knowledge, that such offence has been committed." [Source: Section 210, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cognizance of offences by Magistrate

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 210: Cognizance of offences by Magistrate

Q: Can a Magistrate take cognizance of a case if the police submit their report electronically rather than on paper?
A: Yes, clause (b) explicitly states: "upon a police report (submitted in any mode including electronic mode) of such facts." [Source: Section 210, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cognizance of offences by Magistrate

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 210: Cognizance of offences by Magistrate

Q: Can any Second Class Magistrate automatically take cognizance of offences just like a First Class Magistrate?
A: No, under sub-section (1), a Magistrate of the second class must be "specially empowered in this behalf under sub-section (2)" by the Chief Judicial Magistrate. [Source: Section 210, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cognizance of offences by Magistrate

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 210: Cognizance of offences by Magistrate

Q: What is the overarching legal consequence of a Magistrate "taking cognizance" under this section?
A: The consequence is the formal shift of the matter from a purely investigative police phase into the judicial machinery, activating the court's power to issue summons, warrants, and begin inquiry or trial procedures. [Source: Section 210, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cognizance of offences by Magistrate

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 211: Transfer on application of accused

Q: What right does an accused have if the Magistrate started the case based solely on the Magistrate's own personal knowledge or suspicion?
