A: The accused must be informed before evidence is taken that they have the right to have the case transferred to a different Magistrate. If they object to the current Magistrate, the case must be transferred. [Source: Section 211, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Transfer on application of accused

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 211: Transfer on application of accused

Q: What safeguard is provided by Section 211 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 211 of BNSS 2023 provides a safeguard against judicial bias by granting the accused the right to transfer the case if the Magistrate took cognizance based on their own knowledge or information (suo motu). [Source: Section 211, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Transfer on application of accused

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 211: Transfer on application of accused

Q: A Magistrate witnesses a theft and takes cognizance. The trial begins, and three witnesses give evidence. Then, the Magistrate informs the accused they can transfer the case. Is this legally valid?
A: No, section 211 mandates that the accused "shall, before any evidence is taken, be informed that he is entitled to have the case inquired into or tried by another Magistrate." Informing them after evidence is taken violates this. [Source: Section 211, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Transfer on application of accused

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 211: Transfer on application of accused

Q: Under which specific clause of Section 210 must the cognizance have been taken for this transfer right to apply?
A: It applies only when cognizance is taken "under clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 210" (information received from any person other than police, or own knowledge). [Source: Section 211, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Transfer on application of accused

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 211: Transfer on application of accused

Q: If there are five co-accused in a case, and four want to stay with the original Magistrate but one objects, does the case get transferred?
A: Yes, the section says "if the accused or any of the accused, if there be more than one, objects... the case shall be transferred". [Source: Section 211, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Transfer on application of accused

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 211: Transfer on application of accused

Q: What fundamental principle of natural justice does this section enforce?
A: The consequence is that it enforces the principle that "no man shall be a judge in his own cause," preventing a Magistrate from acting as both the initial witness/informant and the impartial judge in the same trial. [Source: Section 211, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Transfer on application of accused

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 212: Making over of cases to Magistrates

Q: Can a senior Magistrate assign a case to a junior Magistrate for trial?
A: Yes, a Chief Judicial Magistrate can take cognizance of an offence and then make over the case for inquiry or trial to any competent subordinate Magistrate. [Source: Section 212, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Making over of cases to Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 212: Making over of cases to Magistrates

Q: What administrative power is granted by Section 212 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 212 of BNSS 2023 grants the Chief Judicial Magistrate (and specially empowered First Class Magistrates) the power to distribute judicial workload by "making over" cases they have taken cognizance of to competent subordinate Magistrates. [Source: Section 212, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Making over of cases to Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 212: Making over of cases to Magistrates

Q: A regular Magistrate of the First Class takes cognizance of an assault case. Because they are busy, they decide to just hand the case file over to a Second Class Magistrate down the hall to try. Are they allowed to do this automatically?
A: No, under sub-section (2), a Magistrate of the first class can only make over a case if they are "empowered in this behalf by the Chief Judicial Magistrate." [Source: Section 212, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Making over of cases to Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 212: Making over of cases to Magistrates

Q: Who ultimately decides which specific Magistrate a First Class Magistrate can make a case over to?
A: The First Class Magistrate makes it over to "such other competent Magistrate as the Chief Judicial Magistrate may, by general or special order, specify". [Source: Section 212, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Making over of cases to Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 212: Making over of cases to Magistrates

Q: Can a Chief Judicial Magistrate make over a case to a subordinate Magistrate who does not legally have the power to try that specific type of offence?
A: No, sub-section (1) strictly says they may make over the case to "any competent Magistrate subordinate to him." An incompetent Magistrate cannot try the case. [Source: Section 212, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Making over of cases to Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 212: Making over of cases to Magistrates

Q: What is the practical consequence of this section for court administration?
A: The consequence is that it allows the Chief Judicial Magistrate to act as a central funnel for receiving new cases and efficiently distributing them among the subordinate judiciary based on caseloads and jurisdiction, without the police having to figure out exactly which judge to file with. [Source: Section 212, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Making over of cases to Magistrates

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 213: Cognizance of offences by Court of Session

Q: Can a person file a murder complaint directly in the Court of Session to start a trial?
A: No, generally a Court of Session cannot take cognizance of an offence directly. The case must first be filed with a Magistrate, who then "commits" (transfers) it to the Court of Session. [Source: Section 213, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cognizance of offences by Court of Session

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 213: Cognizance of offences by Court of Session

Q: What restriction is placed on the Court of Session by Section 213 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 213 of BNSS 2023 (historically Section 193 CrPC) establishes that a Court of Session does not have original jurisdiction to take cognizance of offences directly; it can only try cases that have been formally committed to it by a Magistrate. [Source: Section 213, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cognizance of offences by Court of Session

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 213: Cognizance of offences by Court of Session

Q: A victim of an acid attack wants the trial to happen quickly, so they bypass the local Magistrate and submit their complaint straight to the Sessions Judge. Can the Sessions Judge begin the trial based on this complaint?
A: No, under section 213, "no Court of Session shall take cognizance of any offence as a Court of original jurisdiction unless the case has been committed to it by a Magistrate." [Source: Section 213, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cognizance of offences by Court of Session

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 213: Cognizance of offences by Court of Session

Q: What is the required procedural step that must happen before a Court of Session can take cognizance of an offence?
A: The case must be "committed to it by a Magistrate under this Sanhita." [Source: Section 213, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cognizance of offences by Court of Session

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 213: Cognizance of offences by Court of Session

Q: Are there absolutely no situations where a Court of Session can take cognizance directly?
A: The section begins with the exception: "Except as otherwise expressly provided by this Sanhita or by any other law for the time being in force," meaning special laws (like the SC/ST Act or Defamation against high dignitaries) might allow direct cognizance. [Source: Section 213, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cognizance of offences by Court of Session

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 213: Cognizance of offences by Court of Session

Q: What is the systemic consequence of this rule for the criminal justice process?
A: The consequence is that Magistrates serve as the mandatory gatekeepers and filter for all serious crimes, ensuring that initial procedures, document supply to the accused, and basic scrutiny are completed before the heavy machinery of a Sessions trial begins. [Source: Section 213, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cognizance of offences by Court of Session

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 214: Additional Sessions Judges to try cases made over to them

Q: Which cases are handled by an Additional Sessions Judge?
A: An Additional Sessions Judge tries cases that are assigned to them by the main Sessions Judge of their division, or cases directed to them by the High Court. [Source: Section 214, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Additional Sessions Judges to try cases made over to them

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 214: Additional Sessions Judges to try cases made over to them

Q: What dictates the caseload of an Additional Sessions Judge under Section 214 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 214 of BNSS 2023 dictates that Additional Sessions Judges derive their specific trial docket entirely through assignment ("making over") by the principal Sessions Judge or by special orders from the High Court. [Source: Section 214, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Additional Sessions Judges to try cases made over to them

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 214: Additional Sessions Judges to try cases made over to them

Q: A Magistrate commits a murder case to the Court of Session. An Additional Sessions Judge in that division decides to take up the file directly and start the trial without asking the principal Sessions Judge. Is this proper?
A: No, an Additional Sessions Judge "shall try such cases as the Sessions Judge of the division may... make over to him." They cannot independently pull cases from the general docket without assignment. [Source: Section 214, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Additional Sessions Judges to try cases made over to them

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 214: Additional Sessions Judges to try cases made over to them

Q: Aside from the Sessions Judge of the division, who else has the authority to direct an Additional Sessions Judge to try a specific case?
A: "the High Court may, by special order, direct him to try." [Source: Section 214, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Additional Sessions Judges to try cases made over to them

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 214: Additional Sessions Judges to try cases made over to them

Q: Does the Sessions Judge have to make a specific order for every single individual case given to an Additional Sessions Judge?
A: No, the section allows the assignment to be done "by general or special order," meaning they can have a standing general order assigning certain types of cases or cases from certain areas. [Source: Section 214, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Additional Sessions Judges to try cases made over to them

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 214: Additional Sessions Judges to try cases made over to them

Q: What is the administrative consequence of this section within a Sessions Division?
A: The consequence is that the principal Sessions Judge acts as the master of the roster for the division, retaining administrative control over the distribution of work among all Additional Sessions Judges to ensure efficient case management. [Source: Section 214, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Additional Sessions Judges to try cases made over to them

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 215: Prosecution for contempt of lawful authority of public servants, for offences against public

Q: Can a regular citizen file a court complaint if someone disobeys a public servant or gives fake evidence in court?
A: No, for offences against the lawful authority of public servants or offences against public justice (like fake evidence), only the public servant concerned, the Court, or an authorized officer can file the written complaint. [Source: Section 215, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prosecution for contempt of lawful authority of public servants, for offences against public

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 215: Prosecution for contempt of lawful authority of public servants, for offences against public

Q: What limitation does Section 215 of BNSS 2023 impose on taking cognizance?
A: Section 215 of BNSS 2023 prohibits courts from taking cognizance of contempt of public servants, offences against public justice, and offences relating to documents given in evidence, except on a written complaint by the concerned public servant or Court. [Source: Section 215, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prosecution for contempt of lawful authority of public servants, for offences against public

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 215: Prosecution for contempt of lawful authority of public servants, for offences against public

Q: A witness commits perjury (gives false evidence) during a civil trial. The opposing party, angry at the lies, tries to file an FIR and get a Magistrate to start a criminal case against the witness. Can the Magistrate take cognizance based on the party's complaint?
A: No, under clause (b)(i), for offences related to proceedings in any Court (which includes perjury under BNS sections 229-233), the Court cannot take cognizance "except on the complaint in writing of that Court or by such officer of the Court as that Court may authorise". [Source: Section 215, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prosecution for contempt of lawful authority of public servants, for offences against public

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 215: Prosecution for contempt of lawful authority of public servants, for offences against public

Q: According to clause (a), who besides the "public servant concerned" can file the written complaint for contempt of their lawful authority?
A: "some other public servant to whom he is administratively subordinate or of some other public servant who is authorised by the concerned public servant so to do". [Source: Section 215, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prosecution for contempt of lawful authority of public servants, for offences against public

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 215: Prosecution for contempt of lawful authority of public servants, for offences against public

Q: If someone forges a document *before* any court case exists, and later that document is used in court, does this section bar a private complaint for the original forgery?
A: This section applies when an offence is alleged to have been committed "in respect of a document produced or given in evidence in a proceeding in any Court." Interpretation of this usually means the offence must relate to the court proceeding, but the strict text requires a court complaint if the document was produced in evidence. [Source: Section 215, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prosecution for contempt of lawful authority of public servants, for offences against public

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 215: Prosecution for contempt of lawful authority of public servants, for offences against public

Q: What is the consequence of making the public servant or Court the exclusive complainant for these offences?
A: The consequence is that it prevents private individuals from using these specific charges (like perjury or disobeying orders) as tools of harassment or retaliation against their opponents; only the aggrieved authority can initiate prosecution. [Source: Section 215, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prosecution for contempt of lawful authority of public servants, for offences against public

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 216: Procedure for witnesses in case of threatening, etc

Q: Who can file a complaint if a witness in a criminal case is being threatened?
A: The threatened witness themselves, or any other person, may file a complaint regarding the threatening of a witness. [Source: Section 216, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure for witnesses in case of threatening, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 216: Procedure for witnesses in case of threatening, etc

Q: What exception to general complaint rules does Section 216 of BNSS 2023 provide?
A: Section 216 of BNSS 2023 provides a broad locus standi for the offence of threatening a witness (under section 232 BNS), allowing the witness or "any other person" to file the complaint, unlike section 215 which restricts complainants. [Source: Section 216, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure for witnesses in case of threatening, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 216: Procedure for witnesses in case of threatening, etc

Q: A gangster's associate threatens a key witness not to testify. A bystander overhears this threat and goes to the magistrate to file a complaint, even though the witness themselves is too scared to do so. Can the magistrate accept the bystander's complaint?
A: Yes, under section 216, "A witness or any other person may file a complaint in relation to an offence under section 232 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023." [Source: Section 216, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure for witnesses in case of threatening, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 216: Procedure for witnesses in case of threatening, etc

Q: What specific section of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) does this provision apply to?
A: "an offence under section 232 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023." [Source: Section 216, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure for witnesses in case of threatening, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 216: Procedure for witnesses in case of threatening, etc

Q: Does this section require the court where the witness is supposed to testify to be the one filing the complaint about the threat?
A: No, unlike section 215 (which handles perjury/forgery in court), section 216 specifically allows "A witness or any other person" to file it directly, bypassing the need for a formal court complaint. [Source: Section 216, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure for witnesses in case of threatening, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 216: Procedure for witnesses in case of threatening, etc

Q: What is the consequence of allowing "any other person" to file this complaint?
A: The consequence is enhanced protection for the justice system; it ensures that intimidation tactics can be prosecuted even if the primary victim (the witness) is successfully silenced or too intimidated to approach the authorities themselves. [Source: Section 216, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure for witnesses in case of threatening, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 217: Prosecution for offences against State and for criminal conspiracy to commit such

Q: Can a citizen file a court case against someone for treason or waging war against the government?
A: No, a court cannot take cognizance of offences against the State or criminal conspiracy to commit them without the previous sanction (permission) of the Central Government, State Government, or District Magistrate. [Source: Section 217, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prosecution for offences against State and for criminal conspiracy to commit such

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 217: Prosecution for offences against State and for criminal conspiracy to commit such

Q: What mandatory requirement is established by Section 217 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 217 of BNSS 2023 establishes the mandatory requirement of prior government sanction before any court can take cognizance of offences against the State, promoting enmity between groups, or criminal conspiracy. [Source: Section 217, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prosecution for offences against State and for criminal conspiracy to commit such

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 217: Prosecution for offences against State and for criminal conspiracy to commit such

Q: A political activist gives a speech that someone believes is promoting hatred between religious groups (an offence under section 196 BNS). The person goes directly to a Magistrate to file a private complaint. Can the Magistrate immediately issue a summons?
A: No, under sub-section (1)(a), no Court shall take cognizance of an offence under section 196 of the BNS "except with the previous sanction of the Central Government or of the State Government." [Source: Section 217, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prosecution for offences against State and for criminal conspiracy to commit such

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 217: Prosecution for offences against State and for criminal conspiracy to commit such

Q: According to sub-section (3), which authorities can give written consent for initiating proceedings for criminal conspiracy (other than conspiracy for very serious crimes)?
A: "the State Government or the District Magistrate". [Source: Section 217, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prosecution for offences against State and for criminal conspiracy to commit such

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 217: Prosecution for offences against State and for criminal conspiracy to commit such

Q: Is government sanction required to prosecute a criminal conspiracy to commit a murder (punishable with death)?
A: No, sub-section (3) requires consent for criminal conspiracy "other than a criminal conspiracy to commit an offence punishable with death, imprisonment for life or rigorous imprisonment for a term of two years or upwards". Therefore, conspiracy to murder does not need this sanction. [Source: Section 217, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prosecution for offences against State and for criminal conspiracy to commit such

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 217: Prosecution for offences against State and for criminal conspiracy to commit such

Q: What is the consequence of sub-section (4) allowing the Government/Magistrate to order a preliminary investigation?
A: The consequence is that the sanctioning authority can gather facts through a police inspector before deciding whether to grant sanction, ensuring that frivolous or politically motivated allegations against the State are filtered out before a formal trial begins. [Source: Section 217, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prosecution for offences against State and for criminal conspiracy to commit such

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 218: Prosecution of Judges and public servants

Q: Can you directly sue a judge or a high-ranking government official in criminal court for something they did while doing their job?
A: Generally no. You cannot prosecute a Judge, Magistrate, or a public servant (removable only by the Government) for acts done in discharge of their official duty without previous sanction from the Central or State Government. [Source: Section 218, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prosecution of Judges and public servants

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 218: Prosecution of Judges and public servants

Q: What protection does Section 218 of BNSS 2023 provide?
A: Section 218 of BNSS 2023 provides immunity from prosecution to Judges, Magistrates, certain public servants, and Armed Forces members for acts committed in the discharge of official duties, requiring prior government sanction to take cognizance. [Source: Section 218, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prosecution of Judges and public servants

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 218: Prosecution of Judges and public servants

Q: A citizen alleges a police officer beat him during a riot control operation. The citizen tries to file a case in court. The officer claims he was discharging his official duty. Does the court need permission to try the officer?
A: Yes, if the officer is a public servant not removable from office save by government sanction, and the act was "while acting or purporting to act in the discharge of his official duty," the court cannot take cognizance "except with the previous sanction" of the relevant Government. [Source: Section 218, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prosecution of Judges and public servants

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 218: Prosecution of Judges and public servants

Q: What happens if the Government receives a request for sanction to prosecute a public servant but just ignores it and doesn't reply for 5 months?
A: Under the second proviso to sub-section (1), the Government must take a decision within 120 days. If it fails to do so, "the sanction shall be deemed to have been accorded by such Government." [Source: Section 218, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prosecution of Judges and public servants

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 218: Prosecution of Judges and public servants

Q: Does a public servant need sanction to be prosecuted for sexual offences like rape or sexual harassment committed while on duty?
A: No, the third proviso explicitly states "no sanction shall be required in case of a public servant accused of any offence alleged to have been committed under section 64, section 65... [and other sexual offence sections] of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023." [Source: Section 218, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prosecution of Judges and public servants

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 218: Prosecution of Judges and public servants

Q: What is the legal consequence of sub-section (5) for a sanctioned prosecution?
A: The consequence is that the Government retains control even after granting sanction, as it "may determine the person by whom, the manner in which... the prosecution... is to be conducted, and may specify the Court before which the trial is to be held." [Source: Section 218, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prosecution of Judges and public servants

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 219: Prosecution for offences against marriage

Q: If a man commits bigamy (marries someone else while already married), can anyone walking down the street file a criminal case against him?
A: No, for offences against marriage (like bigamy or deceitful marriage), the court can only take the case if the complaint is made by the "person aggrieved by the offence" (e.g., the victimized spouse), with some exceptions for relatives. [Source: Section 219, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prosecution for offences against marriage

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 219: Prosecution for offences against marriage

Q: What limitation does Section 219 of BNSS 2023 place on prosecution?
A: Section 219 of BNSS 2023 dictates that offences against marriage (sections 81-84 BNS) can generally only be prosecuted upon a complaint by the "person aggrieved," barring strangers from interfering in matrimonial disputes. [Source: Section 219, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prosecution for offences against marriage

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 219: Prosecution for offences against marriage

Q: A man discovers that his neighbor's wife has committed bigamy. The husband doesn't want to press charges, but the man feels strongly about the law and files a complaint with the Magistrate. Can the Magistrate take cognizance?
A: No, under section 219, no Court shall take cognizance except upon a complaint made by "some person aggrieved by the offence." The neighbor is not an aggrieved person in this context. [Source: Section 219, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prosecution for offences against marriage

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 219: Prosecution for offences against marriage

Q: According to clause (c) of the proviso, if the aggrieved person is a wife whose husband has committed bigamy (section 82 BNS), who else is explicitly allowed to file the complaint on her behalf?
A: "her father, mother, brother, sister, son or daughter or by her father's or mother's brother or sister, or, with the leave of the Court, by any other person related to her by blood, marriage or adoption." [Source: Section 219, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prosecution for offences against marriage

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 219: Prosecution for offences against marriage

Q: If a husband commits an offence under section 84 BNS (enticing or taking away a married woman), can the woman's father be considered the "aggrieved" person and file the complaint?
A: No, sub-section (2) explicitly states: "no person other than the husband of the woman shall be deemed to be aggrieved by any offence punishable under section 84". [Source: Section 219, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prosecution for offences against marriage

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 219: Prosecution for offences against marriage

Q: What is the consequence of the one-year limitation in sub-section (6) regarding marital rape of a minor wife (under 18)?
A: The consequence is that if a husband has sexual intercourse with his own wife who is under 18 (an offence under section 64 BNS), the court cannot take cognizance if more than one year has passed since the offence was committed, acting as a strict statute of limitations. [Source: Section 219, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prosecution for offences against marriage

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 220: Prosecution of offences under section 85 of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023

Q: Who can file a criminal case against a husband or his relatives for subjecting a woman to cruelty?
A: A court can take the case based on a police report, or a complaint made by the aggrieved woman herself, her parents, siblings, aunts/uncles, or with court permission, other relatives by blood, marriage, or adoption. [Source: Section 220, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prosecution of offences under section 85 of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 220: Prosecution of offences under section 85 of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023

Q: What does Section 220 of BNSS 2023 regulate?
A: Section 220 of BNSS 2023 regulates the initiation of prosecution for the offence of cruelty by a husband or his relatives (Section 85 BNS), specifying exactly who has the legal standing to file a complaint. [Source: Section 220, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prosecution of offences under section 85 of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 220: Prosecution of offences under section 85 of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023

Q: A woman is being subjected to cruelty by her husband for dowry. She is too afraid to go to the police. Her brother goes to the Magistrate and files a formal complaint against the husband. Is the Magistrate allowed to take cognizance based on the brother's complaint?
A: Yes, under section 220, cognizance can be taken "upon a complaint made by... her father, mother, brother, sister". The brother has legal standing to file. [Source: Section 220, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prosecution of offences under section 85 of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 220: Prosecution of offences under section 85 of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023

Q: What are the two primary methods by which a Court can take cognizance of an offence under Section 85 of BNS according to this section?
A: "upon a police report of facts which constitute such offence" OR "upon a complaint made by the person aggrieved... or by her [specified relatives]". [Source: Section 220, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prosecution of offences under section 85 of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 220: Prosecution of offences under section 85 of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023

Q: Can a close friend of the victim, who is not related to her by blood, marriage, or adoption, file a direct complaint to the Magistrate under this section?
A: No, the section restricts private complaints to the aggrieved person, specific close relatives, or "with the leave of the Court, by any other person related to her by blood, marriage or adoption." A non-relative friend does not have standing. [Source: Section 220, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prosecution of offences under section 85 of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 220: Prosecution of offences under section 85 of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023

Q: What is the practical consequence of allowing police reports to initiate these cases, unlike general matrimonial offences?
A: The consequence is that cruelty against women is treated as a severe societal issue, allowing state machinery (police) to investigate and prosecute it directly upon receiving information, rather than strictly relying on the victim or her family to initiate a private court battle. [Source: Section 220, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prosecution of offences under section 85 of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 221: Cognizance of offence

Q: What is required for a court to start a case against a husband for having sexual intercourse with his wife during a separation without her consent?
A: The court can only start the case if the wife herself files a complaint against the husband, and the court is prima facie satisfied with the facts. [Source: Section 221, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cognizance of offence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 221: Cognizance of offence

Q: What specific offence is addressed by Section 221 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 221 of BNSS 2023 specifically addresses the cognizance of an offence under section 67 BNS (sexual intercourse by a man with his wife during separation without consent), requiring a complaint by the wife. [Source: Section 221, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cognizance of offence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 221: Cognizance of offence

Q: A husband and wife are legally separated. The husband forces sexual intercourse upon the wife. The wife tells her sister, and the sister goes to the Magistrate to file a complaint under Section 67 BNS. Can the Magistrate take cognizance?
A: No, under section 221, the Court shall not take cognizance "except upon prima facie satisfaction... upon a complaint having been filed or made by the wife against the husband." The sister cannot file it on her behalf. [Source: Section 221, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cognizance of offence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 221: Cognizance of offence

Q: What specific level of judicial scrutiny is mandated before taking cognizance under this section?
A: "except upon prima facie satisfaction of the facts which constitute the offence". [Source: Section 221, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cognizance of offence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 221: Cognizance of offence

Q: Can the police file a charge sheet (police report) to initiate prosecution for an offence under section 67 BNS?
A: No, the section strictly limits cognizance to instances where a complaint has been "filed or made by the wife against the husband," precluding state initiation via a police report. [Source: Section 221, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cognizance of offence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 221: Cognizance of offence

Q: What is the consequence of this strict requirement?
A: The consequence is that it protects the highly private nature of marital separation, ensuring that criminal proceedings for this specific offence can only be triggered by the direct, autonomous decision of the aggrieved wife, preventing third-party interference. [Source: Section 221, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cognizance of offence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 222: Prosecution for defamation

Q: If a regular citizen is defamed, who has to file the criminal complaint?
A: For a regular citizen, the "person aggrieved" (the person who was defamed) must personally make the complaint to the court. [Source: Section 222, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prosecution for defamation

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 222: Prosecution for defamation

Q: What special procedure does Section 222 of BNSS 2023 outline?
A: Section 222 of BNSS 2023 outlines the procedure for prosecuting defamation, establishing the general rule that only the aggrieved person can complain, but creating a special, direct-to-Sessions procedure for defaming high-ranking state officials. [Source: Section 222, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prosecution for defamation

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 222: Prosecution for defamation

Q: A newspaper publishes a highly defamatory article about the President of India's conduct during a state visit. Does the President have to personally go to a Magistrate's court to file a complaint?
A: No, under sub-section (2), when defamation is against the President regarding their public functions, "a Court of Session may take cognizance of such offence... upon a complaint in writing made by the Public Prosecutor." [Source: Section 222, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prosecution for defamation

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 222: Prosecution for defamation

Q: If the Public Prosecutor wants to file a defamation complaint on behalf of a State Minister, whose previous sanction is required under sub-section (4)?
A: The previous sanction "of the State Government". [Source: Section 222, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prosecution for defamation

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 222: Prosecution for defamation

Q: If a public servant is defamed, is the special Public Prosecutor route their *only* option for getting justice?
A: No, sub-section (6) explicitly states: "Nothing in this section shall affect the right of the person... to make a complaint in respect of that offence before a Magistrate having jurisdiction". The public servant can still file a regular private complaint. [Source: Section 222, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prosecution for defamation

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 222: Prosecution for defamation

Q: What is the consequence of the six-month time limit in sub-section (5)?
A: The consequence is that the special, expedited procedure of having a Public Prosecutor file directly in a Court of Session for defaming a public official is only available if initiated swiftly (within 6 months); otherwise, they must use the standard Magistrate complaint route. [Source: Section 222, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prosecution for defamation

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 223: Examination of complainant

Q: When someone files a private criminal complaint directly to a Magistrate, what is the very first thing the Magistrate must do?
A: The Magistrate must examine the complainant and any witnesses present on oath, write down what they say, and have everyone sign it. Crucially, the Magistrate must also give the accused an opportunity to be heard before taking cognizance. [Source: Section 223, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Examination of complainant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 223: Examination of complainant

Q: What mandatory procedural step is introduced by Section 223 of BNSS 2023 for private complaints?
A: Section 223 of BNSS 2023 mandates the examination of the complainant on oath, but importantly adds a new proviso that no cognizance shall be taken without first "giving the accused an opportunity of being heard," preventing ex-parte initiation of cases. [Source: Section 223, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Examination of complainant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 223: Examination of complainant

Q: A man files a written complaint alleging fraud against his business partner. The Magistrate immediately registers the case and issues an arrest warrant for the partner without ever notifying him. Is this allowed under BNSS 2023?
A: No, the first proviso strictly states that "no cognizance of an offence shall be taken by the Magistrate without giving the accused an opportunity of being heard." The Magistrate must give notice to the partner first. [Source: Section 223, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Examination of complainant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 223: Examination of complainant

Q: Before a Magistrate can take cognizance of a complaint against a public servant acting in official duty, what two conditions must be met under sub-section (2)?
A: (a) The public servant must be given an opportunity to make assertions about the situation, and (b) "a report containing facts and circumstances of the incident from the officer superior to such public servant is received." [Source: Section 223, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Examination of complainant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 223: Examination of complainant

Q: Does a Magistrate *always* have to examine the complainant on oath if the complaint is in writing?
A: No, under the second proviso, the Magistrate need not examine them if "a public servant acting or purporting to act in the discharge of his official duties or a Court has made the complaint," or if the Magistrate makes the case over to another Magistrate. [Source: Section 223, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Examination of complainant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 223: Examination of complainant

Q: What is the consequence of requiring a superior officer's report before prosecuting a public servant under sub-section (2)?
A: The consequence is an added layer of administrative scrutiny that protects public servants from frivolous or vindictive criminal complaints regarding their official acts, ensuring the court has institutional context before proceeding. [Source: Section 223, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Examination of complainant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 224: Procedure by Magistrate not competent to take cognizance of case

Q: What should a judge do if someone hands them a written criminal complaint, but the judge realizes they don't have the legal authority (jurisdiction) to handle that specific type of case?
A: The judge must return the written complaint to the person, write an endorsement on it stating it's being returned, and tell them to present it to the proper, competent court. [Source: Section 224, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure by Magistrate not competent to take cognizance of case

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 224: Procedure by Magistrate not competent to take cognizance of case

Q: What does Section 224 of BNSS 2023 instruct a Magistrate to do?
A: Section 224 of BNSS 2023 instructs a Magistrate who receives a complaint they are not competent to take cognizance of (due to lack of territorial or subject-matter jurisdiction) to return it for presentation to the proper Court. [Source: Section 224, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure by Magistrate not competent to take cognizance of case

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 224: Procedure by Magistrate not competent to take cognizance of case

Q: A person verbally complains to a Second Class Magistrate about a murder (a Sessions-triable offence they cannot take cognizance of). What must the Magistrate do?
A: Under clause (b), because the complaint is not in writing, the Magistrate shall "direct the complainant to the proper Court." [Source: Section 224, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure by Magistrate not competent to take cognizance of case

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 224: Procedure by Magistrate not competent to take cognizance of case

Q: If a written complaint is made to an incompetent Magistrate, what specific action must the Magistrate take upon returning the physical document?
A: The Magistrate must return it "with an endorsement to that effect" (i.e., writing on the complaint that it is being returned for lack of jurisdiction). [Source: Section 224, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure by Magistrate not competent to take cognizance of case

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 224: Procedure by Magistrate not competent to take cognizance of case

Q: Does the Magistrate have the power to just throw the complaint away or dismiss the case entirely because they don't have jurisdiction?
A: No, the section does not authorize dismissal on merits; it strictly mandates administrative routing—either returning the document or directing the person to the correct venue, preserving the complainant's right to seek justice. [Source: Section 224, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure by Magistrate not competent to take cognizance of case

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 224: Procedure by Magistrate not competent to take cognizance of case

Q: What is the practical consequence of this rule for the complainant?
A: The consequence is that it saves the complainant from having their case permanently dismissed due to a procedural filing error; instead, they are guided to the correct judicial forum to have their grievances heard. [Source: Section 224, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure by Magistrate not competent to take cognizance of case

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 225: Postponement of issue of process

Q: When a Magistrate gets a complaint, do they have to immediately issue a summons to the accused?
A: No, the Magistrate may (and must, if the accused lives outside their area) postpone issuing process to either inquire into the case themselves or order a police investigation to see if there's sufficient ground to proceed. [Source: Section 225, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Postponement of issue of process

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 225: Postponement of issue of process

Q: What procedure does Section 225 of BNSS 2023 authorize?
A: Section 225 of BNSS 2023 authorizes a Magistrate to postpone the issue of process (summons/warrant) and conduct a preliminary inquiry or direct a police investigation to ascertain if there are sufficient grounds for proceeding with a complaint. [Source: Section 225, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Postponement of issue of process

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 225: Postponement of issue of process

Q: A person files a complaint in a Mumbai court against a businessman living in Delhi. Can the Mumbai Magistrate immediately issue an arrest warrant for the businessman based on the bare complaint?
A: No, under sub-section (1), because "the accused is residing at a place beyond the area in which he exercises his jurisdiction," the Magistrate "shall... postpone the issue of process" and conduct an inquiry or order an investigation first. [Source: Section 225, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Postponement of issue of process

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 225: Postponement of issue of process

Q: Under what specific condition in clause (a) of the proviso is a Magistrate completely forbidden from directing a police investigation under this section?
A: "where it appears to the Magistrate that the offence complained of is triable exclusively by the Court of Session". [Source: Section 225, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Postponement of issue of process

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 225: Postponement of issue of process

Q: If a person who is not a police officer is directed by the Magistrate to conduct the investigation under sub-section (1), what specific police power do they NOT have?
A: Under sub-section (3), they have all powers of an officer in charge of a police station "except the power to arrest without warrant." [Source: Section 225, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Postponement of issue of process

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 225: Postponement of issue of process

Q: What is the main consequence of making the inquiry/investigation mandatory when the accused lives outside the jurisdiction?
A: The consequence is that it protects innocent people living in distant places from being harassed by frivolous or vindictive false complaints, forcing the complainant to establish a prima facie case before forcing the accused to travel across the country. [Source: Section 225, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Postponement of issue of process

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 226: Dismissal of complaint

Q: What happens if a judge investigates a private complaint and decides there's no real evidence?
A: The Magistrate shall dismiss the complaint and must briefly record the reasons for doing so. [Source: Section 226, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dismissal of complaint

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 226: Dismissal of complaint

Q: What power is given to the Magistrate by Section 226 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 226 of BNSS 2023 gives the Magistrate the power to dismiss a complaint at the pre-summoning stage if, after considering statements on oath and any preliminary inquiry/investigation results, there is no sufficient ground for proceeding. [Source: Section 226, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dismissal of complaint

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 226: Dismissal of complaint

Q: A Magistrate receives a complaint, examines the complainant on oath, and reviews a police report requested under section 225. The Magistrate concludes the complaint is a purely civil dispute dressed up as a crime. What should the Magistrate do?
A: The Magistrate should "dismiss the complaint" because there is "no sufficient ground for proceeding." Crucially, the Magistrate must "briefly record his reasons for so doing." [Source: Section 226, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dismissal of complaint

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 226: Dismissal of complaint

Q: What three specific sources of information must the Magistrate consider (if they exist) before dismissing a complaint under this section?
A: "the statements on oath (if any) of the complainant", "and of the witnesses", and "the result of the inquiry or investigation (if any) under section 225". [Source: Section 226, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dismissal of complaint

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 226: Dismissal of complaint

Q: Can a Magistrate dismiss a complaint just by saying "Dismissed," without writing anything else?
A: No, the section explicitly mandates that "in every such case he shall briefly record his reasons for so doing." A dismissal without recorded reasons would violate this rule. [Source: Section 226, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dismissal of complaint

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 226: Dismissal of complaint

Q: What is the consequence of a dismissal under Section 226 for the accused?
A: The consequence is that the accused is entirely spared from the criminal process; they are not summoned, they do not have to appear in court, and they don't even have to hire a lawyer, as the case is thrown out before it officially begins for them. [Source: Section 226, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dismissal of complaint

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 227: Issue of process

Q: What happens when a Magistrate decides there is enough evidence to move forward with a case?
A: The Magistrate issues "process"—a summons for a summons-case, or a warrant (or summons) for a warrant-case—to compel the accused to appear in court. [Source: Section 227, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Issue of process

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 227: Issue of process

Q: What is the core function of Section 227 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 227 of BNSS 2023 dictates the procedure for the "issue of process," where a Magistrate, upon finding sufficient ground to proceed, formally summons the accused or issues an arrest warrant depending on the severity of the case. [Source: Section 227, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Issue of process

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 227: Issue of process

Q: A Magistrate finds sufficient grounds to proceed in a case involving a minor traffic offence (a summons-case). The Magistrate decides to issue an arrest warrant right away to teach the accused a lesson. Is this legal?
A: No, under sub-section (1)(a), if it appears to be a summons-case, the Magistrate "shall issue summons to the accused for his attendance." A warrant cannot be initially issued for a summons-case under this specific clause. [Source: Section 227, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Issue of process

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 227: Issue of process

Q: According to sub-section (2), what crucial document must be filed by the prosecution before any summons or warrant can be issued against the accused?
A: "a list of the prosecution witnesses has been filed." [Source: Section 227, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Issue of process

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 227: Issue of process

Q: If a complaint is made in writing, what must physically or electronically accompany the summons or warrant sent to the accused?
A: Under sub-section (3), it "shall be accompanied by a copy of such complaint." [Source: Section 227, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Issue of process

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 227: Issue of process

Q: What is the consequence if the law requires process-fees to be paid, but the complainant refuses to pay them within a reasonable time?
A: The consequence under sub-section (4) is that "no process shall be issued" and the Magistrate "may dismiss the complaint." [Source: Section 227, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Issue of process

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 228: Magistrate may dispense with personal attendance of accused

Q: Does an accused person always have to physically go to court when they get a summons?
A: Not always. A Magistrate can dispense with the personal attendance of the accused and allow them to appear through their advocate instead. [Source: Section 228, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Magistrate may dispense with personal attendance of accused

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 228: Magistrate may dispense with personal attendance of accused

Q: What discretion does Section 228 of BNSS 2023 give to a Magistrate?
A: Section 228 of BNSS 2023 gives the Magistrate the discretion to dispense with the personal attendance of an accused person who has been summoned, permitting representation by an advocate. [Source: Section 228, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Magistrate may dispense with personal attendance of accused

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 228: Magistrate may dispense with personal attendance of accused

Q: A prominent CEO is summoned for a minor regulatory violation. The Magistrate allows him to appear through his lawyer. Midway through the trial, the Magistrate realizes the CEO needs to be present to identify a specific document. Can the Magistrate force him to come to court now?
A: Yes, under sub-section (2), the Magistrate may "at any stage of the proceedings, direct the personal attendance of the accused, and, if necessary, enforce such attendance". [Source: Section 228, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Magistrate may dispense with personal attendance of accused

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 228: Magistrate may dispense with personal attendance of accused

Q: Under sub-section (1), what specific process must have been issued for the Magistrate to have the power to dispense with personal attendance initially?
A: "Whenever a Magistrate issues a summons". (This generally implies it's not applicable if a warrant was issued). [Source: Section 228, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Magistrate may dispense with personal attendance of accused

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 228: Magistrate may dispense with personal attendance of accused

Q: Does an accused have an absolute *right* to never appear in court if they hire a lawyer?
A: No, it is entirely at the Magistrate's discretion ("if he sees reason so to do"), and that exemption can be revoked at any time under sub-section (2). [Source: Section 228, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Magistrate may dispense with personal attendance of accused

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 228: Magistrate may dispense with personal attendance of accused

Q: What is the consequence of this provision for the accused in minor cases?
A: The consequence is that it prevents minor criminal proceedings from being used as a tool for harassment by forcing unnecessary, time-consuming physical court appearances, allowing the legal process to continue via counsel. [Source: Section 228, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Magistrate may dispense with personal attendance of accused

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 229: Special summons in cases of petty offence

Q: How are very minor offences (like a small fine) handled to save court time?
A: For petty offences (fine under ₹5000), the Magistrate can issue a "special summons" allowing the accused to plead guilty by mail or through a lawyer and just pay the fine without ever physically going to court. [Source: Section 229, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Special summons in cases of petty offence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 229: Special summons in cases of petty offence

Q: What streamlined procedure is introduced by Section 229 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 229 of BNSS 2023 introduces a streamlined "special summons" procedure for petty offences, enabling accused persons to plead guilty and remit fines via post/messenger or an advocate without personal court attendance. [Source: Section 229, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Special summons in cases of petty offence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 229: Special summons in cases of petty offence

Q: A man receives a special summons for littering, which carries a ₹1,000 fine. He wants to plead guilty but doesn't want to travel to the courthouse or hire a lawyer. What can he do under this section?
A: He can "transmit before the specified date, by post or by messenger to the Magistrate, the said plea in writing and the amount of fine specified in the summons." [Source: Section 229, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Special summons in cases of petty offence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 229: Special summons in cases of petty offence

Q: What is the monetary threshold that defines a "petty offence" under sub-section (2) for the purpose of this section?
A: Any offence punishable only with fine "not exceeding five thousand rupees". [Source: Section 229, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Special summons in cases of petty offence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 229: Special summons in cases of petty offence

Q: Does a ₹2,000 fine for a traffic violation under the Motor Vehicles Act qualify for this specific special summons procedure?
A: No, sub-section (2) explicitly states that "petty offence... does not include any offence so punishable under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988... or under any other law which provides for convicting the accused person in his absence on a plea of guilty." [Source: Section 229, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Special summons in cases of petty offence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 229: Special summons in cases of petty offence

Q: What is the systemic consequence of using special summons for petty offences?
A: The consequence is a massive reduction in the backlog of minor cases clogging the lower courts, saving judicial time while still enforcing penalties for minor infractions. [Source: Section 229, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Special summons in cases of petty offence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 230: Supply to accused of copy of police report and other documents

Q: When the police file a charge sheet, what documents does the accused get to see before the trial starts?
A: The accused (and victim) must be given free copies of the police report, the FIR, witness statements, confessions, and any other relevant documents submitted by the police within 14 days. [Source: Section 230, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Supply to accused of copy of police report and other documents

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 230: Supply to accused of copy of police report and other documents

Q: What is the core mandate of Section 230 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 230 of BNSS 2023 mandates that the Magistrate must supply the accused and the victim (free of cost and within 14 days) with copies of the police report, FIR, witness statements, and confessions to ensure a fair trial. [Source: Section 230, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Supply to accused of copy of police report and other documents

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 230: Supply to accused of copy of police report and other documents

Q: The police file a massive 5,000-page charge sheet against a fraudster, along with 50 GB of digital financial records. Printing this out would take weeks. Does the Magistrate have to provide physical paper copies to the accused?
A: No, under the second proviso, if the document is voluminous, the Magistrate "may furnish the copies through electronic means or direct that he will only be allowed to inspect it either personally or through an advocate in Court." Furthermore, the third proviso states "supply of documents in electronic form shall be considered as duly furnished." [Source: Section 230, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Supply to accused of copy of police report and other documents

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 230: Supply to accused of copy of police report and other documents

Q: What is the strict time limit within which the Magistrate must furnish these copies to the accused?
A: "without delay, and in no case beyond fourteen days from the date of production or appearance of the accused". [Source: Section 230, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Supply to accused of copy of police report and other documents

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 230: Supply to accused of copy of police report and other documents

Q: Do the police have to give the accused *every single word* a witness said, even if it threatens national security or the witness's safety?
A: No, under clause (iii) and the first proviso, the Magistrate may exclude a part of a statement if the police officer made a request for exclusion (under section 193(7)) and the Magistrate finds the reasons proper. [Source: Section 230, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Supply to accused of copy of police report and other documents

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 230: Supply to accused of copy of police report and other documents

Q: What fundamental right does this section protect?
A: The consequence is the protection of the right to a fair trial and the right to defend oneself; it prevents "trial by ambush" by ensuring the accused knows exactly what evidence the state plans to use against them well before the trial begins. [Source: Section 230, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Supply to accused of copy of police report and other documents

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 231: Supply of copies of statements and documents to accused in other cases triable by Court of

Q: If a case is filed directly with a Magistrate (not by the police) but it's a serious crime meant for the Sessions Court, what documents does the accused get?
A: The Magistrate must give the accused free copies of the sworn statements of the complainant and witnesses, any recorded confessions, and any documents the prosecution plans to rely on. [Source: Section 231, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Supply of copies of statements and documents to accused in other cases triable by Court of

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 231: Supply of copies of statements and documents to accused in other cases triable by Court of

Q: What procedure does Section 231 of BNSS 2023 outline?
A: Section 231 of BNSS 2023 outlines the procedure for supplying documents to the accused in a complaint case (instituted otherwise than on a police report) when the offence is triable exclusively by the Court of Session. [Source: Section 231, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Supply of copies of statements and documents to accused in other cases triable by Court of

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 231: Supply of copies of statements and documents to accused in other cases triable by Court of

Q: A woman files a private complaint alleging rape (a Sessions-triable offence). The Magistrate examines her and two witnesses on oath. Before committing the case to the Sessions Court, does the Magistrate have to give the accused transcripts of what the woman and witnesses said?
A: Yes, under section 231, the Magistrate shall furnish to the accused "the statements recorded under section 223 or section 225, of all persons examined by the Magistrate." [Source: Section 231, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Supply of copies of statements and documents to accused in other cases triable by Court of

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 231: Supply of copies of statements and documents to accused in other cases triable by Court of

Q: What specific types of prior statements and confessions (if they exist) must be supplied under clause (ii)?
A: "the statements and confessions, if any, recorded under section 180 or section 183". [Source: Section 231, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Supply of copies of statements and documents to accused in other cases triable by Court of

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 231: Supply of copies of statements and documents to accused in other cases triable by Court of

Q: If the complainant produces a 10,000-page ledger as evidence of a massive corporate fraud, does the Magistrate have to photocopy the whole thing for the accused?
A: No, the first proviso states that if the document is "voluminous", the Magistrate can instead direct that the accused "will only be allowed to inspect it either personally or through an advocate in Court." Or provide it electronically as per the second proviso. [Source: Section 231, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Supply of copies of statements and documents to accused in other cases triable by Court of

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 231: Supply of copies of statements and documents to accused in other cases triable by Court of

Q: What is the consequence of this requirement before committal?
A: The consequence is parity with police report cases; it ensures that even in private complaint cases involving serious crimes, the accused is fully aware of the evidentiary basis of the charges before facing trial in the higher Court of Session. [Source: Section 231, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Supply of copies of statements and documents to accused in other cases triable by Court of

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 232: Commitment of case to Court of Session when offence is triable exclusively by it

Q: How does a serious case like murder actually get to the higher Court of Session?
A: The lower Magistrate handles the initial paperwork, gives the accused the necessary documents, remands the accused to custody (or bail), and then formally "commits" (transfers) the case record to the Court of Session. [Source: Section 232, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Commitment of case to Court of Session when offence is triable exclusively by it

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 232: Commitment of case to Court of Session when offence is triable exclusively by it

Q: What major procedural transition is governed by Section 232 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 232 of BNSS 2023 governs the "committal" proceedings, where a Magistrate, recognizing an offence is exclusively triable by the Court of Session, formally transfers the case, the accused, and the evidence to that higher court. [Source: Section 232, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Commitment of case to Court of Session when offence is triable exclusively by it

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 232: Commitment of case to Court of Session when offence is triable exclusively by it

Q: A Magistrate has taken cognizance of a murder case, given the accused the police report copies, and is ready to send the case to the Sessions Court. A victim's rights group files an application with the Magistrate regarding witness protection. What should the Magistrate do with the application?
A: Under the second proviso, "any application filed before the Magistrate... shall be forwarded to the Court of Session with the committal of the case." The Magistrate should send it up to the Sessions Judge. [Source: Section 232, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Commitment of case to Court of Session when offence is triable exclusively by it

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 232: Commitment of case to Court of Session when offence is triable exclusively by it

Q: What is the strict time limit provided in the first proviso for completing committal proceedings from the date of taking cognizance?
A: "within a period of ninety days from the date of taking cognizance". [Source: Section 232, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Commitment of case to Court of Session when offence is triable exclusively by it

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 232: Commitment of case to Court of Session when offence is triable exclusively by it

Q: Can the 90-day time limit for committal proceedings be extended?
A: Yes, the first proviso states "such period may be extended by the Magistrate for a period not exceeding one hundred and eighty days for the reasons to be recorded in writing". [Source: Section 232, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Commitment of case to Court of Session when offence is triable exclusively by it

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 232: Commitment of case to Court of Session when offence is triable exclusively by it

Q: What is the consequence of clause (b) regarding the accused's liberty?
A: The consequence is that once committed, the Magistrate's authority to grant temporary remand ends; the Magistrate remands the accused to custody "during, and until the conclusion of, the trial" (subject to bail provisions), placing their continued custody under the authority of the Sessions Court. [Source: Section 232, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Commitment of case to Court of Session when offence is triable exclusively by it

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 233: Procedure to be followed when there is a complaint case and police investigation in respect

Q: What happens if a person files a private complaint about a crime, but the police are also already investigating the exact same crime?
A: The Magistrate stops the private complaint case, asks the police for a report, and if the police eventually file charges against the same person, the Magistrate merges the private case and the police case and tries them together. [Source: Section 233, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure to be followed when there is a complaint case and police investigation in respect

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 233: Procedure to be followed when there is a complaint case and police investigation in respect

Q: What conflict does Section 233 of BNSS 2023 resolve?
A: Section 233 of BNSS 2023 resolves the conflict of parallel proceedings by outlining the procedure to merge a private complaint case with an ongoing police investigation regarding the same offence. [Source: Section 233, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure to be followed when there is a complaint case and police investigation in respect

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 233: Procedure to be followed when there is a complaint case and police investigation in respect

Q: A man files a private complaint for criminal breach of trust. During the hearing, the Magistrate learns that the police have already registered an FIR for the same fraud and are currently gathering evidence. What must the Magistrate do immediately?
A: Under sub-section (1), the Magistrate "shall stay the proceedings of such inquiry or trial and call for a report on the matter from the police officer conducting the investigation." [Source: Section 233, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure to be followed when there is a complaint case and police investigation in respect

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 233: Procedure to be followed when there is a complaint case and police investigation in respect

Q: If the police eventually submit a report under section 193, and the Magistrate takes cognizance based on it, how are the two cases handled from then on?
A: Under sub-section (2), the Magistrate "shall inquire into or try together the complaint case and the case arising out of the police report as if both the cases were instituted on a police report." [Source: Section 233, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure to be followed when there is a complaint case and police investigation in respect

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 233: Procedure to be followed when there is a complaint case and police investigation in respect

Q: What happens if the police finish their investigation and conclude no crime happened (filing a closure report), so the Magistrate doesn't take cognizance on the police report?
A: Under sub-section (3), if the Magistrate "does not take cognizance of any offence on the police report, he shall proceed with the inquiry or trial, which was stayed by him" (i.e., resume the private complaint case). [Source: Section 233, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure to be followed when there is a complaint case and police investigation in respect

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 233: Procedure to be followed when there is a complaint case and police investigation in respect

Q: What is the main consequence of merging the two cases?
A: The consequence is judicial efficiency and the prevention of conflicting judgments; it ensures the accused doesn't face double jeopardy by having to defend themselves in two separate trials for the exact same set of facts. [Source: Section 233, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure to be followed when there is a complaint case and police investigation in respect

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 234: Contents of charge

Q: How does a court officially tell an accused person what crime they are on trial for?
A: The court drafts a formal "charge" that states the specific offence, the name of the law, the section number, and enough details about the offence to give the accused clear notice of what they are accused of. [Source: Section 234, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Contents of charge

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 234: Contents of charge

Q: What fundamental document is defined by Section 234 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 234 of BNSS 2023 defines the contents of a formal "charge," outlining that it must specify the offence, the law, the section, and the necessary legal conditions to ensure the accused understands the allegations against them. [Source: Section 234, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Contents of charge

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 234: Contents of charge

Q: A man is charged with "Murder." He argues the charge is invalid because it doesn't explicitly state that his act did not fall under any of the self-defense exceptions in the BNS. Is the charge invalid?
A: No, under sub-section (5) and Illustration (a), the mere fact that the charge is made "is equivalent to a statement that every legal condition required by law to constitute the offence charged was fulfilled," which includes the absence of general exceptions like self-defense. [Source: Section 234, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Contents of charge

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 234: Contents of charge

Q: If a law creates an offence but doesn't give it a specific name (like "theft" or "murder"), how must the offence be described in the charge according to sub-section (3)?
