Q: Does the judge have to go through a whole mini-trial to prove the previous conviction if the accused simply admits they were convicted before?
A: No, the section specifies the evidence-taking procedure applies when "the accused does not admit that he has been previously convicted". If they admit it, the judge can simply apply the enhanced punishment. [Source: Section 259, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Previous conviction

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 259: Previous conviction

Q: What fundamental unfairness does this section prevent?
A: The consequence is preventing bias; it ensures the judge evaluates the evidence for the current crime entirely objectively, without being prejudiced by the knowledge that the accused is a known "criminal" from past deeds. [Source: Section 259, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Previous conviction

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 260: Procedure in cases instituted under sub-section (2) of section 222

Q: What happens when a high-ranking official like a Minister is defamed, and the Public Prosecutor files a case directly in the Sessions Court?
A: The Sessions Court tries the case using the procedures normally meant for lower Magistrates handling warrant cases, and usually, the defamed official must testify as a witness. [Source: Section 260, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in cases instituted under sub-section (2) of section 222

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 260: Procedure in cases instituted under sub-section (2) of section 222

Q: What special trial procedure is governed by Section 260 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 260 of BNSS 2023 governs the special trial procedure for defamation cases initiated directly in the Court of Session by a Public Prosecutor (under section 222(2)), prescribing a warrant-case procedure and compensation mechanisms for false accusations. [Source: Section 260, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in cases instituted under sub-section (2) of section 222

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 260: Procedure in cases instituted under sub-section (2) of section 222

Q: A Public Prosecutor files a defamation case in the Sessions Court on behalf of a State Minister. The accused is acquitted, and the Court finds the accusation was completely baseless. Can the Court force the Minister to pay compensation to the accused?
A: Yes, under sub-section (3), the Court may direct the person alleged to have been defamed (the Minister) "to show cause why he should not pay compensation to such accused", up to ₹5,000. [Source: Section 260, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in cases instituted under sub-section (2) of section 222

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 260: Procedure in cases instituted under sub-section (2) of section 222

Q: According to sub-section (3), which three high-ranking officials are completely exempt from ever having to pay compensation to an acquitted accused under this section?
A: "the President, the Vice-President or the Governor of a State or the Administrator of a Union territory". [Source: Section 260, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in cases instituted under sub-section (2) of section 222

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 260: Procedure in cases instituted under sub-section (2) of section 222

Q: Does the defamed public official *always* have to come to court and testify as a witness for the prosecution?
A: Usually yes, but the proviso to sub-section (1) provides an exception: "unless the Court of Session, for reasons to be recorded, otherwise directs". [Source: Section 260, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in cases instituted under sub-section (2) of section 222

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 260: Procedure in cases instituted under sub-section (2) of section 222

Q: What is the consequence of allowing these trials to be held "in camera" (in private) under sub-section (2)?
A: The consequence is the protection of the public official's reputation from further damage and public spectacle during a trial that is specifically about discussing highly defamatory and potentially embarrassing allegations. [Source: Section 260, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in cases instituted under sub-section (2) of section 222

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 261: Compliance with section 230

Q: When a Magistrate starts a trial based on a police report, what is the very first thing they must check?
A: The Magistrate must make sure the accused has been given all the necessary documents (like the police report, FIR, and witness statements) as required by law. [Source: Section 261, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Compliance with section 230

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 261: Compliance with section 230

Q: What preliminary check is mandated by Section 261 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 261 of BNSS 2023 mandates that at the commencement of a warrant-case trial instituted on a police report, the Magistrate must verify compliance with section 230, ensuring the accused has received all required copies of documents. [Source: Section 261, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Compliance with section 230

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 261: Compliance with section 230

Q: An accused is brought before a Magistrate for the start of a warrant-case trial based on a police charge sheet. The accused's lawyer complains they never received a copy of the FIR or the main witness statements. What must the Magistrate do?
A: Under section 261, "the Magistrate shall satisfy himself that he has complied with the provisions of section 230." The Magistrate must pause the proceedings and ensure those documents are supplied to the accused before moving forward. [Source: Section 261, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Compliance with section 230

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 261: Compliance with section 230

Q: In what specific type of case does this compliance check apply?
A: "in any warrant-case instituted on a police report". [Source: Section 261, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Compliance with section 230

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 261: Compliance with section 230

Q: Can the Magistrate just take the police officer's word that the documents were handed over, without asking the accused?
A: The section requires the Magistrate to "satisfy himself." While it doesn't prescribe the exact method, legal standards generally require the Magistrate to actively confirm with the accused or their counsel, not merely rely on police assertions. [Source: Section 261, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Compliance with section 230

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 261: Compliance with section 230

Q: What is the consequence of this mandatory check for the fairness of the trial?
A: The consequence is the prevention of "trial by ambush"; it guarantees the accused's fundamental right to know the evidence against them is upheld right at the starting line, ensuring they can prepare an adequate defense. [Source: Section 261, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Compliance with section 230

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 262: When accused shall be discharged

Q: In a Magistrate's court, what can an accused do if they read the police report and think the charges are completely baseless?
A: The accused can apply for "discharge" within 60 days of getting the documents. If the Magistrate thinks the charge is groundless after reviewing the report and hearing both sides, they will discharge the accused and record the reasons. [Source: Section 262, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: When accused shall be discharged

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 262: When accused shall be discharged

Q: What pre-trial remedy does Section 262 of BNSS 2023 provide in Magistrate courts?
A: Section 262 of BNSS 2023 provides the remedy of discharge in warrant-cases before a Magistrate, allowing the accused to be freed if the Magistrate, upon reviewing the police report and hearing the parties, finds the charge groundless. [Source: Section 262, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: When accused shall be discharged

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 262: When accused shall be discharged

Q: The police file a charge sheet for cheating. The accused reads it and realizes the police attached a completely irrelevant contract that doesn't involve him at all. What is the time limit for his lawyer to file an application arguing the case should be thrown out immediately?
A: Under sub-section (1), the application for discharge must be preferred "within a period of sixty days from the date of supply of copies of documents under section 230." [Source: Section 262, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: When accused shall be discharged

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 262: When accused shall be discharged

Q: What standard must the Magistrate's assessment of the charge meet to order a discharge under sub-section (2)?
A: The Magistrate must consider "the charge against the accused to be groundless". [Source: Section 262, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: When accused shall be discharged

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 262: When accused shall be discharged

Q: Can the Magistrate discharge the accused solely based on reading the written police report without listening to what the prosecutor has to say?
A: No, sub-section (2) explicitly requires the Magistrate to make the decision "after giving the prosecution and the accused an opportunity of being heard". [Source: Section 262, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: When accused shall be discharged

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 262: When accused shall be discharged

Q: What is the consequence of a discharge under this section?
A: The consequence is that the accused is spared the harassment, time, and expense of a full criminal trial, filtering out frivolous, malicious, or legally unsustainable police cases before formal charges are even framed. [Source: Section 262, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: When accused shall be discharged

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 263: Framing of charge

Q: If the Magistrate decides the police report *does* show grounds for a case, what happens next?
A: The Magistrate will formally write down the charge (within 60 days), read and explain it to the accused, and ask if they plead guilty or want a trial. [Source: Section 263, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Framing of charge

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 263: Framing of charge

Q: What procedural step is mandated by Section 263 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 263 of BNSS 2023 mandates the framing of a formal written charge by the Magistrate if they find grounds to presume the accused committed an offence, followed by reading the charge and recording the accused's plea. [Source: Section 263, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Framing of charge

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 263: Framing of charge

Q: A Magistrate reviews a police report for extortion. The Magistrate thinks there is definitely enough evidence to presume the accused did it. What is the deadline for the Magistrate to officially write down the charge?
A: Under sub-section (1), the Magistrate "shall frame in writing a charge against the accused within a period of sixty days from the date of first hearing on charge." [Source: Section 263, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Framing of charge

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 263: Framing of charge

Q: Besides presuming an offence was committed, what two jurisdictional elements must the Magistrate be satisfied with before framing a charge under this section?
A: The offence must be one "which such Magistrate is competent to try" AND "which, in his opinion, could be adequately punished by him". [Source: Section 263, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Framing of charge

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 263: Framing of charge

Q: If the accused is illiterate and doesn't understand legal jargon, is it enough for the Magistrate to just hand them the written charge paper?
A: No, under sub-section (2), "The charge shall then be read and explained to the accused". The Magistrate has a duty to ensure comprehension before taking a plea. [Source: Section 263, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Framing of charge

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 263: Framing of charge

Q: What is the consequence of the requirement that the Magistrate believe the offence can be "adequately punished by him"?
A: The consequence is that if the Magistrate realizes the crime is so severe it deserves a punishment heavier than what their specific court has the power to give, they cannot frame the charge themselves and must commit or transfer the case to a higher court (like the Chief Judicial Magistrate or Sessions Court). [Source: Section 263, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Framing of charge

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 264: Conviction on plea of guilty

Q: What happens in a Magistrate's court if an accused person confesses and pleads guilty to the framed charges?
A: The Magistrate will record the guilty plea and has the discretion to convict the person right then based on their confession. [Source: Section 264, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Conviction on plea of guilty

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 264: Conviction on plea of guilty

Q: What power is granted to the Magistrate by Section 264 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 264 of BNSS 2023 grants the Magistrate the discretionary power to convict an accused person upon a plea of guilty in a warrant-case instituted on a police report. [Source: Section 264, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Conviction on plea of guilty

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 264: Conviction on plea of guilty

Q: An accused is charged with theft. When asked how he pleads, he says, "Yes, I stole it." Is the trial over?
A: Likely yes, but it depends on the Magistrate. Under section 264, "the Magistrate shall record the plea and may, in his discretion, convict him thereon." The Magistrate can choose to convict him immediately, ending the trial phase. [Source: Section 264, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Conviction on plea of guilty

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 264: Conviction on plea of guilty

Q: What is the mandatory action the Magistrate must perform when the accused pleads guilty?
A: The Magistrate "shall record the plea". [Source: Section 264, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Conviction on plea of guilty

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 264: Conviction on plea of guilty

Q: Can a Magistrate refuse to convict someone who pleads guilty?
A: Yes, the conviction is "in his discretion." A Magistrate might refuse to convict on a plea if they suspect the plea was coerced, if the accused clearly doesn't understand the nature of the charge, or if the facts admitted don't actually constitute an offence in law. [Source: Section 264, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Conviction on plea of guilty

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 264: Conviction on plea of guilty

Q: What is the consequence of a conviction under this section?
A: The consequence is rapid case disposal; the court avoids the lengthy process of summoning witnesses, taking evidence, and hearing cross-examinations, moving swiftly to the sentencing phase. [Source: Section 264, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Conviction on plea of guilty

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 265: Evidence for prosecution

Q: In a Magistrate's trial based on a police report, what happens if the accused refuses to plead guilty to the charges?
A: The Magistrate will fix a date to examine witnesses and take evidence from the prosecution to prove the case. The Magistrate must give the accused the police witness statements in advance. [Source: Section 265, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence for prosecution

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 265: Evidence for prosecution

Q: What phase of a warrant-case trial is governed by Section 265 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 265 of BNSS 2023 governs the "Evidence for prosecution" phase in a warrant-case instituted on a police report, triggered when the accused claims a trial instead of pleading guilty. [Source: Section 265, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence for prosecution

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 265: Evidence for prosecution

Q: The trial date is set. The prosecution wants to call an eyewitness, but the witness is ignoring their phone calls. What can the prosecutor do?
A: Under sub-section (2), the prosecutor can apply to the Magistrate, and the Magistrate "may, on the application of the prosecution, issue a summons to any of its witnesses directing him to attend". [Source: Section 265, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence for prosecution

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 265: Evidence for prosecution

Q: What specific document must the Magistrate supply to the accused *before* the examination of witnesses begins?
A: "the statement of witnesses recorded during investigation by the police." [Source: Section 265, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence for prosecution

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 265: Evidence for prosecution

Q: Is it strictly mandatory for every prosecution witness to physically travel to the Magistrate's court to testify?
A: No, the second proviso to sub-section (3) provides an exception: "the examination of a witness under this sub-section may be done by audio-video electronic means at the designated place to be notified by the State Government." [Source: Section 265, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence for prosecution

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 265: Evidence for prosecution

Q: What is the consequence of the Magistrate's power to defer cross-examination under the first proviso of sub-section (3)?
A: The consequence is that the prosecution can present its witnesses in a logical sequence without the defense immediately breaking the narrative flow through cross-examination, allowing the judge to hear the complete story before it is challenged. [Source: Section 265, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence for prosecution

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 266: Evidence for defence

Q: In a Magistrate's trial based on a police report, when does the accused finally get to present their side of the story and call their own witnesses?
A: After the prosecution finishes presenting its evidence, the accused is called upon to "enter upon his defence" and produce their own evidence and witnesses. [Source: Section 266, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence for defence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 266: Evidence for defence

Q: What phase of a warrant-case trial is initiated by Section 266 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 266 of BNSS 2023 initiates the "Evidence for defence" phase in a warrant-case instituted on a police report, detailing the accused's right to produce evidence and the Magistrate's role in summoning defense witnesses. [Source: Section 266, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence for defence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 266: Evidence for defence

Q: During the defense phase, the accused asks the Magistrate to summon 50 different witnesses who live across the country, none of whom actually saw the crime. Can the Magistrate say no?
A: Yes, under sub-section (2), the Magistrate shall issue the process *unless* he considers the application "is made for the purpose of vexation or delay or for defeating the ends of justice," which he must record in writing. [Source: Section 266, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence for defence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 266: Evidence for defence

Q: Under sub-section (3), what financial condition can the Magistrate impose before summoning a defense witness?
A: The Magistrate may "require that the reasonable expenses incurred by the witness in attending for the purposes of the trial be deposited in Court." [Source: Section 266, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence for defence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 266: Evidence for defence

Q: If the accused already heavily cross-examined a prosecution witness earlier in the trial, can they demand the Magistrate summon that same witness again during the defense phase just to ask more questions?
A: Generally no, the first proviso to sub-section (2) states that if the accused already had the opportunity to cross-examine a witness, their attendance shall not be compelled again "unless the Magistrate is satisfied that it is necessary for the ends of justice". [Source: Section 266, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence for defence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 266: Evidence for defence

Q: What is the consequence of allowing defense witnesses to be examined via audio-video electronic means?
A: The consequence is making it easier and cheaper for the accused to mount a defense, as they can call expert witnesses or alibi witnesses who live far away without bearing the heavy financial burden of paying their travel expenses to court. [Source: Section 266, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence for defence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 267: Evidence for prosecution

Q: How does a warrant-case trial start if the case was filed directly by a private citizen (a complaint case) instead of by the police?
A: When the accused appears before the Magistrate, the Magistrate skips the police report review (since there isn't one) and immediately starts hearing the prosecution (the complainant) and taking their evidence. [Source: Section 267, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence for prosecution

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 267: Evidence for prosecution

Q: What procedure does Section 267 of BNSS 2023 establish for non-police cases?
A: Section 267 of BNSS 2023 establishes the initial evidentiary procedure for warrant-cases instituted *otherwise* than on a police report, requiring the Magistrate to directly hear the prosecution and take evidence as soon as the accused appears. [Source: Section 267, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence for prosecution

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 267: Evidence for prosecution

Q: A citizen files a private complaint for major fraud against a company director. The director appears in court. The complainant wants to call an auditor to prove the fraud, but the auditor refuses to come without a court order. What should the complainant do?
A: Under sub-section (2), the complainant (acting as the prosecution) should make an application to the Magistrate, who "may, on the application of the prosecution, issue a summons to any of its witnesses directing him to attend". [Source: Section 267, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence for prosecution

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 267: Evidence for prosecution

Q: What specific event triggers the Magistrate's duty to start taking prosecution evidence in a complaint case under sub-section (1)?
A: "When... the accused appears or is brought before a Magistrate". [Source: Section 267, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence for prosecution

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 267: Evidence for prosecution

Q: Does the Magistrate frame the formal charges *before* taking this initial prosecution evidence in a complaint case?
A: No, unlike cases based on police reports where charges are framed right after reading the report, in complaint cases, the Magistrate must take "all such evidence as may be produced in support of the prosecution" *first*, to determine if a charge is even warranted. [Source: Section 267, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence for prosecution

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 267: Evidence for prosecution

Q: What is the consequence of this distinct procedure for private complaint cases?
A: The consequence is that it places the initial burden heavily on the private complainant to actually produce credible evidence in court right from the start, preventing citizens from harassing others with baseless formal charges that lack any evidentiary backing. [Source: Section 267, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence for prosecution

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 268: When accused shall be discharged

Q: In a private complaint case, what happens if the complainant presents all their evidence to the Magistrate, but the evidence is incredibly weak or proves nothing?
A: If the Magistrate considers that no case has been made out against the accused (meaning even if the evidence wasn't challenged, it wouldn't lead to a conviction), the Magistrate must discharge the accused. [Source: Section 268, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: When accused shall be discharged

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 268: When accused shall be discharged

Q: What safeguard is provided by Section 268 of BNSS 2023 in complaint cases?
A: Section 268 of BNSS 2023 provides the safeguard of "Discharge" in warrant-cases instituted otherwise than on a police report, allowing the Magistrate to dismiss the case if the initial prosecution evidence fails to establish a prima facie case. [Source: Section 268, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: When accused shall be discharged

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 268: When accused shall be discharged

Q: A man files a private complaint accusing his neighbor of criminal breach of trust regarding a lawnmower. The man testifies but provides no contract, no witnesses, and his own story contradicts itself. What should the Magistrate do?
A: Under sub-section (1), if the Magistrate considers that "no case against the accused has been made out which, if unrebutted, would warrant his conviction, the Magistrate shall discharge him." [Source: Section 268, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: When accused shall be discharged

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 268: When accused shall be discharged

Q: What specific legal standard must the prosecution's initial evidence fail to meet for the Magistrate to order a discharge under sub-section (1)?
A: The evidence must fail to make out a case "which, if unrebutted, would warrant his conviction". [Source: Section 268, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: When accused shall be discharged

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 268: When accused shall be discharged

Q: Does the Magistrate *have* to wait until the complainant has presented absolutely every single piece of evidence before discharging the accused?
A: No, sub-section (2) provides an exception: "Nothing in this section shall be deemed to prevent a Magistrate from discharging the accused at any previous stage of the case if... he considers the charge to be groundless." [Source: Section 268, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: When accused shall be discharged

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 268: When accused shall be discharged

Q: What is the consequence of this rule for the accused in a private complaint case?
A: The consequence is that the accused doesn't even have to present a defense or undergo a full trial if the complainant's own initial evidence is inherently defective or insufficient to prove a crime occurred. [Source: Section 268, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: When accused shall be discharged

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 269: Procedure where accused is not discharged

Q: In a private complaint case, what happens if the complainant's initial evidence *does* show there are grounds to presume the accused committed the crime?
A: The Magistrate will officially write down the charge, read it to the accused, ask how they plead, and if they plead not guilty, allow the accused to cross-examine the complainant's witnesses. [Source: Section 269, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where accused is not discharged

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 269: Procedure where accused is not discharged

Q: What procedure follows a successful prima facie showing in a complaint case under Section 269 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 269 of BNSS 2023 mandates that if the accused is not discharged, the Magistrate shall frame the charge in writing, record the plea, and if the accused claims trial, recall the prosecution witnesses for cross-examination by the defense. [Source: Section 269, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where accused is not discharged

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 269: Procedure where accused is not discharged

Q: In a private complaint case for fraud, the complainant provides strong documents and testimony. The Magistrate frames the charge. The accused pleads not guilty. The accused's lawyer says, "I want to cross-examine the complainant right now." Must the Magistrate allow it?
A: Yes. Under sub-section (4), the accused is asked "whether he wishes to cross-examine any... of the witnesses for the prosecution whose evidence has been taken." Under sub-section (5), if he says yes, "the witnesses named by him shall be recalled and, after cross-examination... they shall be discharged." [Source: Section 269, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where accused is not discharged

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 269: Procedure where accused is not discharged

Q: Under sub-section (1), what are the two jurisdictional conditions the Magistrate must meet before framing the charge?
A: The offence must be one "which such Magistrate is competent to try" and "which, in his opinion, could be adequately punished by him". [Source: Section 269, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where accused is not discharged

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 269: Procedure where accused is not discharged

Q: What happens if a prosecution witness testified earlier, but when they are recalled for cross-examination, they completely vanish and cannot be found despite the court's best efforts?
A: Under sub-section (7), if their attendance cannot be secured, "it shall be deemed that such witness has not been examined for not being available". Their earlier unchecked testimony is essentially nullified for the purpose of the trial. [Source: Section 269, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where accused is not discharged

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 269: Procedure where accused is not discharged

Q: What is the consequence of sub-section (7) regarding missing witnesses?
A: The consequence is that it protects the accused's fundamental right to cross-examination; the court cannot base a conviction on the testimony of a complainant's witness if the defense never had the legal opportunity to challenge that testimony's truthfulness. [Source: Section 269, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where accused is not discharged

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 270: Evidence for defence

Q: In a private complaint case, when does the accused get to present their own defense evidence?
A: After the charges are framed, the prosecution's witnesses are cross-examined, and any remaining prosecution evidence is taken, the accused is then called upon to present their defense evidence. [Source: Section 270, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence for defence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 270: Evidence for defence

Q: What phase of a private complaint trial is initiated by Section 270 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 270 of BNSS 2023 initiates the "Evidence for defence" phase in a warrant-case instituted otherwise than on a police report, simply applying the same rules found in section 266 to this stage. [Source: Section 270, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence for defence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 270: Evidence for defence

Q: The prosecution finishes its case in a private complaint trial. The Magistrate turns to the accused. What is the exact legal phrase describing what happens next?
A: "The accused shall then be called upon to enter upon his defence and produce his evidence". [Source: Section 270, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence for defence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 270: Evidence for defence

Q: Which specific earlier section provides the detailed rules for how the accused produces this defense evidence (like summoning witnesses)?
A: "the provisions of section 266 shall apply to the case." [Source: Section 270, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence for defence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 270: Evidence for defence

Q: Does this section create any *new* rules for the defense phase that are different from police-instituted cases?
A: No, it explicitly cross-references section 266, ensuring the rules for presenting a defense and summoning defense witnesses are identical whether the case started via police report or private complaint. [Source: Section 270, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence for defence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 270: Evidence for defence

Q: What is the structural consequence of this section?
A: The consequence is that it synchronizes the two different types of warrant-case trials (police report vs. private complaint); although they start differently, once the prosecution rests, the trial converges into identical procedures for the defense phase. [Source: Section 270, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Evidence for defence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 271: Acquittal or conviction

Q: How does a warrant-case trial in a Magistrate's court finally end?
A: It ends with the Magistrate recording an order of acquittal if the accused is found not guilty, or passing a sentence (after hearing the accused) if found guilty. [Source: Section 271, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Acquittal or conviction

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 271: Acquittal or conviction

Q: What final stage of a warrant-case trial is governed by Section 271 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 271 of BNSS 2023 governs "Acquittal or conviction" at the conclusion of a warrant-case trial, detailing the mandatory recording of acquittal, the hearing on sentencing for convictions, and the post-conviction procedure for proving previous criminal records. [Source: Section 271, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Acquittal or conviction

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 271: Acquittal or conviction

Q: A Magistrate finds an accused guilty of cheating. The Magistrate immediately signs a paper sending the person to jail for 1 year without saying another word. Is this legal?
A: No, under sub-section (2), when the Magistrate finds the accused guilty, "he shall, after hearing the accused on the question of sentence, pass sentence upon him according to law." The mandatory hearing on sentence was skipped. [Source: Section 271, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Acquittal or conviction

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 271: Acquittal or conviction

Q: Under sub-section (3), at what specific point in the trial is the prosecution finally allowed to bring up the fact that the accused has a prior criminal conviction?
A: "after he has convicted the said accused" (meaning after the conviction for the *current* offence is finalized). [Source: Section 271, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Acquittal or conviction

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 271: Acquittal or conviction

Q: Are there any situations where a Magistrate finds an accused guilty but *doesn't* have to pass a sentence of punishment?
A: Yes, sub-section (2) says the Magistrate shall pass sentence "but does not proceed in accordance with the provisions of section 364 or section 401" (which relate to submitting the proceedings to a Chief Judicial Magistrate for higher punishment, or releasing the offender on probation). [Source: Section 271, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Acquittal or conviction

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 271: Acquittal or conviction

Q: What is the consequence of the proviso in sub-section (3) regarding previous convictions?
A: The consequence is that it completely walls off the accused's criminal history from the judge's mind while deciding guilt for the current incident, ensuring the verdict is based strictly on the current evidence, not past bad character. [Source: Section 271, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Acquittal or conviction

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 272: Absence of complainant

Q: In a private complaint case, what happens if the person who filed the complaint just doesn't show up to court on the hearing day?
A: If it's a minor offence (non-cognizable or compoundable), the Magistrate can give the complainant 30 days' notice. If they still don't show up, the Magistrate can just discharge the accused and close the case before charges are even framed. [Source: Section 272, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Absence of complainant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 272: Absence of complainant

Q: What scenario is addressed by Section 272 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 272 of BNSS 2023 addresses the "Absence of complainant" in warrant-cases instituted on complaint, giving the Magistrate discretion to discharge the accused if the complainant fails to appear for a compoundable or non-cognizable offence, after giving 30 days' time. [Source: Section 272, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Absence of complainant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 272: Absence of complainant

Q: A man files a private complaint against his neighbor for a minor, non-cognizable dispute. On the first hearing day, the neighbor (accused) shows up, but the man who filed the complaint doesn't. Can the Magistrate immediately throw the case out?
A: The Magistrate has the discretion to throw it out, but must first give "thirty days' time to the complainant to be present" before discharging the accused under this section. [Source: Section 272, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Absence of complainant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 272: Absence of complainant

Q: What are the two specific types of offences to which this rule of discharge due to complainant absence applies?
A: The offence must be one that "may be lawfully compounded" OR "is not a cognizable offence". [Source: Section 272, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Absence of complainant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 272: Absence of complainant

Q: If a private citizen files a complaint for Murder (a highly cognizable, non-compoundable offence) and misses a court date, can the Magistrate use this section to discharge the accused?
A: No, this section explicitly restricts this power to offences that "may be lawfully compounded or is not a cognizable offence." Serious crimes cannot be dismissed just because the complainant missed a day. [Source: Section 272, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Absence of complainant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 272: Absence of complainant

Q: What is the consequence of this rule for the accused?
A: The consequence is that the accused is protected from endless harassment by a malicious complainant who files a petty case just to drag the accused to court but never bothers to show up to actually prosecute the case. [Source: Section 272, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Absence of complainant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 273: Compensation for accusation without reasonable cause

Q: What happens if someone files a completely fake, malicious police report or court complaint just to harass someone, and the accused gets acquitted?
A: If the Magistrate thinks there was no reasonable ground for making the accusation, they can order the person who made the fake complaint to pay compensation to the accused, and if they don't pay, they can be sent to jail for up to 30 days. [Source: Section 273, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Compensation for accusation without reasonable cause

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 273: Compensation for accusation without reasonable cause

Q: What penalizing mechanism is established by Section 273 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 273 of BNSS 2023 establishes the mechanism for "Compensation for accusation without reasonable cause," allowing Magistrates to fine complainants/informants who initiate baseless criminal cases and award that money to the wrongfully accused. [Source: Section 273, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Compensation for accusation without reasonable cause

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 273: Compensation for accusation without reasonable cause

Q: A woman falsely tells the police her co-worker stole her phone, purely out of spite. The co-worker undergoes a trial and is acquitted because security footage proves he was nowhere near the phone. Can the Magistrate punish the woman?
A: Yes, under sub-section (1), the Magistrate can call upon her to "show cause why he should not pay compensation to such accused", and under sub-section (2), order her to pay compensation not exceeding the amount of fine the Magistrate is empowered to impose. [Source: Section 273, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Compensation for accusation without reasonable cause

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 273: Compensation for accusation without reasonable cause

Q: What specific standard must the Magistrate's opinion meet regarding the initial accusation to trigger this section?
A: The Magistrate must be "of opinion that there was no reasonable ground for making the accusation". [Source: Section 273, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Compensation for accusation without reasonable cause

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 273: Compensation for accusation without reasonable cause

Q: Does paying this compensation mean the malicious complainant cannot be sued for defamation in civil court later?
A: No, sub-section (5) states: "No person who has been directed to pay compensation under this section shall, by reason of such order, be exempted from any civil or criminal liability". However, the compensation paid will be taken into account in a subsequent civil suit. [Source: Section 273, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Compensation for accusation without reasonable cause

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 273: Compensation for accusation without reasonable cause

Q: What is the systemic consequence of having this compensation provision?
A: The consequence is deterrence; it strongly discourages people from using the criminal justice system as a weapon for personal vendettas, knowing that filing a frivolous case could result in them having to personally pay the victim or go to jail themselves. [Source: Section 273, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Compensation for accusation without reasonable cause

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 274: Substance of accusation to be stated

Q: Summons-cases are for minor offences. How does a summons-case trial begin compared to a serious warrant-case trial?
A: It's much simpler. The Magistrate just tells the accused the "substance of the accusation" (what they are accused of) and asks how they plead. The Magistrate doesn't have to write up a formal, complex "charge" document. [Source: Section 274, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Substance of accusation to be stated

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 274: Substance of accusation to be stated

Q: What simplified procedure is introduced in Section 274 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 274 of BNSS 2023 introduces the starting procedure for the "Trial of Summons-Cases," where the Magistrate simply states the particulars of the offence to the accused and takes their plea, explicitly dispensing with the need to frame a formal charge. [Source: Section 274, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Substance of accusation to be stated

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 274: Substance of accusation to be stated

Q: A man is brought to court for a minor traffic violation (a summons-case). His lawyer demands that the trial be paused because the Magistrate hasn't framed a formal written "charge" outlining the exact legal parameters of the offence. Is the lawyer right?
A: No, section 274 explicitly states that in a summons-case, "it shall not be necessary to frame a formal charge." Stating the particulars orally is legally sufficient. [Source: Section 274, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Substance of accusation to be stated

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 274: Substance of accusation to be stated

Q: According to the proviso, what must the Magistrate do if they immediately consider the accusation to be "groundless" right at the start?
A: The Magistrate shall "after recording reasons in writing, release the accused and such release shall have the effect of discharge." [Source: Section 274, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Substance of accusation to be stated

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 274: Substance of accusation to be stated

Q: Is the Magistrate completely exempt from telling the accused what they did wrong just because a formal charge isn't needed?
A: No, the core requirement remains: "the particulars of the offence of which he is accused shall be stated to him". The accused still has a fundamental right to know the allegations. [Source: Section 274, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Substance of accusation to be stated

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 274: Substance of accusation to be stated

Q: What is the practical consequence of not requiring a formal charge in summons-cases?
A: The consequence is immense speed and efficiency; minor offences (like petty theft, traffic violations, or public nuisance) can be processed through the courts rapidly without bogging down the system with heavy procedural paperwork. [Source: Section 274, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Substance of accusation to be stated

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 275: Conviction on plea of guilty

Q: In a summons-case, what must the Magistrate do if the accused pleads guilty right at the start?
A: The Magistrate must record the plea using the exact words of the accused as much as possible, and then has the discretion to immediately convict the accused. [Source: Section 275, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Conviction on plea of guilty

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 275: Conviction on plea of guilty

Q: What procedure does Section 275 of BNSS 2023 establish?
A: Section 275 of BNSS 2023 establishes the procedure for a "Conviction on plea of guilty" in a summons-case, requiring the Magistrate to record the exact words of the plea before exercising discretion to convict. [Source: Section 275, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Conviction on plea of guilty

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 275: Conviction on plea of guilty

Q: A man is charged with a minor assault (a summons-case). When asked how he pleads, he says, "Yeah, I hit him, but he called my mother a name first." Can the Magistrate just record "Accused pleads guilty"?
A: No, under section 275, the Magistrate "shall record the plea as nearly as possible in the words used by the accused". The Magistrate must record the full statement, as the condition ("but he called my mother...") might amount to a legal defense (provocation), meaning it's not actually an unequivocal guilty plea. [Source: Section 275, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Conviction on plea of guilty

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 275: Conviction on plea of guilty

Q: What specific standard is applied to *how* the guilty plea must be recorded?
A: It must be recorded "as nearly as possible in the words used by the accused". [Source: Section 275, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Conviction on plea of guilty

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 275: Conviction on plea of guilty

Q: Is the Magistrate forced to convict every single person who utters the words "I am guilty"?
A: No, the conviction is "in his discretion." A Magistrate might refuse to convict on a guilty plea if they suspect the accused is covering for someone else, or doesn't understand the law. [Source: Section 275, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Conviction on plea of guilty

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 275: Conviction on plea of guilty

Q: What is the consequence of requiring the Magistrate to record the exact words of the accused?
A: The consequence is that appellate courts can review the precise statement to ensure the accused made an unambiguous, voluntary admission of guilt, preventing unfair convictions based on a Magistrate misinterpreting a complex statement as a simple "guilty" plea. [Source: Section 275, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Conviction on plea of guilty

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 276: Conviction on plea of guilty in absence of accused in petty cases

Q: For very petty offences (like a small traffic ticket), does the accused have to physically go to court to plead guilty?
A: No. If the summons allows it, the accused can plead guilty without appearing in court by sending a letter with their plea and the fine money by post or messenger, or they can authorize their lawyer to plead guilty on their behalf. [Source: Section 276, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Conviction on plea of guilty in absence of accused in petty cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 276: Conviction on plea of guilty in absence of accused in petty cases

Q: What convenience mechanism is introduced in Section 276 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 276 of BNSS 2023 introduces a convenience mechanism for petty cases, allowing an accused to plead guilty in absentia by transmitting a letter and the specified fine, or through an authorized advocate. [Source: Section 276, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Conviction on plea of guilty in absence of accused in petty cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 276: Conviction on plea of guilty in absence of accused in petty cases

Q: A woman gets a summons for littering, with a specified fine of ₹500. She lives in another state and cannot attend court. How can she resolve this without traveling?
A: Under sub-section (1), she can "transmit to the Magistrate, by post or by messenger, a letter containing his plea and also the amount of fine specified in the summons." [Source: Section 276, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Conviction on plea of guilty in absence of accused in petty cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 276: Conviction on plea of guilty in absence of accused in petty cases

Q: If an accused chooses to send a letter pleading guilty by post, what two specific things must be included in the transmission?
A: "a letter containing his plea" AND "the amount of fine specified in the summons." [Source: Section 276, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Conviction on plea of guilty in absence of accused in petty cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 276: Conviction on plea of guilty in absence of accused in petty cases

Q: Can the Magistrate sentence the absent accused to jail time based on their mailed-in guilty plea?
A: No, under sub-section (2), the Magistrate may only "sentence him to pay the fine specified in the summons". In-absentia pleas are strictly for fine-only resolutions in petty cases. [Source: Section 276, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Conviction on plea of guilty in absence of accused in petty cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 276: Conviction on plea of guilty in absence of accused in petty cases

Q: What is the systemic consequence of allowing guilty pleas by post or messenger?
A: The consequence is massive relief for both the public and the courts; citizens avoid disproportionate travel expenses for minor fines, and courts can dispose of thousands of petty cases administratively without clogging the courtrooms. [Source: Section 276, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Conviction on plea of guilty in absence of accused in petty cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 277: Procedure when not convicted

Q: If the accused pleads "not guilty" in a summons-case, how does the trial actually happen?
A: The Magistrate simply hears the prosecution and takes their evidence, and then immediately hears the accused and takes their defense evidence. The Magistrate can also issue summons for witnesses if requested. [Source: Section 277, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure when not convicted

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 277: Procedure when not convicted

Q: What trial procedure is outlined in Section 277 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 277 of BNSS 2023 outlines the "Procedure when not convicted" (the actual trial phase) for summons-cases, mandating the Magistrate to take evidence from both the prosecution and the defense in a continuous, streamlined manner. [Source: Section 277, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure when not convicted

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 277: Procedure when not convicted

Q: In a summons-case for public nuisance, the accused pleads not guilty. The prosecutor immediately hands the Magistrate a list of 5 witnesses and asks the Magistrate to force them to attend. Can the Magistrate demand the prosecutor pay for their travel first?
A: Yes, under sub-section (3), the Magistrate "may, before summoning any witness on such application, require that the reasonable expenses of the witness incurred in attending... be deposited in Court." [Source: Section 277, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure when not convicted

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 277: Procedure when not convicted

Q: Whose evidence must the Magistrate hear first according to sub-section (1)?
A: The Magistrate shall "proceed to hear the prosecution and take all such evidence as may be produced in support of the prosecution" before hearing the defense. [Source: Section 277, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure when not convicted

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 277: Procedure when not convicted

Q: In a summons-case, does the Magistrate stop halfway through the trial to frame a formal written charge after hearing the prosecution witnesses?
A: No, section 277 requires hearing the prosecution and then hearing the accused. Summons-cases (as per section 274) do not require the framing of a formal charge at any stage; the trial proceeds straight from prosecution evidence to defense evidence. [Source: Section 277, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure when not convicted

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 277: Procedure when not convicted

Q: What is the consequence of this consolidated evidentiary procedure?
A: The consequence is a highly accelerated trial process; by eliminating the formal charge-framing step and moving directly from prosecution to defense, summons-cases can often be concluded in a single hearing day. [Source: Section 277, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure when not convicted

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 278: Acquittal or conviction

Q: After hearing all the evidence in a summons-case, what are the Magistrate's final options?
A: The Magistrate will either record an order of acquittal if the accused is not guilty, or pass a sentence of punishment if the accused is guilty. [Source: Section 278, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Acquittal or conviction

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 278: Acquittal or conviction

Q: What conclusive actions are mandated by Section 278 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 278 of BNSS 2023 mandates the final judgment in a summons-case: recording an acquittal if evidence is insufficient, or passing a sentence if guilt is proven, while allowing conviction for alternative offences proved during the trial. [Source: Section 278, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Acquittal or conviction

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 278: Acquittal or conviction

Q: An accused is brought in on a summons for "simple hurt." During the trial, the evidence clearly shows they didn't commit hurt, but they did commit "criminal intimidation," which is also a summons-case offence. Can the Magistrate convict them of intimidation even though the original summons was for hurt?
A: Yes, under sub-section (3), the Magistrate may convict the accused of *any* offence triable under this Chapter which the facts prove they committed, "whatever may be the nature of the complaint or summons," provided the accused is not prejudiced by this change. [Source: Section 278, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Acquittal or conviction

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 278: Acquittal or conviction

Q: Under sub-section (1), can the Magistrate rely on evidence that neither the prosecutor nor the defense lawyer actually submitted?
A: Yes, the Magistrate can take the evidence referred to in section 277 "and such further evidence, if any, as he may, of his own motion, cause to be produced". The Magistrate can actively seek out evidence. [Source: Section 278, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Acquittal or conviction

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 278: Acquittal or conviction

Q: If the Magistrate finds the accused guilty, do they *always* have to pass a sentence?
A: No, sub-section (2) provides exceptions if the Magistrate proceeds "in accordance with the provisions of section 364 or section 401" (e.g., sending the case to a higher Magistrate for heavier punishment, or releasing on probation). [Source: Section 278, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Acquittal or conviction

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 278: Acquittal or conviction

Q: What is the consequence of sub-section (3) allowing conviction for a different offence than what was on the summons?
A: The consequence is preventing guilty individuals from escaping justice on minor technicalities; it allows the court to adapt the final conviction to the actual facts proven at trial, without forcing the prosecution to start a whole new case just to fix a categorization error on the initial summons. [Source: Section 278, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Acquittal or conviction

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 279: Non-appearance or death of complainant

Q: In a minor complaint case (summons-case), what happens if the person who filed the complaint doesn't show up for the hearing, or dies?
A: The Magistrate will give the complainant 30 days to appear. If they still don't show up, or if they have died, the Magistrate shall acquit the accused, unless there's a good reason to postpone the trial. [Source: Section 279, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Non-appearance or death of complainant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 279: Non-appearance or death of complainant

Q: What scenario does Section 279 of BNSS 2023 address?
A: Section 279 of BNSS 2023 addresses the "Non-appearance or death of complainant" in summons-cases, mandating the acquittal of the accused after a 30-day waiting period if the complainant fails to appear, with provisions for dispensing with their attendance if represented by counsel. [Source: Section 279, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Non-appearance or death of complainant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 279: Non-appearance or death of complainant

Q: A man files a private complaint for public nuisance. He dies before the first hearing date. Does the accused have to go through a full trial with a ghost complainant?
A: No, under sub-section (2), the provisions regarding non-appearance apply "to cases where the non-appearance of the complainant is due to his death." The Magistrate will likely acquit the accused unless there's a compelling reason to continue. [Source: Section 279, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Non-appearance or death of complainant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 279: Non-appearance or death of complainant

Q: Under the proviso to sub-section (1), what are the two specific situations where a Magistrate can proceed with the trial even if the complainant is physically absent?
A: (1) "where the complainant is represented by an advocate or by the officer conducting the prosecution" or (2) "where the Magistrate is of opinion that the personal attendance of the complainant is not necessary". [Source: Section 279, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Non-appearance or death of complainant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 279: Non-appearance or death of complainant

Q: Is the Magistrate absolutely forced to acquit the accused exactly 30 days after the complainant misses a date?
A: No, the Magistrate shall acquit "unless for some reason he thinks it proper to adjourn the hearing of the case to some other day". [Source: Section 279, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Non-appearance or death of complainant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 279: Non-appearance or death of complainant

Q: What is the consequence of treating the complainant's absence as grounds for an "acquittal" (rather than a mere discharge)?
A: The consequence is finality; because it is an *acquittal*, double jeopardy applies. The complainant (or their heirs) cannot come back a year later and try to file the exact same minor case against the accused again. [Source: Section 279, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Non-appearance or death of complainant

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 280: Withdrawal of complaint

Q: Can a person who filed a minor complaint against someone change their mind and take it back?
A: Yes. At any point before the final order is given, if the complainant convinces the Magistrate there are good reasons, the Magistrate can let them withdraw the complaint, which results in the accused being acquitted. [Source: Section 280, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Withdrawal of complaint

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 280: Withdrawal of complaint

Q: What legal action is authorized by Section 280 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 280 of BNSS 2023 authorizes the "Withdrawal of complaint" in summons-cases, allowing a complainant, with the Magistrate's permission, to drop the charges before the final order, resulting in an acquittal for the accused. [Source: Section 280, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Withdrawal of complaint

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 280: Withdrawal of complaint

Q: A landlord files a private complaint against a tenant for a minor nuisance. Halfway through the trial, they settle their dispute privately. The landlord tells the Magistrate he wants to drop the case. What is the legal effect if the Magistrate agrees?
A: Under section 280, if the Magistrate permits him to withdraw it, the Magistrate "shall thereupon acquit the accused against whom the complaint is so withdrawn." The case is permanently over. [Source: Section 280, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Withdrawal of complaint

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 280: Withdrawal of complaint

Q: What is the absolute time limit for a complainant to request the withdrawal of their complaint under this section?
A: "at any time before a final order is passed". [Source: Section 280, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Withdrawal of complaint

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 280: Withdrawal of complaint

Q: If there are three co-accused in a complaint, can the complainant withdraw the case against just *one* of them and continue prosecuting the other two?
A: Yes, the section explicitly states the complainant can withdraw the complaint against the accused, "or if there be more than one accused, against all or any of them". [Source: Section 280, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Withdrawal of complaint

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 280: Withdrawal of complaint

Q: What is the consequence of requiring the Magistrate to be "satisfied that there are sufficient grounds" for withdrawal?
A: The consequence is that it prevents abuse of process; the court can refuse the withdrawal if it suspects the accused is extorting or violently intimidating the complainant into dropping the charges against their will. [Source: Section 280, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Withdrawal of complaint

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 281: Power to stop proceedings in certain cases

Q: Can a Magistrate just abruptly stop a minor trial that was started by the police, without ever giving a final judgment?
A: Yes, in a summons-case not based on a private complaint (e.g., started by police), a First Class Magistrate can stop the proceedings at any stage for recorded reasons. If the main witnesses already testified, it counts as an acquittal; otherwise, it's just a discharge. [Source: Section 281, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to stop proceedings in certain cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 281: Power to stop proceedings in certain cases

Q: What extraordinary power is granted by Section 281 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 281 of BNSS 2023 grants the "Power to stop proceedings in certain cases," allowing specific Magistrates to halt summons-case trials (instituted otherwise than on complaint) at any stage, resulting in either a discharge or acquittal depending on whether principal witnesses have testified. [Source: Section 281, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to stop proceedings in certain cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 281: Power to stop proceedings in certain cases

Q: The police start a minor summons-case trial. Halfway through, the Magistrate realizes the police investigation was completely botched and continuing the trial is a waste of public money. No witnesses have testified yet. The Magistrate stops the proceedings. What is the legal status of the accused?
A: Under section 281, because the stoppage occurred *before* the evidence of principal witnesses was recorded, the Magistrate shall "release the accused, and such release shall have the effect of discharge." [Source: Section 281, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to stop proceedings in certain cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 281: Power to stop proceedings in certain cases

Q: What specific class of Magistrate can exercise this power without needing anyone else's permission?
A: "a Magistrate of the first class". (Any other Judicial Magistrate requires "the previous sanction of the Chief Judicial Magistrate"). [Source: Section 281, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to stop proceedings in certain cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 281: Power to stop proceedings in certain cases

Q: Can a Magistrate use this power to abruptly stop a trial that was started by a private citizen's complaint?
A: No, this power explicitly applies only "In any summons-case instituted otherwise than upon complaint". It cannot be used to arbitrarily shut down a private citizen's legal grievance. [Source: Section 281, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to stop proceedings in certain cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 281: Power to stop proceedings in certain cases

Q: What is the consequence of distinguishing between stopping the trial before vs. after principal witnesses testify?
A: The consequence is fairness regarding double jeopardy; if the prosecution has already presented its main case (witnesses) and the trial is stopped, the accused gets a final acquittal (cannot be retried). If it's stopped early, they only get a discharge (could potentially be charged again if better evidence arises). [Source: Section 281, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to stop proceedings in certain cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 282: Power of Court to convert summonscases into warrant-cases

Q: What happens if a Magistrate starts a simple trial (summons-case) for a crime, but during the trial realizes the crime is actually much more serious and requires the stricter, more detailed trial process (warrant-case)?
A: If the offence carries a penalty of more than 6 months in prison, the Magistrate can switch the trial mid-way to the stricter warrant-case procedure, re-hear the case, and recall witnesses. [Source: Section 282, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power of Court to convert summonscases into warrant-cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 282: Power of Court to convert summonscases into warrant-cases

Q: What procedural flexibility is provided by Section 282 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 282 of BNSS 2023 provides the "Power of Court to convert summons-cases into warrant-cases," allowing a Magistrate to upgrade the trial procedure mid-stream if justice demands it, provided the offence is punishable by more than six months imprisonment. [Source: Section 282, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power of Court to convert summonscases into warrant-cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 282: Power of Court to convert summonscases into warrant-cases

Q: A Magistrate starts a quick summons-case trial for what police called "simple hurt" (a minor offence). During witness testimony, it becomes clear the victim actually suffered permanent brain damage, making it "grievous hurt" (a serious warrant-case offence). What can the Magistrate do?
A: Under section 282, the Magistrate may "proceed to re-hear the case in the manner provided by this Sanhita for the trial of warrant-cases and may recall any witness who may have been examined." [Source: Section 282, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power of Court to convert summonscases into warrant-cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 282: Power of Court to convert summonscases into warrant-cases

Q: What is the mandatory threshold regarding the punishment of the offence that allows a Magistrate to convert the trial procedure?
A: The offence must be one "punishable with imprisonment for a term exceeding six months". [Source: Section 282, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power of Court to convert summonscases into warrant-cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 282: Power of Court to convert summonscases into warrant-cases

Q: Can the Magistrate convert a trial involving a petty fine-only offence into a complex warrant-case just because they feel like it?
A: No, the conversion is strictly limited to offences punishable with "imprisonment for a term exceeding six months." Petty offences cannot be artificially escalated to warrant-case procedures. [Source: Section 282, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power of Court to convert summonscases into warrant-cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 282: Power of Court to convert summonscases into warrant-cases

Q: What is the consequence of this conversion power for the accused's rights?
A: The consequence is that if a case turns out to be more serious than initially thought, the accused is guaranteed the robust procedural protections of a warrant-case (like the formal framing of charges and multiple opportunities for cross-examination) rather than being railroaded through a simplified summons process. [Source: Section 282, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power of Court to convert summonscases into warrant-cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 283: Power to try summarily

Q: What is a "summary trial," and what kinds of crimes can be tried this way?
A: A summary trial is an extremely fast, simplified trial process used for minor offences. Magistrates must use it for specific petty crimes (like theft of property under ₹20,000, or minor insults). [Source: Section 283, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to try summarily

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 283: Power to try summarily

Q: What mechanism for rapid justice is detailed in Section 283 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 283 of BNSS 2023 details the "Power to try summarily," mandating Chief Judicial Magistrates and First Class Magistrates to use a highly expedited summary trial procedure for a specific list of minor offences (e.g., small thefts, minor intimidation). [Source: Section 283, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to try summarily

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 283: Power to try summarily

Q: A teenager is caught shoplifting a t-shirt worth ₹500. Will this require a massive, multi-year court trial with thousands of pages of documents?
A: No. Because it is theft where the value of the property stolen does not exceed ₹20,000, sub-section (1)(i) mandates that a Magistrate "shall try in a summary way" this offence, resolving it quickly. [Source: Section 283, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to try summarily

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 283: Power to try summarily

Q: What is the exact monetary limit for property stolen, received, or concealed that qualifies the offence for a mandatory summary trial under clauses (i), (ii), and (iii)?
A: "where the value of the property... does not exceed twenty thousand rupees". [Source: Section 283, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to try summarily

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 283: Power to try summarily

Q: If a Magistrate starts a summary trial for a minor theft but suddenly realizes the accused is part of a massive organized crime ring and the case is incredibly complex, are they forced to finish it as a summary trial?
A: No, under sub-section (3), if the Magistrate decides "it is undesirable to try it summarily, the Magistrate shall recall any witnesses... and proceed to re-hear the case in the manner provided by this Sanhita" (e.g., as a regular warrant or summons case). [Source: Section 283, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to try summarily

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 283: Power to try summarily

Q: What is the systemic consequence of making summary trials mandatory ("shall try") for these specific petty offences?
A: The consequence is a drastic reduction in court backlog; by forcing the fastest possible procedure for routine, low-stakes crimes, judicial resources are freed up to handle serious felonies like murder and rape. [Source: Section 283, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to try summarily

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 284: Summary trial by Magistrate of second class

Q: Can a lower-level judge (Magistrate of the second class) conduct these fast summary trials?
A: Yes, but only if the High Court specifically gives them the power to do so, and they can only try very minor offences that are punished only by a fine or a maximum of 6 months in prison. [Source: Section 284, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Summary trial by Magistrate of second class

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 284: Summary trial by Magistrate of second class

Q: What specific delegation of power is authorized by Section 284 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 284 of BNSS 2023 authorizes the High Court to confer the power to conduct summary trials upon a Magistrate of the second class, strictly limiting their jurisdiction to offences punishable by fine only or up to six months imprisonment. [Source: Section 284, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Summary trial by Magistrate of second class

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 284: Summary trial by Magistrate of second class

Q: A Second Class Magistrate wants to conduct a summary trial for a theft case where the maximum punishment under the penal code is 3 years in prison. Can they do this?
A: No, under section 284, a Second Class Magistrate can only be empowered to try summarily offences "which is punishable only with fine or with imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months". They cannot summarily try a 3-year offence. [Source: Section 284, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Summary trial by Magistrate of second class

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 284: Summary trial by Magistrate of second class

Q: Which specific higher authority holds the power to grant a Second Class Magistrate the ability to conduct summary trials?
A: "The High Court". [Source: Section 284, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Summary trial by Magistrate of second class

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 284: Summary trial by Magistrate of second class

Q: Does a Magistrate of the second class automatically have the power to conduct summary trials the moment they are appointed?
