A: No, under sub-section (1), the judge "may, at any subsequent stage of the proceedings, direct the personal attendance of such accused." [Source: Section 355, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Provision for inquiries and trial being held in absence of accused in certain cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 355: Provision for inquiries and trial being held in absence of accused in certain cases

Q: What is the consequence of allowing attendance via audio-video means and dispensing with attendance in certain cases?
A: The consequence is preventing the trial process itself from becoming a punishment; it spares defendants in minor cases the financial ruin of traveling across the country for 5-minute procedural hearings, while also giving judges a tool to stop unruly defendants from intentionally sabotaging the trial process. [Source: Section 355, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Provision for inquiries and trial being held in absence of accused in certain cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 356: Inquiry, trial or judgment in absentia of proclaimed offender

Q: If a hardcore criminal is declared a "proclaimed offender" and completely evades arrest, does the law just wait forever, or can they be tried and convicted in absentia (while they are hiding)?
A: They can be tried, convicted, and sentenced in absentia. By absconding, they legally waive their right to be present. The court appoints a state lawyer to defend them, publishes notices in newspapers, and proceeds with the trial. [Source: Section 356, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Inquiry, trial or judgment in absentia of proclaimed offender

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 356: Inquiry, trial or judgment in absentia of proclaimed offender

Q: How does Section 356 of BNSS 2023 tackle the problem of fugitive offenders stalling justice?
A: Section 356 of BNSS 2023 authorizes "Inquiry, trial or judgment in absentia of proclaimed offender," declaring that absconding waives the right to be present, and allowing courts to proceed with trials, examine witnesses, and pronounce judgments against fugitives after adhering to strict notice procedures. [Source: Section 356, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Inquiry, trial or judgment in absentia of proclaimed offender

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 356: Inquiry, trial or judgment in absentia of proclaimed offender

Q: A terrorist is declared a proclaimed offender and flees the country. The judge frames charges against him on January 1st. On February 1st (30 days later), the judge says, "He's not coming back, let's start examining witnesses tomorrow." Is this allowed?
A: No. The proviso to sub-section (1) explicitly states: "Provided that the Court shall not commence the trial unless a period of ninety days has lapsed from the date of framing of the charge." The judge must wait 90 days. [Source: Section 356, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Inquiry, trial or judgment in absentia of proclaimed offender

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 356: Inquiry, trial or judgment in absentia of proclaimed offender

Q: Under sub-section (2), list at least two of the four specific procedural steps the Court must take to notify the offender before starting a trial in absentia.
A: Any two of: (i) issuing two consecutive arrest warrants at least 30 days apart, (ii) publishing a notice in a national/local newspaper, (iii) informing a relative or friend, (iv) affixing notice on their house and local police station. [Source: Section 356, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Inquiry, trial or judgment in absentia of proclaimed offender

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 356: Inquiry, trial or judgment in absentia of proclaimed offender

Q: If the proclaimed offender is convicted in absentia and sentenced to prison, can their lawyer immediately file an appeal to the High Court while the offender is still hiding abroad?
A: No. Sub-section (7) states "No appeal shall lie against the judgment under this section unless the proclaimed offender presents himself before the Court of appeal". They must surrender to appeal. [Source: Section 356, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Inquiry, trial or judgment in absentia of proclaimed offender

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 356: Inquiry, trial or judgment in absentia of proclaimed offender

Q: What is the severe consequence established by the proviso to sub-section (7) if the convicted fugitive stays hidden for too long?
A: "Provided that no appeal against conviction shall lie after the expiry of three years from the date of the judgment." If they hide for 3 years, their conviction becomes final and unappealable. [Source: Section 356, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Inquiry, trial or judgment in absentia of proclaimed offender

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 357: Procedure where accused does not understand proceedings

Q: What happens if an accused person isn't legally "insane," but they simply cannot understand the court proceedings (for example, they are deaf, mute, and uneducated without any sign language knowledge)?
A: The Magistrate proceeds with the trial. If the trial ends in a conviction, the Magistrate cannot sentence them directly; instead, they must forward the entire case to the High Court, which will decide what to do. [Source: Section 357, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where accused does not understand proceedings

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 357: Procedure where accused does not understand proceedings

Q: How does Section 357 of BNSS 2023 handle defendants with severe communicative or cognitive barriers who are not legally of unsound mind?
A: Section 357 of BNSS 2023 dictates the "Procedure where accused does not understand proceedings," instructing lower courts to proceed with the trial but requiring them to forward any resulting conviction and case report to the High Court for final orders. [Source: Section 357, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where accused does not understand proceedings

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 357: Procedure where accused does not understand proceedings

Q: A person who is profoundly deaf and has never learned to read, write, or sign is put on trial for theft. The Magistrate conducts the trial and finds him guilty. Can the Magistrate immediately sentence him to 6 months in jail?
A: No. Because the accused cannot be made to understand the proceedings, under section 357, "if such proceedings result in a conviction, the proceedings shall be forwarded to the High Court with a report... and the High Court shall pass thereon such order as it thinks fit." [Source: Section 357, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where accused does not understand proceedings

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 357: Procedure where accused does not understand proceedings

Q: What specific mental condition is *excluded* from the application of this section?
A: "though not a person of unsound mind". (Unsoundness of mind is handled by separate chapters). [Source: Section 357, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where accused does not understand proceedings

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 357: Procedure where accused does not understand proceedings

Q: If the trial of a person who cannot understand the proceedings results in an *acquittal* instead of a conviction, does the Magistrate still have to forward the case to the High Court?
A: No. The statute specifically says the proceedings shall be forwarded "if such proceedings result in a conviction". An acquittal ends the matter locally. [Source: Section 357, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where accused does not understand proceedings

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 357: Procedure where accused does not understand proceedings

Q: What is the consequence of forcing the High Court to review these convictions?
A: The consequence is an extreme safeguard against miscarriages of justice; because an accused who cannot understand the trial is utterly defenseless (they cannot instruct a lawyer or cross-examine witnesses), the law strips lower courts of the power to imprison them, demanding the highest court in the state review the fairness of the conviction. [Source: Section 357, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where accused does not understand proceedings

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 358: Power to proceed against other persons appearing to be guilty of offence

Q: What happens if, right in the middle of a trial for Person A, a witness testifies and accidentally proves that Person B (who isn't even charged) actually committed the crime with them?
A: The judge has the power to immediately halt and proceed against Person B as well. The judge can summon or arrest Person B, and add them to the case, though the proceedings against Person B will have to start fresh. [Source: Section 358, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to proceed against other persons appearing to be guilty of offence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 358: Power to proceed against other persons appearing to be guilty of offence

Q: What judicial mechanism for adding new defendants mid-trial is provided by Section 358 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 358 of BNSS 2023 grants the "Power to proceed against other persons appearing to be guilty of offence," allowing a Court, based on evidence emerging during an inquiry/trial, to proceed against, summon, or arrest any person not currently accused who appears to have committed the offence. [Source: Section 358, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to proceed against other persons appearing to be guilty of offence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 358: Power to proceed against other persons appearing to be guilty of offence

Q: During a robbery trial against 'X', the victim testifies that 'X' and another man named 'Y' tied him up. 'Y' happens to be sitting in the back of the courtroom watching the trial. The judge points at 'Y' and tells the police to lock the doors and detain him immediately. Is this legal?
A: Yes. Under sub-section (3), "Any person attending the Court, although not under arrest or upon a summons, may be detained by such Court for the purpose of the inquiry into, or trial of, the offence which he appears to have committed." [Source: Section 358, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to proceed against other persons appearing to be guilty of offence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 358: Power to proceed against other persons appearing to be guilty of offence

Q: If the Court adds a new person to the trial under sub-section (1), what two things *must* happen regarding the proceedings against that newly added person under sub-section (4)(a)?
A: "the proceedings in respect of such person shall be commenced afresh, and the witnesses re-heard". [Source: Section 358, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to proceed against other persons appearing to be guilty of offence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 358: Power to proceed against other persons appearing to be guilty of offence

Q: Can the judge just add the new person to the case and use all the old witness testimonies against them without letting the new person cross-examine them?
A: No, sub-section (4)(a) explicitly mandates that the proceedings be "commenced afresh" and witnesses "re-heard" specifically to protect the new defendant's right to cross-examine. [Source: Section 358, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to proceed against other persons appearing to be guilty of offence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 358: Power to proceed against other persons appearing to be guilty of offence

Q: What is the consequence of giving this power to the trial judge?
A: The consequence is judicial independence from police negligence; if the police purposefully shield a powerful co-conspirator and refuse to charge them, the judge isn't forced to turn a blind eye when the truth emerges in court. The judge can actively drag the shielded criminal into the dock to face justice. [Source: Section 358, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to proceed against other persons appearing to be guilty of offence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 359: Compounding of offences

Q: Can a victim of a crime just agree to "drop the charges" and settle out of court with the criminal?
A: Yes, but only for specific, usually less severe offences (like simple hurt, minor theft, or defamation). This is called "compounding." For some offences, the victim can just do it themselves; for others, they need the judge's permission. If compounded, it counts as an acquittal. [Source: Section 359, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Compounding of offences

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 359: Compounding of offences

Q: How does Section 359 of BNSS 2023 handle out-of-court settlements in criminal law?
A: Section 359 of BNSS 2023 governs the "Compounding of offences," providing strict tables detailing which specific BNS offences can be settled (compounded) by the victim independently, which require Court permission, and establishing that compounding equates to an acquittal. [Source: Section 359, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Compounding of offences

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 359: Compounding of offences

Q: A man is charged with "Word, gesture or act intended to insult the modesty of a woman." He apologizes and pays her money. She tells the judge, "I forgive him, I want to drop the case." Can she just drop it on her own authority?
A: No. According to the table in sub-section (2), this offence (BNS Section 79) is in the category that may only be compounded "with the permission of the Court before which any prosecution for such offence is pending." She needs the judge's approval. [Source: Section 359, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Compounding of offences

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 359: Compounding of offences

Q: According to sub-section (8), what is the ultimate legal effect once an offence has been successfully compounded?
A: "The composition of an offence under this section shall have the effect of an acquittal of the accused". [Source: Section 359, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Compounding of offences

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 359: Compounding of offences

Q: If a criminal is convicted of a compoundable offence, but the judge notes that because of his past criminal record, he is liable to an "enhanced punishment" under the law, can the victim still compound the offence to save him?
A: No. Sub-section (7) explicitly states: "No offence shall be compounded if the accused is, by reason of a previous conviction, liable either to enhanced punishment or to a punishment of a different kind for such offence." [Source: Section 359, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Compounding of offences

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 359: Compounding of offences

Q: What is the consequence of allowing compounding for certain crimes?
A: The consequence is restorative justice and system relief; it acknowledges that for private disputes (like defamation, minor cheating, or simple trespassing), a genuine apology and financial restitution between the parties is often a better outcome than a dragged-out prosecution, freeing up court time for serious, non-compoundable felonies like murder. [Source: Section 359, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Compounding of offences

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 360: Withdrawal from prosecution

Q: If the Public Prosecutor realizes the state's case is weak or politically motivated, can they just withdraw the prosecution and let the accused go?
A: Yes, but the Public Prosecutor MUST get the consent of the Court first, and the Court MUST give the victim a chance to be heard before agreeing to drop the case. [Source: Section 360, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Withdrawal from prosecution

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 360: Withdrawal from prosecution

Q: What mechanism for terminating state prosecutions is governed by Section 360 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 360 of BNSS 2023 controls "Withdrawal from prosecution," allowing a Public Prosecutor to withdraw a case before judgment with the Court's consent, discharging or acquitting the accused, while mandating that the victim be heard and requiring Central Government permission for specific central-level offences. [Source: Section 360, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Withdrawal from prosecution

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 360: Withdrawal from prosecution

Q: A Public Prosecutor decides to withdraw a prosecution against a politician for fraud. The trial has already been going on for a year, and formal charges were framed months ago. The judge agrees to the withdrawal. Does the politician get a "discharge" or an "acquittal"?
A: Because the withdrawal happened *after* the charge had been framed, under clause (b), "he shall be acquitted in respect of such offence". [Source: Section 360, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Withdrawal from prosecution

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 360: Withdrawal from prosecution

Q: Under the second proviso, what mandatory procedural step must the Court take before allowing the prosecutor to withdraw the case?
A: "no Court shall allow such withdrawal without giving an opportunity of being heard to the victim in the case." [Source: Section 360, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Withdrawal from prosecution

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 360: Withdrawal from prosecution

Q: If a state government's Public Prosecutor tries to withdraw a case involving the destruction of Central Government property (like a post office), can the local Magistrate just approve it?
A: No. Under the first proviso (iii), if it involves damage to Central Government property, the Prosecutor cannot move for withdrawal "unless he has been permitted by the Central Government to do so", and the Court must demand to see that permission. [Source: Section 360, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Withdrawal from prosecution

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 360: Withdrawal from prosecution

Q: What is the consequence of requiring the Court's consent and hearing the victim?
A: The consequence is preventing the abuse of prosecutorial discretion; it stops corrupt or heavily politicized state governments from simply ordering their prosecutors to drop all criminal charges against their political allies or wealthy donors, ensuring the judiciary and the victim have a veto over shady backdoor deals. [Source: Section 360, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Withdrawal from prosecution

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 361: Procedure in cases which Magistrate cannot dispose of

Q: What happens if a lower-level Magistrate starts a trial, but realizes halfway through that the crime is actually too serious for them to handle, or that it happened in someone else's jurisdiction?
A: The Magistrate must immediately stop the trial, write a brief report explaining the issue, and send the whole case up to the Chief Judicial Magistrate (their boss) to decide who should handle it. [Source: Section 361, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in cases which Magistrate cannot dispose of

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 361: Procedure in cases which Magistrate cannot dispose of

Q: How does Section 361 of BNSS 2023 handle jurisdictional or competency discoveries mid-trial?
A: Section 361 of BNSS 2023 details the "Procedure in cases which Magistrate cannot dispose of," instructing Magistrates who realize they lack jurisdiction or competency during an inquiry to stay proceedings and submit the case with a report to the Chief Judicial Magistrate for reassignment. [Source: Section 361, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in cases which Magistrate cannot dispose of

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 361: Procedure in cases which Magistrate cannot dispose of

Q: A 2nd Class Magistrate is trying a case of minor theft. During witness testimony, it's revealed the thief used a deadly weapon, turning it into armed robbery—a crime only a higher court can try. What must the 2nd Class Magistrate do?
A: Under section 361(1)(a), because the evidence warrants a presumption "that he has no jurisdiction to try the case", he shall "stay the proceedings and submit the case, with a brief report explaining its nature, to the Chief Judicial Magistrate". [Source: Section 361, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in cases which Magistrate cannot dispose of

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 361: Procedure in cases which Magistrate cannot dispose of

Q: Once the Chief Judicial Magistrate receives the forwarded case, what are their three options under sub-section (2)?
A: The CJM may: (1) "try the case himself", (2) "refer it to any Magistrate subordinate to him having jurisdiction", or (3) "commit the accused for trial". [Source: Section 361, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in cases which Magistrate cannot dispose of

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 361: Procedure in cases which Magistrate cannot dispose of

Q: Can the Magistrate just ignore the jurisdictional issue, finish the trial, and just give a very light sentence so nobody complains?
A: No, the language is mandatory: "he shall stay the proceedings and submit the case". There is no exception allowing them to knowingly act without jurisdiction. [Source: Section 361, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in cases which Magistrate cannot dispose of

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 361: Procedure in cases which Magistrate cannot dispose of

Q: What is the consequence of this rule?
A: The consequence is preventing void trials; if a Magistrate finishes a trial for a crime they aren't legally empowered to judge, the entire verdict is legally void and the whole process has to be done again. This section forces them to hit the brakes the moment they realize they are out of their depth, saving court time. [Source: Section 361, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in cases which Magistrate cannot dispose of

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 362: Procedure when after commencement of inquiry or trial, Magistrate finds case should be committed

Q: If a Magistrate is conducting an inquiry and suddenly realizes the offence is so severe (like a murder) that it has to be tried by a Sessions Court, what do they do?
A: The Magistrate stops the inquiry and "commits" (transfers) the case up to the Court of Session for trial. [Source: Section 362, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure when after commencement of inquiry or trial, Magistrate finds case should be committed

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 362: Procedure when after commencement of inquiry or trial, Magistrate finds case should be committed

Q: What procedure does Section 362 of BNSS 2023 dictate when a Magistrate discovers a case requires a Sessions trial?
A: Section 362 of BNSS 2023 covers the "Procedure when after commencement of inquiry or trial, Magistrate finds case should be committed," requiring the Magistrate to halt and commit the case to the Court of Session if it becomes apparent at any stage before judgment that the case belongs there. [Source: Section 362, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure when after commencement of inquiry or trial, Magistrate finds case should be committed

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 362: Procedure when after commencement of inquiry or trial, Magistrate finds case should be committed

Q: A Magistrate finishes hearing all evidence in what he thought was a serious assault case. Right as he is writing the judgment, he realizes the evidence actually proves attempted murder, which is exclusively triable by the Court of Session. It's the very end of his trial. Does he still have to transfer it?
A: Yes. Under section 362, if it appears to him "at any stage of the proceedings before signing the judgment that the case is one which ought to be tried by the Court of Session, he shall commit it to that Court". He must stop writing the judgment and transfer it. [Source: Section 362, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure when after commencement of inquiry or trial, Magistrate finds case should be committed

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 362: Procedure when after commencement of inquiry or trial, Magistrate finds case should be committed

Q: What specific action is the deadline, after which the Magistrate can no longer use this section to commit the case?
A: "before signing the judgment". [Source: Section 362, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure when after commencement of inquiry or trial, Magistrate finds case should be committed

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 362: Procedure when after commencement of inquiry or trial, Magistrate finds case should be committed

Q: Is there any exception where a Magistrate who realizes the case should be tried by a Sessions Court can just try it themselves to save time?
A: No. The word "shall" is used ("he shall commit it"). It is a mandatory requirement with no exceptions. [Source: Section 362, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure when after commencement of inquiry or trial, Magistrate finds case should be committed

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 362: Procedure when after commencement of inquiry or trial, Magistrate finds case should be committed

Q: What is the consequence of this procedural safeguard?
A: The consequence is ensuring defendants face the correct level of judicial scrutiny; Sessions Courts have more experienced judges and different procedural protections suited for severe crimes carrying life imprisonment or death. This rule ensures serious crimes don't slip through the cracks of the lower courts. [Source: Section 362, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure when after commencement of inquiry or trial, Magistrate finds case should be committed

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 363: Trial of persons previously convicted of offences against coinage, stamp-law or

Q: If someone is a repeat offender who keeps counterfeiting coins or forging stamps, does a low-level Magistrate try them?
A: Generally, no. If they've already been convicted of a serious counterfeiting/forgery crime and get caught doing it again, the Magistrate must send the case up to the Chief Judicial Magistrate or the Sessions Court, who have the power to hand down much harsher sentences. [Source: Section 363, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Trial of persons previously convicted of offences against coinage, stamp-law or

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 363: Trial of persons previously convicted of offences against coinage, stamp-law or

Q: How does Section 363 of BNSS 2023 handle recidivists involved in counterfeiting and forgery?
A: Section 363 of BNSS 2023 regulates the "Trial of persons previously convicted of offences against coinage, stamp-law or property," requiring Magistrates to forward repeat offenders facing 3+ years imprisonment for such crimes to the CJM or Court of Session, unless the Magistrate can independently pass an adequate sentence. [Source: Section 363, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Trial of persons previously convicted of offences against coinage, stamp-law or

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 363: Trial of persons previously convicted of offences against coinage, stamp-law or

Q: A man who previously served 4 years for counterfeiting government stamps is arrested for doing it again. A 1st Class Magistrate (who can only sentence up to 3 years) is handling the inquiry. The Magistrate knows the man deserves at least 7 years for his second offense. What must the Magistrate do?
A: Because the Magistrate is not competent to pass an adequate sentence, under section 363(1), "he shall be sent for trial to the Chief Judicial Magistrate or committed to the Court of Session". [Source: Section 363, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Trial of persons previously convicted of offences against coinage, stamp-law or

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 363: Trial of persons previously convicted of offences against coinage, stamp-law or

Q: Under sub-section (2), if the repeat counterfeiter is put on trial alongside an accomplice who is a first-time offender, what happens to the accomplice when the main guy gets sent to the higher court?
A: The accomplice "shall be similarly sent or committed, unless the Magistrate discharges such other person". The co-accused travel together to the higher court. [Source: Section 363, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Trial of persons previously convicted of offences against coinage, stamp-law or

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 363: Trial of persons previously convicted of offences against coinage, stamp-law or

Q: Is the Magistrate *forced* to send the case up every single time?
A: No, there is an exception: "unless the Magistrate is competent to try the case and is of opinion that he can himself pass an adequate sentence". [Source: Section 363, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Trial of persons previously convicted of offences against coinage, stamp-law or

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 363: Trial of persons previously convicted of offences against coinage, stamp-law or

Q: What is the consequence of targeting coinage and stamp recidivists with this rule?
A: The consequence is protecting the state's economic integrity; repeat counterfeiters pose a systemic threat to the national currency and revenue. Ensuring their second trial occurs in a court empowered to issue devastatingly long sentences acts as a severe deterrent against making counterfeiting a career. [Source: Section 363, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Trial of persons previously convicted of offences against coinage, stamp-law or

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 364: Procedure when Magistrate cannot pass sentence sufficiently severe

Q: What happens if a Magistrate finds a defendant guilty, but realizes the crime is so bad that the maximum punishment the Magistrate is legally allowed to give (like 3 years) just isnt enough?
A: The Magistrate records their opinion that the person is guilty, but instead of sentencing them, forwards the accused to the Chief Judicial Magistrate, who has the power to give a much harsher, appropriate punishment. [Source: Section 364, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure when Magistrate cannot pass sentence sufficiently severe

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 364: Procedure when Magistrate cannot pass sentence sufficiently severe

Q: How does Section 364 of BNSS 2023 address situations where a convicting Magistrate lacks adequate sentencing power?
A: Section 364 of BNSS 2023 defines the "Procedure when Magistrate cannot pass sentence sufficiently severe," permitting a Magistrate who finds an accused guilty but believes a harsher punishment is warranted than they can inflict, to forward the proceedings and the accused to the Chief Judicial Magistrate for sentencing. [Source: Section 364, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure when Magistrate cannot pass sentence sufficiently severe

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 364: Procedure when Magistrate cannot pass sentence sufficiently severe

Q: A 1st Class Magistrate (who can sentence up to 3 years) convicts a man of a horrific, unprovoked assault. The Magistrate thinks the man deserves 7 years in prison. The Magistrate writes "Guilty, I sentence you to 7 years" and signs it. Is this legal?
A: No. The Magistrate cannot exceed their sentencing power. Under section 364(1), because he thinks the accused "ought to receive a punishment... more severe than, that which such Magistrate is empowered to inflict", he must "submit his proceedings, and forward the accused, to the Chief Judicial Magistrate". Only the CJM can pass the 7-year sentence. [Source: Section 364, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure when Magistrate cannot pass sentence sufficiently severe

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 364: Procedure when Magistrate cannot pass sentence sufficiently severe

Q: Under sub-section (3), when the Chief Judicial Magistrate receives the guilty person, what power does the CJM have regarding the evidence that was already taken by the lower Magistrate?
A: The CJM "may... recall and examine any witness who has already given evidence in the case and may call for and take any further evidence". [Source: Section 364, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure when Magistrate cannot pass sentence sufficiently severe

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 364: Procedure when Magistrate cannot pass sentence sufficiently severe

Q: Can a Magistrate use this section to send someone to the CJM *before* hearing all the evidence from the defense?
A: No, sub-section (1) explicitly requires the Magistrate to form their opinion "after hearing the evidence for the prosecution and the accused". [Source: Section 364, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure when Magistrate cannot pass sentence sufficiently severe

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 364: Procedure when Magistrate cannot pass sentence sufficiently severe

Q: What is the consequence of this two-tiered conviction-and-sentencing mechanism?
A: The consequence is maximizing judicial efficiency without sacrificing proportionality; lower Magistrates can handle the bulk of fact-finding trials, but if the facts reveal a monster who needs a massive sentence, the system can seamlessly bump the sentencing phase up to a senior judge without having to completely redo the entire trial. [Source: Section 364, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure when Magistrate cannot pass sentence sufficiently severe

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 365: Conviction or commitment on evidence partly recorded by one Magistrate and partly by

Q: If a judge conducts half a trial but then gets transferred to another city, does the new replacement judge have to start the whole trial from the beginning?
A: No. The new judge can continue exactly where the old judge left off, relying on the witness evidence the previous judge already recorded. However, if the new judge feels it's necessary for justice, they can call back any witness to testify again. [Source: Section 365, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Conviction or commitment on evidence partly recorded by one Magistrate and partly by

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 365: Conviction or commitment on evidence partly recorded by one Magistrate and partly by

Q: How does Section 365 of BNSS 2023 prevent trials from being derailed by the transfer of judicial officers?
A: Section 365 of BNSS 2023 allows for "Conviction or commitment on evidence partly recorded by one Magistrate and partly by another," permitting a succeeding Judge or Magistrate to act on evidence recorded by their predecessor, while retaining the discretion to re-summon witnesses if necessary. [Source: Section 365, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Conviction or commitment on evidence partly recorded by one Magistrate and partly by

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 365: Conviction or commitment on evidence partly recorded by one Magistrate and partly by

Q: A judge hears testimony from the key eyewitness in a murder case, but gets promoted before the defense can cross-examine. The new judge takes over. The defense lawyer demands the new judge completely throw out the eyewitness's testimony and start over. Does the new judge have to?
A: No. Under sub-section (1), the succeeding judge "may act on the evidence so recorded by his predecessor". However, under the proviso, the judge *may* re-summon the witness for "further examination, cross-examination and re-examination". It is at the judge's discretion, not mandatory to start over. [Source: Section 365, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Conviction or commitment on evidence partly recorded by one Magistrate and partly by

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 365: Conviction or commitment on evidence partly recorded by one Magistrate and partly by

Q: Under sub-section (3), name one specific type of proceeding where this rule does NOT apply (meaning if the judge leaves, the new judge *must* start over).
A: "summary trials" (or cases stayed under section 361, or submitted to a superior Magistrate under section 364). [Source: Section 365, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Conviction or commitment on evidence partly recorded by one Magistrate and partly by

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 365: Conviction or commitment on evidence partly recorded by one Magistrate and partly by

Q: If a case is formally transferred from Judge A to Judge B by an order of a higher court, does Judge B count as "succeeding" Judge A under this section?
A: Yes, sub-section (2) explicitly clarifies that when a case is transferred, the former judge "shall be deemed to cease to exercise jurisdiction therein, and to be succeeded by the latter, within the meaning of sub-section (1)." [Source: Section 365, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Conviction or commitment on evidence partly recorded by one Magistrate and partly by

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 365: Conviction or commitment on evidence partly recorded by one Magistrate and partly by

Q: What is the consequence of this continuity provision?
A: The consequence is massive time and resource savings; given the frequent transfer of judges in the Indian legal system, forcing every trial to restart from day one whenever a judge moved would paralyze the courts and traumatize witnesses who would have to testify repeatedly. [Source: Section 365, BNSS 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 366: Court to be open

Q: Are criminal trials open to the public? Can anyone just walk into a courtroom and watch?
A: Yes, generally, criminal courts are open to the public. However, the judge can order people to leave if needed. Also, trials for sexual offences (like rape) are strictly held "in camera" (closed to the public and press). [Source: Section 366, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Court to be open

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 366: Court to be open

Q: How does Section 366 of BNSS 2023 regulate public access to criminal trials?
A: Section 366 of BNSS 2023 mandates the "Court to be open" to the public generally, but provides the judge discretion to restrict access, and strictly mandates that trials for rape and other specified sexual offences against women and children be held "in camera" (privately). [Source: Section 366, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Court to be open

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 366: Court to be open

Q: A journalist walks into a courtroom during a high-profile rape trial to take notes for an article. The judge stops the trial, kicks the journalist out, and bans them from publishing anything about the trial without permission. Did the judge act legally?
A: Yes. Under sub-section (2), a rape trial "shall be conducted in camera". Furthermore, under sub-section (3), it is "not be lawful for any person to print or publish any matter in relation to any such proceedings except with the previous permission of the Court". [Source: Section 366, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Court to be open

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 366: Court to be open

Q: For "in camera" trials dealing with sexual offences, what specific demographic preference for the presiding judicial officer is mandated by the second proviso to sub-section (2)?
A: "in camera trial shall be conducted as far as practicable by a woman Judge or Magistrate." [Source: Section 366, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Court to be open

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 366: Court to be open

Q: During a closed "in camera" rape trial, can the victim request that her mother be allowed to stay in the courtroom with her?
A: Yes. The first proviso to sub-section (2) states the judge may, "on an application made by either of the parties, allow any particular person to have access to, or be or remain in, the room". [Source: Section 366, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Court to be open

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 366: Court to be open

Q: What is the consequence of mandating "in camera" trials for sexual offences?
A: The consequence is protecting the dignity and privacy of survivors; testifying about sexual violence is deeply traumatizing, and doing so in front of a gallery of strangers or sensationalist media often deters victims from pursuing justice. Closed courts create a safer environment for truth-telling. [Source: Section 366, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Court to be open

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 367: Procedure in case of accused being person of unsound mind

Q: What happens if a person arrested for a crime seems to be suffering from severe mental illness (unsound mind) and cannot even understand what is happening to them during the initial inquiry?
A: The Magistrate stops the normal process and has a government doctor examine them. If they are mentally incapable of defending themselves, the proceedings are halted, and they are sent for psychiatric treatment until they are fit to face trial. [Source: Section 367, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in case of accused being person of unsound mind

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 367: Procedure in case of accused being person of unsound mind

Q: What procedure does Section 367 of BNSS 2023 establish for accused persons who appear mentally incapacitated during an inquiry?
A: Section 367 of BNSS 2023 details the "Procedure in case of accused being person of unsound mind," requiring a Magistrate to order a medical/psychiatric examination if an accused seems incapable of making a defense, and to postpone proceedings for treatment if incapacity is confirmed by doctors. [Source: Section 367, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in case of accused being person of unsound mind

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 367: Procedure in case of accused being person of unsound mind

Q: A man is brought before a Magistrate for trespassing. He is hallucinating and clearly doesn't know where he is. The Magistrate simply ignores this, appoints a lawyer for him, and starts the inquiry anyway. Is this correct?
A: No. Under section 367(1), if the Magistrate has reason to believe the person is of unsound mind and incapable of making his defence, he "shall inquire into the fact... and shall cause such person to be examined by the civil surgeon". It is mandatory, not optional. [Source: Section 367, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in case of accused being person of unsound mind

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 367: Procedure in case of accused being person of unsound mind

Q: If the accused is evaluated by a government psychiatrist but disagrees with the doctor's finding, who can the accused appeal to under the proviso to sub-section (2)?
A: They may "prefer an appeal before the Medical Board" (consisting of the head of psychiatry at a Govt hospital and a psychiatry faculty member). [Source: Section 367, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in case of accused being person of unsound mind

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 367: Procedure in case of accused being person of unsound mind

Q: If a person is found to be of unsound mind, does the Magistrate automatically lock them up in a mental hospital forever?
A: No. Under sub-section (4), the Magistrate first checks the prosecution evidence. If the Magistrate "finds that no prima facie case is made out against the accused, he shall... discharge the accused" instead of postponing for treatment. They only postpone for treatment if there is a real case against them. [Source: Section 367, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in case of accused being person of unsound mind

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 367: Procedure in case of accused being person of unsound mind

Q: What is the consequence of explicitly distinguishing between "unsoundness of mind" and "intellectual disability" in sub-sections (4) and (5)?
A: The consequence is scientific accuracy in justice; "unsoundness of mind" (like schizophrenia) might be treatable, so the inquiry is postponed (sub-section 4). But "intellectual disability" is a permanent condition, so if it prevents them from defending themselves, the Magistrate "shall order closure of the inquiry" completely (sub-section 5), avoiding pointless delays. [Source: Section 367, BNSS 2023]
