content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 368: Procedure in case of person of unsound mind tried before Court

Q: What happens if a trial has already started, and the judge realizes the defendant has a severe mental breakdown and can no longer understand the trial or defend themselves?
A: The judge must halt the trial and order a psychiatric evaluation. If the doctor confirms the accused is incapable of defending themselves due to unsound mind, the trial is paused, and the person is sent for treatment. [Source: Section 368, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in case of person of unsound mind tried before Court

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 368: Procedure in case of person of unsound mind tried before Court

Q: How does Section 368 of BNSS 2023 differ from Section 367 regarding mentally incapacitated defendants?
A: Section 368 of BNSS 2023 dictates the "Procedure in case of person of unsound mind tried before Court," applying the same medical examination, appeal, and postponement/treatment protocols as Section 367, but specifically for the *trial* phase rather than the preliminary *inquiry* phase. [Source: Section 368, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in case of person of unsound mind tried before Court

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 368: Procedure in case of person of unsound mind tried before Court

Q: During a murder trial, the accused suffers a psychotic break. The psychiatrist confirms he cannot understand the trial. The judge looks at the evidence and realizes there's absolutely no proof the accused committed the murder anyway. Does the judge still have to pause the trial and send him to a mental hospital for the crime?
A: No. Under sub-section (3), if the judge finds "no prima facie case is made out against the accused, he or it shall, instead of postponing the trial, discharge the accused". [Source: Section 368, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in case of person of unsound mind tried before Court

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 368: Procedure in case of person of unsound mind tried before Court

Q: Under sub-section (4), if the accused cannot defend themselves because of a permanent "intellectual disability" (rather than a treatable mental illness), what must the court order regarding the trial itself?
A: The court "shall not hold the trial and order the accused to be dealt with in accordance with section 369." [Source: Section 368, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in case of person of unsound mind tried before Court

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 368: Procedure in case of person of unsound mind tried before Court

Q: Is the court required to blindly accept the initial psychiatrist's diagnosis that the accused is faking their mental illness?
A: No, under the proviso to sub-section (2), the accused can "prefer an appeal before the Medical Board". [Source: Section 368, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in case of person of unsound mind tried before Court

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 368: Procedure in case of person of unsound mind tried before Court

Q: What is the fundamental legal consequence of Sections 367 and 368?
A: The consequence is upholding the right to a fair trial; it is a fundamental principle of justice that you cannot try a person who lacks the mental capacity to instruct a lawyer, understand the charges, or present a defense. Doing so would be equivalent to trying a person who is unconscious. [Source: Section 368, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in case of person of unsound mind tried before Court

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 369: Release of person of unsound mind pending investigation or trial

Q: While a mentally ill accused person is waiting to be fit for trial, do they just sit in a regular prison cell?
A: No. The court must release them on bail to a family member who promises to get them psychiatric treatment. If that's not possible, they are placed in a proper mental health facility for treatment, never in a standard prison cell. [Source: Section 369, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Release of person of unsound mind pending investigation or trial

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 369: Release of person of unsound mind pending investigation or trial

Q: How does Section 369 of BNSS 2023 manage the custody and care of mentally incapacitated defendants?
A: Section 369 of BNSS 2023 governs the "Release of person of unsound mind pending investigation or trial," mandating bail and out-patient treatment via relatives when safe, or ordering detention in a psychiatric facility governed by the Mental Healthcare Act when bail is inappropriate or unsafe. [Source: Section 369, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Release of person of unsound mind pending investigation or trial

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 369: Release of person of unsound mind pending investigation or trial

Q: A man charged with a non-bailable crime is found to have severe schizophrenia and cannot face trial. His brother offers to take him home, ensure he takes his medication daily, and watch him so he doesn't hurt anyone. The judge says, "The crime is non-bailable, I cannot give him bail." Is the judge correct?
A: No. Under sub-section (1), the Court "shall, whether the case is one in which bail may be taken or not, order release of such person on bail" if a relative undertakes to obtain treatment and prevent injury (as per the proviso). [Source: Section 369, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Release of person of unsound mind pending investigation or trial

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 369: Release of person of unsound mind pending investigation or trial

Q: If bail cannot be granted, under what specific central law's rules must the public mental health establishment operate when detaining the accused, according to the proviso in sub-section (2)?
A: "the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 (10 of 2017)." [Source: Section 369, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Release of person of unsound mind pending investigation or trial

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 369: Release of person of unsound mind pending investigation or trial

Q: Can the Magistrate totally discharge the accused (let them go completely) instead of just giving them bail or sending them to a facility?
A: Yes, under proviso (a) to sub-section (3), "such release may be ordered, if sufficient security is given that the accused shall be prevented from doing injury to himself or to any other person". [Source: Section 369, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Release of person of unsound mind pending investigation or trial

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 369: Release of person of unsound mind pending investigation or trial

Q: What is the consequence of linking criminal detention of mentally ill persons to the Mental Healthcare Act?
A: The consequence is medicalizing the treatment of mentally ill defendants; it prevents the historical abuse of locking severely mentally ill people in brutal solitary confinement in prisons, ensuring they are treated as patients requiring clinical psychiatric care, not just as criminals requiring punishment. [Source: Section 369, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Release of person of unsound mind pending investigation or trial

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 370: Resumption of inquiry or trial

Q: If a trial was paused because the accused was mentally ill, what happens when they get better?
A: Once the accused is cured and mentally sound again, the court resumes the trial or inquiry from where it left off. [Source: Section 370, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Resumption of inquiry or trial

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 370: Resumption of inquiry or trial

Q: What is the mechanism in Section 370 of BNSS 2023 for restarting paused proceedings?
A: Section 370 of BNSS 2023 provides for the "Resumption of inquiry or trial," allowing a Magistrate or Court to resume proceedings once an accused person has ceased to be of unsound mind and is capable of making a defense. [Source: Section 370, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Resumption of inquiry or trial

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 370: Resumption of inquiry or trial

Q: An accused was released on bail to his family for psychiatric treatment. Two years later, he is fully medicated, stable, and completely sane. The family brings him back to court. Can the judge use the official medical certificate to prove he is ready for trial?
A: Yes. Under sub-section (2), when sureties produce him to the appointed officer, "the certificate of such officer that the accused is capable of making his defence shall be receivable in evidence." [Source: Section 370, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Resumption of inquiry or trial

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 370: Resumption of inquiry or trial

Q: Under sub-section (1), when can the Magistrate or Court resume the inquiry or trial?
A: "at any time after the person concerned has ceased to be of unsound mind". [Source: Section 370, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Resumption of inquiry or trial

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 370: Resumption of inquiry or trial

Q: If the trial resumes, does the court have to start over from the very first witness?
A: The section says "resume the inquiry or trial" and "require the accused to appear". It implies picking up where it was paused, though standard procedures for recalling witnesses might apply under other sections. [Source: Section 370, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Resumption of inquiry or trial

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 370: Resumption of inquiry or trial

Q: What is the consequence of having a clear mechanism to resume trials?
A: The consequence is ensuring that a claim of temporary mental illness does not serve as a permanent "get out of jail free" card; once the medical incapacity is resolved, the legal accountability for the alleged crime resumes. [Source: Section 370, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Resumption of inquiry or trial

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 371: Procedure on accused appearing before Magistrate or Court

Q: When an accused person returns to court after mental health treatment, how does the judge decide what to do next?
A: The judge looks at the accused. If the judge thinks they are better, the trial continues. If the judge thinks they are still too sick to defend themselves, they are sent back for more treatment or care. [Source: Section 371, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure on accused appearing before Magistrate or Court

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 371: Procedure on accused appearing before Magistrate or Court

Q: How does Section 371 of BNSS 2023 dictate the court's immediate actions when a treated accused reappears?
A: Section 371 of BNSS 2023 outlines the "Procedure on accused appearing before Magistrate or Court," directing the Court to proceed with the trial if the accused is now capable of defense, or to revert to sections 367/368/369 procedures if they remain incapable. [Source: Section 371, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure on accused appearing before Magistrate or Court

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 371: Procedure on accused appearing before Magistrate or Court

Q: A man was sent to a mental hospital for a year because he couldn't face trial. He is brought back to court. The judge talks to him and realizes he is still deeply delusional and cannot understand the charges. Does the judge have to restart the trial anyway because a year has passed?
A: No. Under sub-section (2), if the Magistrate considers him "still incapable of making his defence", the Magistrate "shall deal with such accused in accordance with the provisions of section 369" (which means sending him back for treatment or care). [Source: Section 371, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure on accused appearing before Magistrate or Court

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 371: Procedure on accused appearing before Magistrate or Court

Q: Under sub-section (1), what must the Magistrate or Court consider before the inquiry or trial shall proceed?
A: The Magistrate or Court must consider "him capable of making his defence". [Source: Section 371, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure on accused appearing before Magistrate or Court

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 371: Procedure on accused appearing before Magistrate or Court

Q: Is the court required to hold a full medical trial just to confirm the accused is better?
A: The section simply states "If... the Magistrate or Court considers him capable". It gives the judicial officer the authority to make the determination based on the accused's appearance and likely medical certificates (as per Sec 370). [Source: Section 371, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure on accused appearing before Magistrate or Court

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 371: Procedure on accused appearing before Magistrate or Court

Q: What is the consequence of this section?
A: The consequence is creating a judicial feedback loop; the court retains ultimate oversight over the accused's fitness for trial, ensuring nobody is forced to face a jury while still mentally incapacitated, regardless of what administrative timelines have passed. [Source: Section 371, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure on accused appearing before Magistrate or Court

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 372: When accused appears to have been of sound mind

Q: What happens if a person is perfectly sane right now during the trial, but the evidence shows they were completely legally insane (of unsound mind) on the exact day they committed the crime?
A: The Magistrate finishes the inquiry and, if it's a serious crime, sends the case up to the Sessions Court for a full trial, noting that the defense of insanity at the time of the crime is the main issue. [Source: Section 372, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: When accused appears to have been of sound mind

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 372: When accused appears to have been of sound mind

Q: How does Section 372 of BNSS 2023 handle the defense of insanity at the time of the offense when the accused is currently sane?
A: Section 372 of BNSS 2023 covers situations "When accused appears to have been of sound mind," requiring a Magistrate to proceed with the case or commit it to a Sessions Court if the accused is currently fit for trial, but evidence suggests they committed the act while mentally incapable of knowing it was wrong. [Source: Section 372, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: When accused appears to have been of sound mind

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 372: When accused appears to have been of sound mind

Q: A woman is on trial. She is perfectly calm and understands everything. However, the evidence shows that when she committed the assault six months ago, she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis and didn't know what she was doing. Does the Magistrate pause the trial and send her to a hospital?
A: No. Because she "appears to be of sound mind at the time of inquiry or trial", she is fit to be tried. The Magistrate "shall proceed with the case, and, if the accused ought to be tried by the Court of Session, commit him for trial". Her past insanity is a defense to be argued at trial, not a reason to stop the trial now. [Source: Section 372, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: When accused appears to have been of sound mind

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 372: When accused appears to have been of sound mind

Q: What are the two specific cognitive failures caused by unsoundness of mind at the time of the act that trigger this section?
A: Being "incapable of knowing the nature of the act or that it was wrong or contrary to law". [Source: Section 372, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: When accused appears to have been of sound mind

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 372: When accused appears to have been of sound mind

Q: If the Magistrate believes the person was insane at the time of the crime, can the Magistrate just acquit them immediately during the preliminary inquiry?
A: No. The section says the Magistrate "shall proceed with the case". The actual acquittal on grounds of insanity requires a full judgment (as dealt with in the next section). [Source: Section 372, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: When accused appears to have been of sound mind

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 372: When accused appears to have been of sound mind

Q: What is the consequence of differentiating present sanity from past insanity?
A: The consequence is procedural clarity; past insanity (insanity at the time of the act) is a substantive legal defense that results in acquittal. Present insanity (insanity at the time of trial) is a procedural block that pauses the trial. Section 372 ensures cases with past insanity defenses proceed to a full verdict if the defendant is currently fit. [Source: Section 372, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: When accused appears to have been of sound mind

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 373: Judgment of acquittal on ground of unsoundness of mind

Q: If a court finds a person "not guilty by reason of insanity," do they just say "acquitted" and leave it at that?
A: No. The court's judgment must specifically state whether or not the person physically committed the act they were accused of, even though they are being acquitted because they were legally insane at the time. [Source: Section 373, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Judgment of acquittal on ground of unsoundness of mind

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 373: Judgment of acquittal on ground of unsoundness of mind

Q: What specific finding is mandated by Section 373 of BNSS 2023 when a defendant successfully pleads insanity?
A: Section 373 of BNSS 2023 dictates the form of a "Judgment of acquittal on ground of unsoundness of mind," requiring that the finding must specifically state whether the accused actually committed the alleged act, despite being acquitted due to lacking criminal intent. [Source: Section 373, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Judgment of acquittal on ground of unsoundness of mind

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 373: Judgment of acquittal on ground of unsoundness of mind

Q: A man who killed his neighbor while experiencing severe schizophrenic delusions is found not guilty by reason of insanity. The judge just writes: "Acquitted due to unsound mind." Is this judgment legally complete under Section 373?
A: No. Under section 373, "the finding shall state specifically whether he committed the act or not." The judge must explicitly write that the man did physically commit the act of killing, before acquitting him for lacking the mental capacity to know it was wrong. [Source: Section 373, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Judgment of acquittal on ground of unsoundness of mind

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 373: Judgment of acquittal on ground of unsoundness of mind

Q: What is the legal threshold for unsoundness of mind mentioned in this section that leads to acquittal?
A: "incapable of knowing the nature of the act alleged as constituting the offence, or that it was wrong or contrary to law". [Source: Section 373, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Judgment of acquittal on ground of unsoundness of mind

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 373: Judgment of acquittal on ground of unsoundness of mind

Q: Can a judge use this section to acquit someone who was just very drunk and didn't know what they were doing?
A: Generally no, as this section specifically relies on "unsoundness of mind" (a medical/legal term for insanity/mental illness), not voluntary intoxication (which is handled differently under the penal code). [Source: Section 373, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Judgment of acquittal on ground of unsoundness of mind

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 373: Judgment of acquittal on ground of unsoundness of mind

Q: What is the consequence of forcing the judge to record whether the physical act was committed?
A: The consequence is critical for post-trial public safety; if the person didn't even commit the physical act, they go entirely free. But if the judge records that they *did* commit a violent act (but were just insane), it triggers the state's power in the next section (374) to detain them in a psychiatric facility to protect the public. [Source: Section 373, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Judgment of acquittal on ground of unsoundness of mind

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 374: Person acquitted on ground of unsoundness of mind to be detained in safe custody

Q: If a person is found "not guilty by reason of insanity" for committing a violent crime, are they instantly set free to walk the streets?
A: Not necessarily. Because they committed the physical act but were legally insane, the court can order them to be detained safely in a psychiatric facility, or hand them over to a family member who promises to keep them safe and prevent them from hurting anyone. [Source: Section 374, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Person acquitted on ground of unsoundness of mind to be detained in safe custody

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 374: Person acquitted on ground of unsoundness of mind to be detained in safe custody

Q: How does Section 374 of BNSS 2023 manage public safety after a successful insanity defense?
A: Section 374 of BNSS 2023 deals with a "Person acquitted on ground of unsoundness of mind to be detained in safe custody," empowering the Court to order the acquitted person's detention in a mental health facility or delivery to a relative under strict security conditions to prevent harm. [Source: Section 374, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Person acquitted on ground of unsoundness of mind to be detained in safe custody

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 374: Person acquitted on ground of unsoundness of mind to be detained in safe custody

Q: A woman is acquitted of arson because she was legally insane. The judge orders her to be sent to a state mental hospital for secure treatment. The state government ignores the Mental Healthcare Act and locks her in a standard prison cell. Is this allowed?
A: No. Under sub-section (2), "No order for the detention of the accused in a public mental health establishment shall be made... otherwise than in accordance with such rules as the State Government may have made under the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017". [Source: Section 374, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Person acquitted on ground of unsoundness of mind to be detained in safe custody

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 374: Person acquitted on ground of unsoundness of mind to be detained in safe custody

Q: If the court decides to deliver the acquitted person to a relative instead of a hospital, what two guarantees must the relative give as security under sub-section (3)?
A: They must guarantee the person shall: (a) "be properly taken care of and prevented from doing injury to himself or to any other person", and (b) "be produced for the inspection of such officer... as the State Government may direct." [Source: Section 374, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Person acquitted on ground of unsoundness of mind to be detained in safe custody

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 374: Person acquitted on ground of unsoundness of mind to be detained in safe custody

Q: Does the court automatically detain the person if the judgment says they *didn't* commit the act?
A: No. Sub-section (1) only applies "Whenever the finding states that the accused person committed the act alleged". If they didn't do it, they are entirely free. [Source: Section 374, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Person acquitted on ground of unsoundness of mind to be detained in safe custody

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 374: Person acquitted on ground of unsoundness of mind to be detained in safe custody

Q: What is the consequence of this section on the concept of an "acquittal"?
A: The consequence is creating a unique legal status; a normal acquittal means absolute freedom. An insanity acquittal means freedom from *criminal punishment*, but it triggers the state's *civil commitment* powers, allowing the state to restrict the person's liberty indefinitely in a medical facility to protect society from a dangerous, uncontrollable illness. [Source: Section 374, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Person acquitted on ground of unsoundness of mind to be detained in safe custody

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 375: Power of State Government to empower officer in charge to discharge

Q: Who has the authority to discharge a mentally ill person from a jail where they are being held for treatment?
A: Normally, the Inspector-General of Prisons has this authority, but the State Government can also give this power directly to the officer in charge of that specific jail. [Source: Section 375, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power of State Government to empower officer in charge to discharge

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 375: Power of State Government to empower officer in charge to discharge

Q: How does Section 375 of BNSS 2023 delegate authority regarding mentally ill detainees?
A: Section 375 of BNSS 2023 addresses the "Power of State Government to empower officer in charge to discharge," allowing the State Government to authorize a jail's officer-in-charge to perform the functions of the Inspector-General of Prisons under sections 376 or 377 regarding detained persons of unsound mind. [Source: Section 375, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power of State Government to empower officer in charge to discharge

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 375: Power of State Government to empower officer in charge to discharge

Q: A mentally ill accused person is detained in a district jail under Section 369. The Inspector-General of Prisons is not available to evaluate him. The State Government has issued an order empowering the District Jail Superintendent under Section 375. Can the Superintendent certify the person is fit for trial?
A: Yes. Because the State Government empowered the officer in charge under section 375, they can "discharge all or any of the functions of the Inspector-General of Prisons under section 376". [Source: Section 375, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power of State Government to empower officer in charge to discharge

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 375: Power of State Government to empower officer in charge to discharge

Q: Which two specific sections define the powers (regarding certifying fitness for trial or fitness for release) that the State Government can delegate to the jail officer under this section?
A: "section 376 or section 377". [Source: Section 375, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power of State Government to empower officer in charge to discharge

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 375: Power of State Government to empower officer in charge to discharge

Q: Can the State Government use this section to empower the head of a "public mental health establishment" (like a hospital) to act like the Inspector-General?
A: No, the text specifically says "empower the officer in charge of the jail". Hospitals are governed by the Mental Health Review Board under other sections. [Source: Section 375, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power of State Government to empower officer in charge to discharge

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 375: Power of State Government to empower officer in charge to discharge

Q: What is the consequence of this delegation of power?
A: The consequence is administrative efficiency; it prevents mentally ill detainees who have recovered from languishing in jail for months just waiting for a high-ranking official (the Inspector-General) to visit their specific facility to sign their release paperwork. [Source: Section 375, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power of State Government to empower officer in charge to discharge

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 376: Procedure where prisoner of unsound mind is reported capable of making his defence

Q: How does a mentally ill prisoner who was paused from facing trial legally prove they are finally sane enough to go to court?
A: The head of their facility (like the Inspector-General of Prisons or the Mental Health Review Board) issues a formal certificate stating they are capable of making a defense, and then they are taken back to the Magistrate or Court. [Source: Section 376, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where prisoner of unsound mind is reported capable of making his defence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 376: Procedure where prisoner of unsound mind is reported capable of making his defence

Q: What is the procedure under Section 376 of BNSS 2023 when a detained person of unsound mind recovers their faculties?
A: Section 376 of BNSS 2023 outlines the "Procedure where prisoner of unsound mind is reported capable of making his defence," requiring the Inspector-General of Prisons or Mental Health Review Board to certify the person's fitness, after which they are brought before the Court to resume proceedings under Section 371. [Source: Section 376, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where prisoner of unsound mind is reported capable of making his defence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 376: Procedure where prisoner of unsound mind is reported capable of making his defence

Q: A man was detained in a public mental health establishment because he couldn't face trial. A single junior nurse tells the police, "He seems fine today, take him to court." The police take him to the Magistrate. Is this the correct procedure?
A: No. Under section 376, for a person in a public mental health establishment, it requires the "Mental Health Review Board constituted under the Mental Healthcare Act" to certify his capability. A nurse's opinion is not sufficient. [Source: Section 376, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where prisoner of unsound mind is reported capable of making his defence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 376: Procedure where prisoner of unsound mind is reported capable of making his defence

Q: Once the certificate of capability is issued, what evidentiary weight does it hold in court?
A: "the certificate of such Inspector-General or visitors as aforesaid shall be receivable as evidence." [Source: Section 376, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where prisoner of unsound mind is reported capable of making his defence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 376: Procedure where prisoner of unsound mind is reported capable of making his defence

Q: Does this section apply to a person who was released on bail to their family for treatment?
A: No, this section explicitly applies if "a person is detained under the provisions of sub-section (2) of section 369" (i.e., detained in a jail or facility). People released on bail to family are handled via Section 370. [Source: Section 376, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where prisoner of unsound mind is reported capable of making his defence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 376: Procedure where prisoner of unsound mind is reported capable of making his defence

Q: What is the consequence of requiring a certificate from the Mental Health Review Board or Inspector-General?
A: The consequence is ensuring rigorous medical-legal oversight; it prevents police or ambitious prosecutors from prematurely dragging a still-sick defendant back into a trial before qualified, high-level authorities have definitively certified their mental restoration. [Source: Section 376, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where prisoner of unsound mind is reported capable of making his defence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 377: Procedure where person of unsound mind detained is declared fit to be released

Q: If a person was locked in a psychiatric facility because they were acquitted due to insanity (and considered dangerous), who decides when they are safe enough to finally be let out?
A: The medical authorities certify they are no longer a danger, and then the State Government makes the final decision. The State Government might even appoint a special Commission (a judge and two doctors) to double-check their sanity before releasing them. [Source: Section 377, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where person of unsound mind detained is declared fit to be released

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 377: Procedure where person of unsound mind detained is declared fit to be released

Q: How does Section 377 of BNSS 2023 govern the final release of individuals detained for criminal insanity?
A: Section 377 of BNSS 2023 covers the "Procedure where person of unsound mind detained is declared fit to be released," empowering the State Government to release, retain, or transfer a detainee after medical authorities certify they are no longer a danger, with the option to appoint a Commission for formal inquiry. [Source: Section 377, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where person of unsound mind detained is declared fit to be released

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 377: Procedure where person of unsound mind detained is declared fit to be released

Q: A serial arsonist was acquitted due to severe insanity and detained in a hospital. Three years later, the hospital doctors certify he is perfectly sane and not a danger to anyone. Does the hospital just unlock the doors and let him go home?
A: No. Even with the certificate, only "the State Government may thereupon order him to be released". The hospital cannot release him independently. [Source: Section 377, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where person of unsound mind detained is declared fit to be released

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 377: Procedure where person of unsound mind detained is declared fit to be released

Q: If the State Government decides to appoint a formal Commission to inquire into the state of mind of the person, what is the mandatory composition of that Commission?
A: "consisting of a Judicial and two medical officers." [Source: Section 377, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where person of unsound mind detained is declared fit to be released

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 377: Procedure where person of unsound mind detained is declared fit to be released

Q: Is the State Government *forced* to release the person the moment the medical certificate says they are safe?
A: No, sub-section (1) says the State Government "may thereupon order him to be released, or to be detained in custody, or to be transferred". It retains discretion, and can use the Commission to double-check. [Source: Section 377, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where person of unsound mind detained is declared fit to be released

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 377: Procedure where person of unsound mind detained is declared fit to be released

Q: What is the consequence of placing the final release decision in the hands of the State Government and a special Commission?
A: The consequence is prioritizing public safety over immediate medical optimism; releasing a violently insane person who merely *appears* cured is a massive risk to society. This section provides multiple layers of bureaucratic and judicial verification to ensure they are truly harmless before re-entering the public. [Source: Section 377, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where person of unsound mind detained is declared fit to be released

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 378: Delivery of person of unsound mind to care of relative or friend

Q: Can a family member take custody of a relative who is locked up because they are unfit for trial due to mental illness?
A: Yes. A relative or friend can apply to the State Government to take them home. However, the relative must guarantee they will take proper care of the person, prevent them from hurting anyone, and bring them to court whenever required. [Source: Section 378, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Delivery of person of unsound mind to care of relative or friend

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 378: Delivery of person of unsound mind to care of relative or friend

Q: How does Section 378 of BNSS 2023 facilitate family care for mentally ill detainees?
A: Section 378 of BNSS 2023 deals with the "Delivery of person of unsound mind to care of relative or friend," allowing the State Government to transfer custody of a detained person to a relative/friend upon receiving satisfactory security regarding care, safety, and future production before the authorities. [Source: Section 378, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Delivery of person of unsound mind to care of relative or friend

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 378: Delivery of person of unsound mind to care of relative or friend

Q: A mother wants to take her mentally ill son home from the jail where he is detained pending trial. She promises the State Government she will care for him, but refuses to promise she will bring him back to court later, saying he's too fragile. Will the government give him to her?
A: No. Under sub-section (1)(c), the relative must give security that the person shall "be produced when required before such Magistrate or Court". If she refuses this condition, the transfer cannot happen. [Source: Section 378, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Delivery of person of unsound mind to care of relative or friend

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 378: Delivery of person of unsound mind to care of relative or friend

Q: Under sub-section (2), if the person was delivered to a relative because they were unfit for trial, and an inspecting officer later certifies the person is now capable of making a defense, what must the Magistrate do?
A: The Magistrate "shall call upon the relative or friend to whom such accused was delivered to produce him before the Magistrate or Court". [Source: Section 378, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Delivery of person of unsound mind to care of relative or friend

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 378: Delivery of person of unsound mind to care of relative or friend

Q: Can the Magistrate or Court directly order the delivery of the detained person to a relative under this specific section?
A: No. Section 378(1) explicitly states "the State Government may... order such person to be delivered". (The Court has its own powers to deliver to relatives under other sections like 369/374, but *this* specific mechanism is an application to the State Government). [Source: Section 378, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Delivery of person of unsound mind to care of relative or friend

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 378: Delivery of person of unsound mind to care of relative or friend

Q: What is the consequence of this custody transfer mechanism?
A: The consequence is humane alternatives to state detention; state psychiatric hospitals or jails are often terrible environments for recovery. Allowing vetted families to take custody (under strict security bonds) promotes better mental health recovery while still ensuring the state can pull the person back for trial if they get better. [Source: Section 378, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Delivery of person of unsound mind to care of relative or friend

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 379: Procedure in cases mentioned in section 215

Q: What happens if someone submits a forged document to a judge, or lies under oath in court? Does the police arrest them directly?
A: No. Crimes committed against the court itself (like forgery in court or perjury) cannot usually be investigated directly by police. The judge whose court was lied to must conduct a preliminary inquiry, write a formal complaint, and send it to a Magistrate to start the criminal case against the liar. [Source: Section 379, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in cases mentioned in section 215

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 379: Procedure in cases mentioned in section 215

Q: How does Section 379 of BNSS 2023 initiate prosecutions for offences against the administration of justice?
A: Section 379 of BNSS 2023 sets out the "Procedure in cases mentioned in section 215," requiring a Court that believes an offence (like perjury or forgery) was committed in its proceedings to conduct a preliminary inquiry, record a finding, make a written complaint, and forward it to a First Class Magistrate. [Source: Section 379, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in cases mentioned in section 215

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 379: Procedure in cases mentioned in section 215

Q: A witness obviously lies on the stand in a civil trial. The judge gets angry, yells "You are a liar!", and immediately sentences the witness to 3 years in prison right then and there. Is this the correct procedure under Section 379?
A: No. Under section 379(1), the court must "make a complaint thereof in writing; (c) send it to a Magistrate of the first class having jurisdiction". The judge cannot try and punish the witness themselves; they must act as the complainant and send the case to another Magistrate. [Source: Section 379, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in cases mentioned in section 215

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 379: Procedure in cases mentioned in section 215

Q: Who must sign the written complaint if the court making the complaint is a High Court?
A: "by such officer of the Court as the Court may appoint" (sub-section 3(a)). [Source: Section 379, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in cases mentioned in section 215

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 379: Procedure in cases mentioned in section 215

Q: If a lower court sees perjury but refuses to file a complaint about it, is there any way for a complaint to still be filed?
A: Yes. Under sub-section (2), the power to make the complaint "may... be exercised by the Court to which such former Court is subordinate". A higher court can file the complaint if the lower court fails to do so. [Source: Section 379, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in cases mentioned in section 215

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 379: Procedure in cases mentioned in section 215

Q: What is the consequence of requiring the Court itself to be the complainant in these cases?
A: The consequence is preventing vindictive retaliation by litigants; if any angry loser in a lawsuit could just call the police and accuse the winning side's witnesses of perjury, the system would collapse into chaos. By forcing the judge to be the gatekeeper who officially files the complaint, it ensures only genuine cases of perjury or forgery are prosecuted. [Source: Section 379, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in cases mentioned in section 215

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 380: Appeal

Q: If you ask a judge to file a criminal complaint against someone for lying in court, and the judge refuses, can you appeal that refusal?
A: Yes. You can appeal to the higher court that the original judge reports to. The higher court can review the situation and order that the complaint be filed. [Source: Section 380, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Appeal

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 380: Appeal

Q: What appellate mechanism is provided by Section 380 of BNSS 2023 regarding complaints by courts?
A: Section 380 of BNSS 2023 governs the "Appeal" process, allowing a person to appeal to a superior court if a lower court refuses to make a complaint under section 379 (for offences against justice), or if the lower court *does* make a complaint against them, empowering the superior court to direct withdrawal or making of the complaint. [Source: Section 380, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Appeal

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 380: Appeal

Q: A trial judge files a formal perjury complaint against a witness under Section 379. The witness appeals to the Sessions Court (the superior court). The Sessions Court agrees the witness didn't lie and orders the withdrawal of the complaint. Can the prosecutor then file a "revision" application against the Sessions Court's order?
A: No. Under sub-section (2), "An order under this section... shall be final, and shall not be subject to revision." The superior court's decision is absolute. [Source: Section 380, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Appeal

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 380: Appeal

Q: Before a superior court can direct the withdrawal of a complaint, what procedural step must it take regarding the involved parties?
A: It must do so "after notice to the parties concerned". [Source: Section 380, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Appeal

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 380: Appeal

Q: Does this appeal mechanism apply if the court that originally refused to make the complaint was a High Court?
A: No. Sub-section (1) explicitly states: "Any person on whose application any Court *other than a High Court* has refused to make a complaint". You cannot use this section to appeal a High Court's refusal. [Source: Section 380, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Appeal

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 380: Appeal

Q: What is the consequence of making these appellate orders "final" and "not subject to revision"?
A: The consequence is preventing endless procedural warfare; disputes about *whether* a perjury trial should happen can drag on for years. By making the first appeal final, the law forces the system to either quickly start the perjury trial or drop the matter entirely, rather than litigating the mere *filing* of the complaint forever. [Source: Section 380, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Appeal

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 381: Power to order costs

Q: If someone frivolously asks a court to file a perjury complaint against their opponent, just to harass them, can the court penalize them financially?
A: Yes. The court handling the application for the complaint, or the court handling the appeal about it, has the power to order costs (making them pay money) as it sees fit. [Source: Section 381, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to order costs

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 381: Power to order costs

Q: What financial power is granted to courts handling Section 379/380 matters under Section 381 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 381 of BNSS 2023 outlines the "Power to order costs," granting any Court dealing with an application for a complaint (under Section 379) or an appeal (under Section 380) the authority to make just orders regarding costs. [Source: Section 381, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to order costs

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 381: Power to order costs

Q: A vengeful ex-husband files an application asking a Magistrate to complain that his ex-wife lied during their divorce. The Magistrate finds the application completely baseless and malicious. Can the Magistrate order the ex-husband to pay 10,000 rupees to the ex-wife for wasting her time?
A: Yes. Under section 381, the Court dealing with the application "shall have power to make such order as to costs as may be just." [Source: Section 381, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to order costs

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 381: Power to order costs

Q: Does this power to order costs only apply to the original trial court, or does it also apply to the appellate court reviewing the decision?
A: It applies to both. The section specifies "Any Court dealing with an application made to it for filing a complaint under section 379 or an appeal under section 380". [Source: Section 381, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to order costs

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 381: Power to order costs

Q: Is there a strict statutory maximum limit (like 1000 rupees) mentioned in this section for the costs a court can order?
A: No, the section simply states "make such order as to costs as may be just", leaving the amount to the court's discretion based on justice. [Source: Section 381, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to order costs

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 381: Power to order costs

Q: What is the consequence of giving courts this power regarding costs?
A: The consequence is deterring the weaponization of the perjury laws; without the threat of financial costs, petty litigants would routinely file baseless applications demanding their opponents be prosecuted for perjury, simply to intimidate them. This section ensures a financial penalty for filing malicious applications. [Source: Section 381, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to order costs

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 382: Procedure of Magistrate taking cognizance

Q: When a judge officially files a complaint that a witness committed perjury, how does the Magistrate treat that complaint? Does it go through the long process of a private citizen's complaint?
A: No. The Magistrate treats a complaint filed by a judge exactly as if it were an official Police Report (a chargesheet), skipping the slow preliminary steps required for private complaints. [Source: Section 382, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure of Magistrate taking cognizance

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 382: Procedure of Magistrate taking cognizance

Q: How does Section 382 of BNSS 2023 dictate the procedure for Magistrates receiving judicial complaints?
A: Section 382 of BNSS 2023 governs the "Procedure of Magistrate taking cognizance," instructing Magistrates to treat complaints received under Section 379 or 380 as if they were instituted on a police report, and allowing them to adjourn hearings if an appeal is pending in the original underlying case. [Source: Section 382, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure of Magistrate taking cognizance

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 382: Procedure of Magistrate taking cognizance

Q: A civil court judge files a complaint against a man for submitting a forged deed. The Magistrate receives the complaint. The man's lawyer demands the Magistrate first hold a lengthy hearing to examine the complainant (the judge) under oath before issuing a summons, just like in normal private complaints. Is the lawyer right?
A: No. Under section 382(1), the Magistrate shall "notwithstanding anything contained in Chapter XVI, proceed... to deal with the case as if it were instituted on a police report." Cases instituted on police reports skip the Chapter XVI complainant examination phase. The judge does not have to be examined. [Source: Section 382, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure of Magistrate taking cognizance

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 382: Procedure of Magistrate taking cognizance

Q: Under sub-section (2), what specific event allows the Magistrate to pause (adjourn) the hearing of the perjury/forgery case?
A: If "an appeal is pending against the decision arrived at in the judicial proceeding out of which the matter has arisen". [Source: Section 382, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure of Magistrate taking cognizance

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 382: Procedure of Magistrate taking cognizance

Q: Is the Magistrate *forced* to pause the perjury trial just because the underlying civil case is being appealed?
A: No, the power is discretionary: "he may, if he thinks fit, at any stage, adjourn the hearing". [Source: Section 382, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure of Magistrate taking cognizance

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 382: Procedure of Magistrate taking cognizance

Q: What is the consequence of treating judicial complaints as "police reports"?
A: The consequence is expediting prosecutions against those who attack the justice system; it shows profound institutional trust in judges. A private citizen's complaint is viewed with suspicion and must be vetted, but a formal written complaint from a sitting Judge is considered as reliable as a fully investigated police chargesheet, allowing the trial to start immediately. [Source: Section 382, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure of Magistrate taking cognizance

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 383: Summary procedure for trial for giving false evidence

Q: If a witness blatantly lies in front of a senior judge, does the judge have to go through the long process of filing a complaint with another Magistrate, or can they just punish the liar right then and there?
A: For perjury (giving false evidence), a Sessions Court or 1st Class Magistrate actually has the power to hold a quick, "summary" trial right after delivering their main judgment. They can ask the witness to explain themselves, and if unsatisfied, instantly sentence them to up to 3 months in jail. [Source: Section 383, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Summary procedure for trial for giving false evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 383: Summary procedure for trial for giving false evidence

Q: What expedited punitive power does Section 383 of BNSS 2023 grant to certain courts regarding perjury?
A: Section 383 of BNSS 2023 provides a "Summary procedure for trial for giving false evidence," allowing a Court of Session or First Class Magistrate, at the time of delivering judgment, to directly take cognizance, try summarily, and sentence a witness (up to 3 months/1000 rupees) for knowingly giving or fabricating false evidence. [Source: Section 383, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Summary procedure for trial for giving false evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 383: Summary procedure for trial for giving false evidence

Q: During a murder trial in a Sessions Court, a witness admits he was bribed to lie under oath. The judge delivers the murder verdict. Then, without filing a complaint elsewhere, the judge asks the witness to show cause, rejects his excuse, and sentences him to 1 month in jail for perjury. Is the judge allowed to do this?
A: Yes. Under section 383(1), a Court of Session may "try such offender summarily and sentence him to imprisonment for a term which may extend to three months" for knowingly giving false evidence. [Source: Section 383, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Summary procedure for trial for giving false evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 383: Summary procedure for trial for giving false evidence

Q: What specific procedural right must the judge give the offending witness before punishing them under this summary procedure?
A: They must be given "a reasonable opportunity of showing cause why he should not be punished for such offence". [Source: Section 383, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Summary procedure for trial for giving false evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 383: Summary procedure for trial for giving false evidence

Q: If a judge realizes a witness lied, but decides 3 months in jail isn't a harsh enough punishment, are they banned from filing a formal complaint under Section 379 for a full trial?
A: No. Sub-section (3) states: "Nothing in this section shall affect the power of the Court to make a complaint under section 379 for the offence, where it does not choose to proceed under this section." [Source: Section 383, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Summary procedure for trial for giving false evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 383: Summary procedure for trial for giving false evidence

Q: What is the consequence of granting this summary power to judges?
A: The consequence is immediate deterrence against perjury; witnesses are far less likely to brazenly lie under oath if they know the judge sitting in front of them has the power to throw them straight into jail the moment the trial ends, bypassing the years-long process of a separate perjury trial. [Source: Section 383, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Summary procedure for trial for giving false evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 384: Procedure in certain cases of contempt

Q: What happens if someone insults a judge, yells during a hearing, or refuses to answer questions in court (contempt)?
A: The judge can immediately detain them. Before the court closes for the day, the judge can give them a chance to explain themselves, and if the excuse isn't good enough, fine them up to 1000 rupees or give them 1 month in jail if they don't pay. [Source: Section 384, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in certain cases of contempt

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 384: Procedure in certain cases of contempt

Q: How does Section 384 of BNSS 2023 handle immediate disruptions or contempt within a courtroom?
A: Section 384 of BNSS 2023 establishes the "Procedure in certain cases of contempt," permitting any Civil, Criminal, or Revenue Court to instantly detain a person committing specified offences (like insulting a public servant or interrupting proceedings) in its presence, and try them on the same day for a fine up to 1000 rupees. [Source: Section 384, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in certain cases of contempt

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 384: Procedure in certain cases of contempt

Q: A man in the gallery starts screaming insults at the Magistrate during a hearing (an offence under BNS 267). The Magistrate orders police to detain him. Before leaving for the day, the Magistrate asks him why he did it, rejects his apology, and sentences him to pay a 500 rupee fine, or spend 15 days in jail if he refuses to pay. Is this legal?
A: Yes. Under section 384(1), the court can detain the offender, take cognizance "before the rising of the Court on the same day", give an opportunity to show cause, and sentence them to a "fine not exceeding one thousand rupees, and, in default of payment of fine, to simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to one month". [Source: Section 384, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in certain cases of contempt

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 384: Procedure in certain cases of contempt

Q: Under sub-section (3), if the offence is interrupting or insulting the court (BNS section 267), what two specific details must the court's written record show?
A: It must show "the nature and stage of the judicial proceeding" and "the nature of the interruption or insult." [Source: Section 384, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in certain cases of contempt

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 384: Procedure in certain cases of contempt

Q: Under this specific section, can the judge bypass the fine entirely and just sentence the heckler directly to 1 month of hard labor in prison?
A: No. The section explicitly limits the punishment to "sentence the offender to fine not exceeding one thousand rupees", with imprisonment only occurring "in default of payment of fine", and that imprisonment must be "simple imprisonment" (not hard labor). [Source: Section 384, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in certain cases of contempt

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 384: Procedure in certain cases of contempt

Q: What is the consequence of empowering all courts (even revenue courts) with this immediate contempt power?
A: The consequence is the preservation of judicial decorum and authority; courts cannot function in chaos. Giving every presiding officer the power to instantly fine and detain hecklers, disrupters, or those who maliciously refuse to answer questions ensures that the physical courtroom remains an orderly environment where justice can be administered without intimidation. [Source: Section 384, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure in certain cases of contempt

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 385: Procedure where Court considers that case should not be dealt with under

Q: If a person commits a severe contempt in court, but the judge thinks the maximum 1000 rupee fine under the "summary" rules is too light and they deserve a longer prison sentence, what does the judge do?
A: The judge cannot sentence them to more than the summary limit directly. Instead, the judge records the facts and sends the person to a different Magistrate to stand trial for the contempt offense under normal procedures. [Source: Section 385, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where Court considers that case should not be dealt with under

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 385: Procedure where Court considers that case should not be dealt with under

Q: How does Section 385 of BNSS 2023 provide an alternative to the summary contempt procedure?
A: Section 385 of BNSS 2023 outlines the "Procedure where Court considers that case should not be dealt with under section 384," allowing a Court that believes a contempt offender deserves imprisonment or a fine exceeding 200 rupees (or for any other reason) to forward the case to a Magistrate for a standard trial. [Source: Section 385, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where Court considers that case should not be dealt with under

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 385: Procedure where Court considers that case should not be dealt with under

Q: A man violently interrupts a civil court. The judge is furious and wants to impose a 5000 rupee fine and 6 months in jail. Since Section 384 only allows a 1000 rupee fine, the judge uses Section 385. Can the judge just impose the 5000 rupee fine himself using Section 385?
A: No. Under Section 385, if the Court considers a higher fine or imprisonment should be imposed, the Court "may forward the case to a Magistrate having jurisdiction to try the same". The original judge cannot impose the higher sentence themselves; they must transfer the case. [Source: Section 385, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where Court considers that case should not be dealt with under

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 385: Procedure where Court considers that case should not be dealt with under

Q: When the Court forwards the accused person to the Magistrate under this section, what two options does the Court have regarding the accused's physical custody during the transfer?
A: The court may "require security to be given for the appearance" (bail/bond) or, if security is not given, "shall forward such person in custody" (arrest). [Source: Section 385, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where Court considers that case should not be dealt with under

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 385: Procedure where Court considers that case should not be dealt with under

Q: Is the threshold for forwarding the case under Section 385 strictly tied to wanting a fine higher than 1000 rupees (the maximum in 384)?
A: Interestingly, no. The text of Section 385(1) says "or that a fine exceeding two hundred rupees should be imposed upon him". (This seems to be a historical anomaly or drafting specific, as 384 allows up to 1000). Furthermore, it allows forwarding if the court is "for any other reason of opinion that the case should not be disposed of under section 384". [Source: Section 385, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procedure where Court considers that case should not be dealt with under

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 385: Procedure where Court considers that case should not be dealt with under

Q: What is the consequence of having Section 385 alongside Section 384?
A: The consequence is providing a graded response to contempt; Section 384 handles minor, immediate disruptions with swift, low-level fines. Section 385 ensures that truly egregious, violent, or deeply insulting behavior against the court isn't artificially capped at a minor fine, ensuring severe contempt faces severe, formalized justice. [Source: Section 385, BNSS 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 386: When Registrar or Sub-Registrar to be deemed a Civil Court

Q: Do property registrars have the same powers as judges to punish people who insult them or cause disruptions in their offices?
A: Yes, if the State Government explicitly directs it, Registrars and Sub-Registrars are legally treated as "Civil Courts," giving them the power to fine or detain people who cause disruptions in their presence. [Source: Section 386, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: When Registrar or Sub-Registrar to be deemed a Civil Court

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 386: When Registrar or Sub-Registrar to be deemed a Civil Court

Q: How does Section 386 of BNSS 2023 extend contempt powers to non-judicial officers?
A: Section 386 of BNSS 2023 dictates "When Registrar or Sub-Registrar to be deemed a Civil Court," stating that upon State Government direction, officers appointed under the Registration Act are deemed Civil Courts for the purposes of wielding contempt powers under sections 384 and 385. [Source: Section 386, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: When Registrar or Sub-Registrar to be deemed a Civil Court

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 386: When Registrar or Sub-Registrar to be deemed a Civil Court

Q: A man gets angry at a Sub-Registrar over a property deed and starts screaming insults in the registration office. The State Government has issued a notification under this section. Can the Sub-Registrar immediately detain the man and fine him 500 rupees for contempt?
A: Yes. Because the State Government directed it, the Sub-Registrar "shall be deemed to be a Civil Court within the meaning of sections 384 and 385", giving them the exact same summary contempt powers as a judge. [Source: Section 386, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: When Registrar or Sub-Registrar to be deemed a Civil Court

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 386: When Registrar or Sub-Registrar to be deemed a Civil Court

Q: What specific central act governs the appointment of the Registrars who can be granted this power?
A: "the Registration Act, 1908 (16 of 1908)". [Source: Section 386, BNSS 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 386: When Registrar or Sub-Registrar to be deemed a Civil Court

Q: Are all Sub-Registrars automatically deemed Civil Courts the moment they are hired?
A: No, it requires a specific trigger: "When the State Government so directs". It is not automatic. [Source: Section 386, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: When Registrar or Sub-Registrar to be deemed a Civil Court

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 386: When Registrar or Sub-Registrar to be deemed a Civil Court

Q: What is the consequence of granting this power to property registrars?
A: The consequence is maintaining order in highly volatile administrative environments; property registration often involves intense, emotional disputes over immense wealth. Treating the registrar as a "Civil Court" deters violence and intimidation in these offices, protecting the integrity of public land records. [Source: Section 386, BNSS 2023]
