content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 387: Discharge of offender on submission of apology

Q: If a person is punished for contempt of court, but they immediately realize their mistake and sincerely apologize to the judge, can the judge cancel the punishment?
A: Yes. The judge has the discretion to forgive the offender, cancel the fine or jail time, or discharge them completely if they offer a satisfactory apology or comply with the court's order. [Source: Section 387, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Discharge of offender on submission of apology

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 387: Discharge of offender on submission of apology

Q: How does Section 387 of BNSS 2023 allow for the resolution of contempt charges without final punishment?
A: Section 387 of BNSS 2023 allows for the "Discharge of offender on submission of apology," granting the Court discretion to discharge a person or remit their punishment (under Section 384 or 385) if they submit to the Court's order or offer a satisfactory apology. [Source: Section 387, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Discharge of offender on submission of apology

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 387: Discharge of offender on submission of apology

Q: A lawyer yells at a judge and is immediately fined 1000 rupees under Section 384. Ten minutes later, the lawyer realizes he crossed a line, stands up, and offers a deep, unconditional apology on the record. The judge accepts it but says, "I already signed the fine order, I legally cannot take it back." Is the judge correct?
A: No. Under section 387, "the Court may, in its discretion, discharge the offender or remit the punishment... on apology being made to its satisfaction." The judge absolutely has the legal power to remit (cancel) the punishment. [Source: Section 387, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Discharge of offender on submission of apology

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 387: Discharge of offender on submission of apology

Q: Besides making an apology, what is the other action the offender can take to convince the court to discharge them under this section?
A: "on his submission to the order or requisition of such Court" (e.g., finally agreeing to answer the question he previously refused to answer). [Source: Section 387, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Discharge of offender on submission of apology

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 387: Discharge of offender on submission of apology

Q: Is the judge *forced* to drop the punishment just because the offender mumbles "sorry"?
A: No. The section says "the Court may, in its discretion" and the apology must be "made to its satisfaction." A fake or insincere apology can be rejected. [Source: Section 387, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Discharge of offender on submission of apology

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 387: Discharge of offender on submission of apology

Q: What is the consequence of this "apology clause"?
A: The consequence is de-escalation; the primary goal of contempt powers isn't vindictive punishment, but forcing compliance and restoring the court's dignity. If an apology achieves that dignity, or compliance achieves the court's goal, grinding the offender through the penal system is unnecessary. [Source: Section 387, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Discharge of offender on submission of apology

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 388: Imprisonment or committal of person refusing to answer or produce document

Q: If a witness takes the stand but stubbornly refuses to answer a legitimate question, or refuses to hand over a document they brought with them, what can the judge do to them?
A: The judge can instantly sentence them to up to 7 days in jail to think about it. If they still refuse after 7 days, the judge can hit them with formal contempt charges. [Source: Section 388, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Imprisonment or committal of person refusing to answer or produce document

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 388: Imprisonment or committal of person refusing to answer or produce document

Q: What coercive power does Section 388 of BNSS 2023 give a court against a recalcitrant witness?
A: Section 388 of BNSS 2023 covers the "Imprisonment or committal of person refusing to answer or produce document," allowing a Criminal Court to sentence an obstinate witness to simple imprisonment for up to seven days to compel their testimony or document production. [Source: Section 388, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Imprisonment or committal of person refusing to answer or produce document

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 388: Imprisonment or committal of person refusing to answer or produce document

Q: A witness is asked a question. They refuse to answer. The judge doesn't ask for an explanation and immediately orders the bailiff to lock the witness in a cell for 7 days. Is this lawful?
A: No. Section 388 states the court can do this if the witness "does not, after a reasonable opportunity has been given to him so to do, offer any reasonable excuse for such refusal". The judge must give them a chance to explain *why* they are refusing (e.g., asserting a legal privilege). [Source: Section 388, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Imprisonment or committal of person refusing to answer or produce document

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 388: Imprisonment or committal of person refusing to answer or produce document

Q: What happens if the witness is sent to jail for 7 days, but on day 3, they tell the guard they are finally ready to answer the question?
A: The section says the imprisonment is "unless in the meantime, such person consents to be examined and to answer, or to produce the document". If they consent, the imprisonment ends. [Source: Section 388, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Imprisonment or committal of person refusing to answer or produce document

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 388: Imprisonment or committal of person refusing to answer or produce document

Q: If the 7 days pass and the witness comes back to court and *still* refuses to answer, does the court just have to let them go?
A: No. The section explicitly states: "in the event of his persisting in his refusal, he may be dealt with according to the provisions of section 384 or section 385" (meaning formal contempt charges and further punishment). [Source: Section 388, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Imprisonment or committal of person refusing to answer or produce document

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 388: Imprisonment or committal of person refusing to answer or produce document

Q: What is the consequence of this specific 7-day committal power?
A: The consequence is providing a short, sharp shock to compel evidence; it acts as a high-pressure coercive tool. Seven days in a cell is often enough to break the stubbornness of a witness who is protecting a friend, ensuring the court gets the vital truth without immediately initiating a massive, separate criminal trial against the witness. [Source: Section 388, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Imprisonment or committal of person refusing to answer or produce document

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 389: Summary procedure for punishment for non-attendance by a witness in obedience to

Q: What happens if a person receives a legal summons to appear in court as a witness, but they just ignore it and stay home without a good reason?
A: The court can hold a quick summary trial and fine them up to 500 rupees for disobeying the summons. [Source: Section 389, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Summary procedure for punishment for non-attendance by a witness in obedience to

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 389: Summary procedure for punishment for non-attendance by a witness in obedience to

Q: How does Section 389 of BNSS 2023 penalize witness truancy?
A: Section 389 of BNSS 2023 outlines the "Summary procedure for punishment for non-attendance by a witness in obedience to summons," allowing a Court to summarily try and fine (up to 500 rupees) any legally summoned witness who neglects to attend or departs early without just excuse. [Source: Section 389, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Summary procedure for punishment for non-attendance by a witness in obedience to

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 389: Summary procedure for punishment for non-attendance by a witness in obedience to

Q: A witness is summoned to court at 10:00 AM. They show up at 10:00 AM, sit in the waiting room for an hour, get bored, and go home at 11:00 AM before being called to the stand. Can they be punished under this section even though they technically "attended"?
A: Yes. The section specifically covers a witness who "departs from the place where he has to attend before the time at which it is lawful for him to depart". Leaving before being officially dismissed triggers the penalty. [Source: Section 389, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Summary procedure for punishment for non-attendance by a witness in obedience to

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 389: Summary procedure for punishment for non-attendance by a witness in obedience to

Q: What procedural right must the truant witness be given before the court can actually impose the fine?
A: They must be given "an opportunity of showing cause why he should not be punished under this section". [Source: Section 389, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Summary procedure for punishment for non-attendance by a witness in obedience to

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 389: Summary procedure for punishment for non-attendance by a witness in obedience to

Q: Can the court use this section to sentence the truant witness to a month in jail?
A: No. The punishment under sub-section (1) is strictly limited to "sentence him to fine not exceeding five hundred rupees." Imprisonment is not an option under this specific summary procedure. [Source: Section 389, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Summary procedure for punishment for non-attendance by a witness in obedience to

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 389: Summary procedure for punishment for non-attendance by a witness in obedience to

Q: What is the consequence of creating a "summary procedure" specifically for non-attendance?
A: The consequence is streamlined judicial administration; courts rely on witnesses to function. If judges had to file massive, formal criminal complaints every time a witness overslept or ignored a subpoena, the system would stall. This allows judges to quickly slap a fine on a truant witness and move on. [Source: Section 389, BNSS 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 390: Appeals from convictions under sections 383, 384, 388 and 389

Q: If a judge uses their special summary powers to punish someone for contempt, perjury, or ignoring a summons, can the punished person appeal that decision to a higher court?
A: Yes. Even though it was a quick summary punishment, the convicted person has the right to appeal to the superior court that normally hears appeals from that specific judge. [Source: Section 390, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Appeals from convictions under sections 383, 384, 388 and 389

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 390: Appeals from convictions under sections 383, 384, 388 and 389

Q: Which section guarantees the right to appeal against summary convictions for offences against the administration of justice?
A: Section 390 of BNSS 2023 governs "Appeals from convictions under sections 383, 384, 388 and 389," guaranteeing an appeal to the normally designated appellate court against these specific summary judicial punishments. [Source: Section 390, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Appeals from convictions under sections 383, 384, 388 and 389

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 390: Appeals from convictions under sections 383, 384, 388 and 389

Q: A Sub-Registrar of properties (acting as a Civil Court under State direction) fines a man for contempt under section 384. The man wants to appeal, but doesn't know where to go since the Sub-Registrar isn't a normal judge. Where does he file the appeal?
A: Under sub-section (4), an appeal from such conviction by a Registrar/Sub-Registrar "shall lie to the Court of Session for the sessions division within which the office of such Registrar or Sub-Registrar is situate." [Source: Section 390, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Appeals from convictions under sections 383, 384, 388 and 389

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 390: Appeals from convictions under sections 383, 384, 388 and 389

Q: According to sub-section (2), what three specific actions can the Appellate Court take regarding the lower court's finding or sentence?
A: The Appellate Court may "alter or reverse the finding, or reduce or reverse the sentence". [Source: Section 390, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Appeals from convictions under sections 383, 384, 388 and 389

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 390: Appeals from convictions under sections 383, 384, 388 and 389

Q: Can a person appeal if they were sentenced by the High Court under these summary sections?
A: No. Sub-section (1) explicitly limits the right of appeal to "Any person sentenced by any Court *other than a High Court*". High Court summary contempt convictions follow different constitutional rules. [Source: Section 390, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Appeals from convictions under sections 383, 384, 388 and 389

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 390: Appeals from convictions under sections 383, 384, 388 and 389

Q: What is the consequence of explicitly guaranteeing appeals for summary punishments?
A: The consequence is preventing judicial tyranny; summary powers allow a judge to act as the victim, prosecutor, and jury all at once (e.g., when insulted). Guaranteeing an appeal ensures that a judge who acts out of personal anger rather than legal justice can be checked by a neutral higher court. [Source: Section 390, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Appeals from convictions under sections 383, 384, 388 and 389

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 391: Certain Judges and Magistrates not to try certain offences when committed before

Q: Can a judge preside over a full criminal trial if the crime being tried is an insult or contempt that was directed at that very same judge earlier?
A: No. A judge cannot be the trial judge for a contempt or justice-related offense that happened in their own courtroom against them, because they are essentially the victim. They must transfer the case to a different judge. (The only exception is the quick "summary" fines discussed earlier). [Source: Section 391, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Certain Judges and Magistrates not to try certain offences when committed before

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 391: Certain Judges and Magistrates not to try certain offences when committed before

Q: How does Section 391 of BNSS 2023 enforce the principle that no one should be a judge in their own cause?
A: Section 391 of BNSS 2023 dictates that "Certain Judges and Magistrates not to try certain offences when committed before themselves," prohibiting a judicial officer from formally trying an accused for offences against justice (like perjury or contempt) if the offence was committed in their presence, forcing them to transfer the case to another court. [Source: Section 391, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Certain Judges and Magistrates not to try certain offences when committed before

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 391: Certain Judges and Magistrates not to try certain offences when committed before

Q: A witness commits perjury. The Magistrate files a formal complaint under Section 379 for a full trial. Instead of sending it to a different court, the Magistrate says, "I will hold the trial myself, I know he lied because I heard him." Can the Magistrate legally conduct this full trial?
A: No. Under section 391, "no Judge... or Magistrate shall try any person for any offence referred to in section 215, when such offence is committed before himself". The Magistrate is barred from trying the case. [Source: Section 391, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Certain Judges and Magistrates not to try certain offences when committed before

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 391: Certain Judges and Magistrates not to try certain offences when committed before

Q: What four specific sections are listed as exceptions to this rule (where the judge *is* allowed to punish someone for an offense committed in front of them)?
A: "Except as provided in sections 383, 384, 388 and 389" (these are the summary, immediate punishment sections). [Source: Section 391, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Certain Judges and Magistrates not to try certain offences when committed before

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 391: Certain Judges and Magistrates not to try certain offences when committed before

Q: Does this prohibition against trying offences committed before themselves apply to a Judge of a High Court?
A: No. The section explicitly states "(other than a Judge of a High Court)". High Court judges have inherent constitutional powers regarding their own contempt. [Source: Section 391, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Certain Judges and Magistrates not to try certain offences when committed before

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 391: Certain Judges and Magistrates not to try certain offences when committed before

Q: What is the consequence of this strict prohibition?
A: The consequence is preserving objective neutrality in formal trials; while judges need immediate summary powers to maintain order, a full criminal trial requires a totally unbiased adjudicator. A judge who was personally insulted or lied to cannot possibly be expected to view the evidence neutrally in a full trial later on. [Source: Section 391, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Certain Judges and Magistrates not to try certain offences when committed before

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 392: Judgment

Q: How does a judge announce their final decision (judgment) at the end of a trial?
A: The judge must pronounce it in open court. They can read the whole thing, or just read the operative part (guilty/not guilty and the sentence) and explain it in a language the accused understands. It must be delivered within 45 days of the trial ending. [Source: Section 392, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Judgment

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 392: Judgment

Q: What are the procedural requirements for delivering a judgment under Section 392 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 392 of BNSS 2023 covers the "Judgment," requiring it to be pronounced in open court within 45 days of trial termination, detailing methods of delivery (reading in full or operative part), and mandating the presence of the accused (physically or electronically). [Source: Section 392, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Judgment

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 392: Judgment

Q: A trial finishes on March 1st. The judge is very busy and doesn't write the judgment. Finally, on June 1st (90 days later), the judge emails a copy of the judgment to the lawyers without ever reading it in court. Is this valid?
A: No. First, sub-section (1) requires the judgment be pronounced "not later than forty-five days". Second, it must be pronounced "in open Court". Emailing it without an open court pronouncement violates the law. [Source: Section 392, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Judgment

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 392: Judgment

Q: If the judge chooses to only read out the "operative part" of the judgment (the conclusion), what must they additionally do according to sub-section (1)(c)?
A: They must "explain the substance of the judgment in a language which is understood by the accused or his advocate." [Source: Section 392, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Judgment

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 392: Judgment

Q: If an accused person is out on bail but fails to show up on the day the judgment is scheduled to be announced, is the judge forbidden from announcing the verdict?
A: No. Under sub-section (6) proviso, if there are multiple accused and some don't attend, the judge "may, in order to avoid undue delay in the disposal of the case, pronounce the judgment notwithstanding their absence." Furthermore, sub-section (7) states the judgment isn't invalid just because a party was absent. [Source: Section 392, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Judgment

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 392: Judgment

Q: What is the consequence of mandating that a copy of the judgment be uploaded to the court's portal within seven days (per the proviso in sub-section 4)?
A: The consequence is modernizing transparency; it stops corrupt lower-level court staff from artificially withholding physical copies of judgments to extort bribes from lawyers and defendants who desperately need the document to file an appeal before their deadline expires. [Source: Section 392, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Judgment

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 393: Language and contents of judgment

Q: What information MUST be written inside a criminal court's final judgment document?
A: The judgment must be in the court's official language. It must list the main questions to be decided, the judge's decision on those questions, the reasons for that decision, and exactly which law and section the person is convicted under (or acquitted of). [Source: Section 393, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Language and contents of judgment

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 393: Language and contents of judgment

Q: What are the mandatory structural contents of a criminal judgment according to Section 393 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 393 of BNSS 2023 dictates the "Language and contents of judgment," requiring it to contain the points for determination, the decision, the reasoning, the specific penal section applied, and requiring special reasons for death sentences or unusually short prison terms. [Source: Section 393, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Language and contents of judgment

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 393: Language and contents of judgment

Q: A judge convicts a man of murder and sentences him to the death penalty. The judgment simply says: "The accused is guilty of murder under BNS. Sentence: Death." Is this judgment legally sufficient under BNSS?
A: No. Under sub-section (3), when the conviction is for an offence punishable with death or life imprisonment, "the judgment shall state the reasons for the sentence awarded, and, in the case of sentence of death, the special reasons for such sentence." A one-line death sentence is invalid. [Source: Section 393, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Language and contents of judgment

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 393: Language and contents of judgment

Q: According to sub-section (4), if a judge convicts someone of a crime that carries a maximum of 3 years in prison, but decides to only sentence them to 1 month in prison (less than three months), what must the judge explicitly record in the judgment?
A: The judge "shall record its reasons for awarding such sentence" (unless it was a summary trial or imprisonment till the rising of the court). [Source: Section 393, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Language and contents of judgment

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 393: Language and contents of judgment

Q: If it is completely unclear whether a thief committed the crime under Section X (theft inside a house) or Section Y (theft by a servant), can the judge convict them of both just to be safe?
A: No, under sub-section (2), if it is doubtful under which of two sections the offence falls, "the Court shall distinctly express the same, and pass judgment in the alternative." [Source: Section 393, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Language and contents of judgment

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 393: Language and contents of judgment

Q: What is the consequence of demanding "the reasons for the decision" in every judgment?
A: The consequence is preventing arbitrary judicial fiat; a judge cannot simply declare someone guilty based on a gut feeling. Forcing the judge to articulate their logical reasoning ensures they actually weighed the evidence, and gives the Appellate Court a clear target to review for legal errors. [Source: Section 393, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Language and contents of judgment

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 394: Order for notifying address of previously convicted offender

Q: If a serious criminal (who served at least 3 years in prison before) gets convicted of another serious crime, can the court order the police to track them after they are finally released?
A: Yes. The court can order repeat offenders to notify the authorities about their home address, and any time they move or leave town, for up to five years after they get out of prison. [Source: Section 394, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order for notifying address of previously convicted offender

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 394: Order for notifying address of previously convicted offender

Q: What post-release surveillance measure can courts impose on repeat offenders under Section 394 of BNSS 2023?
A: Section 394 of BNSS 2023 allows an "Order for notifying address of previously convicted offender," permitting courts to mandate that recidivists convicted of offences carrying 3+ years imprisonment notify authorities of their residence and any changes for up to five years post-release. [Source: Section 394, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order for notifying address of previously convicted offender

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 394: Order for notifying address of previously convicted offender

Q: A man was convicted of a minor theft and served 1 year. Ten years later, he is convicted of another minor theft. Can the Magistrate order him to report his address to the police for 5 years after his release under this section?
A: No. Sub-section (1) requires that the previous conviction *and* the current conviction must be for an "offence punishable with imprisonment for a term of three years, or upwards". Minor thefts usually don't meet this threshold, so the tracking order cannot be applied. [Source: Section 394, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order for notifying address of previously convicted offender

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 394: Order for notifying address of previously convicted offender

Q: Under sub-section (2), what two related types of criminal activity (besides actually committing the crime) can also trigger this address notification order?
A: "criminal conspiracies to commit such offences and to the abetment of such offences and attempts to commit them." [Source: Section 394, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order for notifying address of previously convicted offender

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 394: Order for notifying address of previously convicted offender

Q: Can a 2nd Class Magistrate issue an order forcing a repeat offender to notify the police of their address?
A: No. Sub-section (1) explicitly says "by any Court *other than that of a Magistrate of the second class*". Only higher courts can issue this order. [Source: Section 394, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order for notifying address of previously convicted offender

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 394: Order for notifying address of previously convicted offender

Q: What is the consequence of this notification order?
A: The consequence is enhanced proactive policing; it acknowledges that hardcore recidivists are highly likely to reoffend upon release. Forcing them to register their address allows local police to keep tabs on them, preventing them from melting anonymously into new communities to start a new crime spree. [Source: Section 394, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order for notifying address of previously convicted offender

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 395: Order to pay compensation

Q: If a court orders a convicted criminal to pay a heavy fine, does the money just go to the government, or can the victim get some of it?
A: The court can order that the fine money be given to the victim as compensation for their injuries or losses. It can also be used to pay for the prosecution's expenses or to compensate people who unknowingly bought stolen goods from the criminal. [Source: Section 395, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order to pay compensation

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 395: Order to pay compensation

Q: How does Section 395 of BNSS 2023 allow fines to be repurposed for restitution?
A: Section 395 of BNSS 2023 details the "Order to pay compensation," empowering a Court to apply recovered fines to defray prosecution costs, compensate victims for loss/injury, compensate dependents in fatal accidents, or compensate bona fide purchasers of stolen property. [Source: Section 395, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order to pay compensation

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 395: Order to pay compensation

Q: A man is convicted of fraud and fined 1 Lakh rupees. The victim asks the trial court for that money as compensation. However, the convict immediately files an appeal to the High Court. Can the trial court hand the 1 Lakh rupees to the victim right away?
A: No. Under sub-section (2), "If the fine is imposed in a case which is subject to appeal, no such payment shall be made before the period allowed for presenting the appeal has elapsed, or, if an appeal be presented, before the decision of the appeal." [Source: Section 395, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order to pay compensation

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 395: Order to pay compensation

Q: Under sub-section (3), if the court imposes a sentence that does *not* include a fine (e.g., just imprisonment), can the court still order the accused to pay money to the victim?
A: Yes. The court may "order the accused person to pay, by way of compensation, such amount as may be specified in the order to the person who has suffered any loss or injury". [Source: Section 395, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order to pay compensation

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 395: Order to pay compensation

Q: If a victim receives 50,000 rupees as compensation under this section during the criminal trial, are they banned from filing a separate civil lawsuit against the criminal for more money?
A: No, they are not banned. However, sub-section (5) states that "At the time of awarding compensation in any subsequent civil suit relating to the same matter, the Court shall take into account any sum paid or recovered as compensation under this section." [Source: Section 395, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order to pay compensation

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 395: Order to pay compensation

Q: What is the consequence of empowering criminal courts to award compensation directly?
A: The consequence is providing swift, accessible justice to victims; instead of forcing a victim who just survived a grueling criminal trial to immediately hire a new lawyer and start a years-long civil lawsuit just to get their stolen money back or medical bills paid, the criminal judge can order restitution on the spot. [Source: Section 395, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order to pay compensation

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 396: Victim compensation scheme

Q: What happens if a victim is severely injured by a crime, needs money for medical rehab, but the criminal is poor and can't pay compensation, or the criminal is never even caught?
A: The State Government has a special "Victim Compensation Scheme" fund. The Legal Services Authority can award money from this government fund to the victim to help them recover, even if the criminal is acquitted or never identified. [Source: Section 396, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Victim compensation scheme

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 396: Victim compensation scheme

Q: How does Section 396 of BNSS 2023 ensure victim rehabilitation independent of the offender's ability to pay?
A: Section 396 of BNSS 2023 establishes the "Victim compensation scheme," mandating State Governments to create funds to compensate victims. The Legal Services Authority determines the quantum based on court recommendations or direct applications (even if the offender is untraced or acquitted). [Source: Section 396, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Victim compensation scheme

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 396: Victim compensation scheme

Q: A woman is attacked by a masked man who is never identified or caught. She needs extensive surgery. Since there is no criminal trial, can she still get state compensation under this scheme?
A: Yes. Under sub-section (4), "Where the offender is not traced or identified, but the victim is identified, and where no trial takes place, the victim or his dependents may make an application to the State or the District Legal Services Authority for award of compensation." [Source: Section 396, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Victim compensation scheme

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 396: Victim compensation scheme

Q: What is the mandatory time limit for the Legal Services Authority to complete its enquiry and award adequate compensation after receiving an application or recommendation?
A: "within two months." (sub-section 5). [Source: Section 396, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Victim compensation scheme

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 396: Victim compensation scheme

Q: If a judge already ordered the criminal to pay compensation out of their fine under Section 395, can the judge *also* recommend state compensation under Section 396?
A: Yes, under sub-section (3), if the trial Court "is satisfied, that the compensation awarded under section 395 is not adequate for such rehabilitation... it may make recommendation for compensation." [Source: Section 396, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Victim compensation scheme

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 396: Victim compensation scheme

Q: What is the consequence of this state-funded scheme?
A: The consequence is shifting the burden of victim care to the state; it recognizes that the state failed in its fundamental duty to protect the citizen from crime. Therefore, regardless of whether the specific criminal is caught or has money, the state takes financial responsibility for the victim's physical and psychological rehabilitation. [Source: Section 396, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Victim compensation scheme

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 397: Treatment of victims

Q: If a victim of a serious crime like rape or acid attack goes to a private hospital, can the hospital demand payment upfront or refuse to treat them?
A: Absolutely not. All hospitals (public or private) are legally mandated to immediately provide free first-aid and medical treatment to victims of specified violent crimes against women and children, and they must inform the police right away. [Source: Section 397, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Treatment of victims

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 397: Treatment of victims

Q: What mandatory duty does Section 397 of BNSS 2023 impose on healthcare facilities regarding crime victims?
A: Section 397 of BNSS 2023 dictates the "Treatment of victims," requiring all hospitals (public and private) to immediately provide free first-aid or medical treatment to victims of specified serious offences (primarily sexual offences and acid attacks under BNS and POCSO) and to inform the police. [Source: Section 397, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Treatment of victims

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 397: Treatment of victims

Q: An acid attack survivor is rushed to a highly expensive, exclusive private hospital. The hospital administrators refuse her at the door, saying they only treat members and she should go to a government clinic. Is the hospital breaking the law?
A: Yes. Section 397 explicitly states "All hospitals, public or private... shall immediately, provide the first-aid or medical treatment, free of cost, to the victims of any offence covered under... section 124 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita". Acid attack (BNS 124) is covered. Refusal is a crime. [Source: Section 397, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Treatment of victims

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 397: Treatment of victims

Q: Which specific specialized central Act regarding crimes against minors is explicitly referenced in this section alongside the BNS?
A: "the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 (32 of 2012)". [Source: Section 397, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Treatment of victims

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 397: Treatment of victims

Q: Can a hospital provide the free treatment but choose to keep it confidential and not tell the police to protect the victim's privacy?
A: No, the section strictly mandates that they "shall immediately inform the police of such incident." [Source: Section 397, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Treatment of victims

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 397: Treatment of victims

Q: What is the consequence of this strict medical mandate?
A: The consequence is prioritizing human life over medical bureaucracy and profit; it eliminates the cruel "golden hour" delays where victims of horrific violence bleed out or suffer permanent damage while hospitals argue over police paperwork (FIRs) or demand cash deposits before initiating life-saving care. [Source: Section 397, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Treatment of victims

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 398: Witness protection scheme

Q: Does the law require states to have a system to keep witnesses safe from intimidation or murder by the criminals they are testifying against?
A: Yes. The law explicitly requires every State Government to prepare and notify a formal Witness Protection Scheme to ensure the safety of people testifying in criminal cases. [Source: Section 398, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Witness protection scheme

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 398: Witness protection scheme

Q: What administrative mandate does Section 398 of BNSS 2023 place on State Governments regarding trial evidence?
A: Section 398 of BNSS 2023 mandates a "Witness protection scheme," legally requiring every State Government to prepare and notify a scheme to ensure the protection of witnesses in criminal trials. [Source: Section 398, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Witness protection scheme

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 398: Witness protection scheme

Q: A key witness in a gang murder case refuses to testify because the gang threatened his family. The prosecutor tells the judge, "We don't have any formal rules for hiding witnesses in this state, so there's nothing we can do." Is this acceptable under BNSS?
A: No. Under Section 398, "Every State Government shall prepare and notify a Witness Protection Scheme". It is a mandatory statutory duty, not an optional policy. [Source: Section 398, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Witness protection scheme

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 398: Witness protection scheme

Q: What is the stated goal or view of preparing this scheme according to the text?
A: "with a view to ensure protection of the witnesses." [Source: Section 398, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Witness protection scheme

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 398: Witness protection scheme

Q: Does this section provide the specific logistical details (like changing names or relocating families) of how the protection must be done?
A: No, it is a brief enabling provision. It forces the State Government to "prepare and notify" a scheme, leaving the actual logistical and operational rules to the state's executive rule-making power. [Source: Section 398, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Witness protection scheme

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 398: Witness protection scheme

Q: What is the consequence of elevating witness protection to a statutory requirement?
A: The consequence is combating the plague of "hostile witnesses"; organized crime and powerful politicians routinely derail trials by intimidating witnesses into changing their stories. Mandating formal protection schemes helps secure the integrity of the trial process by shielding truth-tellers from violent reprisal. [Source: Section 398, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Witness protection scheme

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 399: Compensation to persons groundlessly arrested

Q: If someone maliciously lies to the police and causes you to get arrested for no reason, can the Magistrate force that liar to pay you for ruining your day?
A: Yes. If a Magistrate finds there was no sufficient ground for the arrest, they can order the person who caused the false arrest to pay you up to 1000 rupees for your loss of time and expenses. [Source: Section 399, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Compensation to persons groundlessly arrested

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 399: Compensation to persons groundlessly arrested

Q: How does Section 399 of BNSS 2023 penalize malicious complaints that result in unwarranted police action?
A: Section 399 of BNSS 2023 covers "Compensation to persons groundlessly arrested," allowing a Magistrate to award up to 1000 rupees in compensation (payable by the person who baselessly caused the arrest) to a victim for loss of time and expenses, enforceable as a fine or via imprisonment. [Source: Section 399, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Compensation to persons groundlessly arrested

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 399: Compensation to persons groundlessly arrested

Q: A man falsely tells police his neighbor stole his car, leading to the neighbor's arrest. The Magistrate realizes it was a lie and orders the man to pay the neighbor 1000 rupees compensation. The man refuses to pay. Can the Magistrate send him to jail just for not paying this compensation?
A: Yes. Under sub-section (3), "if it cannot be so recovered, the person by whom it is payable shall be sentenced to simple imprisonment for such term not exceeding thirty days as the Magistrate directs". [Source: Section 399, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Compensation to persons groundlessly arrested

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 399: Compensation to persons groundlessly arrested

Q: What is the maximum financial amount the Magistrate can award to *each* arrested person under this section?
A: "not exceeding one thousand rupees" (per person, as per sub-section 2). [Source: Section 399, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Compensation to persons groundlessly arrested

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 399: Compensation to persons groundlessly arrested

Q: Can the Magistrate use this section to force the *police officer* who made the arrest to pay the compensation out of their own pocket?
A: No. The section specifies the compensation is "to be paid by the person *so causing* the arrest". It is aimed at malicious complainants/informants who misuse the police, not the police themselves (unless the police acted entirely on their own malice). [Source: Section 399, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Compensation to persons groundlessly arrested

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 399: Compensation to persons groundlessly arrested

Q: What is the consequence of this immediate compensatory power?
A: The consequence is providing a swift, low-level deterrent against frivolous or vindictive police complaints; it offers immediate, tangible redress for the humiliation of a false arrest without forcing the victim to launch a massive civil defamation lawsuit. [Source: Section 399, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Compensation to persons groundlessly arrested

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 400: Order to pay costs in non-cognizable cases

Q: In minor "non-cognizable" cases (where the victim usually has to hire their own lawyer and file a complaint directly to the Magistrate), if the victim wins the case, can they force the criminal to pay for their lawyer fees?
A: Yes. If the court convicts the accused in a non-cognizable case, it can order the convicted person to pay the complainant's prosecution costs, including witness fees and advocate's fees. [Source: Section 400, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order to pay costs in non-cognizable cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 400: Order to pay costs in non-cognizable cases

Q: How does Section 400 of BNSS 2023 address the financial burden of private prosecutions?
A: Section 400 of BNSS 2023 allows an "Order to pay costs in non-cognizable cases," permitting the Court, upon convicting an accused in a privately filed non-cognizable case, to order the accused to reimburse the complainant for prosecution expenses (including advocate fees), with default resulting in imprisonment. [Source: Section 400, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order to pay costs in non-cognizable cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 400: Order to pay costs in non-cognizable cases

Q: A woman files a private complaint against her neighbor for simple nuisance (a non-cognizable offense). She spends 20,000 rupees on a lawyer. The neighbor is convicted. The Magistrate orders the neighbor to pay the 20,000 back to the woman. The neighbor refuses. Can he be jailed for refusing to pay these lawyer fees?
A: Yes. Under sub-section (1), the Court "may further order that in default of payment, the accused shall suffer simple imprisonment for a period not exceeding thirty days". [Source: Section 400, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order to pay costs in non-cognizable cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 400: Order to pay costs in non-cognizable cases

Q: What three specific types of expenses are explicitly listed as things that can be included in the "costs" awarded by the Court?
A: "any expenses incurred in respect of process-fees, witnesses and advocate's fees". [Source: Section 400, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order to pay costs in non-cognizable cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 400: Order to pay costs in non-cognizable cases

Q: Does this rule apply if the police filed a formal chargesheet for a major, cognizable crime like murder?
A: No, the section explicitly begins: "Whenever any complaint of a *non-cognizable* offence is made to a Court". [Source: Section 400, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order to pay costs in non-cognizable cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 400: Order to pay costs in non-cognizable cases

Q: What is the consequence of allowing cost recovery in non-cognizable cases?
A: The consequence is making minor justice accessible; in non-cognizable cases, the State doesn't provide a free prosecutor. If victims couldn't recover their legal fees upon winning, they would never bother filing complaints for minor offenses because the lawyer would cost more than the dispute itself. [Source: Section 400, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order to pay costs in non-cognizable cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 401: Order to release on probation of good conduct or after admonition

Q: Does a judge have to send a first-time offender to prison for a minor crime, or can the judge just give them a strict warning and let them go on "probation"?
A: For minor crimes (and for youth/women in slightly more serious crimes), if it's their first offense, the judge can release them on "probation of good conduct." They sign a bond promising to behave for up to 3 years. For extremely trivial crimes, the judge can release them with just a stern warning (admonition). [Source: Section 401, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order to release on probation of good conduct or after admonition

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 401: Order to release on probation of good conduct or after admonition

Q: How does Section 401 of BNSS 2023 provide alternatives to incarceration for certain demographics and first-time offenders?
A: Section 401 of BNSS 2023 governs the "Order to release on probation of good conduct or after admonition," allowing courts to release first-time adult offenders (crimes up to 7 years), and youth/women (crimes not punishable by death/life), on behavioral bonds instead of prison, or with an admonition for trivial theft/cheating offenses. [Source: Section 401, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order to release on probation of good conduct or after admonition

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 401: Order to release on probation of good conduct or after admonition

Q: A 30-year-old man is convicted of a crime punishable by 10 years in prison. It is his very first offense and he has excellent character. Can the judge release him on probation under Section 401 instead of sending him to jail?
A: No. Under sub-section (1), for a "person not under twenty-one years of age" (an adult male), probation is only available if convicted of an offence "punishable with fine only or with imprisonment for a term of *seven years or less*". Since his crime carries 10 years, he is ineligible. [Source: Section 401, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order to release on probation of good conduct or after admonition

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 401: Order to release on probation of good conduct or after admonition

Q: For trivial offenses like minor theft, what is the action the Court takes when it decides not to punish or use a probation bond, as per sub-section (3)?
A: The court may "release him after due admonition" (a formal reprimand/warning). [Source: Section 401, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order to release on probation of good conduct or after admonition

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 401: Order to release on probation of good conduct or after admonition

Q: If a 19-year-old (under 21) is convicted of a serious crime punishable by 14 years in prison, are they eligible for probation under this section?
A: Yes. Under sub-section (1), "any person under twenty-one years of age or any woman" is eligible as long as they are "convicted of an offence *not punishable with death or imprisonment for life*". Since 14 years is less than life, the youth is eligible. [Source: Section 401, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order to release on probation of good conduct or after admonition

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 401: Order to release on probation of good conduct or after admonition

Q: What is the consequence of this probation system?
A: The consequence is breaking the cycle of criminality; sending a young, first-time offender to a harsh prison for a minor mistake often turns them into a hardened, lifelong criminal due to prison influence. Probation allows the state to hold a threat of prison over their head (the bond) while allowing them to remain productive members of society. [Source: Section 401, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Order to release on probation of good conduct or after admonition

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 402: Special reasons to be recorded in certain cases

Q: If a young offender or a first-time offender is legally eligible for probation, but the judge decides to send them to prison anyway, does the judge have to explain why?
A: Yes. If a judge refuses to use the available probation laws or juvenile laws to help a young/first-time offender and sends them to jail instead, the judge must explicitly write down the "special reasons" for choosing harsh punishment over rehabilitation. [Source: Section 402, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Special reasons to be recorded in certain cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 402: Special reasons to be recorded in certain cases

Q: What mandatory justification does Section 402 of BNSS 2023 require when courts deny rehabilitative sentencing?
A: Section 402 of BNSS 2023 requires "Special reasons to be recorded in certain cases," dictating that if a Court could have dealt with an offender under Section 401 (probation), the Probation of Offenders Act, or the Juvenile Justice Act, but chooses not to, it must explicitly record its special reasons for denying that rehabilitative treatment. [Source: Section 402, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Special reasons to be recorded in certain cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 402: Special reasons to be recorded in certain cases

Q: A 19-year-old first-time offender is convicted of simple theft. He is perfectly eligible for probation under Section 401. The Magistrate is in a bad mood and simply sentences him to 1 year in jail without writing any explanation. Is this sentence procedurally flawed?
A: Yes. Because the Magistrate *could* have dealt with him under Section 401 but didn't, Section 402 strictly mandates that the court "shall record in its judgment the special reasons for not having done so." Failing to record reasons makes the judgment legally vulnerable. [Source: Section 402, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Special reasons to be recorded in certain cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 402: Special reasons to be recorded in certain cases

Q: Which specific central Act regarding young offenders (besides the Probation of Offenders Act) is explicitly protected by this "special reasons" requirement?
A: "the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015". [Source: Section 402, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Special reasons to be recorded in certain cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 402: Special reasons to be recorded in certain cases

Q: Does the judge have to record special reasons if they send a 40-year-old repeat offender to prison?
A: No. Section 402 only applies "Where in any case the Court *could have* dealt with" the person under probation/juvenile laws. A 40-year-old repeat offender is legally ineligible for Section 401 probation, so the judge doesn't need to justify not using it. [Source: Section 402, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Special reasons to be recorded in certain cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 402: Special reasons to be recorded in certain cases

Q: What is the consequence of forcing judges to record "special reasons" for denying probation?
A: The consequence is creating a strong judicial presumption in favor of rehabilitation; it forces judges to pause and think before ruining a young life with a prison sentence. It makes probation the default expectation for eligible offenders, requiring the judge to logically justify why this specific individual is too dangerous to be given a second chance. [Source: Section 402, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Special reasons to be recorded in certain cases

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 403: Court not to alter judgment

Q: Once a judge signs the final judgment in a criminal case, can they change their mind the next day and rewrite the verdict or change the prison sentence?
A: Absolutely not. Once a criminal judgment is signed, the judge loses all power to alter or review it. They can only fix minor clerical typos or math errors. [Source: Section 403, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Court not to alter judgment

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 403: Court not to alter judgment

Q: How does Section 403 of BNSS 2023 enforce the finality of judicial decisions?
A: Section 403 of BNSS 2023 establishes the rule of "Court not to alter judgment," explicitly forbidding any Court from altering or reviewing its own judgment or final order once signed, except to correct minor clerical or arithmetical mistakes. [Source: Section 403, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Court not to alter judgment

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 403: Court not to alter judgment

Q: A Magistrate convicts a man of theft and sentences him to 2 years in prison, signing the judgment. That evening, the Magistrate reads a new Supreme Court ruling and realizes he made a terrible legal error and the man should have been acquitted. Can the Magistrate rip up the old judgment and issue a new one acquitting the man the next morning?
A: No. Under Section 403, "no Court, when it has signed its judgment... shall alter or review the same except to correct a clerical or arithmetical error." The Magistrate is powerless; the man must appeal to a higher court to fix the legal error. [Source: Section 403, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Court not to alter judgment

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 403: Court not to alter judgment

Q: What are the only two types of errors a judge is legally allowed to correct in a signed judgment under this section?
A: "a clerical or arithmetical error." [Source: Section 403, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Court not to alter judgment

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 403: Court not to alter judgment

Q: Are there *any* situations where a judgment can be altered, other than for typos?
A: Only if explicitly allowed elsewhere in the law. The section begins with the caveat: "Save as otherwise provided by this Sanhita or by any other law for the time being in force". [Source: Section 403, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Court not to alter judgment

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 403: Court not to alter judgment

Q: What is the consequence of stripping a judge's power to review their own signed judgment?
A: The consequence is the legal doctrine of "functus officio" (having performed his office); it ensures absolute certainty and finality in criminal trials. If judges could constantly change their minds, lawyers would harass them endlessly in their chambers to rewrite verdicts, leading to immense corruption and a total lack of closure for both victims and defendants. [Source: Section 403, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Court not to alter judgment

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 404: Copy of judgment to be given to accused and other persons

Q: After a criminal trial finishes, does the convicted person have a right to get a copy of the judge's written decision? Do they have to pay for it?
A: If the person is sentenced to prison, they must immediately be given a free copy of the judgment. Anyone else can apply to get a copy by paying a standard fee. If it's a death sentence, they get a free copy immediately whether they ask for it or not. [Source: Section 404, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Copy of judgment to be given to accused and other persons

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 404: Copy of judgment to be given to accused and other persons

Q: How does Section 404 of BNSS 2023 regulate the distribution of judgments?
A: Section 404 of BNSS 2023 mandates "Copy of judgment to be given to accused and other persons," requiring free, immediate copies for imprisoned or death-sentenced convicts, providing translated/certified copies for appealable cases, and allowing affected parties or the government to obtain copies upon application. [Source: Section 404, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Copy of judgment to be given to accused and other persons

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 404: Copy of judgment to be given to accused and other persons

Q: A man is convicted and sentenced to 5 years in prison. The court tells him, "You can have a copy of your judgment next week, but you must pay a 500 rupee copying fee first." Is the court following the law?
A: No. Under sub-section (1), when the accused is sentenced to imprisonment, a copy "shall, immediately after the pronouncement of the judgment, be given to him free of cost." Delaying it and charging a fee are both illegal. [Source: Section 404, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Copy of judgment to be given to accused and other persons

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 404: Copy of judgment to be given to accused and other persons

Q: Under sub-section (4), if a Court sentences someone to death, what specific piece of information must the Court verbally inform the accused of?
A: The Court "shall inform him of the period within which, if he wishes to appeal, his appeal should be preferred." [Source: Section 404, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Copy of judgment to be given to accused and other persons

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 404: Copy of judgment to be given to accused and other persons

Q: Can a random citizen, who was not a victim, witness, or defendant in a case, walk into court and demand a copy of the judgment just because they are curious?
A: Not automatically under this section. Sub-section (5) grants copies to "any person affected by a judgment". However, sub-section (6) allows the High Court to make rules to grant copies to "any person who is not affected... subject to such conditions, as the High Court may... provide." [Source: Section 404, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Copy of judgment to be given to accused and other persons

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 404: Copy of judgment to be given to accused and other persons

Q: What is the consequence of ensuring free, immediate copies of judgments to prisoners?
A: The consequence is safeguarding the fundamental right to appeal; an imprisoned person cannot draft a legal appeal without seeing the exact reasons the judge used to convict them. Charging them money or delaying the document could cause them to miss their strict statutory deadline to file an appeal, unjustly trapping them in prison. [Source: Section 404, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Copy of judgment to be given to accused and other persons

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 405: Judgment when to be translated

Q: If a judge writes their final decision in English, but the official court language is Hindi, what happens to the document?
A: The original English judgment is kept in the file, but if either party asks for it, a translated version in the court's official language (Hindi) must be added to the official record. [Source: Section 405, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Judgment when to be translated

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 405: Judgment when to be translated

Q: How does Section 405 of BNSS 2023 handle judgments written in a language different from the Court's language?
A: Section 405 of BNSS 2023 dictates "Judgment when to be translated," requiring that if an original judgment is recorded in a language other than the Court's language, a translation into the Court's language must be added to the record if either party requires it. [Source: Section 405, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Judgment when to be translated

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 405: Judgment when to be translated

Q: A Magistrate in a district where the official court language is Marathi writes his 50-page judgment entirely in English. The accused man, who only speaks Marathi, demands a Marathi copy for his records. Is the court legally obligated to translate the entire judgment?
A: Yes. Under section 405, "if either party so requires, a translation thereof into the language of the Court shall be added to such record." Since Marathi is the language of the court and the party required it, the translation must be provided. [Source: Section 405, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Judgment when to be translated

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 405: Judgment when to be translated

Q: What happens to the original version of the judgment (the one written in the non-court language) after it is translated?
A: "The original judgment shall be filed with the record of the proceedings". It is not discarded. [Source: Section 405, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Judgment when to be translated

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 405: Judgment when to be translated

Q: Is the court forced to automatically translate every single judgment written in a different language, even if no one asks for it?
A: No, the translation requirement is triggered "if either party so requires". It is not automatically mandatory without a request. [Source: Section 405, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Judgment when to be translated

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 405: Judgment when to be translated

Q: What is the consequence of this translation rule?
A: The consequence is ensuring linguistic accessibility while allowing judicial efficiency; many Indian judges are educated and draft complex legal reasoning in English. This section allows them to write in their comfortable language, but strictly protects the right of the local litigants to understand their own fate in the local official language if they ask. [Source: Section 405, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Judgment when to be translated

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 406: Court of Session to send copy of finding and sentence to District Magistrate

Q: When a serious case finishes in a Sessions Court, who needs to be officially informed about the result besides the people involved?
A: The trial judge must send a copy of the final verdict and sentence to the District Magistrate (the chief executive officer) of the district where the trial took place. [Source: Section 406, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Court of Session to send copy of finding and sentence to District Magistrate

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 406: Court of Session to send copy of finding and sentence to District Magistrate

Q: What administrative notification is required by Section 406 of BNSS 2023 following certain trials?
A: Section 406 of BNSS 2023 requires the "Court of Session to send copy of finding and sentence to District Magistrate," mandating that a Court of Session or Chief Judicial Magistrate forward a copy of their trial results to the District Magistrate of that local jurisdiction. [Source: Section 406, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Court of Session to send copy of finding and sentence to District Magistrate

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 406: Court of Session to send copy of finding and sentence to District Magistrate

Q: A Sessions Court acquits a notorious gang leader of murder. The trial concludes and the gang leader walks free. The judge files the judgment but doesn't tell the local District Magistrate (DM) about the acquittal. Is this an administrative failure under BNSS?
A: Yes. Section 406 explicitly states the Court of Session "shall forward a copy of its... finding and sentence (if any) to the District Magistrate". Even an acquittal (a finding with no sentence) must be forwarded. [Source: Section 406, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Court of Session to send copy of finding and sentence to District Magistrate

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 406: Court of Session to send copy of finding and sentence to District Magistrate

Q: Which two specific types of judicial officers are mandated by this section to send their findings to the District Magistrate?
A: "the Court of Session or a Chief Judicial Magistrate". [Source: Section 406, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Court of Session to send copy of finding and sentence to District Magistrate

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 406: Court of Session to send copy of finding and sentence to District Magistrate

Q: Does a Second Class Magistrate have to send a copy of every petty theft conviction to the District Magistrate under this specific section?
A: No, this section only applies "In cases tried by the Court of Session or a Chief Judicial Magistrate". [Source: Section 406, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Court of Session to send copy of finding and sentence to District Magistrate

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 406: Court of Session to send copy of finding and sentence to District Magistrate

Q: What is the consequence of forcing the courts to notify the District Magistrate?
A: The consequence is executive awareness; the District Magistrate is responsible for the overall law and order of the district. If a serial killer is sentenced to death, or a dangerous gang is suddenly acquitted, the DM needs to know immediately to manage jail logistics, prevent riots, or prepare for police appeals. [Source: Section 406, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Court of Session to send copy of finding and sentence to District Magistrate

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 407: Sentence of death to be submitted by Court of Session for confirmation

Q: If a local trial judge sentences a murderer to death, is the murderer executed right away?
A: Absolutely not. A death sentence passed by a Sessions Court cannot be executed until it is sent to the state's High Court and the High Court explicitly reviews and confirms the death penalty. [Source: Section 407, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sentence of death to be submitted by Court of Session for confirmation

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 407: Sentence of death to be submitted by Court of Session for confirmation

Q: How does Section 407 of BNSS 2023 act as a safeguard against premature executions?
A: Section 407 of BNSS 2023 governs the "Sentence of death to be submitted by Court of Session for confirmation," mandating that all death sentences passed by a Court of Session must be submitted forthwith to the High Court, and execution is strictly barred until High Court confirmation. [Source: Section 407, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sentence of death to be submitted by Court of Session for confirmation

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 407: Sentence of death to be submitted by Court of Session for confirmation

Q: A Sessions Judge sentences a terrorist to death. The judge writes in the order: "This crime is so heinous that the execution shall take place tomorrow at dawn." Can the prison warden legally hang the terrorist the next morning based on this order?
A: No. Under Section 407(1), "the sentence shall not be executed unless it is confirmed by the High Court." The Sessions Judge has no legal power to order an immediate execution bypassing the High Court. [Source: Section 407, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sentence of death to be submitted by Court of Session for confirmation

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 407: Sentence of death to be submitted by Court of Session for confirmation

Q: While the death sentence is waiting to be reviewed by the High Court, what is the legal status of the convicted person according to sub-section (2)?
A: The Court "shall commit the convicted person to jail custody under a warrant." [Source: Section 407, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sentence of death to be submitted by Court of Session for confirmation

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 407: Sentence of death to be submitted by Court of Session for confirmation

Q: If the convicted person refuses to file an appeal because they want to die, does the High Court still have to confirm the sentence?
A: Yes. The section says "the proceedings shall forthwith be submitted... and the sentence shall not be executed unless it is confirmed". This is an automatic, mandatory statutory submission, independent of whether the convict actually files an appeal. [Source: Section 407, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sentence of death to be submitted by Court of Session for confirmation

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 407: Sentence of death to be submitted by Court of Session for confirmation

Q: What is the consequence of this automatic confirmation requirement?
A: The consequence is the ultimate fail-safe against judicial error; death is irreversible. This section ensures that no single trial judge, no matter how senior, has the absolute power to end a human life without a mandatory, automatic review by the highest constitutional court in the state. [Source: Section 407, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sentence of death to be submitted by Court of Session for confirmation

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 408: Power to direct further inquiry to be made or additional evidence to be taken

Q: When the High Court is reviewing a death sentence to decide if it should be confirmed, can they ask for more evidence or a further investigation, even though the trial is technically over?
A: Yes. If the High Court feels something was missed, they can order a further inquiry or demand new evidence be taken before they make their final decision on the death penalty. [Source: Section 408, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to direct further inquiry to be made or additional evidence to be taken

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 408: Power to direct further inquiry to be made or additional evidence to be taken

Q: What investigatory powers does Section 408 of BNSS 2023 grant the High Court during death sentence confirmations?
A: Section 408 of BNSS 2023 outlines the "Power to direct further inquiry to be made or additional evidence to be taken," allowing the High Court, while reviewing a death sentence, to conduct or order a further inquiry or take additional evidence regarding the convict's guilt or innocence. [Source: Section 408, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to direct further inquiry to be made or additional evidence to be taken

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 408: Power to direct further inquiry to be made or additional evidence to be taken

Q: The High Court is reviewing a death sentence for a poisoning case. The judges realize a crucial blood test was never done during the trial. The prosecutor argues it's too late because the trial is closed. Can the High Court order the blood test to be done now?
A: Yes. Under Section 408(1), if the High Court thinks "additional evidence taken upon, any point bearing upon the guilt or innocence of the convicted person, it may make such inquiry or take such evidence itself, or direct it to be made or taken by the Court of Session." [Source: Section 408, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to direct further inquiry to be made or additional evidence to be taken

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 408: Power to direct further inquiry to be made or additional evidence to be taken

Q: If the High Court orders the lower Court of Session to take this additional evidence, does the convicted person (who is locked on death row) have to be physically brought back to the lower court to watch?
A: No, not necessarily. Sub-section (2) states: "Unless the High Court otherwise directs, the presence of the convicted person may be dispensed with when such inquiry is made or such evidence is taken." [Source: Section 408, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to direct further inquiry to be made or additional evidence to be taken

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 408: Power to direct further inquiry to be made or additional evidence to be taken

Q: Can the High Court use this power to gather evidence just to see if the convict was involved in a completely different, unrelated crime?
A: No. The section limits the inquiry/evidence to "any point bearing upon the guilt or innocence of the convicted person" (meaning, regarding the specific crime for which they were sentenced to death). [Source: Section 408, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to direct further inquiry to be made or additional evidence to be taken

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 408: Power to direct further inquiry to be made or additional evidence to be taken

Q: What is the consequence of granting this power at the confirmation stage?
A: The consequence is prioritizing absolute truth over procedural finality in capital cases; in normal appeals, new evidence is rarely allowed. But because a life is at stake, the High Court is given broad inquisitorial powers to actively hunt for any missing piece of truth before confirming the execution. [Source: Section 408, BNSS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Power to direct further inquiry to be made or additional evidence to be taken

content:
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS) - Section 409: Power of High Court to confirm sentence or annul conviction

Q: When reviewing a death sentence, what are the different choices the High Court can make?
